overview:
# nuvui

nuvui is a React component library for business software. The components wrap Radix UI primitives, which handle focus, keys and ARIA. nuvui adds the styles: SCSS compiled to plain CSS, with BEM class names that begin with `nuv-`, in cascade layers, themed with CSS custom properties.

Three things are different from the libraries you may expect, and most mistakes come from them:

- **It's installed, not copied.** Components are imported from `@nuvui/react` and its add-on packages. There's no `components/ui` folder to edit and no command that generates a component.
- **It isn't Tailwind.** No component takes utility classes to look right, and the project may not have Tailwind at all. Looks are changed with props, CSS variables and tokens.
- **One stylesheet per package, loaded once by the app.** A component never imports its own CSS. Without the stylesheet it renders unstyled.

## Before writing anything

1. Read the project's `package.json` for which `@nuvui/*` packages are installed, and at which versions. Use only what's installed, or install what's missing with the project's package manager.
2. Find where the app loads `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, usually the root layout or the entry file. If it isn't loaded, add it there, and the stylesheet of each add-on after it.
3. See how the app styles its own layout: CSS modules, SCSS, Tailwind, plain CSS. Follow that for what you add around the components. Don't bring in a styling tool the app doesn't have. Where the app has nothing yet, write a plain CSS file beside the component, with the theme's tokens: [rules/styling.md](rule:styling).
4. Read the reference file for each component you're about to use. [reference.md](tool:list_components) lists them. Props and parts are easy to guess wrong, and each file has a working example of each thing the component does.

## The packages

| Package | What's in it | Also needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@nuvui/react` | The core: seventy-six components, the tokens and the themes. | `react`, `react-dom` 18.2 or newer |
| `@nuvui/date-picker` | `Calendar`, `DatePicker`, `DateRangePicker` | |
| `@nuvui/table` | `Table` and its parts, `DataTable` with sorting, filtering, selection, paging and virtual rows | `@tanstack/react-table`, and `@tanstack/react-virtual` only for virtual rows |
| `@nuvui/charts` | `ChartContainer`, tooltip and legend, around Recharts | `recharts` |
| `@nuvui/barcodes` | `Barcode`, `QRCode` | |
| `@nuvui/chat` | Messages, a prompt box, markdown, code blocks, tool calls, sources, threads | `shiki`, only for colored code |
| `@nuvui/kanban` | `Kanban`, a board with cards that drag and move by keyboard | |
| `@nuvui/editor` | `RichTextEditor`, on Tiptap | |
| `@nuvui/emoji` | `EmojiPicker`, `EmojiReaction` | |
| `@nuvui/map` | `MapView`, markers, popups, controls, routes, clusters, on MapLibre | `maplibre-gl` |
| `@nuvui/flow` | `Flow`, a diagram of shapes joined by arrows that pans, zooms and can be edited | |
| `@nuvui/icons` | 317 line icons in three styles, such as `ArrowRightIcon` | |

Every add-on but `@nuvui/icons` needs `@nuvui/react` beside it, and its own stylesheet after the core's:

```tsx
import "@nuvui/react/styles.css";
import "@nuvui/table/styles.css";
```

`@nuvui/icons` needs only React, and has no stylesheet.

The first page of each package's reference says how to install it and what it needs set up. Some have a step that's easy to miss: [rules/packages.md](rule:packages).

## Rules

Each links to a file with the reasons and the code. Read the file before working in that area.

**Styling**: [rules/styling.md](rule:styling)

- Change how a component looks with its props first, then its `--nuv-*` variables, then tokens. Not with a heavier selector, and never `!important`.
- Every color is a token: `var(--color-primary)`, never a hex value or a named color.
- Don't put Tailwind utilities on a component to restyle it. `className` is for placing it: margin, grid area, width.
- Dark mode is `data-theme` on `<html>`. Density is `data-density`. Neither is a prop or a provider.
- Your own CSS for a block of UI uses BEM with the block's own name, never the `nuv-` prefix.

**Putting components together**: [rules/composition.md](rule:composition)

- Most components are several parts. Use every part the reference shows: a `Dialog` needs `DialogContent` with a `DialogTitle`, a `Select` needs `SelectTrigger`, `SelectValue`, `SelectContent` and `SelectItem`.
- `asChild` hands a part's behavior and classes to the one child inside it. It's how a trigger takes your `Button`, and how a `Button` becomes a link.
- A link that looks like a button is `<Button asChild><a href>`. A button that navigates is wrong.
- Use the component that exists: `Empty` for nothing to show, `Alert` for a message in the page, `toast()` for one that passes, `Skeleton` and `Spinner` for waiting, `Badge` for a status.
- `Toaster` is rendered once, near the root. `toast()` is called from anywhere.

**Forms**: [rules/forms.md](rule:forms)

- Every control goes in a `Field`, with `FieldLabel`, the control inside `FieldControl`, and `FieldDescription` or `FieldError` as needed. That's what ties the label and the error to the control.
- There's no form component and no validation in the library. Use the browser's, or React Hook Form.
- A `Button` is `type="button"` unless you say `type="submit"`.

**Accessibility**: [rules/accessibility.md](rule:accessibility)

- A button with only an icon needs `aria-label`.
- Every `nav` on a page needs its own name: `aria-label="Main"`.
- Each reference file has "What you need to handle". Do what it lists. The component can't.
- Don't say something with color alone.

**Text and direction**: [rules/text-and-direction.md](rule:text-and-direction)

- The few words a component writes itself, such as "Close", are English by default and each has a prop. In an app with translations, pass them.
- Right to left needs `dir="rtl"` on `<html>` and `DirectionProvider` around the app. Both.

**Server components**: [rules/server-components.md](rule:server-components)

- The parts that hold state carry `"use client"` themselves, so they can be rendered from a server component. Your file needs `"use client"` only for what it does itself: calling a hook, the library's included, passing a function as a prop, or calling `toast()`.
- A child that's a function, or a prop that's one, can't cross from a server component.

## Choosing a component

| For | Use |
| --- | --- |
| An action | `Button`. Several that belong together: `ButtonGroup`, `Toolbar` |
| A choice from a few | `RadioGroup`, `ToggleGroup`, `ChoiceCard` for choices with a description |
| A choice from many | `Select`. With search: `Combobox`. The browser's own: `NativeSelect` |
| On or off | `Switch` for a setting that applies at once, `Checkbox` for one sent with a form |
| Text | `Input`, `Textarea`, `PasswordInput`, `NumberField`, `OtpField`. With an icon or a button inside: `InputGroup` |
| A date | `DatePicker`, `DateRangePicker`, from [`@nuvui/date-picker`](page:date-picker/index) |
| Files | `FileUpload` |
| Something over the page that needs an answer | `Dialog`. For a destructive one: `AlertDialog`. From the edge: `Sheet` |
| Something beside its trigger | `Popover`, `DropdownMenu`, `HoverCard`, `Tooltip` for a name only |
| Commands by typing | `Command` |
| A message in the page | `Alert`. One that passes: `toast()`. Nothing to show: `Empty` |
| Waiting | `Skeleton` for a shape, `Spinner` for a moment, `Progress` for a known amount |
| Rows | `Table` for plain rows, `DataTable` for sorting, filtering and selection, from [`@nuvui/table`](page:table/index). A list of things with actions: `ListView`, `Item` |
| Figures | `Stat`, `Trend`, `FormattedNumber`. Charts: [`@nuvui/charts`](page:charts/index) |
| A barcode or a QR code | [`@nuvui/barcodes`](page:barcodes/index) |
| An emoji to pick, or a reaction | [`@nuvui/emoji`](page:emoji/index) |
| Getting around | `Sidebar`, `Navbar`, `NavigationMenu`, `Breadcrumb`, `Tabs`, `Pagination`, `Stepper`, `TableOfContents` |
| A tree | `Tree` |
| Grouping | `Card`, `Fieldset`, `Accordion`, `Collapsible`, `Separator`, `Resizable`, `ScrollArea` |
| People and status | `Avatar`, `Badge`, `Timeline` |
| A conversation with an assistant | [`@nuvui/chat`](page:chat/index) |
| A board of cards | [`@nuvui/kanban`](page:kanban/index) |
| Formatted text to edit | [`@nuvui/editor`](page:editor/index) |
| A place | [`@nuvui/map`](page:map/index) |
| Steps joined by arrows, a process or an approval path | [`@nuvui/flow`](page:flow/index) |
| An icon | [`@nuvui/icons`](page:icons/index) |

A core component's file is `reference/components/<name>.md`, with the name in lower case and hyphens: `reference/components/alert-dialog.md`.

Icons are in [`@nuvui/icons`](page:icons/index): 317 line icons in three styles, each named for what it shows with `Icon` at the end, such as `ArrowRightIcon`. The reference lists every name. Don't guess one. An app that already has an icon set keeps using it. The blocks use `lucide-react`.

## Start from a block

Before building a screen from nothing, look in [blocks.md](tool:list_blocks). There are blocks for signing in, dashboards, tables with toolbars, settings pages, chat screens and more, each one TSX file and one SCSS file built from these components. [recipes.md](page:recipes) says which to start from for the screens people ask for most.

A block's files aren't in this skill. They're fetched, and [blocks.md](tool:list_blocks) has the addresses. A block does more than most requests ask for, so take the structure and leave out what wasn't asked for. Where a block can't be fetched, or the app has no Sass, build from the reference files, which have everything a block uses.

## Checking your work

- The project's own lint and typecheck pass. TypeScript catches a wrong prop and a part that can't take `asChild`.
- Every component you used has its stylesheet loaded.
- No color in what you wrote is anything but a token.
- Each interactive thing has a name a screen reader can say, and can be reached and worked with the keyboard.
- It reads right at 320 pixels wide. The components do. Check the layout you put around them.

## More

- [reference.md](tool:list_components): a file for each component and guide.
- [tokens.md](tool:get_tokens): every design token.
- [blocks.md](tool:list_blocks): the blocks, and how to add one.
- [recipes.md](page:recipes): common screens, and what to build them from.
- The docs, for people: https://nuvui.nuvraxis.com/docs

# Accessibility

The components handle what a component can: roles, focus, the keyboard, what's announced. Each reference file has a section, "What the component handles", and another, "What you need to handle". The second is a list of things only the app can do. Do them.

## Names

Everything a person can press or type in needs a name a screen reader can say.

```tsx
// Wrong: a button nobody can name
<Button intent="ghost">
  <Trash />
</Button>

// Right
<Button intent="ghost" aria-label="Delete invoice 1042">
  <Trash aria-hidden="true" />
</Button>
```

- A button with only an icon: `aria-label`, saying what it does and to what.
- A control: a `FieldLabel`, through `Field`. See [forms.md](rule:forms).
- A dialog, a sheet, a popover with a heading: its `...Title` part.
- A table: a caption. A chart: `aria-label`. A map: `aria-label`.
- In a list, names that tell the rows apart: "Delete invoice 1042", not "Delete" twenty times.

## Landmarks

Every `nav` on a page needs its own name, since a page usually has more than one:

```tsx
<NavbarNav aria-label="Main">…</NavbarNav>
<Breadcrumb>…</Breadcrumb>          {/* named "Breadcrumb" already */}
<nav aria-label="Account">…</nav>
```

A page has one `main`, and one `h1`. Headings go down a level at a time and aren't picked for their size: set the size in CSS.

## Not by color alone

A status needs words or a shape as well as its color: a `Badge` that says "Overdue", an icon beside the red text. A chart's series are told apart by pattern or dash as well as by color, which the chart components can do. A required field says so, and isn't only a red star.

## The keyboard

- Everything that works with a pointer has to work with the keyboard. Use `Button` and the library's components and it does. An `onClick` on a `div` doesn't.
- Don't take the focus ring away. It's the library's, and it follows the theme.
- When something opens, the focus goes into it, and comes back when it closes. The overlays do this, so don't move the focus yourself around them. The one time you do: when what had the focus is gone, such as the row a dialog has just deleted, or its trigger. Then the focus would be lost, so put it somewhere that makes sense: the next row, the list's heading, a line that says what happened. Give that element `tabIndex={-1}` if it isn't something that takes the focus.
- Menus, tabs, radio groups and toolbars are one stop for the Tab key, and the arrow keys move inside them. Don't add `tabIndex` to their items.

## Things that change by themselves

What appears without being asked for has to be said: use `toast()`, or put the text in an element with `role="status"`. What's gone wrong goes in an `Alert`, which has the role for it. A `FieldError` is different: it's read with its control and not announced by itself, so after a submit with errors, move the focus to the first control that has one.

Content that's loading says so. `Spinner` and `Skeleton` have what's needed. Put the name of what's loading in the `Spinner`'s label where there's more than one.

## Touch and small screens

- Every target is at least 44 pixels on a touch screen. The components are. Keep it true for what you add, and don't shrink a control with CSS on a phone.
- Nothing scrolls sideways at 320 pixels wide. A wide table scrolls inside its own box.
- Motion is wrapped in `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference`.

## In a test

When writing tests for what you build, find elements the way a person does, by role and name: `getByRole("button", { name: "Save" })`. If that can't find something, a screen reader can't either.

One thing to know when testing with a real browser: some Radix controls act on an arrow key a moment after it goes down. Wait for the result, the focused or selected element, and don't assert on the same tick as the key press.

# Putting components together ## A component is its parts Most components are several parts, each exported by name, and you write all of them. There's no single tag that takes everything as props. ```tsx // Wrong: props that don't exist Delete} /> // Right Delete this project? This can't be undone. ``` The reference file for a component begins with a working example, and lists each part and what it's for. Copy the structure from there. Don't guess a part's name from another library: check it. Things that are always needed: - `Dialog`, `AlertDialog`, `Sheet`: a `...Title` inside the content. It's the name a screen reader says. Where the design shows no title, hide it with `VisuallyHidden`. Don't leave it out. - `Select`: `SelectTrigger` with a `SelectValue` in it, and `SelectContent` with `SelectItem`s. Each item needs a `value`. - `Tabs`: each `TabsTrigger` and its `TabsContent` share a `value`. - `Tooltip`: `TooltipTrigger` and `TooltipContent`. A tooltip names a control. It isn't a place for things to read or press. - `Accordion`: `type="single"` or `type="multiple"`, and a `value` on each item. ## `asChild` A part with `asChild` renders no element of its own. It gives its props, its classes and its behavior to the one child inside it. ```tsx // A trigger that is your button // A link that looks like a button // With a router's link ``` - Without `asChild`, a trigger renders its own ` ``` An icon from `@nuvui/icons` is hidden from screen readers unless it has a `title` or an `aria-label`, so it needs no `aria-hidden`. Its names are in [reference/icons/index.md](page:icons/index). ## Refs and other props Every component forwards its ref to its element and passes on the props it doesn't use, so `id`, `data-*`, `aria-*`, `style` and event handlers work as they do on the element.

# Forms nuvui has no form component and no validation of its own. The controls are native elements, or Radix controls that keep a hidden native input in step, so a plain `
` submits them. `Field` ties a label, a hint and an error to each one. [reference/forms.md](page:forms) has all of it, with whole forms to copy. ## Every control goes in a Field ```tsx // Wrong: a label that isn't tied to its control, an error nobody is told of
Enter an email address
// Right Email The invite goes to this address. {error} ``` `Field` gives the control its `id`, points the label at it, and adds the hint and the error to what a screen reader reads with it. The control has to be the one child of `FieldControl`. `FieldError` renders nothing while it's empty, so it isn't rendered conditionally, and while it has something in it the control is marked invalid. Check [reference/components/field.md](page:components/field) for the props before using them: this file shows the shape, and the reference has the exact names. - Don't write `id`, `htmlFor` or `aria-describedby` by hand inside a `Field`. - A control that's a group, such as a `RadioGroup`, goes in a `Field` too, so it can have a `FieldError`. Its label can't be a `label` element, which names one control, so it's `Role`. [reference/components/field.md](page:components/field) has it under "With other controls". Each option inside keeps its own `label` with `htmlFor`. - Several fields that belong together, such as an address, go in a `Fieldset` with a `FieldsetLegend`. - A placeholder isn't a label. Every control has a `FieldLabel`, or an `aria-label` where the design has no room for one. ## Give controls a name A control is in the form's data when it has a `name`. | Control | What's submitted | | --- | --- | | `Input`, `Textarea`, `NativeSelect`, `PasswordInput` | The element's value | | `Checkbox`, `Switch` | `"on"`, or the `value` you set, while checked | | `RadioGroup`, `Select` | The picked `value` | | `Slider` | One number per handle | | `OtpField` | The whole code as one value | | `FileUpload` | The chosen files | ## Validation Three ways. Use the one the app already has: - **The browser's.** Put `required`, `type="email"`, `minLength` or `pattern` on the control. It costs no JavaScript and suits a short form. The message is the browser's own bubble, so nothing is shown under the field. [reference/forms.md](page:forms) has a form this way. - **Your own, with state.** For messages under the fields, in an app with no form library: `noValidate` on the form, read the values from `FormData` on submit, keep the messages in state, and give each to its `FieldError`. [reference/components/field.md](page:components/field) has it under "Errors". Don't install a form library for one form. - **React Hook Form**, version 7, where the app has it or has many forms. Native controls take `register`. Radix controls, `Select`, `Checkbox`, `Switch`, `RadioGroup`, `Slider`, go through `Controller`, with `onValueChange` or `onCheckedChange` wired to `field.onChange`. Put `noValidate` on the form, and each message in a `FieldError`. [reference/forms.md](page:forms) has a form this way too. When to check: on submit. After that, a field that has a message is checked again as it's changed, so the message goes when it's put right. A field that hasn't been found wrong yet isn't checked while it's typed in. What's checked in the browser is checked again on the server. A server action, or any function that returns a message per field, fits: put what comes back into the same `FieldError`s. ## Buttons in a form `Button` is `type="button"` by default, which is not what HTML does. A button in a form does nothing until you say: ```tsx ``` One submit button, and it's the `primary` one. ## While it's sending, and after - Disable the submit button while the form is being sent, and say so: a `Spinner` in it, or other words on it. - When it's sent, say so where a screen reader hears it: a `toast()`, or text in an element with `role="status"`. A toast needs a `Toaster` near the root. Look for one, and add it if the app has none. - When there are errors, move the focus to the first control that has one. A `FieldError` is read with its control, and isn't announced by itself. - When the server says no, put its message in the field's `FieldError`, or in an `Alert` at the top of the form for one that belongs to no field. ## Choosing the control - Two to about five choices: `RadioGroup`, so they're all seen. With a description each: `ChoiceCard`. - More than that: `Select`. So many that they need a search: `Combobox`. On a phone, or where the browser's own is wanted: `NativeSelect`. - Yes or no, sent with the form: `Checkbox`. A setting that applies the moment it's flipped: `Switch`. - A number with steps: `NumberField`. Within a range, roughly: `Slider`. - A date: `DatePicker` from `@nuvui/date-picker`. Its value is a `Date`. Don't turn it into text with `toISOString()`, which gives the day in UTC: [reference/date-picker/index.md](page:date-picker/index) says what to use. - A code sent by email or text: `OtpField`.

# The add-on packages

Each add-on is installed next to `@nuvui/react`, which it needs, and has a stylesheet of its own to load after the core's. Its first reference page, `reference/<package>/index.md`, has the install command and the setup. These are the steps that are easy to miss.

```tsx
import "@nuvui/react/styles.css";
import "@nuvui/<package>/styles.css";
```

## @nuvui/table

- Install `@tanstack/react-table` with it: it's a peer dependency. `@tanstack/react-virtual` is needed only for virtual rows.
- `Table` and its parts are plain styled elements. `DataTable` is the one with sorting, filtering, selection and paging, and takes a table made by `useDataTable`, which is TanStack Table's.
- The hook comes from an entry that says how much of TanStack to bring: `@nuvui/table/full` for everything, which also draws a search box, a column chooser and paging. For a table that does one thing, such as sorting, make a hook with only that feature. [reference/table/index.md](page:table/index) has both.
- A column is TanStack's. What a cell shows is its `cell`: `cell: ({ getValue }) => <FormattedNumber value={getValue()} />`. A date in a cell is written with `Intl.DateTimeFormat`, with the time zone said, inside a `time` element.
- Keep `columns` outside the component, or in `useMemo`. An array made during render is new every time, and the rows are worked out again.
- A data table needs a name: `caption`, `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`. TypeScript reports one with none.
- The file that calls `useDataTable` has `"use client"`.
- It's ESM only.

## @nuvui/charts

- Install `recharts` with it. The chart itself is Recharts' own components, inside a `ChartContainer`.
- The container needs a `config`, with an entry for each series, and an `aria-label`.
- Color a series with `chartFill("key")` or its like, which is a CSS variable the container sets, so the chart follows the theme. Never a color written out.
- The file a chart is in has `"use client"`.
- reference/charts/ has a page for each kind: bar, line, area, pie, radar, radial, scatter, composed.

## @nuvui/date-picker

- `react-day-picker` and `date-fns` come with it. Don't install them.
- Values are `Date` objects. Don't turn one into text with `toISOString()`, which gives the day in UTC and can be the day before. Use the form value, or date-fns' `format(date, "yyyy-MM-dd")`.
- Other languages are a `locale` from date-fns. A time zone is said on purpose. [reference/date-picker/index.md](page:date-picker/index) has both.

## @nuvui/chat

- The components draw a conversation. They don't talk to a model or a server: messages come in as props, and a callback says when something is sent.
- `Markdown` and `CodeBlock` color code with a highlighter you pass in. The ready one is `createShikiHighlighter` from `@nuvui/chat/shiki`, which needs `shiki` installed. Make one for the whole app, outside any component.
- Without a highlighter, code is shown plain. That's allowed.

## @nuvui/kanban

- The board keeps the order: which card ids are in which column. What a card is stays with you, looked up by id when it's drawn.
- `onValueChange` is called once per move, with the columns as they are now. That's when to save.

## @nuvui/editor

- It's about 120 kB compressed. Load it with the screen that has it: `lazy` and `Suspense`, or `next/dynamic`.
- The value is a string of HTML. Before HTML from a database is put in a page, sanitize it on the server, or show it with the editor itself, read only.

## @nuvui/emoji

- Emoji are drawn as text in the device's own font. There are no pictures to load, and they look different from one device to the next.
- Comparing two emoji with `===` can fail: the same emoji is sometimes written with an extra invisible character, U+FE0F. Strip it from both before comparing.

## @nuvui/map

- Install `maplibre-gl` with it, version 6.4.1 or newer.
- **Say where MapLibre's worker is**, once, before a map is drawn. Without it the map stays on "Loading map".

  ```tsx
  // Next.js, with Turbopack or webpack, and webpack alone
  "use client";
  import { setMapWorkerUrl } from "@nuvui/map";

  setMapWorkerUrl(
    new URL("maplibre-gl/dist/maplibre-gl-worker.mjs", import.meta.url),
  );
  ```

  ```tsx
  // Vite
  import { setMapWorkerUrl } from "@nuvui/map";
  import workerUrl from "maplibre-gl/dist/maplibre-gl-worker.mjs?url";

  setMapWorkerUrl(workerUrl);
  ```

  Put it in a file of its own, such as `components/map-worker.ts`, and import that file from the client component that draws the map.

- **It has no tiles.** `mapStyle` is required: the address of a MapLibre style from a tile provider the app's owner has chosen. Ask which, and don't pick one for them. A provider has terms and a cost.

  The examples in the reference use OpenFreeMap's address, so that they run. It's a stand-in. Don't copy it into an app. Where the provider isn't known yet, read the address from the app's configuration, such as an environment variable, show the places in words where there's no address, and say what's still to be decided.

- A place is `[longitude, latitude]`, in that order. The types are exported: `MapLngLat` is that pair, and `MapBounds` is two of them, the south-west corner and the north-east. `mapBoundsOf` makes one from a list of places.
- A marker's popup closes on a press anywhere else on the map, another marker included, so one is open at a time without your keeping it. `open` and `onOpenChange` are for opening one from outside the map, such as from a list beside it.
- Don't load MapLibre's own stylesheet.
- Give the map an `aria-label`, each marker a `label`, and the same places in words beside the map.
- It's ESM only.

## @nuvui/flow

- Nothing else to install. A diagram is data: `nodes`, each with an `id`, a `label` and a `position` (its top left corner), and `edges`, each `from` one id `to` another. Positions come from the app. Nothing lays a diagram out by itself.
- `aria-label` is required, and each node's `label` is its name for a screen reader: make each one tell it from the others.
- With `editable`, `onNodesChange` and `onEdgesChange` are called once per change, a drag when it ends, with the lists as they are now and the change. That's when to save. Don't save from `onNodeDrag`, which comes every frame.
- Keep the lists in state, or in `useMemo` for generated ones. The nodes that didn't change are the same objects, and a new object is read again.
- A node holds words, not React content: it's drawn in SVG.
- The frame's height is `--nuv-flow-height`, 24rem by default.

## @nuvui/barcodes

- A code is black on white in every theme, on purpose: a scanner needs the contrast. Don't theme it.
- Check a value before drawing it. [reference/barcodes/index.md](page:barcodes/index) has the function for that.

# Text and direction

## The words a component writes itself

Nearly all the text in an interface is the app's: labels, headings, what's on the buttons. A few words the components write themselves, mostly names for screen readers on buttons that are only an icon: "Close" on a dialog, "Loading" on a spinner, "More pages" in a pagination. Each is a prop, with an English default.

```tsx
// In an app with translations
<DialogContent closeLabel={t("close")}>…</DialogContent>
<Spinner label={t("loading")} />
```

- [reference/translation.md](page:translation) lists every one for the core, by component, with its prop and its default.
- The add-ons take theirs together, in a `labels` prop: `DataTable`, `Kanban`, `MapView` and others. Each one's reference file has a "Translation" or "Text and translation" section.
- There's no provider that takes all the strings at once. With many dialogs in an app, wrap the library's part in a component of the app's that passes the prop.

When the app has translations, pass these props wherever you render one of those components. When it has none and is in English, leave them.

Dates and numbers follow a locale and not these props: `FormattedNumber` and the date picker take one. [reference/date-picker/index.md](page:date-picker/index) covers the calendar's.

## Right to left

Arabic, Hebrew and other languages that read from the right need two things, and both:

```tsx
import { DirectionProvider } from "@nuvui/react";

<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">
  <body>
    <DirectionProvider dir="rtl">{children}</DirectionProvider>
  </body>
</html>
```

`dir="rtl"` mirrors the layout: text, padding, which side a sheet comes from. `DirectionProvider` tells the components that work with arrow keys which way is forward: tabs, sliders, menus that open a submenu. With only the first, a slider looks mirrored and its arrow keys go the wrong way. [reference/right-to-left.md](page:right-to-left) has what each one changes.

In CSS of your own, write for both directions from the start:

- `margin-inline-start`, `padding-inline-end`, `inset-inline-start`, `border-inline-end`, `text-align: start`. Not `left` and `right`.
- An icon that points, such as an arrow for "next", has to be mirrored. One that doesn't point, such as a clock, stays.
- Numbers, code and phone numbers stay left to right: put `dir="ltr"` on that element.

pages.title: Getting started
pages.description: Install nuvui, load its stylesheet once, and render your first component.
pages.markdown: # Getting started Install nuvui, load its stylesheet once, and render your first component. nuvui is a set of React components for enterprise applications: the forms, tables, charts and dashboards that business software is made of. The components wrap [Radix UI](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives) primitives. Radix handles the behavior: focus, keyboard support, ARIA. nuvui adds the styles, written in SCSS with BEM class names and themed through CSS custom properties. There are seventy-six components, listed under Components in the menu. Three more, for dates, are in a package of their own, [`@nuvui/date-picker`](page:date-picker/index), tables are in another, [`@nuvui/table`](page:table/index), charts in a third, [`@nuvui/charts`](page:charts/index), barcodes and QR codes in a fourth, [`@nuvui/barcodes`](page:barcodes/index), the parts of a conversation with an assistant in a fifth, [`@nuvui/chat`](page:chat/index), a kanban board in a sixth, [`@nuvui/kanban`](page:kanban/index), a rich text editor in a seventh, [`@nuvui/editor`](page:editor/index), an emoji picker in an eighth, [`@nuvui/emoji`](page:emoji/index), a map in a ninth, [`@nuvui/map`](page:map/index), and flow diagrams in a tenth, [`@nuvui/flow`](page:flow/index). An eleventh, [`@nuvui/icons`](page:icons/index), is a set of icons, and needs only React. ## Install ```sh pnpm add @nuvui/react ``` npm, yarn and bun work the same way. You also need `react` and `react-dom`, version 18.2 or newer. ## Load the styles Import the stylesheet once, somewhere that runs for every page. In a Next.js app that's the root layout: ```tsx title="app/layout.tsx" import "@nuvui/react/styles.css"; ``` It's a plain CSS file. The components never import CSS themselves, so there's no loader or build plugin to set up, and it works the same with server components. ## Use a component ```tsx import { Button } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function Page() { return ; } ``` ## Rendering another element Many parts take `asChild`. With it, the part doesn't render an element of its own. It gives its props, its classes and its behavior to the one child you put inside: ```tsx ``` That's a link that looks like a button, and it's how a trigger takes your own button: ``. It only works where there's one child to become. A part that draws something of its own beside what you give it doesn't take `asChild`, and TypeScript says so: a dialog's content has its close button, a checkbox has its tick, a select's trigger has its arrow. Style those with `className`, or with the CSS variables on the component's page. ## Dark mode Components are light unless you ask for something else. Set `data-theme` on ``, or on any element to theme just that part of the page: | Value | Result | | --- | --- | | `data-theme="light"` | Light | | `data-theme="dark"` | Dark | | `data-theme="system"` | Follows the visitor's operating system | ```html ``` `system` is handled in CSS, so there's no script and no flash of the wrong theme on load. We don't switch to dark automatically. If we did, a site with only a light design would show light text on its white background to everyone whose system is set to dark. Colors, radii and spacing are all CSS custom properties. [Theming and tokens](page:theming) covers changing them, and has an editor to try it in. It also covers the five [presets](page:theming#presets) that come with the package, and [density](page:theming#density). ## Loading less `styles.css` contains every component. If you only use a few, import their stylesheets one by one. Each needs the tokens and the base styles loaded as well: ```tsx import "@nuvui/react/tokens.css"; import "@nuvui/react/base.css"; import "@nuvui/react/css/button.css"; ``` The JavaScript has an entry per component too. Bundlers tree-shake the main entry, so this mostly matters if yours doesn't: ```tsx import { Button } from "@nuvui/react/button"; ``` ## Browser support The styles use cascade layers, `oklch()` colors, `color-mix()` and `dvh` units. That means Chrome and Edge 111, Firefox 113 and Safari 16.4, or newer. There's no fallback for older browsers. The [support policy](page:support) has the versions of React and Node as well, and says which of them the tests run on. ## With Tailwind or Sass Neither is needed. If your app already uses one, there's a guide for each: - [Using with Tailwind](page:tailwind) covers the layer order and how to get utilities such as `bg-primary`. - [Using with SCSS](page:scss) covers the mixins and changing the breakpoints. For Arabic, Hebrew and other languages that read from the right, see [Right-to-left](page:right-to-left). The few words the components write themselves, and the prop for each, are listed in [Translation](page:translation). ## What isn't here yet - A 1.0. Until then a minor version may rename or remove things, and the [changelog](https://nuvui.nuvraxis.com/docs/changelog) says where one does. - Testing in Safari itself. The tests run in Chromium, Firefox and the WebKit build that Playwright ships, which is close to Safari and isn't Safari. - More components. There are seventy-six, and no date for the next ones.

## Install


npm, yarn and bun work the same way. You also need `react` and `react-dom`, version 18.2 or newer.

## Load the styles

Import the stylesheet once, somewhere that runs for every page. In a Next.js app that's the root layout:

```tsx title="app/layout.tsx"
import "@nuvui/react/styles.css";
```

It's a plain CSS file. The components never import CSS themselves, so there's no loader or build plugin to set up, and it works the same with server components.

sections.heading: Use a component
Rendering another element
sections.markdown: ## Rendering another element Many parts take `asChild`. With it, the part doesn't render an element of its own. It gives its props, its classes and its behavior to the one child you put inside: ```tsx ``` That's a link that looks like a button, and it's how a trigger takes your own button: ``. It only works where there's one child to become. A part that draws something of its own beside what you give it doesn't take `asChild`, and TypeScript says so: a dialog's content has its close button, a checkbox has its tick, a select's trigger has its arrow. Style those with `className`, or with the CSS variables on the component's page.

sections.heading: Dark mode
sections.markdown:
## Dark mode

Components are light unless you ask for something else. Set `data-theme` on `<html>`, or on any element to theme just that part of the page:

| Value | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `data-theme="light"` | Light |
| `data-theme="dark"` | Dark |
| `data-theme="system"` | Follows the visitor's operating system |

```html
<html lang="en" data-theme="system">
```

`system` is handled in CSS, so there's no script and no flash of the wrong theme on load.

We don't switch to dark automatically. If we did, a site with only a light design would show light text on its white background to everyone whose system is set to dark.

Colors, radii and spacing are all CSS custom properties. [Theming and tokens](page:theming) covers changing them, and has an editor to try it in. It also covers the five [presets](page:theming#presets) that come with the package, and [density](page:theming#density).

The styles use cascade layers, `oklch()` colors, `color-mix()` and `dvh` units. That means Chrome and Edge 111, Firefox 113 and Safari 16.4, or newer. There's no fallback for older browsers.

- [Using with SCSS](page:scss) covers the mixins and changing the breakpoints.

For Arabic, Hebrew and other languages that read from the right, see [Right-to-left](page:right-to-left). The few words the components write themselves, and the prop for each, are listed in [Translation](page:translation).

pages.title: Theming and tokens
pages.description: How nuvui's design tokens are layered, the presets that ship with it, density, how to override tokens for a site, a section or one component, and a live editor to try changes in.

sections.heading: Try it
sections.markdown:
## Try it

Change a value and the components in the box follow. The editor sets the variables on that box only, so the rest of the page keeps its own look. The CSS underneath is what you'd paste into your own stylesheet to get the same result.

Colors are kept apart for light and dark. Switch the site's theme with the toggle in the navigation and you're editing the other set.

**Start from** puts the preview in one of the [presets](#presets). Your changes then sit on top of that preset, and the CSS says which one to load.

The editor will let you pick colors nobody can read. The contrast figures are there to catch that. Text needs 4.5:1 against what's behind it, and the edge of a control or a focus ring needs 3:1.

sections.heading: How the tokens are layered
sections.markdown:
## How the tokens are layered

There are three levels, and each one reads from the one before it.

**Raw scales** are plain values with no meaning attached: `--color-blue-600`, `--radius-md`, `--text-sm`. The names and values are the ones in Tailwind v4's default theme.

**Semantic tokens** say what a value is for: `--color-primary`, `--color-background`, `--color-border`. Each points at a raw color, and has one value for light and another for dark. For color, the components only ever read these.

**Component variables** belong to one component: `--nuv-button-radius`, `--nuv-dialog-width`. The library never declares them. Each component reads its own, with a token as the fallback:

```css
.nuv-button {
  border-radius: var(--nuv-button-radius, var(--radius-md));
}
```

So changing `--radius-md` rounds everything that uses it, and setting `--nuv-button-radius` changes buttons alone.

sections.heading: Changing tokens
Presets
Density
Dark mode for part of a page
Fonts
The focus ring
sections.markdown:
## The focus ring

Every component draws the same ring on keyboard focus. Three variables change it everywhere at once.

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-focus-ring-width` | `2px` | Thickness of the ring. |
| `--nuv-focus-ring-color` | `var(--color-ring)` | Its color. Keep it at 3:1 or better against whatever is behind it. |
| `--nuv-focus-ring-offset` | `2px`, `3px`, `-2px`, `0`, `4px` | Gap between the element and the ring. Tabs and the toast region draw theirs inside the edge, which is the negative default. |

The rows in a menu or a select list are filled in when focused, not ringed. The [DropdownMenu](page:components/dropdown-menu) page explains why.

sections.heading: Token reference
sections.markdown:
## Token reference

These tables are read from the `tokens.css` that the package ships.

### Semantic colors

| Name | What it's for |
| --- | --- |
| `--color-background` | The page. Also the thumb of a switch. |
| `--color-foreground` | Text on the page. |
| `--color-surface` | Things that sit above the page: dialogs, popovers, menus, select lists and toasts. |
| `--color-surface-foreground` | Text on a surface. |
| `--color-muted` | Quiet fills, such as a secondary button or the hover state of a close button. |
| `--color-muted-foreground` | Text that matters less: descriptions, placeholders, group labels. |
| `--color-primary` | The main action: a primary button, a checked checkbox or switch, the selected tab, the focused row in a menu. |
| `--color-primary-foreground` | Text and icons on top of primary. |
| `--color-danger` | Destructive actions and errors. |
| `--color-danger-foreground` | Text on top of danger. |
| `--color-success` | The edge of a success toast. |
| `--color-warning` | No component reads it yet. It's defined so your own warnings can match. |
| `--color-border` | Dividers and the edges of panels. |
| `--color-border-strong` | The edge of a control you have to be able to find: a checkbox, a switch, a select. It keeps 3:1 against the page. |
| `--color-ring` | The focus ring. |
| `--color-overlay` | The dimmed layer behind a dialog. |

### Chart colors

Eight colors for the series of a chart, to be used in this order. No component reads them yet. They're here so charts you draw now match the chart components when those arrive.

_The docs page shows this as a table: https://nuvui.nuvraxis.com/docs/theming. The tokens themselves are in tokens.md, beside SKILL.md._

Each one reaches 3:1 against the page and against a surface, in light and in dark. The order alternates hue and lightness so that neighbours can still be told apart with protanopia, deuteranopia or tritanopia. That was checked by simulating each one, and it's part of the test suite. Color alone is still not enough for a chart: label the series as well.

They don't change with a preset.

### Color scales

Five of Tailwind's scales, plus black and white. The values are in `oklch()`.

_The docs page shows this as a table: https://nuvui.nuvraxis.com/docs/theming. The tokens themselves are in tokens.md, beside SKILL.md._

### Spacing

_The docs page shows this as a table: https://nuvui.nuvraxis.com/docs/theming. The tokens themselves are in tokens.md, beside SKILL.md._

One unit. Sizes are written as multiples of it, so `calc(var(--spacing) * 4)` is `1rem`. Change it and every padding and gap in the library scales together.

### Type

_The docs page shows this as a table: https://nuvui.nuvraxis.com/docs/theming. The tokens themselves are in tokens.md, beside SKILL.md._

Each `--text-*` size has a line height to go with it, named like `--text-sm--line-height`.

### Radius

_The docs page shows this as a table: https://nuvui.nuvraxis.com/docs/theming. The tokens themselves are in tokens.md, beside SKILL.md._

### Shadows

_The docs page shows this as a table: https://nuvui.nuvraxis.com/docs/theming. The tokens themselves are in tokens.md, beside SKILL.md._

### Motion

_The docs page shows this as a table: https://nuvui.nuvraxis.com/docs/theming. The tokens themselves are in tokens.md, beside SKILL.md._

Transitions and animations are only declared under `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference`. Someone who has asked their system for less motion gets none, and there's nothing for you to switch off.

### Breakpoints

_The docs page shows this as a table: https://nuvui.nuvraxis.com/docs/theming. The tokens themselves are in tokens.md, beside SKILL.md._

These are for reading in your own CSS or JavaScript. A custom property can't be used in a media query, so changing one here doesn't move the point where a dialog stops being a sheet. [Using with SCSS](page:scss#breakpoints) covers how to do that.

### Controls

_The docs page shows this as a table: https://nuvui.nuvraxis.com/docs/theming. The tokens themselves are in tokens.md, beside SKILL.md._

`--nuv-border-width` is the width of every border the components draw. `--nuv-disabled-opacity` is how far a disabled control fades.

`--nuv-touch-size` is the smallest a control gets on a touch screen. The three heights are what [density](#density) changes.

### Stacking order

_The docs page shows this as a table: https://nuvui.nuvraxis.com/docs/theming. The tokens themselves are in tokens.md, beside SKILL.md._

Popovers sit above dialogs because a menu or a select can open from inside one. If something of yours has to sit above or between them, move these rather than raising your own `z-index` until it works.

Whose values win

The dark variant
What this site does
sections.markdown:
## What this site does

This site runs both. Tailwind is here for the page layout, through Fumadocs, and the previews are nuvui. It uses the `@theme` block above as it's printed, and the two previews on this page are rendered with it. The layer order is `theme, tokens, base, components, utilities`, for the reason given earlier.

pages.title: Using with SCSS
pages.description: Load nuvui's Sass mixins into your own stylesheets, change the breakpoints, and see which build tools resolve the package's SCSS entry.

sections.heading: Use the mixins
The mixins
sections.markdown:
## The mixins

| Name | What it's for |
| --- | --- |
| `breakpoint` | Wraps its content in a min-width media query for a named breakpoint. An unknown name stops the compile with a list of the ones that exist. |
| `dark` | For setting tokens. Use it at the top level of a file: it writes its content for data-theme="dark", and again for data-theme="system" when the system is dark. |
| `motion-safe` | Wraps its content in prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference. Put transitions and animations in here and they don't exist for people who asked for less motion. |
| `reduced-motion` | The opposite query, for when less motion needs a style of its own. |
| `rtl` | For what has to be mirrored where the page reads right to left: an arrow, the side a panel slides in from. It goes by the dir attribute, on the element or around it, and leaves a part marked dir="ltr" alone. |
| `hover` | A :hover rule that only applies on devices that can hover. On a touch screen, hover styles stick after a tap. |
| `fine-pointer` | For the denser sizes that suit a mouse or trackpad. Everything outside it keeps its touch size. |
| `focus-ring` | The library's focus ring, on :focus-visible. The argument is the gap between the element and the ring. |
| `touch-target` | A minimum width and height of 44 pixels. |
| `touch-area` | Widens the area that responds to a tap to 44 pixels without changing what's drawn, for controls that have to look small. The element needs position: relative. |

There's no `max-width` version of `breakpoint`, on purpose. The library is written smallest screen first, and one direction keeps overrides predictable.

sections.heading: Breakpoints
What your build tool needs
sections.markdown:
## What your build tool needs

`@use "@nuvui/react/scss/mixins"` is a path through the package's `exports` map. Sass can't follow that by itself, so whether it works depends on what runs Sass for you. This is what we've run. Every row was run on Windows, and the Turbopack row on Linux as well:

| Tool | `scss/mixins` | `scss` (the whole library) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Next.js 16 with Turbopack | Works | Works on Linux, fails on Windows |
| Next.js 16 with webpack | Works | Works |
| Vite 8 | Works | Works |
| Sass 1.105, command line or API | Works with `pkg:` | Works with `pkg:` |

### Next.js with Turbopack on Windows

Compiling the whole library fails with "Can't find stylesheet to import". Turbopack finds the file in the package, then can't follow that file's own relative `@use` lines. The code that passes paths from Sass to Turbopack builds them with backslashes on Windows. The same build works on Linux. We haven't run it on macOS.

Next.js has this as [issue 87243](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/87243). It was still open, and still happening in 16.4.0-canary.61, when this page was last checked in October 2026.

The mixins file is one file that loads nothing else, which is why it isn't affected.

If you need to compile the whole library in a Next.js app on Windows, run Next with webpack (`next dev --webpack` and `next build --webpack`).

### Sass on its own

Without a bundler, use Sass's package importer and the `pkg:` prefix:

```scss
@use "pkg:@nuvui/react/scss/mixins" as nuv;
```

```sh
sass --pkg-importer=node styles.scss styles.css
```

From JavaScript, the equivalent is `importers: [new NodePackageImporter()]`.

sections.heading: What isn't in the package
sections.markdown:
## What isn't in the package

- There's no SCSS entry per component. To load only some components, use the [per-component CSS files](page:index#loading-less).
- `scss/tokens` and `scss/base` exist and compile to the same thing as `tokens.css` and `base.css`. They're only worth using if you're compiling everything yourself anyway.
- The partials the components share between themselves aren't part of the public API. If a file isn't in the list above, it can change without notice.

pages.title: Forms
pages.description: Build a form from nuvui's fields, validate it with the browser or with React Hook Form, and show errors that a screen reader reads with the control.

sections.heading: What submits, and how
sections.markdown:
## What submits, and how

Every control with a `name` is part of the form's data.

| Control | What's submitted |
| --- | --- |
| Input, Textarea, NativeSelect, PasswordInput | The element's own value. These are native elements. |
| FileUpload | The chosen files, from a native file input. |
| Checkbox, Switch | `"on"`, or the `value` you set, while checked. Radix renders a hidden checkbox. |
| RadioGroup, Select | The picked `value`. Radix renders hidden inputs. |
| Slider | One number per handle. |
| OtpField | The whole code as one value. |

`disabled` works on all of them, and `required` on all but the slider, which always has a value.

sections.heading: With the browser's validation
With React Hook Form
What a screen reader is told
sections.markdown:
## What a screen reader is told

A screen reader builds what it says from four things the browser works out for each control: its role, its name, its description and its states. Field sets all four. This is what they are for the email field above, before and after a failed submit.

| | Before | After submitting it empty |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Role | Text field | Text field |
| Name | "Email" | "Email" |
| Description | "The invite goes to this address." | "The invite goes to this address. Enter their email address." |
| States | Required | Required, invalid |

The asterisk isn't in the name. It's hidden from screen readers, because "required" already comes from the control.

The library's tests check these values in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. How they're worded, and in what order, differs from one screen reader to the next, and that hasn't been tested with each of them. Try your own forms with the screen readers your users have.

Two more things decide whether someone who can't see the form finds the errors.

- **Focus has to move.** The description is read when focus lands on the control, not when the message appears. React Hook Form focuses the first failed field after a submit, as long as it has the control's ref. The browser's validation does the same.
- **A message that appears while typing needs announcing.** If you validate on every keystroke or on blur, add `aria-live="polite"` to that `FieldError`. A message that appears on submit doesn't need it, since focus is about to move there.

sections.heading: Writing the messages
sections.markdown:
## Writing the messages

- Say what to do, not what's wrong. "Enter a date after today", not "Invalid date".
- Name the field when messages are collected in one place. Next to the field, the label already does.
- Don't blame. "Enter your email address" reads better than "You forgot your email address".
- Keep the hint and the error apart. The hint in `FieldDescription` says what's expected before anything goes wrong, and stays there after.

sections.heading: Long forms
sections.markdown:
## Long forms

On a form too long to see at once, list the errors at the top after a failed submit, each one a link to its field, and move focus to that list. The list tells people how many problems there are, which a message next to each field can't. Group related fields with a [Fieldset](page:components/fieldset).

sections.heading: Checking on the server
sections.markdown:
## Checking on the server

Whatever runs in the browser is a convenience for the person filling the form in. Check everything again on the server. Send the server's messages back keyed by field name, and pass each to the `FieldError` of its field. With React Hook Form that's `setError("email", { message })`.

pages.title: Right-to-left
pages.description: Use nuvui in Arabic, Hebrew, Persian and other languages that read from the right, with the dir attribute and DirectionProvider.
pages.markdown:
# Right-to-left Use nuvui in Arabic, Hebrew, Persian and other languages that read from the right, with the dir attribute and DirectionProvider. Every component works in a right-to-left layout. Two things turn it on, and both are needed: the `dir` attribute, which the styles follow, and `DirectionProvider`, which the keyboard behavior follows. ```tsx "use client"; import { Breadcrumb, BreadcrumbItem, BreadcrumbLink, BreadcrumbList, BreadcrumbPage, BreadcrumbSeparator, type Direction, DirectionProvider, Progress, Slider, Tabs, TabsContent, TabsList, TabsTrigger, ToggleGroup, ToggleGroupItem, } from "@nuvui/react"; import { useState } from "react"; export default function Example() { const [dir, setDir] = useState("rtl"); return (
value && setDir(value as Direction)} > Left to right Right to left {/* In an app both of these go at the top: the attribute on , and the provider around everything. */}
