); } ``` ## Setting it up Put `dir="rtl"` on the `` element, and `DirectionProvider` around the app with the same value. ```tsx title="app/layout.tsx" import { DirectionProvider } from "@nuvui/react"; import type { ReactNode } from "react"; export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) { return ( {children} ); } ``` `DirectionProvider` is a client component that adds no element of its own. It can be rendered from a server component, as here. In an app with several languages, work the direction out from the language once and pass it to both places. ## Why there are two **The attribute is what CSS sees.** The styles are written with logical properties, such as `padding-inline-start`, and with a selector on the `dir` attribute where something has to be mirrored. Both go by the `dir` of the element or of what's around it. So the layout flips with the attribute alone: text aligns to the right, icons move to the other side, a progress bar fills from the right. **The provider is what the components' code sees.** Radix decides in JavaScript which arrow key moves to the next tab and which way a submenu opens, and it doesn't read the attribute. It reads a `dir` prop on the component, or this provider. With the attribute and no provider, the tabs are laid out from the right and the left arrow still moves to the previous one. That's the mistake this page is here to prevent. ## What each one changes | | With `dir="rtl"` | With `DirectionProvider` as well | | --- | --- | --- | | Text, padding, borders | Mirrored | | | The arrows in Breadcrumb, Pagination and the rows that open a submenu | Point the other way | | | Progress, and the sliding bar of an unknown amount | Fill and move from the right | | | A sheet with `side="start"` | Comes from the right | | | Tabs, RadioGroup, ToggleGroup, Toolbar, Menubar | Laid out from the right | The left arrow moves forward | | Slider | | The low end is on the right, and the left arrow raises the value | | A submenu in DropdownMenu, ContextMenu and Menubar | | Opens with the left arrow, to the left | | ScrollArea | | The scrollbar is on the left | | NavigationMenu | Laid out from the right | The left arrow moves forward | The up and down arrows, Home, End and Tab do the same thing in both directions. ## One part of a page A page can hold a section in the other direction, such as a quotation in Arabic on an English page. Give the section's element the attribute and wrap it in a provider. The nearest provider wins, so a section can also go back to left-to-right inside a right-to-left app. ```tsx
...
``` Overlays need one more step there. Dialogs, popovers, menus and tooltips render at the end of ``, outside the section, so they get the page's direction and not the section's. Pass the section's element as the `container` prop of the overlay's content, and it renders inside. With the attribute on ``, there's nothing to do: `` has the direction too. ## One component Radix components that depend on the direction also take a `dir` prop, which wins over the provider. That's rarely the right tool, because the styles still follow the attribute, and the two then disagree. Use the attribute and the provider together. ## In your own components `useDirection` returns the direction from the nearest provider, or `"ltr"` when there is none. ```tsx "use client"; import { useDirection } from "@nuvui/react"; function NextArrow() { const dir = useDirection(); return {dir === "rtl" ? "←" : "→"}; } ``` Most of the time CSS is enough and no hook is needed: - Use logical properties: `margin-inline-start`, `inset-inline-end`, `border-start-start-radius`, `text-align: start`. - Mirror what can't be expressed that way with the `dir` attribute. ```css [dir="rtl"] .back-arrow { transform: scaleX(-1); } ``` In SCSS the library's [`rtl` mixin](page:scss) writes that selector for you, and leaves a part marked `dir="ltr"` inside a right-to-left page alone: ```scss @use "@nuvui/react/scss/mixins"; .back-arrow { @include mixins.rtl { transform: scaleX(-1); } } ``` The `:dir(rtl)` selector says the same in fewer words, and isn't used here for a reason. A build that supports browsers without it, which is Next.js by default, rewrites it to a list of `:lang()` selectors. After that nothing is mirrored on a page that sets `dir="rtl"` and not one of those languages. ## What shouldn't flip Not everything mirrors. These stay as they are in a right-to-left layout: - Numbers, phone numbers and code. - Icons that don't show a direction, and icons of real things, such as a clock or a check mark. - Media controls. Play points the same way everywhere, because it shows the direction of the tape and not of reading. - A chart's axes, unless the people who read it expect otherwise. Arrows that mean "back" and "forward", "previous" and "next" do flip. ## API ### DirectionProvider | Prop | Type | What it does | | --- | --- | --- | | `dir` | `"ltr" \| "rtl"` | The reading direction of everything inside. Required. | | `children` | `ReactNode` | The part of the app it applies to. | ### useDirection ```ts function useDirection(dir?: "ltr" | "rtl"): "ltr" | "rtl"; ``` Pass a component's own `dir` prop and it's returned when set. Otherwise the result is the nearest provider's direction, or `"ltr"`. Both are exported from `@nuvui/react`, and from `@nuvui/react/direction` by themselves. ## Checking your work - Tab through each page and press the arrow keys in every tab list, menu and slider. The key that points at the next item should move to it. - Open every overlay. It should be mirrored like the rest. - Look for anything pinned with `left` or `right` in your own CSS. - Read a page with mixed text, such as an English product name inside an Arabic sentence. The browser's own algorithm orders it, and `` around the foreign part keeps punctuation in place. The library's tests cover each component with a direction in both layouts, in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. They can't cover your content.

sections.heading: Setting it up
Why there are two
sections.markdown:
## Why there are two

**The attribute is what CSS sees.** The styles are written with logical properties, such as `padding-inline-start`, and with a selector on the `dir` attribute where something has to be mirrored. Both go by the `dir` of the element or of what's around it. So the layout flips with the attribute alone: text aligns to the right, icons move to the other side, a progress bar fills from the right.

**The provider is what the components' code sees.** Radix decides in JavaScript which arrow key moves to the next tab and which way a submenu opens, and it doesn't read the attribute. It reads a `dir` prop on the component, or this provider.

With the attribute and no provider, the tabs are laid out from the right and the left arrow still moves to the previous one. That's the mistake this page is here to prevent.

sections.heading: What each one changes
sections.markdown:
## What each one changes

| | With `dir="rtl"` | With `DirectionProvider` as well |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Text, padding, borders | Mirrored | |
| The arrows in Breadcrumb, Pagination and the rows that open a submenu | Point the other way | |
| Progress, and the sliding bar of an unknown amount | Fill and move from the right | |
| A sheet with `side="start"` | Comes from the right | |
| Tabs, RadioGroup, ToggleGroup, Toolbar, Menubar | Laid out from the right | The left arrow moves forward |
| Slider | | The low end is on the right, and the left arrow raises the value |
| A submenu in DropdownMenu, ContextMenu and Menubar | | Opens with the left arrow, to the left |
| ScrollArea | | The scrollbar is on the left |
| NavigationMenu | Laid out from the right | The left arrow moves forward |

The up and down arrows, <kbd>Home</kbd>, <kbd>End</kbd> and <kbd>Tab</kbd> do the same thing in both directions.

sections.heading: One part of a page
sections.markdown:
## One part of a page

A page can hold a section in the other direction, such as a quotation in Arabic on an English page. Give the section's element the attribute and wrap it in a provider. The nearest provider wins, so a section can also go back to left-to-right inside a right-to-left app.

```tsx
<DirectionProvider dir="rtl">
  <section dir="rtl" lang="ar">
    ...
  </section>
</DirectionProvider>
```

Overlays need one more step there. Dialogs, popovers, menus and tooltips render at the end of `<body>`, outside the section, so they get the page's direction and not the section's. Pass the section's element as the `container` prop of the overlay's content, and it renders inside.

With the attribute on `<html>`, there's nothing to do: `<body>` has the direction too.

sections.heading: One component
sections.markdown:
## One component

Radix components that depend on the direction also take a `dir` prop, which wins over the provider. That's rarely the right tool, because the styles still follow the attribute, and the two then disagree. Use the attribute and the provider together.

sections.heading: In your own components
What shouldn't flip
sections.markdown:
## What shouldn't flip

Not everything mirrors. These stay as they are in a right-to-left layout:

- Numbers, phone numbers and code.
- Icons that don't show a direction, and icons of real things, such as a clock or a check mark.
- Media controls. Play points the same way everywhere, because it shows the direction of the tape and not of reading.
- A chart's axes, unless the people who read it expect otherwise.

Arrows that mean "back" and "forward", "previous" and "next" do flip.

sections.heading: API
sections.markdown:
## API

### DirectionProvider

| Prop | Type | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dir` | `"ltr" \| "rtl"` | The reading direction of everything inside. Required. |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | The part of the app it applies to. |

### useDirection

```ts
function useDirection(dir?: "ltr" | "rtl"): "ltr" | "rtl";
```

Pass a component's own `dir` prop and it's returned when set. Otherwise the result is the nearest provider's direction, or `"ltr"`.

Both are exported from `@nuvui/react`, and from `@nuvui/react/direction` by themselves.

sections.heading: Checking your work
sections.markdown:
## Checking your work

- Tab through each page and press the arrow keys in every tab list, menu and slider. The key that points at the next item should move to it.
- Open every overlay. It should be mirrored like the rest.
- Look for anything pinned with `left` or `right` in your own CSS.
- Read a page with mixed text, such as an English product name inside an Arabic sentence. The browser's own algorithm orders it, and `<bdi>` around the foreign part keeps punctuation in place.

The library's tests cover each component with a direction in both layouts, in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. They can't cover your content.

pages.title: Translation
pages.description: Every piece of text nuvui writes by itself, such as "Close" and "Loading", with the prop that changes each one. A list for translators, taken from the components' own types.
pages.markdown:
# Translation

Every piece of text nuvui writes by itself, such as "Close" and "Loading", with the prop that changes each one. A list for translators, taken from the components' own types.

Almost all the text in an interface built with nuvui is yours: the labels, the headings, what's on the buttons. A few words the components write themselves, mostly names for screen readers on buttons that are only an icon. Each has a prop, with an English default.

This page lists all of them. The tables are made from the components' types when the docs are built, so a default shown here is the one in the code.

## How to translate them

Pass the prop wherever you render the component. With many dialogs in an app, that's easiest in a component of your own that wraps the library's:

```tsx
import { DialogContent, type DialogContentProps } from "@nuvui/react";
import { useTranslations } from "your-i18n-library";

export function AppDialogContent(props: DialogContentProps) {
  const t = useTranslations();
  return <DialogContent closeLabel={t("close")} {...props} />;
}
```

There's no provider that takes all the strings at once. A prop is found by TypeScript when its name changes, works in a server component, and keeps a component's text next to the component.

Text direction is a separate matter, covered in [right-to-left](page:right-to-left).

## Components

### Breadcrumb

The trail is a landmark named "Breadcrumb". Pass `aria-label` to `Breadcrumb` to change it.

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `string` | `"More"` | What a screen reader says for the three dots. |

### Combobox

On `ComboboxContent`:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `string` | `"Search"` | The search field's name, and the popup's. |
| `listLabel` | `string` | `"Options"` | The list's name. |
| `searchPlaceholder` | `string` |  | The search field's placeholder. There's none by default. |

On `ComboboxLoading`:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `string` | `"Loading"` | What a screen reader hears while options are fetched, when the part has no children. |

What `ComboboxEmpty` says is its children, which you write.

### Command

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `string` | `"Search"` | The search field's name. |

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `string` | `"Suggestions"` | The list's name. |

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `string` | `"Loading"` | What a screen reader hears while items are fetched, when the part has no children. |

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `title` | `string` | `"Command palette"` | The dialog's name. It isn't drawn. |

### Compare

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `beforeLabel` | `string` | `"Before"` | The name of before, on the picture and on the switch. |
| `afterLabel` | `string` | `"After"` | The name of after, on the picture and on the switch. |
| `dividerLabel` | `string` | `"Before and after"` | The divider's name, which a screen reader reads as a slider. |
| `valueLabel` | `((position: number, before: string, after: string) => string)` | `(position, before, after) => '${position}% ${before}, ${100 - position}% ${after}'` | What a screen reader says the divider's position is, given the position and the two names. |
| `switchLabel` | `string` | `"Show"` | The name of the switch, when one picture shows at a time. |

### Dialog and Sheet

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `closeLabel` | `string` | `"Close"` | The name of the close button in the corner. |

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `closeLabel` | `string` | `"Close"` | The name of the close button in the corner. |

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `string` | `"Change size", or "Dismiss" in a sheet with no stops` | The name of the bar a sheet is dragged by, which says what pressing it does. |

An alert dialog has no close button, and nothing of its own to translate.

### FileUpload

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | `"Drop files here, or choose them from your device"` | The words in the drop area. |
| `removeLabel` | `((name: string) => string)` | `(name) => 'Remove ${name}'` | The name of the button that removes a file from the list, given the file's name. |
| `formatSize` | `((bytes: number) => string)` | `The size in the visitor's own number format, such as "1.2 MB"` | How a file's size is written. The default uses the browser's language for the number and the unit. |

Why a file was refused is yours to say. `onReject` gives you the reason as `"type"`, `"size"` or `"count"`.

### HoldToConfirm

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `hint` | `string` | `"Hold down to confirm."` | What a screen reader says about the button, and says again when it's let go of too soon. |
| `againLabel` | `string` | `"Press again to confirm."` | What a screen reader says after the first of two presses. |

What the button says is its children, which you write. Start it with the words for "Hold to".

### Navbar

On `NavbarMenu`:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `string` | `"Menu"` | The name of the button that opens the links on a narrow screen, and the title of the panel. |
| `closeLabel` | `string` | `"Close"` | The name of the button that closes that panel. |

### NumberField

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `incrementLabel` | `string` | `"Increase"` | The name of the button that raises the number. |
| `decrementLabel` | `string` | `"Decrease"` | The name of the button that lowers it. |

How the number is written, and how what's typed is read, follows its `format`, which takes a `locale`.

### OtpField

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `inputLabel` | `((position: number, length: number) => string)` | `(position, length) => 'Character ${position} of ${length}'` | The name of each box, given its position and how many there are. |

### Pagination

The bar is a landmark named "Pagination". Pass `aria-label` to `Pagination` to change it. `PaginationPrevious` and `PaginationNext` say "Previous" and "Next" unless you give them children.

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `string` | `"More pages"` | What a screen reader says for the three dots. |

### PasswordInput

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `showLabel` | `string` | `"Show password"` | The name of the button while the password is hidden. |
| `hideLabel` | `string` | `"Hide password"` | The name of the button while the password is shown. |

### Rating

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `itemLabel` | `((value: number, max: number) => string)` | `(value) => (value === 1 ? "1 star" : '${value} stars')` | The name of one star, given its number and how many there are. |
| `valueLabel` | `((value: number, max: number) => string)` | `(value, max) => '${value} out of ${max}'` | The name of a rating that can't be changed, given its value and how many stars there are. |

### Sidebar

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `string` | `"Sidebar"` | The sidebar's name as a landmark, and the name of the panel it becomes on a phone. |
| `closeLabel` | `string` | `"Close"` | The name of the button that closes that panel. |

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `string` | `"Toggle sidebar"` | The name of the button that opens and closes the sidebar. |

### Spinner

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `string` | `"Loading"` | What a screen reader hears when the spinner appears. |

### Stepper

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `completedLabel` | `string` | `"Completed"` | What a screen reader says after the title of a step that's done. |

### Toast

On `Toaster`:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `closeLabel` | `string` | `"Close"` | The name of the close button on each toast. |
| `toastLabel` | `string` | `"Notification"` | What a screen reader says before the text of each toast. |

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `string` |  | The name of the list of toasts as a landmark. It's `"Notifications ({hotkey})"` unless you say otherwise, and `{hotkey}` is filled in for you. |

### Trend

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `upLabel` | `string` | `"Up"` | What a screen reader says before the amount of a rise. |
| `downLabel` | `string` | `"Down"` | What a screen reader says before the amount of a fall. |
| `flatLabel` | `string` | `"No change"` | What a screen reader says for no change, in place of the amount. |

How the amount itself is written follows its `format`, which takes a `locale`. So does every [`FormattedNumber`](page:components/formatted-number): pass it the language your app is in.

## Dates

A calendar's month and day names, and the names a screen reader hears on its buttons, come from a `locale`. [Dates](page:date-picker/index#languages) has how to pass one. These are what the two fields add, on `DatePicker` and `DateRangePicker`:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `calendarLabel` | `string` | `"Choose date"` | The name of the button that opens the calendar. `"Choose date"` on a date picker. |
| `title` | `string` | `"Choose date"` | The name of the calendar's panel, and the heading of the sheet on a phone. `"Choose date"` on a date picker. |
| `closeLabel` | `string` | `"Close"` | The name of the sheet's close button. |
| `invalidMessage` | `string` | `"Enter a valid date."` | What the browser shows for text that isn't a date. |
| `startLabel` | `string` | `"Start date"` | The name of the first field. A range only. |
| `endLabel` | `string` | `"End date"` | The name of the second field. A range only. |
| `orderMessage` | `string` | `"The end date is before the start date."` | What the browser shows for a range typed the wrong way round. A range only. |

## Tables

A data table takes all its text in one prop, `labels`. Pass the ones to change:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `search` (required) | `string` |  | The search field's name and placeholder. |
| `columns` (required) | `string` |  | The column chooser's button. |
| `empty` (required) | `string` |  | Shown in place of rows when there are none. |
| `noMatches` (required) | `string` |  | Shown in place of rows when a filter leaves none. |
| `clearFilters` (required) | `string` |  |  |
| `error` (required) | `string` |  | Shown when `error` is `true` and not a message of your own. |
| `retry` (required) | `string` |  |  |
| `selectAll` (required) | `string` |  |  |
| `selectPage` (required) | `string` |  | The header checkbox of a table with pages. |
| `selectRow` (required) | `(row: string) => string` |  |  |
| `rowName` (required) | `(position: number) => string` |  | A row's name when it has no `rowHeader` column: its place in the list. |
| `expandRow` (required) | `(row: string) => string` |  |  |
| `collapseRow` (required) | `(row: string) => string` |  |  |
| `selected` (required) | `(count: number) => string` |  |  |
| `clearSelection` (required) | `string` |  |  |
| `bulkActions` (required) | `string` |  | The name of the bar that holds the actions for selected rows. |
| `pagination` (required) | `string` |  |  |
| `rowsPerPage` (required) | `string` |  |  |
| `pageRange` (required) | `(from: number, to: number, total: number) => string` |  | "21-40 of 143". |
| `page` (required) | `(page: number, pages: number) => string` |  |  |
| `firstPage` (required) | `string` |  |  |
| `previousPage` (required) | `string` |  |  |
| `nextPage` (required) | `string` |  |  |
| `lastPage` (required) | `string` |  |  |
| `resizeColumn` (required) | `(column: string) => string` |  |  |
| `filterColumn` (required) | `(column: string) => string` |  |  |
| `sortedAscending` (required) | `(column: string) => string` |  | Read out after a sort. |
| `sortedDescending` (required) | `(column: string) => string` |  |  |
| `sortCleared` (required) | `string` |  |  |
| `results` (required) | `(count: number) => string` |  | Read out after a filter changes how many rows there are. |

`empty` and `error`, on `DataTable`, replace "No rows." and the error message for one table.

## Charts

A chart writes no text of its own. Its name is the `aria-label` you give it, a series is named by its `label` in the config, and numbers are written by `formatValue`.

## Flow diagrams

A diagram's name is the `aria-label` you give it, and a node's is its `label`. What it adds, the meaning of each shape, where a node leads, the buttons and what's said as it changes, is in one prop, `labels`:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `roleDescription` | `string` |  | What kind of thing the diagram is, read after its name. |
| `shapes` | `Partial<Record<FlowShape, string>>` |  | What each shape means, read after a node's name. |
| `leadsTo` | `((targets: FlowLinkTarget[]) => string)` |  | Where a node leads, read after its name and shown in the list. |
| `instructions` | `string` |  | How to get around the diagram with the keyboard. |
| `editInstructions` | `string` |  | How to change it with the keyboard, read after `instructions`. |
| `controls` | `string` |  | The name of the group of buttons. |
| `zoomIn` | `string` |  |  |
| `zoomOut` | `string` |  |  |
| `fit` | `string` |  |  |
| `showList` | `string` |  | The button that shows the diagram as a list. |
| `hideList` | `string` |  |  |
| `list` | `string` |  | The name of the list. |
| `showMore` | `((count: number) => string)` |  | The button at the end of a long list. |
| `find` | `((label: string) => string)` |  | A step's button in the list, which finds it in the diagram. |
| `removeLink` | `((from: string, to: string) => string)` |  | A link's button in the list of an editable diagram. |
| `linking` | `((from: string) => string)` |  | Said when a link is started with the keyboard. |
| `linked` | `((from: string, to: string) => string)` |  | Said when a link is made. |
| `linkCancelled` | `string` |  | Said when a link that was started is let go. |
| `moved` | `((labels: string[]) => string)` |  | Said when nodes are moved. |
| `removed` | `((nodes: number, links: number) => string)` |  | Said when nodes and links are removed. |

## What isn't text

- A [field](page:components/field) marks a required label with `*`, which `FieldLabel` changes with `requiredIndicator`. Screen readers don't hear it. They hear "required" from the control, in the browser's own language.
- A [progress bar](page:components/progress) says its value as a percentage, such as "40%". `getValueLabel` changes that.
- Messages a browser shows for a field that fails its own validation, such as a required one left empty, are the browser's and in its language.

## What hasn't been checked

The list was made by searching the source of the four packages for text, and by reading what Radix UI, cmdk, react-day-picker and Recharts add by themselves. It was not checked by running an interface in another language through a screen reader.

Components
sections.markdown:
## Components

### Breadcrumb

The trail is a landmark named "Breadcrumb". Pass `aria-label` to `Breadcrumb` to change it.

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `string` | `"More"` | What a screen reader says for the three dots. |

### Combobox

sections.markdown:
## Dates

A calendar's month and day names, and the names a screen reader hears on its buttons, come from a `locale`. [Dates](page:date-picker/index#languages) has how to pass one. These are what the two fields add, on `DatePicker` and `DateRangePicker`:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `calendarLabel` | `string` | `"Choose date"` | The name of the button that opens the calendar. `"Choose date"` on a date picker. |
| `title` | `string` | `"Choose date"` | The name of the calendar's panel, and the heading of the sheet on a phone. `"Choose date"` on a date picker. |
| `closeLabel` | `string` | `"Close"` | The name of the sheet's close button. |
| `invalidMessage` | `string` | `"Enter a valid date."` | What the browser shows for text that isn't a date. |

sections.heading: Charts
sections.markdown:
## Charts

A chart writes no text of its own. Its name is the `aria-label` you give it, a series is named by its `label` in the config, and numbers are written by `formatValue`.

sections.heading: Flow diagrams
sections.markdown:
## Flow diagrams

A diagram's name is the `aria-label` you give it, and a node's is its `label`. What it adds, the meaning of each shape, where a node leads, the buttons and what's said as it changes, is in one prop, `labels`:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `roleDescription` | `string` |  | What kind of thing the diagram is, read after its name. |
| `shapes` | `Partial<Record<FlowShape, string>>` |  | What each shape means, read after a node's name. |
| `leadsTo` | `((targets: FlowLinkTarget[]) => string)` |  | Where a node leads, read after its name and shown in the list. |
| `instructions` | `string` |  | How to get around the diagram with the keyboard. |
| `editInstructions` | `string` |  | How to change it with the keyboard, read after `instructions`. |
| `controls` | `string` |  | The name of the group of buttons. |
| `zoomIn` | `string` |  |  |
| `zoomOut` | `string` |  |  |
| `fit` | `string` |  |  |
| `showList` | `string` |  | The button that shows the diagram as a list. |
| `hideList` | `string` |  |  |
| `list` | `string` |  | The name of the list. |
| `showMore` | `((count: number) => string)` |  | The button at the end of a long list. |
| `find` | `((label: string) => string)` |  | A step's button in the list, which finds it in the diagram. |
| `removeLink` | `((from: string, to: string) => string)` |  | A link's button in the list of an editable diagram. |
| `linking` | `((from: string) => string)` |  | Said when a link is started with the keyboard. |
| `linked` | `((from: string, to: string) => string)` |  | Said when a link is made. |
| `linkCancelled` | `string` |  | Said when a link that was started is let go. |
| `moved` | `((labels: string[]) => string)` |  | Said when nodes are moved. |
| `removed` | `((nodes: number, links: number) => string)` |  | Said when nodes and links are removed. |

sections.heading: What isn't text
sections.markdown:
## What isn't text

- A [field](page:components/field) marks a required label with `*`, which `FieldLabel` changes with `requiredIndicator`. Screen readers don't hear it. They hear "required" from the control, in the browser's own language.
- A [progress bar](page:components/progress) says its value as a percentage, such as "40%". `getValueLabel` changes that.
- Messages a browser shows for a field that fails its own validation, such as a required one left empty, are the browser's and in its language.

sections.heading: What hasn't been checked
sections.markdown:
## What hasn't been checked

The list was made by searching the source of the four packages for text, and by reading what Radix UI, cmdk, react-day-picker and Recharts add by themselves. It was not checked by running an interface in another language through a screen reader.

pages.title: Support policy
pages.description: Which versions of React, Node and browsers nuvui works with, which of those are tested, how versions are numbered, and what a fix in a supported setup means.
pages.markdown:
# Support policy

Which versions of React, Node and browsers nuvui works with, which of those are tested, how versions are numbered, and what a fix in a supported setup means.

This page says what the library is meant to work with, and separately what it's tested with. Where the two differ, it says so.

The policy applies to every released version, from the first.

## React

| Version | Status |
| --- | --- |
| 19 | Supported, and what the component tests run on. |
| 18.2 and later 18 releases | Supported. Built, type-checked and rendered on a server on 18.2. |
| 17 and older | Not supported. |

The packages declare `react` and `react-dom` as peers at `^18.2.0 || ^19.0.0`, and `@nuvui/icons` only `react`. The code is written for both: components use `forwardRef`, which React 18 needs, and nothing uses an API that only React 19 has.

On React 18.2.0 and its types, one app installs the packed packages, type-checks, builds, and renders every package's components to HTML with React 18's server renderer. That catches a type, an import or a hook that React 18 doesn't have. What it doesn't catch is behavior in a browser: the component tests, with their keys, focus and effects, run on React 19 only. Treat a problem there on 18 as likely to be found by you first, and report it.

Server components are supported. A component that needs the browser is marked `"use client"` in the package, so it can be imported from a server component. This is tested with Next.js.

## Node

Node is only involved where your app renders on a server or builds. Each package says the oldest version it runs on in its `engines` field:

| Package | Node |
| --- | --- |
| `@nuvui/react` | 18 or newer |
| `@nuvui/date-picker` | 18 or newer |
| `@nuvui/charts` | 18 or newer |
| `@nuvui/barcodes` | 18 or newer |
| `@nuvui/chat` | 18 or newer |
| `@nuvui/kanban` | 18 or newer |
| `@nuvui/editor` | 18 or newer |
| `@nuvui/emoji` | 18 or newer |
| `@nuvui/map` | 18 or newer |
| `@nuvui/flow` | 18 or newer |
| `@nuvui/icons` | 18 or newer |
| `@nuvui/table` | 20 or newer, because TanStack Table 9 asks for it |

The tests run on Node 24. Older versions on this list aren't tested.

Working on the library itself needs Node 22.18 or newer, which runs TypeScript files without a build step.

## Browsers

Chrome and Edge 111, Firefox 113 and Safari 16.4, or newer. The styles use cascade layers, `oklch()` colors, `color-mix()` and `dvh` units, and there's no fallback for a browser without them.

The tests run in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, in the current versions that Playwright ships, on a desktop and at a phone's size. WebKit there is close to Safari and isn't Safari. Nothing is tested in an old version of any browser: the versions above are where the features the styles need arrived.

## Build tools

The end-to-end tests pack the packages, install them into three apps and build those: one with Vite, one with Next.js as a static export, and one with Vite on React 18.2. Other bundlers that read a package's `exports` should work, and aren't tested.

The styles are plain CSS files. The SCSS source is there for apps that compile Sass, with [one known problem](page:scss) in Next.js with Turbopack on Windows.

## TypeScript

The packages ship their own types. They're built and checked with the TypeScript version in the repository, and with `@arethetypeswrong/cli` for both ES modules and CommonJS. Older TypeScript versions aren't tested.

## Assistive technology

Every component is tested for the roles, names and states a browser passes to a screen reader, and with axe. What a screen reader then says hasn't been checked by a person. Each component's page has a section that says this for that component.

## Versions

The packages follow semantic versioning:

- A **patch** fixes a bug and changes nothing else.
- A **minor** adds something. Code written for the version before still works.
- A **major** may rename or remove things. The changelog says what to change.

Before 1.0, a minor may also rename or remove things. The [changelog](https://nuvui.nuvraxis.com/docs/changelog) says so where it does.

What counts as the public API: the components and their props, the functions the packages export, the CSS variables and the class names on each component's page, and the tokens. What doesn't: the DOM inside a component beyond the classes its page lists, and anything imported from a path that isn't in a package's `exports`.

Dropping a version of React, Node or a browser from this page is a major change.

## What supported means

A bug you can reproduce in a setup this page calls supported is a bug in the library, and is fixed in the next release. Fixes go into the latest release only.

{/* TODO(Nuvraxis): say here whether an older major gets fixes after a new one is out, and for how long. Nothing has been decided, so nothing is promised. */}

A security problem is reported privately. The repository's `SECURITY.md` says how.

To report anything else, open an issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/Nuvraxis/nuvui/issues) with the versions you're on and the smallest example that shows it.

pages.title: Content Security Policy
pages.description: The policy a site with a strict Content Security Policy needs for nuvui, what each line is for, and what breaks without it.
pages.markdown:
# Content Security Policy

The policy a site with a strict Content Security Policy needs for nuvui, what each line is for, and what breaks without it.

A Content Security Policy tells the browser what a page may load and run. nuvui works under a strict one, with one allowance: `style` attributes. This page says which, and why.

## The policy

These are the lines nuvui needs. Your framework adds its own, mostly for its scripts.

```txt title="Content-Security-Policy"
default-src 'self';
style-src 'self' 'nonce-{nonce}';
style-src-attr 'unsafe-inline';
img-src 'self' blob:;
connect-src 'self';
worker-src 'self' blob:;
```

`{nonce}` is a value made fresh for every response. It needs a server that sends each page. A site exported as static files has no nonce to give, and a component that needs one can't be used there under this policy.

| Line | What it's for |
| --- | --- |
| `style-src 'self'` | The packages' stylesheets, served from your site. |
| `'nonce-{nonce}'` | The one `<style>` element in the library, written by `ScrollArea`. Pass it the same value: `<ScrollArea nonce={nonce}>`. No other component writes a `<style>` element. |
| `style-src-attr 'unsafe-inline'` | `style` attributes in the HTML. See below. |
| `img-src blob:` | A picture of a file before it's sent, in `PromptInput`, and saving a barcode or a QR code as a PNG. Leave it out if you use neither. |
| `worker-src blob:` | Where MapLibre starts its worker from, for `@nuvui/map`. With `setMapWorkerUrl` pointing at a file on your site, `'self'` is enough. |

No package runs code from a string, so `script-src` needs no `'unsafe-eval'`. The chat package's code colors come from Shiki's JavaScript engine, which needs no WebAssembly either.

## Why `style` attributes

A component sets some of its styles on the element itself, where the value is only known while it runs: how far a progress bar has filled, where a slider's handle sits, the colors of a chart's series. So do the libraries under it: Radix places its own parts this way, and Recharts sizes its charts this way.

A page that's built in the browser sets these from JavaScript, and a policy doesn't stop that. A page rendered on a server sends them in its HTML, as `style` attributes, and without `style-src-attr 'unsafe-inline'` the browser drops them. React doesn't put them back when it takes the page over. On a page rendered on a server, this is what goes wrong:

| Component | Without `style` attributes |
| --- | --- |
| `Progress` | The bar is empty, whatever its value. |
| `Slider` | The filled part is empty, and the handle is at the start. |
| `ScrollArea` | The box doesn't scroll. |
| A chart | The series lose their colors. |
| `Rating` | A part of a star isn't filled. |
| `AspectRatio` | The box has no height. |
| `ColorPicker` | The swatch in the trigger is empty. |
| `TextReveal` | The lines rise together rather than one after another. |
| `Compare` | Until the page's script runs, the divider is in the middle, whatever `defaultPosition` says. It sets the position again once it runs. |
| `DataTable` | A nested row isn't indented. |
| `Checkbox`, `RadioGroup`, `Switch` and `Select` in a form | Radix's hidden copy of the control shows on the page. |

A `style` attribute can only style the element it's on. It can't select other elements, so it can't be used to read what's on the page, which is what a `<style>` element can be made to do. That's why the line is allowed and `<style>` elements stay behind the nonce.

## The add-on packages

- **`@nuvui/map`:** the tiles and the style come from a provider. Add its address to `connect-src`.
- **`@nuvui/chat`:** what your app sends a model and gets back is your app's own requests, under your `connect-src`.
- **`@nuvui/flow`:** nothing. Every position is an SVG attribute, so a diagram sent by a server is drawn whole under a policy without `style-src-attr 'unsafe-inline'`.
- **`@nuvui/barcodes`:** a picture laid over a QR code is fetched once to save it in the file, from its own address, under `connect-src`.

## How it was checked

Every page of these docs was loaded in Chromium under this policy, with the scripts allowed, and nothing the packages draw was blocked. The same pages with `style` attributes blocked gave the table above. A test in the docs repeats the first for the components in that table, in each browser the docs are tested in.

sections.heading: Install
sections.markdown:
## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/react
```

sections.heading: Import
Parts
sections.markdown:
## Parts

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `Accordion` | Holds which items are open. |
| `AccordionItem` | One heading together with its panel. |
| `AccordionTrigger` | The button that opens and closes the panel. It renders the heading element around itself, and the chevron. |
| `AccordionContent` | The panel. |

These are separate exports, not properties of `Accordion`. `Accordion.Item` isn't available, because property access on a client component doesn't work from a server component.

sections.heading: Props
sections.markdown:
## Props

### Accordion

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `type` (required) | `"multiple" \| "single"` |  | Whether one item can be open at a time or any number. Required. |
| `value` | `string \| string[]` |  | The open item, when you control it yourself. A string for `"single"`, an array of strings for `"multiple"`. |
| `defaultValue` | `string \| string[]` |  | What's open at first, when you don't control it. |
| `onValueChange` | `((value: string) => void) \| ((value: string[]) => void)` |  | Called with the new value when an item opens or closes. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` |  | Stops every item from being opened or closed. |

One more prop exists only with `type="single"`:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `collapsible` | `boolean` | `false` | Lets the open item be closed again by pressing its trigger. Without it, one item always stays open once any has been opened. |

### AccordionItem

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value` (required) | `string` |  | Identifies the item. It has to be unique within the accordion. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` |  | Stops this item from being opened or closed. |

### AccordionTrigger

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `headingLevel` | `2 \| 3 \| 4 \| 5 \| 6` | `3` | The heading level each trigger is wrapped in. Pick the one that fits the page's outline: 2 if the accordion sits right under the page title. |

Every part also takes what its element takes, including `ref` and `className`. The [Radix Accordion reference](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/components/accordion#api-reference) has the full list.

Heading level
sections.markdown:
## Heading level Each trigger sits inside a real heading, so the accordion shows up in the page's outline and in a screen reader's list of headings. It's an `

` unless you say otherwise. Pick the level that follows the heading above the accordion: ```tsx

Questions

How long does shipping take? Three to five working days. ``` The heading takes its size and weight from the trigger, not from its level, so changing the level doesn't change how it looks.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### Keyboard

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Moves to the next trigger, or into an open panel if it has something focusable. |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Space</kbd> | Opens or closes the focused item. |
| <kbd>↓</kbd> and <kbd>↑</kbd> | Move to the next or previous trigger. From the last one it goes to the first. Disabled items are skipped. |
| <kbd>Home</kbd> | Moves to the first trigger. |
| <kbd>End</kbd> | Moves to the last trigger. |

### What the component handles

- Each trigger is a `<button>` inside a heading, with `aria-expanded`. An open panel has `role="region"` and is named by its trigger. This part is Radix.
- A closed panel's content isn't rendered, so it can't be reached with <kbd>Tab</kbd> or read by a screen reader.
- Triggers are at least 44 pixels tall.
- The chevron is hidden from screen readers. `aria-expanded` already says whether the item is open.
- The panel slides open and the chevron turns only when the visitor hasn't asked for reduced motion. Otherwise both change at once.

### What you need to handle

- Set `headingLevel` to fit the page's outline.
- Keep links and buttons out of the trigger. It's a button, and HTML doesn't allow a control inside a button. Browsers and screen readers each handle that differently.
- Pass `collapsible` with `type="single"` unless one item really has to stay open. Without it, the open item's trigger is marked `aria-disabled` and pressing it does nothing.

sections.heading: CSS variables
sections.markdown:
## CSS variables

Set any of these on `Accordion`, or on anything around it.

```css
.faq {
  --nuv-accordion-padding-block: calc(var(--spacing) * 5);
}
```

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-accordion-border` | `var(--color-border)` | Color of the lines between items. |
| `--nuv-accordion-padding-block` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 3)` | Padding above and below each trigger's label, and below each panel's content. |
| `--nuv-accordion-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Text color of the triggers. |
| `--nuv-accordion-content-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Text color of the panels. |

sections.heading: Classes
sections.markdown:
## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-accordion` | Accordion. |
| `.nuv-accordion__body` | The element inside the panel that holds your content and its padding. |
| `.nuv-accordion__chevron` | The arrow at the end of each trigger. |
| `.nuv-accordion__content` | AccordionContent. This is the element whose height is animated. |
| `.nuv-accordion__header` | The heading around each trigger. |
| `.nuv-accordion__item` | AccordionItem. |
| `.nuv-accordion__trigger` | AccordionTrigger. |

Radix sets `data-state="open"` or `data-state="closed"` on the item, the heading, the trigger and the panel, and `data-disabled` on a disabled item's parts. The chevron and the animation hang off those.

sections.heading: Server components
sections.markdown:
## Server components

The accordion parts are client components. They carry `"use client"`, and the build checks that the directive is still there in the published files.

You can put an accordion together inside a server component, as both examples on this page do. It only needs a client component of your own when you control `value`.

A closed panel's content isn't in the HTML the server sends. That matters for a page of questions and answers that search engines should read. Either start with the items open through `defaultValue`, or pass `forceMount` to each `AccordionContent` and hide the ones with `data-state="closed"` in your own CSS.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Write each heading so it makes sense without opening it.
- Use `type="multiple"` when people may want to compare two panels.
- Keep the panels short. A long one pushes the next heading off the screen.

**Don't**

- Don't hide content that everyone needs behind a click.
- Don't put an accordion inside an accordion.
- Don't use one for navigation. Opening a panel shouldn't take anyone to another page.

pages.title: ActionBar
pages.description: A bar that appears while something is selected, with what can be done to it, and tells a screen reader how much is selected.
pages.markdown:
# ActionBar A bar that appears while something is selected, with what can be done to it, and tells a screen reader how much is selected. Use an action bar for what can be done to a selection: messages ticked in a list, files in a grid, cards on a board. It's there while something is selected and gone when nothing is. A [data table](page:table/index) has a bar of its own for selected rows. ```tsx "use client"; import { ActionBar, ActionBarSelection, Button, Checkbox, Label, } from "@nuvui/react"; import { useState } from "react"; const messages = [ { id: "invoice", subject: "Invoice for March" }, { id: "renewal", subject: "Your plan renews soon" }, { id: "welcome", subject: "Welcome to the team" }, { id: "export", subject: "Your export is ready" }, ]; export default function Example() { const [selected, setSelected] = useState(["invoice"]); const toggle = (id: string) => setSelected((current) => current.includes(id) ? current.filter((other) => other !== id) : [...current, id], ); return (
    {messages.map((message) => (
  • toggle(message.id)} />
    • ))}
0} position="static" aria-label="Selected messages" > {selected.length} selected
); } ``` ## Install ```sh pnpm add @nuvui/react ``` ## Import ```tsx import { ActionBar, ActionBarSelection } from "@nuvui/react"; ``` The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that, and how to load only this component's CSS. ## Parts | Part | What it is | | --- | --- | | `ActionBar` | The bar: a named group. It's told whether it's open. | | `ActionBarSelection` | How much is selected, in words. | The rest is yours: [buttons](page:components/button), a [separator](page:components/separator), a [menu](page:components/dropdown-menu) for what doesn't fit. ## Props | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `open` (required) | `boolean` | | Whether the bar is shown. Usually: whether anything is selected. | | `position` | `"fixed" \| "static" \| "sticky"` | `"fixed"` | Where the bar is. `"fixed"` is the bottom of the window. `"sticky"` is the bottom of whatever scrolls around it, and it takes room in the page. `"static"` is where you put it, with nothing else done. | `ActionBar` also takes what a `div` takes. `ref`, `className` and the rest go on the bar itself, which is in the page only while it's open. `ActionBarSelection` adds no props of its own. ## Where the bar is `position` has three values. - `"fixed"`, the default, puts the bar along the bottom of the window, over the page. Leave room at the end of the page so the bar doesn't cover the last row. - `"sticky"` keeps it at the bottom of whatever scrolls around it, and it takes room there. - `"static"` leaves it where you put it. ```tsx "use client"; import { ActionBar, ActionBarSelection, Button, Checkbox, Label, } from "@nuvui/react"; import { useState } from "react"; const files = Array.from({ length: 12 }, (_, index) => ({ id: `file-${index + 1}`, name: `Report ${index + 1}.pdf`, })); export default function Example() { const [selected, setSelected] = useState(["file-2", "file-3"]); const toggle = (id: string) => setSelected((current) => current.includes(id) ? current.filter((other) => other !== id) : [...current, id], ); return (
    {files.map((file) => (
  • toggle(file.id)} />
    • ))}
0} position="sticky" aria-label="Selected files" > {selected.length} selected
); } ``` A closed bar takes no room in any of the three. ## What's selected is yours The bar keeps no state. `open` is usually whether your selection has anything in it, and the buttons call your own functions. Clear the selection when an action is done, and the bar closes. ## Accessibility An action bar has no keyboard behavior of its own. Its buttons are reached with Tab, in the order they're written. ### What the component handles - The bar is a group with the name you give it. - What `ActionBarSelection` says is read out when the bar appears, and again whenever it changes. The element a screen reader listens to is in the page all the time, open or not, because a change is only read out from something that was already there. - The same words describe the group, so someone who tabs into the bar hears its name and how much is selected. - The words that are drawn are hidden from screen readers, so they aren't read twice. - The bar slides in. For a visitor who asked for less motion it appears. ### What you need to handle - Name the bar with `aria-label`, such as "Selected messages". - Put the bar in the page right after what it acts on. Tab goes from the list to the bar, wherever the bar is drawn. - Give it a way to clear the selection: a button in the bar, and Escape in your list. - Keep `ActionBarSelection` to text. It's in the page twice, so an `id` inside it would be too. - When an action removes what was selected, move focus back to the list. ## On small screens The bar is as wide as its content and no wider than the screen, and its buttons wrap onto a second row when they don't fit. Three actions is about what fits beside the count on a phone. Put the rest in a menu. A fixed bar keeps clear of the home indicator on a phone. ## CSS variables Set any of these on anything around the `ActionBar`. Some are read by the bar and some by what holds it, so a wrapper is the place. ```css .inbox { --nuv-action-bar-offset: 1.5rem; } ``` | Variable | Default | What it sets | | --- | --- | --- | | `--nuv-action-bar-z` | `calc(var(--nuv-z-overlay) - 1)` | Stacking order of a fixed bar. Under a dialog by default. | | `--nuv-action-bar-offset` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 4)` | Space between a fixed or sticky bar and the edges it's against. | | `--nuv-action-bar-gap` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 2)` | Space between the things in the bar. | | `--nuv-action-bar-padding` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 2)` | Space inside the bar. | | `--nuv-action-bar-border` | `var(--color-border)` | Border color. | | `--nuv-action-bar-radius` | `var(--radius-lg)` | Corner radius. | | `--nuv-action-bar-bg` | `var(--color-surface)` | Background color. | | `--nuv-action-bar-shadow` | `var(--shadow-lg)`, `none` | Shadow. None by default with position="static". | | `--nuv-action-bar-fg` | `var(--color-surface-foreground)` | Text color. | ## Classes | Class | What it's on | | --- | --- | | `.nuv-action-bar` | What holds the bar, and is in the page whether it's open or not. | | `.nuv-action-bar--fixed` | position="fixed" | | `.nuv-action-bar--static` | position="static" | | `.nuv-action-bar--sticky` | position="sticky" | | `.nuv-action-bar__content` | The bar. `className` is added here. | | `.nuv-action-bar__selection` | ActionBarSelection | | `.nuv-action-bar__status` | What a screen reader listens to, drawn for nobody. | Whether the bar is open is in a `data-state` attribute on what holds it: `open` or `closed`. ## Server components ActionBar starts with `"use client"`: it hands the element that's listened to on to `ActionBarSelection`. A selection is state in any case, so the component that renders the bar is a client component. ## Do and don't **Do** - Put the count first and the most used action next to it. - Keep destructive actions last, and in the danger intent. **Don't** - Don't use it for actions that don't need a selection. Those go in a [toolbar](page:components/toolbar). - Don't cover the thing being selected. Leave room under a list for a fixed bar.

## Accessibility

An action bar has no keyboard behavior of its own. Its buttons are reached with Tab, in the order they're written.

### What the component handles

- The bar is a group with the name you give it.
- What `ActionBarSelection` says is read out when the bar appears, and again whenever it changes. The element a screen reader listens to is in the page all the time, open or not, because a change is only read out from something that was already there.
- The same words describe the group, so someone who tabs into the bar hears its name and how much is selected.
- The words that are drawn are hidden from screen readers, so they aren't read twice.
- The bar slides in. For a visitor who asked for less motion it appears.

- Name the bar with `aria-label`, such as "Selected messages".
- Put the bar in the page right after what it acts on. Tab goes from the list to the bar, wherever the bar is drawn.
- Give it a way to clear the selection: a button in the bar, and Escape in your list.
- Keep `ActionBarSelection` to text. It's in the page twice, so an `id` inside it would be too.
- When an action removes what was selected, move focus back to the list.

```css

```

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-action-bar-z` | `calc(var(--nuv-z-overlay) - 1)` | Stacking order of a fixed bar. Under a dialog by default. |
| `--nuv-action-bar-offset` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 4)` | Space between a fixed or sticky bar and the edges it's against. |
| `--nuv-action-bar-gap` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 2)` | Space between the things in the bar. |
| `--nuv-action-bar-padding` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 2)` | Space inside the bar. |
| `--nuv-action-bar-border` | `var(--color-border)` | Border color. |
| `--nuv-action-bar-radius` | `var(--radius-lg)` | Corner radius. |
| `--nuv-action-bar-bg` | `var(--color-surface)` | Background color. |
| `--nuv-action-bar-shadow` | `var(--shadow-lg)`, `none` | Shadow. None by default with position="static". |

sections.heading: Classes
sections.markdown:
## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-action-bar` | What holds the bar, and is in the page whether it's open or not. |
| `.nuv-action-bar--fixed` | position="fixed" |
| `.nuv-action-bar--static` | position="static" |
| `.nuv-action-bar--sticky` | position="sticky" |
