sections.heading: Server components
sections.markdown:
## Server components

ActionBar starts with `"use client"`: it hands the element that's listened to on to `ActionBarSelection`. A selection is state in any case, so the component that renders the bar is a client component.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Put the count first and the most used action next to it.
- Keep destructive actions last, and in the danger intent.

**Don't**

- Don't use it for actions that don't need a selection. Those go in a [toolbar](page:components/toolbar).
- Don't cover the thing being selected. Leave room under a list for a fixed bar.

pages.title: Alert
pages.description: A message that sits in the page, with an icon and a color that say what kind of message it is.
pages.markdown:
# Alert A message that sits in the page, with an icon and a color that say what kind of message it is. Use an alert for something people should read before they carry on with the page: a payment that failed, a trial about to end, a change that's coming. It stays where it is until the reason for it is gone. For a message about something that just happened and needs no action, use a [toast](page:components/toast). For a question that has to be answered first, use an [alert dialog](page:components/alert-dialog). ```tsx import { Alert, AlertDescription, AlertTitle } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function Example() { return ( Maintenance on Saturday Reports will be read-only from 22:00 to midnight while the database is moved. ); } ``` ## Install ```sh pnpm add @nuvui/react ``` ## Import ```tsx import { Alert, AlertDescription, AlertTitle } from "@nuvui/react"; ``` The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that, and how to load only this component's CSS. ## Parts | Part | What it is | | --- | --- | | `Alert` | The box, with the icon. | | `AlertTitle` | What happened, in a few words. | | `AlertDescription` | The detail, and what to do about it. | | `AlertActions` | A row of buttons or links under the text. | ## Props ### Alert | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `intent` | `"danger" \| "info" \| "success" \| "warning"` | `"info"` | What kind of message it is. It sets the icon and the color, and the default `role`. | | `icon` | `ReactNode` | | An icon to draw in place of the intent's own. Pass `null` or `false` for none. | It also takes what a `
` takes. `role` is the one to know about, and [the section below](#when-a-screen-reader-reads-it) covers it. ### AlertTitle | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `asChild` | `boolean` | `false` | Render the single child element instead of a `div`, and give it the title's class and props. Use it to make the title a heading. | `AlertDescription` and `AlertActions` add no props of their own. ## Intents Each intent has its own icon as well as its own color, so the kind of message doesn't depend on telling colors apart. ```tsx import { Alert, AlertDescription, AlertTitle } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function Example() { return (
A new version is ready Reload the page to get it. Invoice sent Northwind Traders will get it by email. Your trial ends in three days Add a card to keep the projects you've made. Payment failed The card ending in 4242 was declined.
); } ``` The color is on the edge and the icon. The text keeps the ordinary text color in every intent, which is what keeps it readable in every theme. ## With actions Put the buttons in `AlertActions`. They wrap onto a second line when the alert is narrow. ```tsx import { Alert, AlertActions, AlertDescription, AlertTitle, Button, } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function Example() { return ( Payment failed The card ending in 4242 was declined. The plan stays active until 1 March. ); } ``` ## When a screen reader reads it An alert has a `role` that depends on its intent. | Intent | Role | What a screen reader does when the alert is added to the page | | --- | --- | --- | | `info`, `success` | `status` | Reads it at the next pause. | | `warning`, `danger` | `alert` | Stops what it's saying and reads it at once. | That only happens for an alert that's added after the page has loaded, as in the example below. One that's in the page from the start isn't read out. It's read when the visitor gets to it, like any other text. ```tsx "use client"; import { Alert, AlertDescription, AlertTitle, Button } from "@nuvui/react"; import { useState } from "react"; export default function Example() { const [failed, setFailed] = useState(false); return (
{failed ? ( The changes weren't saved The server didn't answer. Try again in a moment. ) : null}
); } ``` Two cases call for a different role: - **A warning that's part of the page**, such as a note above a form about what the form does. It was never news, so `role="note"` describes it better. Nothing changes for an alert that's there from the start, but the role is also what a screen reader says when the visitor reaches it. - **Many alerts added at once.** Each one with `role="alert"` interrupts the one before. Put the messages in one alert. A screen reader only notices an alert that's added to the page. One that's there all the time and shown with CSS, or whose text you change, is announced in some combinations of browser and screen reader and not in others. Render the alert when there's something to say, as the example does. ## On small screens An alert takes the width it's given, and its text wraps. A long word or address breaks, so the page doesn't scroll sideways. The icon stays at the top, next to the title. ## Accessibility An alert has no keyboard behavior of its own. It doesn't take focus, and it shouldn't: moving focus to a message takes it away from what the visitor was doing. ### What the component handles - The `role`, by intent. - The icon is hidden from screen readers. The title says what the icon shows. - The icon and the edge have at least 3:1 against the alert in every theme, and the text at least 4.5:1. - The edge is a border, which is still drawn where the browser forces its own colors. - In a right-to-left layout the icon is on the right. ### What you need to handle - Write a title that says what happened without the icon or the color: "Payment failed", not "Error". - Say what to do next in the description, or offer it as a button. - If a danger alert is about a form that was just sent, also move focus to the first field with a problem. The [forms guide](page:forms) shows how. - Don't remove an alert on a timer. People read at different speeds, and some use a screen magnifier that shows a small part of the page at a time. ## CSS variables Set any of these on `Alert`, or on anything around it. A variable set this way applies whatever the intent. ```css .billing { --nuv-alert-radius: var(--radius-md); } ``` | Variable | Default | What it sets | | --- | --- | --- | | `--nuv-alert-gap` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 3)` | Space between the icon and the text. | | `--nuv-alert-padding` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 4)` | Padding inside the box. | | `--nuv-alert-border` | `var(--color-border)`, `var(--color-primary)`, `var(--color-success)`, `var(--color-warning)`, `var(--color-danger)` | Border color. The intent's color by default. | | `--nuv-alert-radius` | `var(--radius-lg)` | Corner radius. | | `--nuv-alert-bg` | `var(--color-surface)` | Background color. | | `--nuv-alert-fg` | `var(--color-surface-foreground)` | Text color of the title, and of anything outside the description. | | `--nuv-alert-icon` | `var(--color-primary)`, `var(--color-success)`, `var(--color-warning)`, `var(--color-danger)` | Color of the icon. The intent's color by default. | | `--nuv-alert-muted-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Text color of the description. | ## Classes | Class | What it's on | | --- | --- | | `.nuv-alert` | Every alert. | | `.nuv-alert--danger` | intent="danger" | | `.nuv-alert--info` | intent="info" | | `.nuv-alert--success` | intent="success" | | `.nuv-alert--warning` | intent="warning" | | `.nuv-alert__actions` | AlertActions. | | `.nuv-alert__body` | The element around everything that isn't the icon. | | `.nuv-alert__description` | AlertDescription. | | `.nuv-alert__icon` | The element around the icon. | | `.nuv-alert__title` | AlertTitle. | ## Server components The alert parts have no `"use client"` directive and use no state, so they render in a server component as they are. ## Do and don't **Do** - Put an alert next to what it's about: above the form, inside the card. - Use `danger` for something that went wrong and `warning` for something that will if nothing is done. **Don't** - Don't use an alert for praise or for marketing. People learn to skip a box they've seen cry wolf. - Don't stack three alerts at the top of a page. Decide which one matters.

sections.heading: Install
sections.markdown:
## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/react
```

sections.heading: Import
sections.markdown:
## Import

```tsx
import { Alert, AlertDescription, AlertTitle } from "@nuvui/react";
```

The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that, and how to load only this component's CSS.

sections.heading: Parts
sections.markdown:
## Parts

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `Alert` | The box, with the icon. |
| `AlertTitle` | What happened, in a few words. |
| `AlertDescription` | The detail, and what to do about it. |
| `AlertActions` | A row of buttons or links under the text. |

sections.heading: Props
sections.markdown:
## Props

### Alert

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `intent` | `"danger" \| "info" \| "success" \| "warning"` | `"info"` | What kind of message it is. It sets the icon and the color, and the default `role`. |
| `icon` | `ReactNode` |  | An icon to draw in place of the intent's own. Pass `null` or `false` for none. |

It also takes what a `<div>` takes. `role` is the one to know about, and [the section below](#when-a-screen-reader-reads-it) covers it.

### AlertTitle

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `asChild` | `boolean` | `false` | Render the single child element instead of a `div`, and give it the title's class and props. Use it to make the title a heading. |

`AlertDescription` and `AlertActions` add no props of their own.

sections.heading: Intents
sections.markdown:
## Intents Each intent has its own icon as well as its own color, so the kind of message doesn't depend on telling colors apart. ```tsx import { Alert, AlertDescription, AlertTitle } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function Example() { return (
A new version is ready Reload the page to get it. Invoice sent Northwind Traders will get it by email. Your trial ends in three days Add a card to keep the projects you've made. Payment failed The card ending in 4242 was declined.
); } ``` The color is on the edge and the icon. The text keeps the ordinary text color in every intent, which is what keeps it readable in every theme.

sections.heading: With actions
sections.markdown:
## With actions

Put the buttons in `AlertActions`. They wrap onto a second line when the alert is narrow.

```tsx
import {
  Alert,
  AlertActions,
  AlertDescription,
  AlertTitle,
  Button,
} from "@nuvui/react";

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <Alert intent="danger" style={{ width: "100%", maxWidth: 480 }}>
      <AlertTitle>Payment failed</AlertTitle>
      <AlertDescription>
        The card ending in 4242 was declined. The plan stays active until 1
        March.
      </AlertDescription>
      <AlertActions>
        <Button size="sm">Update the card</Button>
        <Button size="sm" intent="ghost">
          Contact support
        </Button>
      </AlertActions>
    </Alert>
  );
}
```

sections.heading: When a screen reader reads it
On small screens
sections.markdown:
## On small screens

An alert takes the width it's given, and its text wraps. A long word or address breaks, so the page doesn't scroll sideways. The icon stays at the top, next to the title.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

An alert has no keyboard behavior of its own. It doesn't take focus, and it shouldn't: moving focus to a message takes it away from what the visitor was doing.

### What the component handles

- The `role`, by intent.
- The icon is hidden from screen readers. The title says what the icon shows.
- The icon and the edge have at least 3:1 against the alert in every theme, and the text at least 4.5:1.
- The edge is a border, which is still drawn where the browser forces its own colors.
- In a right-to-left layout the icon is on the right.

### What you need to handle

- Write a title that says what happened without the icon or the color: "Payment failed", not "Error".
- Say what to do next in the description, or offer it as a button.
- If a danger alert is about a form that was just sent, also move focus to the first field with a problem. The [forms guide](page:forms) shows how.
- Don't remove an alert on a timer. People read at different speeds, and some use a screen magnifier that shows a small part of the page at a time.

sections.heading: CSS variables
sections.markdown:
## CSS variables

Set any of these on `Alert`, or on anything around it. A variable set this way applies whatever the intent.

```css
.billing {
  --nuv-alert-radius: var(--radius-md);
}
```

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-alert-gap` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 3)` | Space between the icon and the text. |
| `--nuv-alert-padding` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 4)` | Padding inside the box. |
| `--nuv-alert-border` | `var(--color-border)`, `var(--color-primary)`, `var(--color-success)`, `var(--color-warning)`, `var(--color-danger)` | Border color. The intent's color by default. |
| `--nuv-alert-radius` | `var(--radius-lg)` | Corner radius. |
| `--nuv-alert-bg` | `var(--color-surface)` | Background color. |
| `--nuv-alert-fg` | `var(--color-surface-foreground)` | Text color of the title, and of anything outside the description. |
| `--nuv-alert-icon` | `var(--color-primary)`, `var(--color-success)`, `var(--color-warning)`, `var(--color-danger)` | Color of the icon. The intent's color by default. |
| `--nuv-alert-muted-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Text color of the description. |

sections.heading: Classes
sections.markdown:
## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-alert` | Every alert. |
| `.nuv-alert--danger` | intent="danger" |
| `.nuv-alert--info` | intent="info" |
| `.nuv-alert--success` | intent="success" |
| `.nuv-alert--warning` | intent="warning" |
| `.nuv-alert__actions` | AlertActions. |
| `.nuv-alert__body` | The element around everything that isn't the icon. |
| `.nuv-alert__description` | AlertDescription. |
| `.nuv-alert__icon` | The element around the icon. |
| `.nuv-alert__title` | AlertTitle. |

sections.heading: Server components
sections.markdown:
## Server components

The alert parts have no `"use client"` directive and use no state, so they render in a server component as they are.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Put an alert next to what it's about: above the form, inside the card.
- Use `danger` for something that went wrong and `warning` for something that will if nothing is done.

**Don't**

- Don't use an alert for praise or for marketing. People learn to skip a box they've seen cry wolf.
- Don't stack three alerts at the top of a page. Decide which one matters.

pages.title: Alert dialog
pages.description: A dialog that stops everything to ask one question, with a button to go ahead and a button to back out.

sections.heading: Install
sections.markdown:
## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/react
```

sections.heading: Import
sections.markdown:
## Import

```tsx
import {
  AlertDialog,
  AlertDialogAction,
  AlertDialogCancel,
  AlertDialogContent,
  AlertDialogDescription,
  AlertDialogFooter,
  AlertDialogTitle,
  AlertDialogTrigger,
} from "@nuvui/react";
```

The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that. If you load one stylesheet per component, this one needs `button.css` next to `alert-dialog.css`, because its two buttons are the library's [Button](page:components/button).

sections.heading: Parts
sections.markdown:
## Parts

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `AlertDialog` | Holds the open state. Renders nothing itself. |
| `AlertDialogTrigger` | The button that opens the dialog. Wrap your own with `asChild`. |
| `AlertDialogContent` | The panel. It also renders the overlay behind it. |
| `AlertDialogTitle` | The question. Required, because it's the dialog's accessible name. |
| `AlertDialogDescription` | What will happen. It becomes the dialog's accessible description. |
| `AlertDialogFooter` | A row for the two buttons. |
| `AlertDialogCancel` | The button that backs out. It closes the dialog, and is where focus starts. |
| `AlertDialogAction` | The button that goes ahead. It closes the dialog after its `onClick` has run. |

These are separate exports, not properties of `AlertDialog`. `AlertDialog.Content` isn't available, because property access on a client component doesn't work from a server component.

sections.heading: Props
sections.markdown:
## Props

### AlertDialogContent

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `size` | `"lg" \| "md" \| "sm"` | `"md"` | The widest the dialog gets once the screen is big enough to center it. On a phone it's always a full-width sheet. |
| `container` | `DocumentFragment \| Element \| null` | `document.body` | The element the dialog is rendered into. Set this when the dialog should pick up a `data-theme` from a section of the page. |

### AlertDialogAction and AlertDialogCancel

Both are a [Button](page:components/button) and take every prop a button does. `AlertDialogCancel` starts with `intent="secondary"`, and `AlertDialogAction` with the button's own default, `"primary"`.

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `intent` | `"danger" \| "ghost" \| "primary" \| "secondary"` | `"primary"` | How the button looks. Use `"danger"` on the action when it destroys something. |
| `onClick` | `MouseEventHandler<HTMLButtonElement>` |  | Runs before the dialog closes. Call `event.preventDefault()` in it to keep the dialog open. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` |  | Stops the button from being pressed. |
| `asChild` | `boolean` | `false` | Renders the element you pass in place of a `button`, such as a link, with the button's look and the closing behavior. |

### AlertDialog

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `open` | `boolean` |  | Whether it's open, when you control it yourself. Use it with `onOpenChange`. |
| `defaultOpen` | `boolean` |  | Whether it starts open, when you don't control it. |
| `onOpenChange` | `((open: boolean) => void)` |  | Called when it opens or closes. |

`AlertDialogTrigger`, `AlertDialogTitle` and `AlertDialogDescription` take the same props as the Radix parts they wrap. The [Radix Alert Dialog reference](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/components/alert-dialog#api-reference) lists them. `AlertDialogFooter` is a plain `div`.

sections.heading: Waiting for the action to finish
Opening one from a menu
Sizes
sections.markdown:
## Sizes

`size` sets the maximum width once the screen is at least 40rem wide: 24rem for `sm`, 32rem for `md` and 48rem for `lg`. Below that the dialog is a sheet across the bottom of the screen, with the action on top and cancel under it, each as wide as the sheet.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### Keyboard

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Space</kbd> | On the trigger, opens the dialog. On a button inside, presses it. |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Moves between the two buttons. From the last it goes back to the first. |
| <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>Tab</kbd> | The same, backwards. |
| <kbd>Esc</kbd> | Closes the dialog, as cancel does. |

### What the component handles

Most of this is Radix. The library doesn't change it.

- The panel has `role="alertdialog"`, named by `AlertDialogTitle` and described by `AlertDialogDescription`.
- Opening moves focus to `AlertDialogCancel`, so that pressing <kbd>Enter</kbd> without reading does no harm. Closing returns focus to the trigger.
- Focus can't leave the dialog while it's open, and the rest of the page is hidden from screen readers.
- A click or tap on the page behind does nothing. The person has to pick one of the two buttons, or press <kbd>Esc</kbd>.
- Both buttons are at least 44 pixels tall on a touch screen.
- The open and close animations only run when the visitor hasn't asked for reduced motion.

### What you need to handle

- Write the title as the question, and name the action after what it does: "Delete project", not "OK" or "Yes".
- Always include an `AlertDialogCancel`. Without one, focus has nowhere safe to start.
- Always include an `AlertDialogDescription` that says what will happen. If the title says it all, pass `aria-describedby={undefined}` to `AlertDialogContent`, or Radix logs a warning.
- If <kbd>Esc</kbd> must not close the dialog, call `event.preventDefault()` in `onEscapeKeyDown` on `AlertDialogContent`. Then the two buttons are the only ways out, so make sure both work.

sections.heading: CSS variables
sections.markdown:
## CSS variables

Alert dialogs render at the end of `<body>`, so set these on `:root` or `body`, not on the element around the trigger. They're separate from the dialog's variables: changing `--nuv-dialog-radius` doesn't change an alert dialog.

```css
:root {
  --nuv-alert-dialog-width: 28rem;
}
```

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-alert-dialog-overlay-bg` | `var(--color-overlay)` | Color of the layer that dims the page. |
| `--nuv-alert-dialog-padding` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 6)` | Padding inside the panel. One length, used on every side. |
| `--nuv-alert-dialog-border` | `var(--color-border)` | Border color of the panel. |
| `--nuv-alert-dialog-bg` | `var(--color-surface)` | Background color of the panel. |
| `--nuv-alert-dialog-shadow` | `var(--shadow-xl)` | Shadow under the panel. |
| `--nuv-alert-dialog-fg` | `var(--color-surface-foreground)` | Text color. |
| `--nuv-alert-dialog-radius` | `var(--radius-xl)` | Corner radius. As a sheet on phones, only the top corners are rounded. |
| `--nuv-alert-dialog-width` | `32rem`, `24rem`, `48rem` | Maximum width once the dialog is centered. Differs by size. |

The two buttons read the [button's variables](page:components/button#css-variables).

sections.heading: Classes
sections.markdown:
## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-alert-dialog` | The panel. |
| `.nuv-alert-dialog--lg` | The panel with size="lg". |
| `.nuv-alert-dialog--sm` | The panel with size="sm". |
| `.nuv-alert-dialog__description` | AlertDialogDescription. |
| `.nuv-alert-dialog__footer` | AlertDialogFooter. |
| `.nuv-alert-dialog__overlay` | The layer behind the panel. |
| `.nuv-alert-dialog__title` | AlertDialogTitle. |

The panel also gets `nuv-alert-dialog--md` at the default size. No styles are attached to it, since medium is the base. The two buttons have the button's classes, such as `nuv-button` and `nuv-button--danger`.

Radix sets `data-state="open"` or `data-state="closed"` on the overlay and the panel. The animations hang off those.

sections.heading: Server components
sections.markdown:
## Server components

The alert dialog parts are client components. They carry `"use client"`, and the build checks that the directive is still there in the published files.

You can put one together inside a server component, as the first example on this page does. It needs a client component of your own once the action has an `onClick`, which is most of the time.

sections.heading: Themed sections
sections.markdown:
## Themed sections

An alert dialog opened from inside a `data-theme="dark"` section doesn't inherit that theme, because it isn't rendered inside the section. Pass the section's element as `container` and it will be.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Keep it for actions that can't be undone, or that cost something to undo.
- Say what will be lost, in numbers when you have them: "its 12 files".
- Give the action `intent="danger"` when it destroys something.

**Don't**

- Don't use one for an action that can be undone. Do it, and offer the undo in a [toast](page:components/toast).
- Don't use one to report an error or a success. Nothing is being asked.
- Don't put a form in one. That's a [dialog](page:components/dialog).

pages.title: AnimatedNumber
pages.description: A number that moves to its new value. The digits that change roll like a counter or pop in, and the rest stay still. It's still for anyone who asked for less motion.
pages.markdown:
# AnimatedNumber A number that moves to its new value. The digits that change roll like a counter or pop in, and the rest stay still. It's still for anyone who asked for less motion. Use an animated number for a figure that changes while someone is looking at it: a total that goes up as items are added, a count that's refreshed, a price that changes with the plan. The movement says the number changed, and roughly by how much. For a number that doesn't change on the page, use [FormattedNumber](page:components/formatted-number). ```tsx "use client"; import { AnimatedNumber, Button } from "@nuvui/react"; import { useState } from "react"; export default function Example() { const [seats, setSeats] = useState(1280); return (
); } ``` ## Install ```sh pnpm add @nuvui/react ``` ## Import ```tsx import { AnimatedNumber } from "@nuvui/react"; ``` The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that, and how to load only this component's CSS. ## Props | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `format` | `"currency" \| "decimal" \| "percent"` | `"decimal"` | `"percent"` takes a ratio, so 0.25 is written as 25%. `"currency"` needs `currency`. | | `value` (required) | `number` | | The number. When it changes, the digits that differ move to it. | | `animation` | `"pop" \| "roll"` | `"roll"` | How a digit that changes moves. `"roll"` turns it through the digits between, like a counter. `"pop"` lets the old digit rise out as the new one rises in, coming into focus. Either way it's still for anyone who asked for less motion. | | `locale` | `string` | `"en-US"` | The language and region whose rules the number is written by, as a BCP 47 tag such as `"de-DE"`. It's `"en-US"` unless you say otherwise, and never the visitor's own: the server and the browser would then write two different texts for one page. | | `currency` | `string` | | The currency, as an ISO 4217 code such as `"EUR"`. Giving one is enough to get a currency: `format` can be left out. | | `compact` | `boolean` | `false` | Writes a large number short, as in 1.2M. | | `signDisplay` | `"always" \| "auto" \| "exceptZero" \| "never"` | `"auto"` | When the sign is written. `"exceptZero"` writes a plus on a gain, for a number that's a change. | | `minimumFractionDigits` | `number` | | The fewest digits after the decimal point. | | `maximumFractionDigits` | `number` | | The most digits after the decimal point. | | `options` | `Intl.NumberFormatOptions` | | Anything else `Intl.NumberFormat` takes, such as a unit. What's here wins over the props above. | It's a `data` element, as `FormattedNumber` is, with the plain number in its `value`. It takes what a `data` element takes, including `ref` and `className`. ## Roll or pop With `animation="roll"`, the default, each digit that changes turns through the digits between the old one and the new one, the way the number went: up through nine to zero when it rose, down when it fell. With `animation="pop"`, the old digit rises out of sight as the new one rises into place, coming into focus. ```tsx "use client"; import { AnimatedNumber, Button } from "@nuvui/react"; import { useState } from "react"; const prices = [19, 24, 49]; export default function Example() { const [plan, setPlan] = useState(1); return (
); } ``` Either way only the digits that changed move, from the left, each a moment after the one before. Separators, signs, currency symbols and the letters of a short form such as 1.2K stay where they are. ## What changes and what doesn't The first value is drawn as it is. The page from the server has it, and nothing moves when the page opens. Only a change after that moves. The number takes the width it ends at as soon as it changes, and keeps it while the digits move. With digits of one width, as the component gives them, a number with as many digits as before takes the same room, so nothing beside it moves. ## Languages and currencies It writes the number as [FormattedNumber](page:components/formatted-number) does, with the same props: a language, a currency, a percentage, a short form. Any currency is given by its ISO 4217 code, such as `"EUR"`, `"GBP"` or `"JPY"`, and `locale` says how it's written: the sign before the number or after it, a comma or a point, and how many decimals the currency has. The sign stays where it is, and only the digits move. ```tsx "use client"; import { AnimatedNumber, Button } from "@nuvui/react"; import { useState } from "react"; // One plan's price in four markets, each written the way its own // customers write money: the sign before the number or after it, a comma // or a point, and yen with no cents. const markets = [ { name: "Germany", currency: "EUR", locale: "de-DE", price: 49 }, { name: "United Kingdom", currency: "GBP", locale: "en-GB", price: 42 }, { name: "Japan", currency: "JPY", locale: "ja-JP", price: 7800 }, { name: "India", currency: "INR", locale: "en-IN", price: 3999 }, ]; export default function Example() { const [yearly, setYearly] = useState(false); return (
{markets.map((market) => (
{market.name}
))}
); } ``` The two have to agree with your customer, not with each other: a price in euros for someone in Ireland is `locale="en-IE"`, and for someone in Germany `locale="de-DE"`. In a language whose numbers have digits of their own, such as Arabic or Hindi, those are the digits that roll. In a language read from the right, the number is laid out the way the browser lays it out, and what moves is drawn over it. ## Saying that it changed A screen reader doesn't read out a number because it changed. That's on purpose: a dashboard where every refresh was read out would be hard to use. For a number whose change someone needs to hear, such as the items in a cart, put it in an element with `aria-live="polite"`. It's read once, when the number has changed, and the moving digits aren't read at all. ```tsx "use client"; import { AnimatedNumber, Button } from "@nuvui/react"; import { useState } from "react"; export default function Example() { const [items, setItems] = useState(2); return (
{/* Read out once, when the number has changed. */} items in your cart
); } ``` ## Accessibility An animated number has no role and no keyboard behavior. It can't take focus. ### What the component handles - The number is ordinary text, read as one number while it moves and after. What moves is a copy drawn over it, which is hidden from screen readers. - A copy and paste gets the number once. The moving copy can't be selected. - For a visitor who asked for less motion, the new number is there at once and nothing moves. - Where the browser forces its own colors, the digits are drawn in the browser's text color while they move and after. - Only position, opacity and a slight blur move. Nothing around the number is laid out again. ### What you need to handle - Say a change out loud where it matters, with `aria-live` around it, as above. - Don't change it every second. A number that never stops moving can't be read, and motion that goes on for more than five seconds beside other content is something WCAG asks for a way to stop. ## CSS variables Set any of these on the `AnimatedNumber`, or on anything around it. ```css .revenue { --nuv-animated-number-duration: 1.2s; } ``` | Variable | Default | What it sets | | --- | --- | --- | | `--nuv-animated-number-numeric` | `tabular-nums` | The digits' font-variant-numeric. Digits of one width keep a changing number from pushing what's next to it. | | `--nuv-animated-number-to` | | Where a rolling column stops. The component writes this. Don't set it. | | `--nuv-animated-number-duration` | `800ms`, `500ms` | How long one digit takes to move. The first default is for roll, the second for pop. | | `--nuv-animated-number-easing` | `var(--ease-out)` | How a digit speeds up and slows down. | | `--nuv-animated-number-order` | `0` | Which of the digits that change this is, from the left. The component writes this. Don't set it. | | `--nuv-animated-number-stagger` | `40ms` | How long each digit that changes waits after the one before it. | | `--nuv-animated-number-from` | | Where a rolling column starts. The component writes this. Don't set it. | | `--nuv-animated-number-blur` | `0.12em` | With pop, how out of focus a digit is as it comes in or goes out. | | `--nuv-animated-number-sign` | `1` | 1 for a digit that went up and -1 for one that went down, which turns pop over. Set by the component's stylesheet. | | `--nuv-animated-number-rise` | `0.6em` | With pop, how far a digit travels as it comes in or goes out. | ## Classes | Class | What it's on | | --- | --- | | `.nuv-animated-number` | AnimatedNumber. | | `.nuv-animated-number--roll` | With animation="roll". | | `.nuv-animated-number__digit` | A digit that moves, over its place. | | `.nuv-animated-number__gap` | In the copy, the place a moving digit ends up. | | `.nuv-animated-number__motion` | The copy that moves, over the text. Only there while it moves. | | `.nuv-animated-number__new` | With pop, the digit that comes in. | | `.nuv-animated-number__numeral` | With roll, one digit in the column. | | `.nuv-animated-number__old` | With pop, the digit that leaves. | | `.nuv-animated-number__reel` | With roll, the column of digits that turns. | | `.nuv-animated-number__text` | The number as text. See-through while it moves. | While it moves, the element has `data-state="moving"`, and `data-state="still"` otherwise. The copy has `data-direction`: `up` or `down`. ## Server components AnimatedNumber starts with `"use client"`: it remembers the last number to move from it. It takes no functions, so a server component can render it, and the page from the server has the number written out. ## Do and don't **Do** - Use it for a figure that changes in front of someone, after they did something or when it's refreshed. - Keep its format the same from one value to the next, so the places line up. **Don't** - Don't use it for a number that's only drawn once. There's nothing to move from. - Don't put many on a screen that all change at once. Movement draws the eye, and twenty numbers moving together draw it nowhere.

## Props

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `format` | `"currency" \| "decimal" \| "percent"` | `"decimal"` | `"percent"` takes a ratio, so 0.25 is written as 25%. `"currency"` needs `currency`. |
| `value` (required) | `number` |  | The number. When it changes, the digits that differ move to it. |
| `animation` | `"pop" \| "roll"` | `"roll"` | How a digit that changes moves. `"roll"` turns it through the digits between, like a counter. `"pop"` lets the old digit rise out as the new one rises in, coming into focus. Either way it's still for anyone who asked for less motion. |

| `currency` | `string` |  | The currency, as an ISO 4217 code such as `"EUR"`. Giving one is enough to get a currency: `format` can be left out. |
| `compact` | `boolean` | `false` | Writes a large number short, as in 1.2M. |
| `signDisplay` | `"always" \| "auto" \| "exceptZero" \| "never"` | `"auto"` | When the sign is written. `"exceptZero"` writes a plus on a gain, for a number that's a change. |
| `minimumFractionDigits` | `number` |  | The fewest digits after the decimal point. |
| `maximumFractionDigits` | `number` |  | The most digits after the decimal point. |
| `options` | `Intl.NumberFormatOptions` |  | Anything else `Intl.NumberFormat` takes, such as a unit. What's here wins over the props above. |

What changes and what doesn't

## What changes and what doesn't

The first value is drawn as it is. The page from the server has it, and nothing moves when the page opens. Only a change after that moves.

The number takes the width it ends at as soon as it changes, and keeps it while the digits move. With digits of one width, as the component gives them, a number with as many digits as before takes the same room, so nothing beside it moves.

sections.heading: Languages and currencies
Saying that it changed
Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

An animated number has no role and no keyboard behavior. It can't take focus.

### What the component handles

- The number is ordinary text, read as one number while it moves and after. What moves is a copy drawn over it, which is hidden from screen readers.

- Where the browser forces its own colors, the digits are drawn in the browser's text color while they move and after.

pages.title: AspectRatio
pages.description: A box that keeps its shape at any width, for pictures, videos, maps and anything else that loads late.

sections.heading: Install
sections.markdown:
## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/react
```

sections.heading: Import
sections.markdown:
## Import

```tsx
import { AspectRatio } from "@nuvui/react";
```

The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that, and how to load only this component's CSS.

sections.heading: Props
sections.markdown:
## Props

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ratio` | `number` |  | Width divided by height: `16 / 9`, `4 / 3`, `1`. Leave it out to set `--nuv-aspect-ratio-value` in CSS instead, where it can change at a breakpoint. |

Everything else is passed to the `<div>`, including `ref`, `className` and `style`.

sections.heading: Ratios
What goes inside
sections.markdown:
## What goes inside

Give it one child. The child fills the box.

- A picture or a video keeps its own proportions and is cropped to fit, from the center. Set `--nuv-aspect-ratio-fit` to `contain` to show all of it with empty bands instead.
- Anything else, such as an `iframe` or a `div`, is stretched to the box.

Content that's taller than the box is cut off. This is a frame for media, not a container for text.

sections.heading: A different ratio on a larger screen
Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

The box has no role and no keyboard behavior. What's inside it carries the meaning.

### What you need to handle

- Give a picture an `alt` that says what it shows, or `alt=""` if it's decoration.
- Cropping can cut off the part of a picture that matters. Check the picture at the widths the layout uses, or set `object-position` on it.
- Give an `iframe` a `title`.

sections.heading: CSS variables
sections.markdown:
## CSS variables

Set any of these on the box, or on anything around it.

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-aspect-ratio-radius` | `0` | Corner radius. The content is clipped to it. |
| `--nuv-aspect-ratio-value` | `1` | The ratio, as CSS writes it: 16 / 9. The ratio prop sets this on the element. |
| `--nuv-aspect-ratio-fit` | `cover` | How a picture or a video fits the box: cover crops it, contain shows all of it. |

sections.heading: Classes
sections.markdown:
## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-aspect-ratio` | The box. |

sections.heading: Server components
sections.markdown:
## Server components

AspectRatio has no `"use client"` directive and uses no state, so it renders in a server component as it is.

It's built on the CSS `aspect-ratio` property and not on Radix's primitive. That gives one element in place of two, and a ratio that CSS can change at a breakpoint.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Use the same ratio for every picture in a grid.
- Pick a ratio close to the pictures you have, so little is cropped.

**Don't**

- Don't use it to square off a box of text. Text needs the height it needs.
- Don't set a height on it. The width and the ratio decide the height.

pages.title: Avatar
pages.description: A small picture of a person or a thing, with initials or an icon in its place when there's no picture.
pages.markdown:
# Avatar A small picture of a person or a thing, with initials or an icon in its place when there's no picture. Use an avatar next to a name, in a list of people or at the top of a profile. It shows the picture once the picture has loaded, and the fallback until then, or for good if the picture can't be had. ```tsx import { Avatar, AvatarFallback, AvatarImage } from "@nuvui/react"; // A picture kept in the file, so the example doesn't depend on another site. const picture = "data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' viewBox='0 0 80 80'%3E%3Crect width='80' height='80' fill='%23314158'/%3E%3Ccircle cx='40' cy='30' r='14' fill='%23e2e8f0'/%3E%3Cpath d='M12 80a28 28 0 0 1 56 0z' fill='%23e2e8f0'/%3E%3C/svg%3E"; export default function Example() { return ( <> AL GH ); } ``` ## Install ```sh pnpm add @nuvui/react ``` ## Import ```tsx import { Avatar, AvatarFallback, AvatarImage } from "@nuvui/react"; ``` The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that, and how to load only this component's CSS. ## Parts | Part | What it is | | --- | --- | | `Avatar` | The frame. It sets the size and the shape. | | `AvatarImage` | The picture. It's only in the page once it has loaded. | | `AvatarFallback` | What shows while there's no picture. | | `AvatarGroup` | A row of avatars that overlap. | ## Props ### Avatar | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `size` | `"lg" \| "md" \| "sm"` | `"md"` | | | `shape` | `"circle" \| "square"` | `"circle"` | A circle suits a person. A rounded square suits a company, a team or a project. | ### AvatarImage It takes what an `` takes, `src` and `alt` included, and one prop from Radix. | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `onLoadingStatusChange` | `((status: ImageLoadingStatus) => void)` | | Called with `"loading"`, `"loaded"` or `"error"` as the picture's state changes. | ### AvatarFallback | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `delayMs` | `number` | | How long to wait before showing the fallback, in milliseconds. A few hundred keeps it from flashing before a picture that loads quickly. | `AvatarGroup` takes what a `
` takes. ## Sizes and shapes ```tsx import { Avatar, AvatarFallback } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function Example() { return ( <> AL AL AL NT ); } ``` The sizes are 32, 40 and 56 pixels. Use a circle for a person and a rounded square for a company, a team or a project, so the two can be told apart in a list that has both. Any other size is `--nuv-avatar-size`, with `--nuv-avatar-font-size` for the initials. ## A group `AvatarGroup` overlaps its avatars and draws a ring in the page's color around each, which reads as a gap between them. ```tsx import { Avatar, AvatarFallback, AvatarGroup } from "@nuvui/react"; const people = [ ["AL", "Ada Lovelace"], ["GH", "Grace Hopper"], ["KJ", "Katherine Johnson"], ] as const; export default function Example() { return ( {people.map(([initials, name]) => ( {initials} ))} +4 ); } ``` On a surface that isn't the page's background, such as a card, set `--nuv-avatar-group-ring` to that surface's color. ## While the picture loads `AvatarImage` isn't rendered until the browser has the picture. So a slow or broken address never shows as a broken-image icon, or as an empty frame that fills in from the top. The fallback shows from the start by default. With a picture that's usually cached, that's a flash of initials on every page. `delayMs` on `AvatarFallback` holds the fallback back, and the frame stays empty for that long. The frame has its size from the start, so nothing on the page moves when the picture arrives. ## Accessibility An avatar has no keyboard behavior. It isn't a control. ### What the component handles - The picture is an ``, so its `alt` is what a screen reader reads. - The fallback is text in the page, read as it's written. - The fallback's text has at least 4.5:1 against its background in every theme. - Where the browser forces its own colors, the fallback gets a border in place of its fill. ### What you need to handle - **Next to the person's name, the avatar is decoration.** Give the picture `alt=""` and the fallback `aria-hidden="true"`, or a screen reader says the name twice, or says "AL, Ada Lovelace". - **Where the avatar is the only thing that says who it is,** as in the group above, give the picture the person's name as its `alt`. Initials alone don't name anyone, so for a fallback put `role="img"` and `aria-label` on `Avatar` and hide the initials, as the group example does. - An avatar that opens a menu or a profile goes inside a button or a link, and that element gets the name. ## CSS variables Set any of these on `Avatar` or `AvatarGroup`, or on anything around them. ```css .comment { --nuv-avatar-size: 1.5rem; --nuv-avatar-font-size: 0.625rem; } ``` | Variable | Default | What it sets | | --- | --- | --- | | `--nuv-avatar-size` | `2.5rem`, `2rem`, `3.5rem` | Width and height. Differs by size. | | `--nuv-avatar-radius` | `var(--radius-full)`, `var(--radius-md)` | Corner radius. A circle by default. | | `--nuv-avatar-font-size` | `var(--text-sm)`, `var(--text-xs)`, `var(--text-lg)` | Font size of the fallback. Differs by size. | | `--nuv-avatar-bg` | `var(--color-muted)` | Background color of the fallback. | | `--nuv-avatar-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Text color of the fallback. | | `--nuv-avatar-group-ring-width` | `2px` | Thickness of the ring around each avatar in a group. | | `--nuv-avatar-group-ring` | `var(--color-background)` | Color of that ring. Set it to the color of the surface the group sits on. | | `--nuv-avatar-group-overlap` | `calc(var(--spacing) * -2)` | How far each avatar in a group sits over the one before. A negative length. | ## Classes | Class | What it's on | | --- | --- | | `.nuv-avatar` | Avatar. | | `.nuv-avatar--lg` | size="lg" | | `.nuv-avatar--sm` | size="sm" | | `.nuv-avatar--square` | shape="square" | | `.nuv-avatar-group` | AvatarGroup. | | `.nuv-avatar__fallback` | AvatarFallback. | | `.nuv-avatar__image` | AvatarImage. | A medium avatar also has the class `nuv-avatar--md`. It has no rules of its own, because medium is how every avatar starts. ## Server components Avatar is a client component, because it has to know when the picture has loaded. It carries `"use client"`, and the build checks that the directive is still there in the published files. You can render it from a server component, as the examples on this page do. On the server, and in the first paint, an avatar shows its fallback, or nothing where `delayMs` is set. The picture comes in once the browser has loaded it. ## Do and don't **Do** - Always give a fallback. Pictures fail to load. - Use two initials at most. Three don't fit the small size. **Don't** - Don't rely on a picture to say who someone is. Show the name too, wherever there's room. - Don't use the picture's file name or "avatar" as its `alt`.

sections.markdown:


sections.heading: Import
sections.markdown:
## Import

```tsx
import { Avatar, AvatarFallback, AvatarImage } from "@nuvui/react";
```

The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that, and how to load only this component's CSS.

sections.heading: Parts
sections.markdown:
## Parts

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `Avatar` | The frame. It sets the size and the shape. |
| `AvatarImage` | The picture. It's only in the page once it has loaded. |
| `AvatarFallback` | What shows while there's no picture. |
| `AvatarGroup` | A row of avatars that overlap. |

sections.heading: Props
sections.markdown:
## Props ### Avatar | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `size` | `"lg" \| "md" \| "sm"` | `"md"` | | | `shape` | `"circle" \| "square"` | `"circle"` | A circle suits a person. A rounded square suits a company, a team or a project. | ### AvatarImage It takes what an `` takes, `src` and `alt` included, and one prop from Radix. | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `onLoadingStatusChange` | `((status: ImageLoadingStatus) => void)` | | Called with `"loading"`, `"loaded"` or `"error"` as the picture's state changes. | ### AvatarFallback | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `delayMs` | `number` | | How long to wait before showing the fallback, in milliseconds. A few hundred keeps it from flashing before a picture that loads quickly. | `AvatarGroup` takes what a `
` takes.

sections.heading: Sizes and shapes
sections.markdown:
## Sizes and shapes

```tsx
import { Avatar, AvatarFallback } from "@nuvui/react";

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <>
      <Avatar size="sm">
        <AvatarFallback>AL</AvatarFallback>
      </Avatar>
      <Avatar size="md">
        <AvatarFallback>AL</AvatarFallback>
      </Avatar>
      <Avatar size="lg">
        <AvatarFallback>AL</AvatarFallback>
      </Avatar>
      <Avatar size="lg" shape="square">
        <AvatarFallback>NT</AvatarFallback>
      </Avatar>
    </>
  );
}
```

The sizes are 32, 40 and 56 pixels. Use a circle for a person and a rounded square for a company, a team or a project, so the two can be told apart in a list that has both.

Any other size is `--nuv-avatar-size`, with `--nuv-avatar-font-size` for the initials.

sections.heading: A group
While the picture loads
sections.markdown:
## While the picture loads

`AvatarImage` isn't rendered until the browser has the picture. So a slow or broken address never shows as a broken-image icon, or as an empty frame that fills in from the top.

The fallback shows from the start by default. With a picture that's usually cached, that's a flash of initials on every page. `delayMs` on `AvatarFallback` holds the fallback back, and the frame stays empty for that long.

The frame has its size from the start, so nothing on the page moves when the picture arrives.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown: ## Accessibility An avatar has no keyboard behavior. It isn't a control. ### What the component handles - The picture is an ``, so its `alt` is what a screen reader reads. - The fallback is text in the page, read as it's written. - The fallback's text has at least 4.5:1 against its background in every theme. - Where the browser forces its own colors, the fallback gets a border in place of its fill. ### What you need to handle - **Next to the person's name, the avatar is decoration.** Give the picture `alt=""` and the fallback `aria-hidden="true"`, or a screen reader says the name twice, or says "AL, Ada Lovelace". - **Where the avatar is the only thing that says who it is,** as in the group above, give the picture the person's name as its `alt`. Initials alone don't name anyone, so for a fallback put `role="img"` and `aria-label` on `Avatar` and hide the initials, as the group example does. - An avatar that opens a menu or a profile goes inside a button or a link, and that element gets the name.

sections.heading: CSS variables
sections.markdown:
## CSS variables

Set any of these on `Avatar` or `AvatarGroup`, or on anything around them.

```css
.comment {
  --nuv-avatar-size: 1.5rem;
  --nuv-avatar-font-size: 0.625rem;
}
```

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-avatar-size` | `2.5rem`, `2rem`, `3.5rem` | Width and height. Differs by size. |
| `--nuv-avatar-radius` | `var(--radius-full)`, `var(--radius-md)` | Corner radius. A circle by default. |
| `--nuv-avatar-font-size` | `var(--text-sm)`, `var(--text-xs)`, `var(--text-lg)` | Font size of the fallback. Differs by size. |
| `--nuv-avatar-bg` | `var(--color-muted)` | Background color of the fallback. |
| `--nuv-avatar-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Text color of the fallback. |
| `--nuv-avatar-group-ring-width` | `2px` | Thickness of the ring around each avatar in a group. |
| `--nuv-avatar-group-ring` | `var(--color-background)` | Color of that ring. Set it to the color of the surface the group sits on. |
| `--nuv-avatar-group-overlap` | `calc(var(--spacing) * -2)` | How far each avatar in a group sits over the one before. A negative length. |

sections.markdown:
## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-avatar` | Avatar. |
| `.nuv-avatar--lg` | size="lg" |
| `.nuv-avatar--sm` | size="sm" |
| `.nuv-avatar--square` | shape="square" |
| `.nuv-avatar-group` | AvatarGroup. |
| `.nuv-avatar__fallback` | AvatarFallback. |
| `.nuv-avatar__image` | AvatarImage. |

A medium avatar also has the class `nuv-avatar--md`. It has no rules of its own, because medium is how every avatar starts.

sections.heading: Server components
sections.markdown:
## Server components

Avatar is a client component, because it has to know when the picture has loaded. It carries `"use client"`, and the build checks that the directive is still there in the published files. You can render it from a server component, as the examples on this page do.

On the server, and in the first paint, an avatar shows its fallback, or nothing where `delayMs` is set. The picture comes in once the browser has loaded it.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Always give a fallback. Pictures fail to load.
- Use two initials at most. Three don't fit the small size.

**Don't**

- Don't rely on a picture to say who someone is. Show the name too, wherever there's room.
- Don't use the picture's file name or "avatar" as its `alt`.

pages.title: Badge
pages.description: A short label that says what state something is in, or how many of something there are.
pages.markdown:
# Badge

A short label that says what state something is in, or how many of something there are.

Use a badge for a word or a number next to the thing it describes: the status of an invoice, the plan a customer is on, a count of unread messages. A badge is text, not a control. For something people press, use a [button](page:components/button) or a [toggle](page:components/toggle).

```tsx
import { Badge } from "@nuvui/react";

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <>
      <Badge>Draft</Badge>
      <Badge intent="primary">New</Badge>
      <Badge intent="success">Paid</Badge>
      <Badge intent="warning">Due soon</Badge>
      <Badge intent="danger">Overdue</Badge>
    </>
  );
}
```

## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/react
```

## Import

```tsx
import { Badge } from "@nuvui/react";
```

The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that, and how to load only this component's CSS.

## Props

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `intent` | `"danger" \| "neutral" \| "primary" \| "success" \| "warning"` | `"neutral"` | What the badge says about the thing it's on. The color is extra: the text has to carry the meaning by itself. |
| `variant` | `"outline" \| "solid"` | `"solid"` | `"solid"` is filled with the intent's color. `"outline"` has an edge in that color on a plain background, for a row where many filled badges would be too loud. |

Everything else is passed to the `<span>`, including `ref` and `className`.

## Outline

`variant="outline"` gives a plain background with an edge in the intent's color. Use it where a column of filled badges would pull the eye away from everything else, as in a long table.

```tsx
import { Badge } from "@nuvui/react";

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <>
      <Badge variant="outline">Draft</Badge>
      <Badge variant="outline" intent="primary">
        New
      </Badge>
      <Badge variant="outline" intent="success">
        Paid
      </Badge>
      <Badge variant="outline" intent="warning">
        Due soon
      </Badge>
      <Badge variant="outline" intent="danger">
        Overdue
      </Badge>
    </>
  );
}
```

An outlined success, warning or danger badge has its text in that color too. An outlined primary badge keeps the ordinary text color: a theme's primary color only has to stand out as an edge, at 3:1, and that isn't enough for text.

## With an icon or a number

An icon goes inside, before the text. A badge that only shows a number needs words for a screen reader, since "12" by itself says nothing. Put them in [`VisuallyHidden`](page:components/visually-hidden).

```tsx
import { Badge, VisuallyHidden } from "@nuvui/react";

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <>
      <Badge intent="success">
        <svg
          aria-hidden="true"
          viewBox="0 0 12 12"
          width="12"
          height="12"
          fill="none"
          stroke="currentColor"
          strokeWidth="1.75"
          strokeLinecap="round"
          strokeLinejoin="round"
        >
          <path d="M2.5 6.5l2.25 2.25L9.5 3.5" />
        </svg>
        Verified
      </Badge>
      <Badge intent="danger">
        12
        <VisuallyHidden> failed jobs</VisuallyHidden>
      </Badge>
    </>
  );
}
```

## The colors

A filled badge takes its colors from the theme's tokens, so it follows every preset and both modes.

| Intent | Fill | Text |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `neutral` | `--color-muted` | `--color-foreground` |
| `primary` | `--color-primary` | `--color-primary-foreground` |
| `success` | `--color-success` | `--color-background` |
| `warning` | `--color-warning` | `--color-background` |
| `danger` | `--color-danger` | `--color-danger-foreground` |

The success and warning colors are chosen to be readable as text on the page's background. Contrast is the same both ways round, so the background color is readable as text on them. Every pair in the table has at least 4.5:1 in every theme, and the tests measure each one.

## Accessibility

A badge has no keyboard behavior. It isn't a control and can't take focus.

### What the component handles

- It's a `<span>`, read in place with the text around it.
- Text has at least 4.5:1 against the badge in every intent, variant and theme.
- A filled badge has a border that only shows where the browser forces its own colors, as Windows high contrast does. The fill isn't drawn there, and the border is what keeps the badge a badge.

### What you need to handle

- Say the state in words. Color is extra: plenty of people can't tell red from green, and a badge that says "Overdue" works for them where a red dot doesn't.
- Give a count its unit, in `VisuallyHidden` if there's no room for it.
- A badge that changes while the page is open isn't announced. If the change matters, such as a job that just failed, say it in a [toast](page:components/toast) or an element with `role="status"`.

## CSS variables

Set any of these on the badge, or on anything around it. A variable set this way applies whatever the intent.

```css
.plan-badge {
  --nuv-badge-radius: var(--radius-sm);
}
```

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-badge-gap` | `var(--spacing)` | Space between an icon and the text. |
| `--nuv-badge-padding-block` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 0.5)` | Padding above and below the text. |
| `--nuv-badge-padding-inline` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 2)` | Padding left and right. |
| `--nuv-badge-border` | `transparent`, `var(--color-border-strong)`, `var(--color-primary)`, `var(--color-success)`, `var(--color-warning)`, `var(--color-danger)` | Border color. Transparent on a filled badge, and the intent's color on an outlined one. |
| `--nuv-badge-radius` | `var(--radius-full)` | Corner radius. A pill by default. |
| `--nuv-badge-font-size` | `var(--text-xs)` | Font size. |
| `--nuv-badge-bg` | `var(--color-muted)`, `var(--color-primary)`, `var(--color-success)`, `var(--color-warning)`, `var(--color-danger)`, `var(--color-surface)` | Background color. Differs by intent. |
| `--nuv-badge-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)`, `var(--color-primary-foreground)`, `var(--color-background)`, `var(--color-danger-foreground)`, `var(--color-surface-foreground)`, `var(--color-success)`, `var(--color-warning)`, `var(--color-danger)` | Text color. Differs by intent. Keep it at 4.5:1 against the background. |

## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-badge` | Every badge. |
| `.nuv-badge--danger` | intent="danger" |
| `.nuv-badge--neutral` | intent="neutral" |
| `.nuv-badge--outline` | variant="outline", next to the intent's class. |
| `.nuv-badge--primary` | intent="primary" |
| `.nuv-badge--success` | intent="success" |
| `.nuv-badge--warning` | intent="warning" |

## Server components

Badge has no `"use client"` directive and uses no state, so it renders in a server component as it is.

## Do and don't

**Do**

- Keep it to one or two words.
- Use the same intent for the same state everywhere in the app.

**Don't**

- Don't use a badge as a button. It has no focus ring and no keyboard behavior.
- Don't put a sentence in one. A badge stays on one line and doesn't wrap.

pages.title: Breadcrumb
pages.description: A trail of links that shows where the current page sits in a site, from the top level down.
pages.markdown: # Breadcrumb A trail of links that shows where the current page sits in a site, from the top level down. Use a breadcrumb on pages that sit a few levels deep, so people can see where they are and step back up. It shows the structure of the site, not the path someone took to get here. ```tsx import { Breadcrumb, BreadcrumbItem, BreadcrumbLink, BreadcrumbList, BreadcrumbPage, BreadcrumbSeparator, } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function Example() { return ( Home Docs Breadcrumb ); } ``` ## Install ```sh pnpm add @nuvui/react ``` ## Import ```tsx import { Breadcrumb, BreadcrumbItem, BreadcrumbLink, BreadcrumbList, BreadcrumbPage, BreadcrumbSeparator, } from "@nuvui/react"; ``` The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that, and how to load only this component's CSS. ## Parts | Part | What it is | | --- | --- | | `Breadcrumb` | The `nav` landmark around the trail. | | `BreadcrumbList` | The trail. An `ol`, because the order means something. | | `BreadcrumbItem` | One level. A `li`. | | `BreadcrumbLink` | The link to a level above the current page. | | `BreadcrumbPage` | The current page, last in the trail. Text, not a link. | | `BreadcrumbSeparator` | The mark between two levels. A `li` of its own, between two items. | | `BreadcrumbEllipsis` | Three dots that stand for levels left out of a long trail. | ## Props ### BreadcrumbLink | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `asChild` | `boolean` | `false` | Render the single child element instead of an `a`, and give it the link's class and props. This is how you use your router's link. | It also takes what an `a` takes, `href` included. ### BreadcrumbEllipsis | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `label` | `string` | `"More"` | What a screen reader says for the three dots. Translate it with the rest of your interface. | ### BreadcrumbSeparator | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `children` | `ReactNode` | | What to draw in place of the arrow: a slash, a dot, an icon of your own. | `Breadcrumb`, `BreadcrumbList`, `BreadcrumbItem` and `BreadcrumbPage` take what their elements take, including `ref` and `className`. ## Another separator Give `BreadcrumbSeparator` children and it draws them in place of the arrow. ```tsx import { Breadcrumb, BreadcrumbItem, BreadcrumbLink, BreadcrumbList, BreadcrumbPage, BreadcrumbSeparator, } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function Example() { return ( Docs / Theming / Presets ); } ``` ## A long trail When there are more levels than there's room for, leave out the middle ones and put `BreadcrumbEllipsis` where they were. Keep the first level and the last two. The dots alone tell people something is missing and give them no way to get to it. Putting them in the trigger of a [dropdown menu](page:components/dropdown-menu) that lists the missing levels fixes that. ```tsx import { Breadcrumb, BreadcrumbEllipsis, BreadcrumbItem, BreadcrumbLink, BreadcrumbList, BreadcrumbPage, BreadcrumbSeparator, Button, DropdownMenu, DropdownMenuContent, DropdownMenuItem, DropdownMenuTrigger, } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function Example() { return ( Home {/* The button's own name replaces the one the dots have. */} Docs Theming Button Variants ); } ``` ## With your router's link Pass `asChild` and put the router's link inside. It gets the look, and keeps its own way of changing page. ```tsx import { Breadcrumb, BreadcrumbItem, BreadcrumbLink, BreadcrumbList, BreadcrumbPage, BreadcrumbSeparator, } from "@nuvui/react"; import Link from "next/link"; export default function Example() { return ( Docs Forms Validation ); } ``` ## On small screens A trail that doesn't fit wraps onto a second line. A single long name breaks inside itself, so the page never scrolls sideways. Links are 44 pixels tall on a touch screen, which is taller than their text. The text stays on its line, and the extra height is above and below it. On a phone, a trail of five levels takes a lot of the screen. Showing only the level above, as a "back" link, is often the better use of the room. ## Accessibility ### Keyboard | Key | What it does | | --- | --- | | Tab | Moves through the links in order. The current page isn't a link, so it's skipped. | | Enter | Follows the focused link. | Safari only stops at links with Tab when "Press Tab to highlight each item on a webpage" is turned on in its settings. That applies to every link on every site, not to this component in particular. ### What the component handles - The trail is a `nav` landmark named "Breadcrumb", around an ordered list. - The current page has `aria-current="page"`. - The separators are hidden from screen readers. sections.heading: Install
sections.markdown:
## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/react
```

sections.heading: Import
sections.markdown:
## Import

```tsx
import {
  Breadcrumb,
  BreadcrumbItem,
  BreadcrumbLink,
  BreadcrumbList,
  BreadcrumbPage,
  BreadcrumbSeparator,
} from "@nuvui/react";
```

The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that, and how to load only this component's CSS.

sections.heading: Parts
sections.markdown:
## Parts

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `Breadcrumb` | The `nav` landmark around the trail. |
| `BreadcrumbList` | The trail. An `ol`, because the order means something. |
| `BreadcrumbItem` | One level. A `li`. |
| `BreadcrumbLink` | The link to a level above the current page. |
| `BreadcrumbPage` | The current page, last in the trail. Text, not a link. |
| `BreadcrumbSeparator` | The mark between two levels. A `li` of its own, between two items. |
| `BreadcrumbEllipsis` | Three dots that stand for levels left out of a long trail. |

sections.heading: Props
sections.markdown:
## Props

### BreadcrumbLink

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `asChild` | `boolean` | `false` | Render the single child element instead of an `a`, and give it the link's class and props. This is how you use your router's link. |

It also takes what an `a` takes, `href` included.

### BreadcrumbEllipsis

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `string` | `"More"` | What a screen reader says for the three dots. Translate it with the rest of your interface. |

### BreadcrumbSeparator

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `children` | `ReactNode` |  | What to draw in place of the arrow: a slash, a dot, an icon of your own. |

`Breadcrumb`, `BreadcrumbList`, `BreadcrumbItem` and `BreadcrumbPage` take what their elements take, including `ref` and `className`.

sections.heading: Another separator
sections.markdown:
## Another separator

Give `BreadcrumbSeparator` children and it draws them in place of the arrow.

```tsx
import {
  Breadcrumb,
  BreadcrumbItem,
  BreadcrumbLink,
  BreadcrumbList,
  BreadcrumbPage,
  BreadcrumbSeparator,
} from "@nuvui/react";

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <Breadcrumb>
      <BreadcrumbList>
        <BreadcrumbItem>
          <BreadcrumbLink href="/docs">Docs</BreadcrumbLink>
        </BreadcrumbItem>
        <BreadcrumbSeparator>/</BreadcrumbSeparator>
        <BreadcrumbItem>
          <BreadcrumbLink href="/docs/theming">Theming</BreadcrumbLink>
        </BreadcrumbItem>
        <BreadcrumbSeparator>/</BreadcrumbSeparator>
        <BreadcrumbItem>
          <BreadcrumbPage>Presets</BreadcrumbPage>
        </BreadcrumbItem>
      </BreadcrumbList>
    </Breadcrumb>
  );
}
```

sections.heading: A long trail
sections.markdown: ## A long trail When there are more levels than there's room for, leave out the middle ones and put `BreadcrumbEllipsis` where they were. Keep the first level and the last two. The dots alone tell people something is missing and give them no way to get to it. Putting them in the trigger of a [dropdown menu](page:components/dropdown-menu) that lists the missing levels fixes that. ```tsx import { Breadcrumb, BreadcrumbEllipsis, BreadcrumbItem, BreadcrumbLink, BreadcrumbList, BreadcrumbPage, BreadcrumbSeparator, Button, DropdownMenu, DropdownMenuContent, DropdownMenuItem, DropdownMenuTrigger, } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function Example() { return ( Home {/* The button's own name replaces the one the dots have. */} Docs Theming Button Variants ); } ```

sections.heading: With your router's link
sections.markdown:
## With your router's link

Pass `asChild` and put the router's link inside. It gets the look, and keeps its own way of changing page.

```tsx
import {
  Breadcrumb,
  BreadcrumbItem,
  BreadcrumbLink,
  BreadcrumbList,
  BreadcrumbPage,
  BreadcrumbSeparator,
} from "@nuvui/react";
import Link from "next/link";

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <Breadcrumb>
      <BreadcrumbList>
        <BreadcrumbItem>
          <BreadcrumbLink asChild>
            <Link href="/">Docs</Link>
          </BreadcrumbLink>
        </BreadcrumbItem>
        <BreadcrumbSeparator />
        <BreadcrumbItem>
          <BreadcrumbLink asChild>
            <Link href="/forms">Forms</Link>
          </BreadcrumbLink>
        </BreadcrumbItem>
        <BreadcrumbSeparator />
        <BreadcrumbItem>
          <BreadcrumbPage>Validation</BreadcrumbPage>
        </BreadcrumbItem>
      </BreadcrumbList>
    </Breadcrumb>
  );
}
```

sections.heading: On small screens
sections.markdown:
## On small screens

A trail that doesn't fit wraps onto a second line. A single long name breaks inside itself, so the page never scrolls sideways.

Links are 44 pixels tall on a touch screen, which is taller than their text. The text stays on its line, and the extra height is above and below it.

On a phone, a trail of five levels takes a lot of the screen. Showing only the level above, as a "back" link, is often the better use of the room.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### Keyboard

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Moves through the links in order. The current page isn't a link, so it's skipped. |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> | Follows the focused link. |

Safari only stops at links with <kbd>Tab</kbd> when "Press Tab to highlight each item on a webpage" is turned on in its settings. That applies to every link on every site, not to this component in particular.

### What the component handles

- The trail is a `nav` landmark named "Breadcrumb", around an ordered list.
- The current page has `aria-current="page"`.
- The separators are hidden from screen readers. The list already says where one level ends and the next begins.
- `BreadcrumbEllipsis` has a name, "More".
- The arrow points the other way in a right-to-left layout.
- The current page is heavier as well as darker than the links, so it doesn't depend on telling two colors apart.
- Links have a focus ring.

### What you need to handle

- Translate the landmark's name with `aria-label` on `Breadcrumb`, and the dots' name with `label` on `BreadcrumbEllipsis`.
- End the trail with `BreadcrumbPage`, not with a link to the page people are already on.
- When the dots are inside a button, give the button an `aria-label` that says what it opens. It replaces the dots' own name.
- A page with two breadcrumbs needs a different `aria-label` on each.

sections.heading: CSS variables
sections.markdown:
## CSS variables

Set any of these on `Breadcrumb`, or on anything around it.

```css

}
```

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-breadcrumb-gap` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 1.5)` | Space between a level and the mark beside it. |
| `--nuv-breadcrumb-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of the links, the separators and the dots. |
| `--nuv-breadcrumb-current-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Color of the current page, and of a link under the pointer. |

sections.heading: Classes
sections.markdown:
## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-breadcrumb__chevron` | The arrow a separator draws when it has no children. |
| `.nuv-breadcrumb__ellipsis` | BreadcrumbEllipsis. |
| `.nuv-breadcrumb__item` | BreadcrumbItem. |
| `.nuv-breadcrumb__link` | BreadcrumbLink. |
| `.nuv-breadcrumb__list` | BreadcrumbList. |
| `.nuv-breadcrumb__page` | BreadcrumbPage. |
| `.nuv-breadcrumb__separator` | BreadcrumbSeparator. |

`Breadcrumb` itself gets `nuv-breadcrumb`. No styles are attached to it.

**Do**

**Don't**
