## Parts

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `Stat` | One figure. A card unless you say otherwise. |
| `StatLabel` | What the number counts. |
| `StatValue` | The number, large. |
| `StatDescription` | A line under it: how it changed, and against what. |
| `StatChart` | Room for a small chart, 48 pixels high. |
| `StatGroup` | Several stats, as many to a row as fit. |

Only `Stat`, `StatLabel` and `StatValue` are needed. Put the label first: a screen reader reads the parts in the order they're written, and "Revenue, $48,250" makes sense where "$48,250, Revenue" makes someone wait.

sections.heading: Props
sections.markdown:
## Props

### Stat

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `variant` | `"card" \| "plain"` | `"card"` | `"card"` draws a surface with an edge around the figure. `"plain"` draws nothing, for a figure that's already inside a card or a table. |

The other parts add no props of their own. Each takes what its element takes, including `ref` and `className`.

sections.heading: The number and its change
sections.markdown:
## The number and its change

The parts take any children. [`FormattedNumber`](page:components/formatted-number) writes the number for a language and region, and [`Trend`](page:components/trend) says which way it moved. Neither is required: a value can be plain text, such as "4m 12s".

sections.heading: With a chart
sections.markdown:
## With a chart

`StatChart` is a box with a height, after the rest. What's drawn in it is yours: a sparkline from [`@nuvui/charts`](page:charts/index), or a few lines of SVG as here. The core doesn't depend on a charting library, so it draws nothing itself.

```tsx
import {
  FormattedNumber,
  Stat,
  StatChart,
  StatDescription,
  StatLabel,
  StatValue,
  Trend,
} from "@nuvui/react";

const weeks = [31, 34, 33, 38, 41, 39, 44, 47, 46, 52, 55, 61];

// The line, in a box 110 wide and 40 high, with the first week at the left.
const points = weeks
  .map((value, index) => `${index * 10},${40 - ((value - 30) / 32) * 40}`)
  .join(" ");

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <Stat style={{ inlineSize: "16rem" }}>
      <StatLabel>Active teams</StatLabel>
      <StatValue>
        <FormattedNumber value={61} />
      </StatValue>
      <StatDescription>
        <Trend value={0.109} /> in twelve weeks
      </StatDescription>
      {/* The number and the trend already say it, so the picture is hidden
          from screen readers. */}
      <StatChart>
        <svg
          aria-hidden="true"
          viewBox="0 0 110 40"
          preserveAspectRatio="none"
          width="100%"
          height="100%"
          fill="none"
          stroke="var(--color-chart-1)"
          strokeWidth="2"
          strokeLinecap="round"
          strokeLinejoin="round"
        >
          <polyline points={points} vectorEffect="non-scaling-stroke" />
        </svg>
      </StatChart>
    </Stat>
  );
}
```

When the number and the trend already say what the chart shows, hide the chart from screen readers with `aria-hidden="true"`. When the chart says more, give it a name and a table of its numbers, as the [charts](page:charts/index) pages describe.

sections.heading: Plain, inside something else
sections.markdown:
## Plain, inside something else

`variant="plain"` draws no edge, no fill and no padding, for a stat that sits in a [card](page:components/card) or a table cell that already has them.

```tsx
import {
  Card,
  CardContent,
  CardHeader,
  CardTitle,
  FormattedNumber,
  Stat,
  StatDescription,
  StatGroup,
  StatLabel,
  StatValue,
} from "@nuvui/react";

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <Card style={{ inlineSize: "100%" }}>
      <CardHeader>
        <CardTitle>This billing period</CardTitle>
      </CardHeader>
      <CardContent>
        <StatGroup>
          <Stat variant="plain">
            <StatLabel>Seats in use</StatLabel>
            <StatValue>
              <FormattedNumber value={42} />
            </StatValue>
            <StatDescription>of 50 on the plan</StatDescription>
          </Stat>
          <Stat variant="plain">
            <StatLabel>Next invoice</StatLabel>
            <StatValue>
              <FormattedNumber value={1260} currency="USD" />
            </StatValue>
            <StatDescription>on 1 November</StatDescription>
          </Stat>
        </StatGroup>
      </CardContent>
    </Card>
  );
}
```

sections.markdown:
## In a group

`StatGroup` is a grid that fits as many columns as it can at a least width of 13rem, all the same width. On a phone that's one column. It sets no number of columns, so it works in a full-width page and in a narrow panel without a breakpoint. Change the least width with `--nuv-stat-group-min`.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

A stat has no keyboard behavior. It isn't a control and can't take focus.

### What the component handles

- The parts are read in the order they're written, with nothing hidden and nothing added.

- The label and the description have at least 4.5:1 against the card in every theme.

- Write the label first, then the value.
- Say what a change is measured against, in `StatDescription`.

- A value that changes while the page is open isn't announced. For one that matters, such as an error count passing a limit, say it in a [toast](page:components/toast) or an element with `role="status"`.

pages.title: Stepper
pages.description: Where someone is in a row of steps, with the ones that are done, the current one and the ones still to come, across or down.
pages.markdown:
# Stepper Where someone is in a row of steps, with the ones that are done, the current one and the ones still to come, across or down. Use a stepper to show progress through something with a known number of steps: setting up an account, checking out, an order on its way. It shows where things stand. Moving between steps is your app's. ```tsx import { Stepper, StepperContent, StepperIndicator, StepperItem, StepperTitle, } from "@nuvui/react"; const steps = ["Account", "Team", "Billing", "Review"]; export default function Example() { return ( {steps.map((title, index) => ( {title} ))} ); } ``` ## Install ```sh pnpm add @nuvui/react ``` ## Import ```tsx import { Stepper, StepperContent, StepperDescription, StepperIndicator, StepperItem, StepperTitle, } from "@nuvui/react"; ``` The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that, and how to load only this component's CSS. ## Parts | Part | What it is | | --- | --- | | `Stepper` | The list. An `ol`. It's told which step is current. | | `StepperItem` | One step. An `li`. It's told which step it is. | | `StepperIndicator` | The circle: the step's number, or a tick once it's done. | | `StepperContent` | The title and the description. | | `StepperTitle` | The step's name. | | `StepperDescription` | More about it. | `StepperItem` needs its indicator first and its content second. ## Props ### Stepper | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `value` (required) | `number` | | The step someone is on, counted from 1. The steps before it are done, and the ones after it are still to come. One more than the last step means all of them are done. | | `orientation` | `"horizontal" \| "vertical"` | `"horizontal"` | `"vertical"` stacks the steps, with their text beside them. Use it on a narrow screen, and wherever steps have descriptions. | | `variant` | `"dot" \| "number"` | `"number"` | `"dot"` draws a small circle with nothing in it in place of the step's number. | | `completedLabel` | `string` | `"Completed"` | What a screen reader says after the title of a step that's done. The tick is a picture. Translate it with the rest of your interface. | ### StepperItem | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `step` (required) | `number` | | Which step this is, counted from 1. | The other parts add no props of their own. Each takes what its element takes, including `ref` and `className`. ## Which step is current `value` on the `Stepper` is the step someone is on, counted from 1, and `step` on each item is which one it is. An item works out the rest: before the value it's done, at the value it's current, after it it's still to come. One more than the last step means every step is done. The stepper keeps no state. Your form, your router or your order's status decides the value, and the stepper draws it. ## Down the page `orientation="vertical"` stacks the steps with their text beside them. It's the one to use on a narrow screen, and wherever steps have descriptions: across, four titles fit and four paragraphs don't. ```tsx "use client"; import { Button, Stepper, StepperContent, StepperDescription, StepperIndicator, StepperItem, StepperTitle, } from "@nuvui/react"; import { useState } from "react"; const steps = [ { title: "Order placed", text: "We have your order and your payment." }, { title: "Packed", text: "Two parcels, leaving from Rotterdam." }, { title: "On its way", text: "With the carrier, due on Thursday." }, { title: "Delivered", text: "Signed for at the front desk." }, ]; export default function Example() { const [current, setCurrent] = useState(2); return (
{steps.map((step, index) => ( {step.title} {step.text} ))}
); } ``` To switch at a breakpoint, render it twice and hide one with CSS, or read the width in your own code. The component doesn't change direction by itself, because where it should is a decision about your layout. ## Dots `variant="dot"` draws a small circle with nothing in it, for a quiet row where the place in the order is enough. ```tsx import { Stepper, StepperContent, StepperIndicator, StepperItem, StepperTitle, } from "@nuvui/react"; const steps = ["Draft", "In review", "Approved", "Published"]; export default function Example() { return ( {steps.map((title, index) => ( {title} ))} ); } ``` ## An icon in the circle Children of `StepperIndicator` replace the number and the tick. The circle keeps its look for each state, so an icon is filled over once the step is done unless you change it by state yourself. ## Going back to a step The parts are plain elements. To let someone go back, put a link or a button in `StepperTitle` for the steps that are done. Keep steps that can't be reached yet as text. ## Accessibility A stepper has no keyboard behavior of its own. Links and buttons you put in it work as they do anywhere. ### What the component handles - It's an ordered list, so a screen reader says how many steps there are and where it is among them. The list says it's a list in so many words, because Safari stops treating a list as one once its numbers are styled away. - The current step has `aria-current="step"`. - A step that's done has "Completed" after its title, in the page and drawn for nobody. The tick is a picture. - The circle is hidden from screen readers. The list already gives the step's number. - The three states differ by shape as well as color: filled with a tick, a ring with a number, a ring in a quieter color. Where the browser forces its own colors the fill is gone, and the tick and the words still say which steps are done. - The lines are borders, which are still drawn there. ### What you need to handle - Name the list with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`, such as "Setting up". - Translate `completedLabel`. [Translation](page:translation) lists it. - When the step changes, move focus to the new step's heading or its first field. A screen reader user isn't told that the stepper changed. - An icon you put in the circle is hidden with it. Don't make it the only place something is said. ## On small screens Across, each step takes an equal share of the width and its title wraps inside its share. Four short titles fit on a phone. More steps, longer titles or any description call for `orientation="vertical"`. ## CSS variables Set any of these on the `Stepper`, or on anything around it. ```css .checkout { --nuv-stepper-indicator-size: 1.5rem; } ``` | Variable | Default | What it sets | | --- | --- | --- | | `--nuv-stepper-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Text color. | | `--nuv-stepper-gap` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 2)`, `calc(var(--spacing) * 3)` | Space between the circle and the text. | | `--nuv-stepper-space` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 2)`, `calc(var(--spacing) * 6)` | Space between one step and the next. Across, it's the room at each end of a line. Down, it's the room under a step's text. | | `--nuv-stepper-indicator-size` | `2rem`, `0.875rem` | Width and height of the circle. The line and the text move with it. Smaller by default with variant="dot". | | `--nuv-stepper-line-width` | `2px` | Thickness of the line and of the circle's edge. | | `--nuv-stepper-line` | `var(--color-border)` | Color of the line after a step that isn't done. | | `--nuv-stepper-line-complete` | `var(--color-primary)` | Color of the line after a step that's done. | | `--nuv-stepper-indicator-border` | `var(--color-border-strong)`, `var(--color-primary)` | Border color of the circle. Differs by state. Keep it at 3:1 against the background. | | `--nuv-stepper-indicator-radius` | `var(--radius-full)` | Corner radius of the circle. | | `--nuv-stepper-indicator-bg` | `var(--color-surface)`, `var(--color-primary)` | Background color of the circle. Differs by state. | | `--nuv-stepper-indicator-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)`, `var(--color-surface-foreground)`, `var(--color-primary-foreground)` | Color of the number or the tick. Differs by state. | | `--nuv-stepper-muted-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of the description, and of the title of a step still to come. Keep it at 4.5:1 against the background. | ## Classes | Class | What it's on | | --- | --- | | `.nuv-stepper` | Stepper | | `.nuv-stepper--dot` | variant="dot" | | `.nuv-stepper--vertical` | orientation="vertical" | | `.nuv-stepper__check` | The tick in the circle of a step that's done. | | `.nuv-stepper__content` | StepperContent | | `.nuv-stepper__description` | StepperDescription | | `.nuv-stepper__indicator` | StepperIndicator | | `.nuv-stepper__item` | StepperItem. The line is its `::after`. | | `.nuv-stepper__status` | "Completed", drawn for nobody. | | `.nuv-stepper__title` | StepperTitle | A step's state is in a `data-state` attribute on its item: `complete`, `current` or `upcoming`. The direction is in `data-orientation` on the list. ## Server components The stepper starts with `"use client"`: each step has to find out which one is current. You can still render it from a server component, with a number for `value`. ## Do and don't **Do** - Keep titles to a word or two. - Show every step from the start, so people know how long it is. **Don't** - Don't use it for more than about six steps across. Group them, or go vertical. - Don't use it for a history of what happened. That's a [timeline](page:components/timeline).

| `--nuv-stepper-line` | `var(--color-border)` | Color of the line after a step that isn't done. |
| `--nuv-stepper-line-complete` | `var(--color-primary)` | Color of the line after a step that's done. |
| `--nuv-stepper-indicator-border` | `var(--color-border-strong)`, `var(--color-primary)` | Border color of the circle. Differs by state. Keep it at 3:1 against the background. |
| `--nuv-stepper-indicator-radius` | `var(--radius-full)` | Corner radius of the circle. |
| `--nuv-stepper-indicator-bg` | `var(--color-surface)`, `var(--color-primary)` | Background color of the circle. Differs by state. |
| `--nuv-stepper-indicator-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)`, `var(--color-surface-foreground)`, `var(--color-primary-foreground)` | Color of the number or the tick. Differs by state. |
| `--nuv-stepper-muted-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of the description, and of the title of a step still to come. Keep it at 4.5:1 against the background. |

sections.markdown:
## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-stepper` | Stepper |
| `.nuv-stepper--dot` | variant="dot" |
| `.nuv-stepper--vertical` | orientation="vertical" |
| `.nuv-stepper__check` | The tick in the circle of a step that's done. |
| `.nuv-stepper__content` | StepperContent |
| `.nuv-stepper__description` | StepperDescription |
| `.nuv-stepper__indicator` | StepperIndicator |
| `.nuv-stepper__item` | StepperItem. The line is its `::after`. |
| `.nuv-stepper__status` | "Completed", drawn for nobody. |
| `.nuv-stepper__title` | StepperTitle |

A step's state is in a `data-state` attribute on its item: `complete`, `current` or `upcoming`. The direction is in `data-orientation` on the list.

sections.heading: Server components
sections.markdown:
## Server components

The stepper starts with `"use client"`: each step has to find out which one is current. You can still render it from a server component, with a number for `value`.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Keep titles to a word or two.
- Show every step from the start, so people know how long it is.

**Don't**

- Don't use it for more than about six steps across. Group them, or go vertical.
- Don't use it for a history of what happened. That's a [timeline](page:components/timeline).

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `checked` | `boolean` |  | Whether it's on, when you control it yourself. Use it with `onCheckedChange`. |
| `defaultChecked` | `boolean` |  | Whether it starts on, when you don't control it. |
| `onCheckedChange` | `((checked: boolean) => void)` |  | Called with the new state when someone flips it. |

sections.heading: States
Size
sections.markdown:
## Size

On a touch screen the track is 44 pixels wide and 24 tall, and the area that responds to a tap is 44 by 44. When a mouse or trackpad is the main input, the track is 36 by 20.

The thumb is sized from the track's height, so setting `--nuv-switch-height` and `--nuv-switch-width` is enough to resize the whole control.

sections.heading: In a form
sections.markdown:
## In a form

Give the switch a `name` and it's submitted like a native checkbox. Inside a `<form>`, Radix renders a hidden `<input type="checkbox">` next to the button.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### Keyboard

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Moves focus to the switch. Disabled ones are skipped. |
| <kbd>Space</kbd> | Turns it on or off. |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> | Turns it on or off. |

### What the component handles

- It renders a `<button>` with `role="switch"` and `aria-checked`. This part is Radix.
- A click on a `<label>` that points at it flips it.
- On and off differ by where the thumb sits as well as by color, so the state doesn't depend on telling two colors apart.
- The track while off uses `--color-border-strong`, which has at least 3:1 contrast with the page in light and dark.
- The thumb moves toward the end of the line, so in a right-to-left layout it travels the other way.
- Keyboard focus shows a 2 pixel ring in `--color-ring`.
- The thumb only slides when the visitor hasn't asked for reduced motion. Otherwise it jumps.
- Where the browser forces its own colors, as Windows high contrast does, backgrounds aren't drawn. The track gets an outline there, and the thumb a system color that changes when the switch is on.

### What you need to handle

- Give it a name. Use a `<label>` whose `htmlFor` matches the switch's `id`, or `aria-label` when there's no visible text.
- Name the setting, not the state. "Email updates" stays true whether it's on or off. "On" doesn't.
- Apply the change straight away. If it can fail, put the switch back and say why.

sections.heading: CSS variables
sections.markdown:
## CSS variables

Set any of these on the switch, or on anything around it.

```css
.settings {
  --nuv-switch-checked-bg: var(--color-success);
}
```

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-switch-bg` | `var(--color-border-strong)` | Track color while off. |
| `--nuv-switch-width` | `2.75rem`, `2.25rem` | Width of the track. The default differs between touch screens and a mouse. |
| `--nuv-switch-height` | `1.5rem`, `1.25rem` | Height of the track. The thumb takes its size from it. |
| `--nuv-switch-checked-bg` | `var(--color-primary)` | Track color while on. |
| `--nuv-switch-thumb` | `var(--color-background)` | Color of the thumb. |

sections.heading: Classes
sections.markdown:
## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-switch` | The track, which is the button itself. |
| `.nuv-switch__thumb` | The circle that moves. |

Radix sets `data-state` to `checked` or `unchecked` on both elements, and `data-disabled` when the switch is disabled. Style those, not a modifier class.

sections.heading: Server components
sections.markdown:
## Server components

Switch is a client component. It carries `"use client"`, and the build checks that the directive is still there in the published files.

You can render it from a server component, as the first example on this page does. It needs a client component of your own once you pass `onCheckedChange` or control `checked`, which is most real uses, since a switch is there to do something when it's flipped.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Put the label next to the switch and link the two with `htmlFor`.
- Keep the label the same in both states.
- Use it for one setting at a time.

**Don't**

- Don't use a switch in a form that needs a save button. People expect a switch to have already happened.
- Don't use one to pick between two unrelated options, such as "List" and "Grid". Use [tabs](page:components/tabs) or two buttons.
- Don't shrink the track on pages people use on phones.

pages.title: TableOfContents
pages.description: The headings of a page as a list of links, with the one being read marked as the page scrolls.
pages.markdown:
# TableOfContents

The headings of a page as a list of links, with the one being read marked as the page scrolls.

Use a table of contents on a long page with headings: documentation, a policy, a report. It shows what's on the page and where the reader is in it. The example below lists the headings of this page, and follows it.

```tsx
import { TableOfContents, type TableOfContentsItem } from "@nuvui/react";

// The headings of the page this example is on.
const items: TableOfContentsItem[] = [
  { id: "install", title: "Install" },
  { id: "import", title: "Import" },
  { id: "props", title: "Props" },
  { id: "accessibility", title: "Accessibility" },
  {
    id: "what-the-component-handles",
    title: "What the component handles",
    depth: 2,
  },
  { id: "css-variables", title: "CSS variables" },
];

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <TableOfContents
      aria-label="On this page"
      items={items}
      // This site's headings stop 112 pixels down when a link jumps to
      // them, under its header.
      offset={128}
      style={{ inlineSize: "100%", maxInlineSize: 260 }}
    />
  );
}
```

## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/react
```

## Import

```tsx
import { TableOfContents } from "@nuvui/react";
```

The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that, and how to load only this component's CSS.

## Props

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `items` (required) | `TableOfContentsItem[]` |  | The headings, in the order they come in the page. |
| `value` | `string \| null` |  | The `id` of the heading that's marked, when you control it. `null` marks none. Left out, the component follows the page as it scrolls. |
| `onValueChange` | `((value: string \| null) => void)` |  | Called with the `id` of the heading the page has scrolled to, or `null` above the first one. |
| `offset` | `number` | `96` | How far down the window, in pixels, a heading counts as reached. Set it to the height of whatever is stuck to the top of your page, and a little more. |

It also takes what a `nav` takes, including `ref` and `className`.

### An item

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` (required) | `string` |  | The `id` of the heading in the page. The link goes to `#id`. |
| `title` (required) | `ReactNode` |  | What the link says: the heading's text. |
| `depth` | `1 \| 2 \| 3 \| 4` | `1` | How far in the link is set. 1 is a section, 2 a section inside one, and so on to 4. |

## Where the headings come from

`items` is yours to build. Most things that turn Markdown into pages hand you the headings with their ids, and a page written by hand can list its own. The component doesn't look through the page for headings: which ones belong in the list, and how deep to go, is a decision about your content.

Each heading in the page needs the `id` its item names. An item whose heading isn't in the page is still a link, and is never marked.

## Which heading is marked

The marked heading is the last one to have reached the top of the window, or more exactly a line `offset` pixels down from it. Above the first heading none is marked. At the end of the page, where the last headings can't get to the top, the last one is marked, or the one whose link was just followed.

Set `offset` to the height of whatever is stuck to the top of your page, and a little more. Give your headings a `scroll-margin-top` no larger than that, so a heading that a link jumps to lands above the line and not under your header. The example above sets `offset={128}`, because this site's headings stop 112 pixels down.

```css
h2,
h3 {
  scroll-margin-top: 5rem;
}
```

It follows the window, and anything inside the page that scrolls by itself.

## Controlling it

`value` marks the heading you say and stops the component deciding. `onValueChange` still reports what the page has scrolled to, so you can follow it and overrule it where you need to.

## Behind a button

On a narrow screen there's no room beside the page. Put the same list in a [popover](page:components/popover) or a [collapsible](page:components/collapsible) with a button that says "On this page". It's the same component with the same items, so it stays in step.

## Accessibility

A table of contents has no keyboard behavior of its own. Its links are reached with Tab and followed with Enter.

### What the component handles

- It's a navigation landmark, which a screen reader can jump to.
- It's an ordered list, so a screen reader says how many headings there are. The list says it's a list in so many words, because Safari stops treating a list as one once its numbers are styled away.
- The marked link has `aria-current="location"`.
- The marked link differs by more than color: a bar beside it and heavier text. The bar is a border, which is still drawn where the browser forces its own colors.
- It measures once a frame at most while the page scrolls, and listens passively, so it doesn't slow scrolling down.

### What you need to handle

- Name the landmark with `aria-label`, such as "On this page". A page usually has other navigation, and they have to be told apart.
- Keep the list in the order of the page.
- Following a link moves the page and leaves focus on the link. To have a screen reader start reading at the section, give each heading `tabindex="-1"` and move focus to it yourself when its link is followed.

## On small screens

A link is 44 pixels tall with a finger and 32 with a mouse, and a long title wraps. The list is as wide as you make it.

## CSS variables

Set any of these on the `TableOfContents`, or on anything around it.

```css
.docs {
  --nuv-table-of-contents-indent: 1rem;
}
```

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-table-of-contents-line-width` | `2px` | Thickness of the line down the side, and of the bar on the marked link. |
| `--nuv-table-of-contents-line` | `var(--color-border)` | Color of the line. |
| `--nuv-table-of-contents-item-height` | `var(--nuv-touch-size)`, `calc(var(--spacing) * 8)` | Least height of a link. Taller by default with a finger than with a mouse. |
| `--nuv-table-of-contents-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of a link that isn't marked. Keep it at 4.5:1 against the background. |
| `--nuv-table-of-contents-active-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Color of the marked link, and of a link under the pointer. |
| `--nuv-table-of-contents-indent` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 3)` | How much further in each depth is set. |
| `--nuv-table-of-contents-active-line` | `var(--color-primary)` | Color of the bar on the marked link. Keep it at 3:1 against the background. |

## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-table-of-contents` | TableOfContents |
| `.nuv-table-of-contents__item` | One heading's place in the list. |
| `.nuv-table-of-contents__link` | The link. The bar on the marked one is its `::before`. |
| `.nuv-table-of-contents__list` | The list. The line is its border. |

The marked link is the one with `aria-current`. A link's depth is in its `data-depth` attribute, from 1 to 4.

## Server components

TableOfContents starts with `"use client"`: it watches the page scroll. You can render it from a server component, with a list of plain objects for `items`. On the server no heading is marked. The first measurement is made when the page has loaded.

## Do and don't

**Do**

- List two levels of heading, three at most.
- Use the headings' own words.

**Don't**

- Don't use it for moving between pages. That's a [sidebar](page:components/sidebar) or a [navigation menu](page:components/navigation-menu).
- Don't put it on a page with two or three headings. The page is its own table of contents.

pages.title: Tabs
pages.description: Panels of content with a row of tabs to switch between them. The row scrolls sideways when it doesn't fit the screen.
pages.markdown:
# Tabs

Panels of content with a row of tabs to switch between them. The row scrolls sideways when it doesn't fit the screen.

Use tabs to split one subject into a few views of equal weight, where people look at one at a time: the sections of a settings page, or the details and reviews of a product.

```tsx
import { Tabs, TabsContent, TabsList, TabsTrigger } from "@nuvui/react";

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <Tabs defaultValue="account" style={{ inlineSize: "100%" }}>
      <TabsList aria-label="Settings">
        <TabsTrigger value="account">Account</TabsTrigger>
        <TabsTrigger value="team">Team</TabsTrigger>
        <TabsTrigger value="billing">Billing</TabsTrigger>
      </TabsList>
      <TabsContent value="account">Your name, email and password.</TabsContent>
      <TabsContent value="team">
        The people who can see this project.
      </TabsContent>
      <TabsContent value="billing">Your plan and past invoices.</TabsContent>
    </Tabs>
  );
}
```

## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/react
```

## Import

```tsx
import { Tabs, TabsContent, TabsList, TabsTrigger } from "@nuvui/react";
```

The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that, and how to load only this component's CSS.

## Parts

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `Tabs` | Holds which tab is selected, and lays out the list and the panels. |
| `TabsList` | The row of tabs. |
| `TabsTrigger` | One tab. Its `value` ties it to a panel. |
| `TabsContent` | The panel for one tab. Only the selected panel's content is rendered. |

These are separate exports, not properties of `Tabs`. `Tabs.List` isn't available, because property access on a client component doesn't work from a server component.

## Props

### Tabs

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value` | `string` |  | The selected tab, when you control it yourself. Use it with `onValueChange`. |
| `defaultValue` | `string` |  | The tab selected at first, when you don't control it. Without it, no tab is selected and no panel shows. |
| `onValueChange` | `((value: string) => void)` |  | Called with the new tab's value when the selection changes. |
| `orientation` | `"horizontal" \| "vertical"` |  | Whether the tabs sit in a row above the panel or in a column beside it. It also decides which arrow keys move between them. |
| `activationMode` | `"automatic" \| "manual"` |  | With `"manual"`, the arrow keys only move focus, and Enter or Space selects the tab. |
| `dir` | `"ltr" \| "rtl"` |  | The reading direction. With `"rtl"`, the left and right arrow keys swap. |

### TabsList

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `loop` | `boolean` |  | Whether the arrow keys wrap from the last tab to the first and back. On unless you pass `false`. |

### TabsTrigger

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value` (required) | `string` |  | Matches the `value` of the panel this tab shows. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` |  | Stops the tab from being selected. The arrow keys skip it. |

### TabsContent

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value` (required) | `string` |  | Matches the `value` of the tab that shows this panel. |
| `forceMount` | `true` |  | Keeps the panel's content rendered while its tab isn't selected. The panel is then no longer hidden for you. |

Every part also takes what its element takes, including `ref`, `className` and `asChild`. The [Radix Tabs reference](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/components/tabs#api-reference) has the full list.

## Vertical

```tsx
import { Tabs, TabsContent, TabsList, TabsTrigger } from "@nuvui/react";

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <Tabs
      defaultValue="account"
      orientation="vertical"
      style={{ inlineSize: "100%" }}
    >
      <TabsList aria-label="Settings">
        <TabsTrigger value="account">Account</TabsTrigger>
        <TabsTrigger value="team">Team</TabsTrigger>
        <TabsTrigger value="billing">Billing</TabsTrigger>
      </TabsList>
      <TabsContent value="account">Your name, email and password.</TabsContent>
      <TabsContent value="team">
        The people who can see this project.
      </TabsContent>
      <TabsContent value="billing">Your plan and past invoices.</TabsContent>
    </Tabs>
  );
}
```

A vertical list takes its width from the panel. On a phone that leaves little room for the content, so the horizontal layout is usually the better fit there.

## On small screens

When the tabs don't fit, the list scrolls sideways inside itself and the page stays put. There's no scrollbar. The tab that's cut off at the edge is the hint that there are more.

That hint is easy to miss, so keep the labels short and the number of tabs small.

## When the arrow keys select

By default, moving to a tab with the arrow keys selects it, so the panel changes as you go. Set `activationMode="manual"` if showing a panel is slow or loads data. The arrow keys then only move focus, and the tab is selected with <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Space</kbd>.

## Accessibility

### Keyboard

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Moves focus to the selected tab. Pressed again, it moves to the panel. |
| <kbd>→</kbd> and <kbd>←</kbd> | Move to the next or previous tab and select it. From the last tab it goes to the first. In a vertical list, <kbd>↓</kbd> and <kbd>↑</kbd> do this. |
| <kbd>Home</kbd> | Moves to the first tab. |
| <kbd>End</kbd> | Moves to the last tab. |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Space</kbd> | Selects the focused tab. Only needed with `activationMode="manual"`. |

### What the component handles

Most of this is Radix. The library doesn't change it.

- The parts have the `tablist`, `tab` and `tabpanel` roles. Each tab has `aria-selected` and `aria-controls`, and each panel is named by its tab.
- Only the selected tab is in the tab order. The arrow keys move between tabs and skip disabled ones.
- The panel can take focus, so a keyboard user can reach a panel that has nothing focusable in it.
- Tabs are at least 44 pixels tall on a touch screen and 40 with a mouse.
- The focus ring is drawn inside the tab, because the scrolling list would clip one drawn outside.
- The selected tab is marked by a line as well as by its text color, so it doesn't depend on telling two colors apart.
- Where the browser forces its own colors, as Windows high contrast does, the line is still only under the selected tab.

### What you need to handle

- Name the list with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`, as the examples do.
- In a right-to-left layout, pass `dir="rtl"` so the arrow keys follow the reading direction.

## CSS variables

Set any of these on `Tabs`, or on anything around it.

```css
.product {
  --nuv-tabs-indicator: var(--color-foreground);
}
```

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-tabs-gap` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 4)` | Space between the list and the panel. |
| `--nuv-tabs-border` | `var(--color-border)` | Color of the line under the list, or beside it when vertical. |
| `--nuv-tabs-indicator-width` | `2px` | Thickness of that line. |
| `--nuv-tabs-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Text color of the tabs that aren't selected. |
| `--nuv-tabs-active-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Text color of the selected tab, and of any tab while hovered. |
| `--nuv-tabs-indicator` | `var(--color-primary)` | Color of the line that marks the selected tab. |

## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-tabs` | Tabs. |
| `.nuv-tabs__content` | TabsContent. |
| `.nuv-tabs__list` | TabsList. |
| `.nuv-tabs__trigger` | TabsTrigger. |

Radix sets `data-orientation` on every part, `data-state="active"` or `data-state="inactive"` on the tabs and the panels, and `data-disabled` on a disabled tab. The vertical layout and the selected styles hang off those.

## Server components

The tabs parts are client components. They carry `"use client"`, and the build checks that the directive is still there in the published files.

You can put tabs together inside a server component, as both examples on this page do. They only need a client component of your own when you control `value`.

Only the selected panel's content is in the HTML the server sends. If the other panels have to be in the page too, for search engines or for the browser's find, pass `forceMount` to each `TabsContent` and hide the ones with `data-state="inactive"` in your own CSS.

## Do and don't

**Do**

- Keep the labels to a word or two.
- Put the tab people need most first, and select it by default.
- Use tabs for views of the same thing.

**Don't**

- Don't use tabs for steps that have to be done in order.
- Don't use them to move between pages. Those are links.
- Don't put tabs inside tabs.

# TextReveal Lines of text that rise into place one after another, for a heading that opens a page. It's still for anyone who asked for less motion, and the text is in the page from the server. Use a text reveal for the one heading a page opens with, such as the headline of a home page or the title of a launch. Each line rises from under its own edge, a moment after the one before. It's for a few short lines, once. ```tsx "use client"; import { Button, TextReveal } from "@nuvui/react"; import { useState } from "react"; export default function Example() { // A new key draws it again, so the rise can be seen again here. const [run, setRun] = useState(0); return (

); } ``` ## Install ```sh pnpm add @nuvui/react ``` ## Import ```tsx import { TextReveal } from "@nuvui/react"; ``` The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that, and how to load only this component's CSS. ## Props | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `lines` (required) | `ReactNode[]` | | The lines, in order. Each one rises into place a moment after the one before it. A line can hold markup, such as a link or an `em`. | | `trigger` | `"mount" \| "view"` | `"mount"` | When the lines rise. `"mount"` is as soon as it's drawn, for text at the top of a page. `"view"` is the first time it's scrolled into view, for text further down. Text that's already in view when the page opens is shown as it is. | It's a `span`, and takes what a `span` takes, including `ref` and `className`. Put it inside the heading or the paragraph it's for, which keeps its own level, size and font: ```tsx

``` ## Lines You say where the lines break: each item in `lines` is a line. A line can hold markup, such as a link or an `em`, and a line that's too long for its box wraps like any other text, and rises as one. A screen reader reads the lines as one text, with a space between them, and a copy and paste gets them the same way. ## When it rises With `trigger="mount"`, the default, the lines rise as soon as the page is drawn. The rise is in the stylesheet, so it runs before the page's script has loaded, and ends with the text in place if the script never does. With `trigger="view"`, the lines rise the first time they're scrolled into view. Text that's already in view when the page opens is shown as it is: hiding it then would make it flash. Out of view, the text waits under its edge until it's scrolled to, and it's hidden only once the script knows it's out of view. So the page from the server, and a page whose script fails, show every word. ```tsx import { TextReveal } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function Example() { return (

it's scrolled into view. , ]} />

); } ``` To play it again, give it a new `key`. ## Accessibility A text reveal has no role and no keyboard behavior. It can't take focus. ### What the component handles - The text is ordinary text, in the page from the server, read and found and selected like any other. - For a visitor who asked for less motion, every line is in place from the start. - Only position moves. Nothing around the text is laid out again, and the lines are spaced as they would be without it. - Where the browser forces its own colors, the text is drawn in the browser's text color. ### What you need to handle - Use it once on a page, for the text that opens it. Text that moves each time it's scrolled past is hard to read. - Keep it to a few lines. ## CSS variables Set any of these on the `TextReveal`, or on anything around it. ```css .headline { --nuv-text-reveal-stagger: 200ms; } ``` | Variable | Default | What it sets | | --- | --- | --- | | `--nuv-text-reveal-distance` | `calc(100% + 0.2em)` | How far below its edge a line starts. Far enough that none of it shows. | | `--nuv-text-reveal-duration` | `700ms` | How long one line takes to rise. | | `--nuv-text-reveal-easing` | `var(--ease-out)` | How a line speeds up and slows down. | | `--nuv-text-reveal-index` | `0` | Which line this is, from 0. The component writes this. Don't set it. | | `--nuv-text-reveal-stagger` | `120ms` | How long each line waits after the one before it. | ## Classes | Class | What it's on | | --- | --- | | `.nuv-text-reveal` | TextReveal. | | `.nuv-text-reveal__line` | A line, cut to its own height. | | `.nuv-text-reveal__text` | What's in a line. It's what rises. | Where it is is in a `data-state` attribute: `rising`, `waiting` while it's out of view and waiting to be scrolled to, or `shown` when it was in view from the start. ## Server components TextReveal starts with `"use client"`: with `trigger="view"` it watches for the text to be scrolled to. It takes no functions, so a server component can render it, with lines it wrote. ## Do and don't **Do** - Break the lines where they read well: "Every report" and "your team asks for", not one word on its own. - Keep it for the opening of a page. **Don't** - Don't use it for body text, a list or a form. - Don't put several on one screen.

sections.heading: While something is worked on
When the wait is over
sections.markdown:
## When the wait is over

Take the shimmer out and put the result in its place. Where the same words stay, such as a step that has finished in a list of steps, set `active={false}`: the text keeps its color and stops moving.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

A text shimmer has no keyboard behavior. It can't take focus.

### What the component handles

- The text is ordinary text. A screen reader reads it, and it can be selected and found.
- For a visitor who asked for less motion, nothing moves and the text is drawn in one color.
- The resting color is the muted text color, which the theme holds to 4.5:1 against the background, and the highlight is the stronger text color. So the words can be read at every moment of the sweep.
- Where the browser forces its own colors, the text is drawn in the browser's text color and nothing moves.
- In a right-to-left page the highlight runs from the right.

### What you need to handle

- Give it words. A shimmer on a blank shape is a [skeleton](page:components/skeleton).
- Put it in a `role="status"` element when its appearing should be read out.
- Don't leave it running. Motion that goes on for more than five seconds beside other content is something WCAG asks for a way to stop, and a wait that long deserves more than three words anyway.

sections.heading: CSS variables
sections.markdown:
## CSS variables

Set any of these on the `TextShimmer`, or on anything around it.

```css
.assistant {
  --nuv-text-shimmer-duration: 3s;
}
```

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-text-shimmer-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of the text at rest. Keep it at 4.5:1 against the background. |
| `--nuv-text-shimmer-highlight` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Color of the moving highlight. Keep it at 4.5:1 against the background too. |
| `--nuv-text-shimmer-duration` | `2s` | How long one sweep takes. |

sections.heading: Classes
sections.markdown:
## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-text-shimmer` | TextShimmer |
| `.nuv-text-shimmer--active` | While the highlight moves. Left off with active={false}. |

Whether it's moving is also in a `data-state` attribute: `active` or `still`.

sections.heading: Server components
sections.markdown:
## Server components

TextShimmer has no `"use client"` directive and uses no state, so it renders in a server component as it is.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Keep it to a few words on one line.
- Say what's happening: "Searching the docs" tells more than "Loading".

**Don't**

- Don't use it for a heading or anything else that stays. Moving text is hard to read.
- Don't show several at once.

For a single line, use an [input](page:components/input). ```tsx import { Label, Textarea } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function Example() { return (

sections.heading: Props
sections.markdown:
## Props

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `autoResize` | `boolean` | `false` | Grow with the text, so that all of it shows without scrolling. Set `--nuv-textarea-max-height` to stop it at a height and scroll from there. |

Everything else is passed to the `<textarea>` element, including `ref`, `rows`, `value`, `disabled`, `required` and `name`.

States

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### Keyboard

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Moves focus to the textarea, and on from it. It doesn't type a tab. |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> | Starts a new line. |

### What the component handles

- It renders a native `<textarea>`, so the role, the keyboard and form submission come from the browser.
- The edge uses `--color-border-strong`, which has at least 3:1 contrast with the page in every theme.
- The placeholder has at least 4.5:1 against the box.
- Focus shows a 2 pixel ring in `--color-ring`.
- Text is 16 pixels on a touch screen, so iOS doesn't zoom in when it takes focus.

### What you need to handle

- Give it a name. Use a [label](page:components/label) whose `htmlFor` matches its `id`, or `aria-label` when there's no visible text.
- If there's a length limit, say so before people start, and say how much room is left as they type.
- When the value is wrong, set `aria-invalid` and describe the problem in text. [Field](page:components/field) ties the message to the textarea.

```css
.comment {
  --nuv-textarea-max-height: 20rem;
}
```

| `--nuv-textarea-min-height` | `5rem` | The height it starts at, and never goes under. |
| `--nuv-textarea-max-height` | `none` | The tallest it gets, by growing or by being dragged. Past that it scrolls. |
| `--nuv-textarea-padding-block` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 2)` | Padding above and below. |
| `--nuv-textarea-padding-inline` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 3)` | Padding left and right. |
| `--nuv-textarea-border` | `var(--color-border-strong)` | Border color. |
| `--nuv-textarea-radius` | `var(--radius-md)` | Corner radius. |
| `--nuv-textarea-bg` | `var(--color-surface)` | Background color. |
| `--nuv-textarea-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Text color. |
| `--nuv-textarea-font-size` | `var(--text-base)`, `var(--text-sm)` | Font size. The default differs between touch screens and a mouse. |

sections.heading: Classes
sections.markdown:
## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-textarea` | The textarea. |
| `.nuv-textarea--auto-resize` | autoResize |

States are attributes, not modifier classes: `:disabled`, `[readonly]` and `[aria-invalid="true"]`.

sections.heading: Server components
sections.markdown:
## Server components

Textarea is a client component, because growing with the text takes an effect in browsers without `field-sizing`. It carries `"use client"`, and the build checks that the directive is still there in the published files. You can render it from a server component, as the examples on this page do.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Start it at a height that hints at how much to write.
- Set a maximum height with `autoResize`, so a pasted essay doesn't push the rest of the form off the screen.

**Don't**

- Don't use a textarea for a value that has to be one line.
- Don't cut off what people type without telling them there's a limit.

pages.title: Timeline
pages.description: Events in the order they happened, each with a marker on a line, a title, a time and a description.
pages.markdown:
# Timeline

Events in the order they happened, each with a marker on a line, a title, a time and a description.

Use a timeline for the history of one thing: an invoice, a deploy, an order, a support ticket. It's an ordered list with a line down its side.

```tsx
import {
  Timeline,
  TimelineContent,
  TimelineDescription,
  TimelineItem,
  TimelineMarker,
  TimelineTime,
  TimelineTitle,
} from "@nuvui/react";

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <Timeline aria-label="History of invoice 1042">
      <TimelineItem>
        <TimelineMarker />
        <TimelineContent>
          <TimelineTitle>Paid in full</TimelineTitle>
          <TimelineDescription>By card ending 4242.</TimelineDescription>
          <TimelineTime dateTime="2026-10-06T14:12:00Z">
            6 October, 14:12
          </TimelineTime>
        </TimelineContent>
      </TimelineItem>
      <TimelineItem>
        <TimelineMarker />
        <TimelineContent>
          <TimelineTitle>Reminder sent</TimelineTitle>
          <TimelineDescription>
            To billing@northwind.example.
          </TimelineDescription>
          <TimelineTime dateTime="2026-10-03T09:00:00Z">
            3 October, 09:00
          </TimelineTime>
        </TimelineContent>
      </TimelineItem>
      <TimelineItem>
        <TimelineMarker />
        <TimelineContent>
          <TimelineTitle>Invoice created</TimelineTitle>
          <TimelineDescription>By Ada Osei.</TimelineDescription>
          <TimelineTime dateTime="2026-09-19T16:40:00Z">
            19 September, 16:40
          </TimelineTime>
        </TimelineContent>
      </TimelineItem>
    </Timeline>
  );
}
```

## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/react
```

## Import

```tsx
import {
  Timeline,
  TimelineContent,
  TimelineDescription,
  TimelineItem,
  TimelineMarker,
  TimelineTime,
  TimelineTitle,
} from "@nuvui/react";
```

The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that, and how to load only this component's CSS.

## Parts

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `Timeline` | The list. An `ol`. |
| `TimelineItem` | One event. An `li`, holding a marker and then the content. |
| `TimelineMarker` | The point on the line. A ring, or a filled circle with an icon in it. |
| `TimelineContent` | Everything beside the marker. |
| `TimelineTitle` | What happened, in a line. |
| `TimelineDescription` | More about it. |
| `TimelineTime` | When. A `time` element. |

`TimelineItem` needs its marker first and its content second. Inside the content, any of the three parts can be left out, and they can go in any order.

## Props

### TimelineMarker

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `intent` | `"danger" \| "neutral" \| "primary" \| "success" \| "warning"` | `"neutral"` | What kind of event it is. The color is extra: the event's text has to say it too. |

The other parts add no props of their own. Each takes what its element takes, including `ref` and `className`. `TimelineTime` takes `dateTime`.

## Kinds of event

A marker's `intent` fills it with one of the theme's colors, and an icon can go inside. With no intent it's a ring.

```tsx
import {
  Timeline,
  TimelineContent,
  TimelineDescription,
  TimelineItem,
  TimelineMarker,
  TimelineTime,
  TimelineTitle,
} from "@nuvui/react";
import type { ReactNode } from "react";

function Icon({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <svg
      aria-hidden="true"
      viewBox="0 0 12 12"
      width="12"
      height="12"
      fill="none"
      stroke="currentColor"
      strokeWidth="1.75"
      strokeLinecap="round"
      strokeLinejoin="round"
    >
      {children}
    </svg>
  );
}

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <Timeline aria-label="Deploys of the billing service">
      <TimelineItem>
        <TimelineMarker intent="danger">
          <Icon>
            <path d="M3 3l6 6M9 3l-6 6" />
          </Icon>
        </TimelineMarker>
        <TimelineContent>
          <TimelineTitle>Deploy failed</TimelineTitle>
          <TimelineDescription>
            The health check timed out after 90 seconds.
          </TimelineDescription>
          <TimelineTime dateTime="2026-10-08T11:02:00Z">
            Today, 11:02
          </TimelineTime>
        </TimelineContent>
      </TimelineItem>
      <TimelineItem>
        <TimelineMarker intent="warning">
          <Icon>
            <path d="M6 3v3.5M6 9h.01" />
          </Icon>
        </TimelineMarker>
        <TimelineContent>
          <TimelineTitle>Deployed with warnings</TimelineTitle>
          <TimelineDescription>
            Two migrations took over a minute.
          </TimelineDescription>
          <TimelineTime dateTime="2026-10-07T16:30:00Z">
            Yesterday, 16:30
          </TimelineTime>
        </TimelineContent>
      </TimelineItem>
      <TimelineItem>
        <TimelineMarker intent="success">
          <Icon>
            <path d="M2.5 6.5l2.25 2.25L9.5 3.5" />
          </Icon>
        </TimelineMarker>
        <TimelineContent>
          <TimelineTitle>Deployed</TimelineTitle>
          <TimelineTime dateTime="2026-10-06T10:15:00Z">
            6 October, 10:15
          </TimelineTime>
        </TimelineContent>
      </TimelineItem>
      <TimelineItem>
        <TimelineMarker intent="primary">
          <Icon>
            <path d="M6 2.5v7M2.5 6h7" />
          </Icon>
        </TimelineMarker>
        <TimelineContent>
          <TimelineTitle>Service created</TimelineTitle>
          <TimelineTime dateTime="2026-10-01T09:00:00Z">
            1 October, 09:00
          </TimelineTime>
        </TimelineContent>
      </TimelineItem>
    </Timeline>
  );
}
```

The marker is hidden from screen readers. Its color and its icon are for the eye, and the title has to say the same thing in words: "Deploy failed", not "Deploy" beside a red cross.

## The time

`TimelineTime` is a `time` element. Write the time the way people read it as its children, and give the exact one in `dateTime`, in ISO 8601. The children can be relative, such as "Yesterday, 16:30", as long as `dateTime` isn't.

The component doesn't format dates. Whatever writes dates in the rest of your app writes these, so they're in the same language and time zone.

## Order

The list is read in the order it's written. Newest first suits a history someone checks for what just happened. Oldest first suits the steps something went through. Pick one for the whole app.

For a long history, show the latest events and a button that loads more. The component has no paging of its own.

## Accessibility

A timeline has no keyboard behavior of its own. Links and buttons inside an event work as they do anywhere.

### What the component handles

- It's an ordered list, so a screen reader says how many events there are and where it is among them. The list says it's a list in so many words, because Safari stops treating a list as one once its numbers are styled away.
- The marker has `aria-hidden="true"`.
- The line is a border, and a filled marker has a border that can't be seen until the browser forces its own colors. Both are still drawn there.
- The description and the time have at least 4.5:1 against the page in every theme.

### What you need to handle

- Name the list with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`, such as "History of invoice 1042".
- Say in the title what the marker's color and icon show.
- Give every `TimelineTime` a `dateTime`.
- An event added while the page is open isn't announced. If it matters, say it in a [toast](page:components/toast) or an element with `role="status"`.

## CSS variables

Set any of these on the `Timeline`, or on anything around it.

```css
.compact-history {
  --nuv-timeline-space: calc(var(--spacing) * 3);
  --nuv-timeline-marker-size: 1rem;
}
```

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-timeline-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Text color. |
| `--nuv-timeline-marker-size` | `1.5rem` | Width and height of a marker. The line and the text move with it. |
| `--nuv-timeline-gap` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 3)` | Space between the marker and the text. |
| `--nuv-timeline-space` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 6)` | Space between one event and the next. |
| `--nuv-timeline-line-width` | `var(--nuv-border-width)` | Thickness of the line. |
| `--nuv-timeline-line` | `var(--color-border)` | Color of the line. |
| `--nuv-timeline-marker-border` | `transparent`, `var(--color-border-strong)` | Border color of a marker. The strong border color on a ring, and transparent on a filled one. |
| `--nuv-timeline-marker-radius` | `var(--radius-full)` | Corner radius of a marker. A circle by default. |
| `--nuv-timeline-marker-bg` | `var(--color-surface)`, `var(--color-primary)`, `var(--color-success)`, `var(--color-warning)`, `var(--color-danger)` | Background color of a marker. Differs by intent. |
| `--nuv-timeline-marker-fg` | `var(--color-surface-foreground)`, `var(--color-primary-foreground)`, `var(--color-background)`, `var(--color-danger-foreground)` | Color of an icon in a marker. Differs by intent. Keep it at 3:1 against the marker. |
| `--nuv-timeline-muted-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of the description and the time. Keep it at 4.5:1 against the background. |

## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-timeline` | Timeline |
| `.nuv-timeline__content` | TimelineContent |
| `.nuv-timeline__description` | TimelineDescription |
| `.nuv-timeline__item` | TimelineItem. The line is its `::before`. |
| `.nuv-timeline__marker` | TimelineMarker |
| `.nuv-timeline__marker--danger` | intent="danger" |
| `.nuv-timeline__marker--neutral` | intent="neutral", the default: a ring. |
| `.nuv-timeline__marker--primary` | intent="primary" |
| `.nuv-timeline__marker--success` | intent="success" |
| `.nuv-timeline__marker--warning` | intent="warning" |
| `.nuv-timeline__time` | TimelineTime |
| `.nuv-timeline__title` | TimelineTitle |

## Server components

No part has a `"use client"` directive or uses state, so all of them render in a server component as they are.

## Do and don't

**Do**

- Keep a title to one line that says what happened and, where it matters, who did it.
- Use an intent for the events that need to be found, and leave the rest as rings.

**Don't**

- Don't use it for steps someone still has to take. A timeline is for what has already happened, and has no way to say which step is the current one.
- Don't put the only copy of a fact in the marker. It's hidden from screen readers.

| `--nuv-timeline-muted-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of the description and the time. Keep it at 4.5:1 against the background. |

## Server components

No part has a `"use client"` directive or uses state, so all of them render in a server component as they are.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Keep a title to one line that says what happened and, where it matters, who did it.
- Use an intent for the events that need to be found, and leave the rest as rings.

**Don't**

- Don't use it for steps someone still has to take. A timeline is for what has already happened, and has no way to say which step is the current one.
- Don't put the only copy of a fact in the marker. It's hidden from screen readers.

pages.title: Toast
pages.description: A brief message at the edge of the screen that goes away on its own. You show one by calling toast().
pages.markdown:
# Toast A brief message at the edge of the screen that goes away on its own. You show one by calling toast(). Use a toast to confirm something that just happened: a save, a sent invitation, a deleted file with a chance to undo. It's gone after a few seconds, so don't use one for anything people have to read or act on. ```tsx "use client"; import { Button, toast } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function Example() { return ; } ``` ## Install ```sh pnpm add @nuvui/react ``` ## Import ```tsx import { Toaster, toast } from "@nuvui/react"; ``` The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that, and how to load only this component's CSS. ## Setup There are two pieces. `Toaster` is the component that shows toasts, and `toast()` is the function that sends it one. Render `Toaster` once, near the root of the app: ```tsx title="app/layout.tsx" import { Toaster } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) { return ( {children} ); } ``` Then call `toast()` from any client component. It doesn't need a hook, a context or a ref to the `Toaster`: ```tsx "use client"; import { Button, toast } from "@nuvui/react"; export function SaveButton() { return ; } ``` Render only one `Toaster`. With two on the page, each would show every toast. ## API ### toast(title, options) Shows a toast and returns its id, a string. `title` is the main line, and can be text or JSX. Everything in `options` is optional: | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `id` | `string` | | Pass the id of a toast that's already showing to replace it instead of adding another. | | `description` | `ReactNode` | | A second line under the title. | | `intent` | `"danger" \| "info" \| "neutral" \| "success" \| "warning"` | `"neutral"` | Colors the toast's edge. A `"warning"` or `"danger"` toast also interrupts a screen reader to be read out at once, as an alert with that intent does. The others wait until it's quiet. | | `duration` | `number` | | How long the toast stays, in milliseconds. `Infinity` keeps it until it's dismissed. Without this, the Toaster's `duration` applies. | | `action` | `ToastAction` | | A button in the toast, such as "Undo". | `action` takes these: | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `label` (required) | `ReactNode` | | The text on the button. | | `altText` (required) | `string` | | Another way to do the same thing, for screen reader users, who may not reach the button before the toast has gone. For example "Undo with Ctrl+Z". | | `onClick` (required) | `() => void` | | Called when the button is pressed. The toast closes afterwards. | ### toast.dismiss(id) Closes the toast with that id. Called with no id, it closes all of them. ```tsx const id = toast("Uploading photo.jpg", { duration: Infinity }); // Later toast.dismiss(id); ``` ### Toaster | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `position` | `"bottom-center" \| "bottom-end" \| "bottom-start" \| "top-center" \| "top-end" \| "top-start"` | `"bottom-end"` | Where toasts appear once the screen is at least 40rem wide. On a narrower screen they span its width, and only the top or bottom part of this applies. | | `duration` | `number` | `5000` | How long a toast stays, in milliseconds, unless it sets its own. | | `limit` | `number` | `3` | The most toasts shown at once. Any others wait, and each shows when one before it closes. A waiting toast's `duration` starts when it shows. | | `closeLabel` | `string` | `"Close"` | Accessible name of the close button on each toast. Translate it with the rest of your interface. | | `toastLabel` | `string` | `"Notification"` | What a screen reader says before the text of each toast. Translate it with the rest of your interface. | | `swipeDirection` | `"down" \| "left" \| "right" \| "up"` | `"right"` | The direction a toast is swiped in to dismiss it. | Two more come from Radix: | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `label` | `string` | | The name of the list of toasts as a landmark. It's `"Notifications ({hotkey})"` unless you say otherwise, and `{hotkey}` is filled in for you. | | `hotkey` | `string[]` | | The keys that move focus to the list. It's `["F8"]` unless you say otherwise. | `Toaster` also takes `ref` and `className`, which go to the list element. ## Intents ```tsx "use client"; import { Button, toast } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function Example() { return ( <> ); } ``` The colored edge is decoration. Say what happened in the title, so the message works without it. ## With an action A toast can carry one button. Pressing it runs `onClick` and closes the toast. ```tsx "use client"; import { Button, toast } from "@nuvui/react"; import { useState } from "react"; export default function Example() { const [deleted, setDeleted] = useState(false); function remove() { setDeleted(true); toast("report.pdf deleted", { // Long enough to read it and get to the button. duration: 10000, action: { label: "Undo", altText: "Restore it from the trash", onClick: () => setDeleted(false), }, }); } return (

{deleted ? "The file is in the trash." : "report.pdf"}

); } ``` `altText` is required. A screen reader user may not get to the button before the toast has gone, so it tells them another way to do the same thing. ## Changing a toast that's showing Pass the id of a toast that's already up and it's replaced where it is, instead of a second one appearing. This suits anything with a start and a finish. ```tsx "use client"; import { Button, toast } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function Example() { function upload() { // Stays until the same id is used again below. const id = toast("Uploading photo.jpg", { duration: Infinity }); setTimeout(() => { toast("photo.jpg uploaded", { id, intent: "success" }); }, 2000); } return ; } ``` ## How long it stays A toast stays for 5 seconds unless `duration` says otherwise, on `Toaster` for all of them or in `options` for one. `Infinity` keeps a toast up until it's dismissed. The clock stops while the pointer is over a toast, and while keyboard focus is anywhere in the list. It starts again when they leave. ## Several at once Three toasts show at a time. A fourth waits, and shows when one of the three closes. The button below sends five to show it happening. ```tsx "use client"; import { Button, toast } from "@nuvui/react"; const messages = [ "Draft saved", "Link copied", "Invitation sent", "Export ready", "Comment posted", ]; export default function Example() { function send() { for (const message of messages) toast(message); } return ; } ``` A toast that's waiting isn't on the page yet. Its clock starts when it shows, so it gets its full time, and that's also when a screen reader hears it. Change the number with `limit` on `Toaster`. A toast with `duration: Infinity` holds its place until someone closes it, so three of those keep everything behind them waiting. `toast.dismiss()` with no id clears the ones that are waiting as well as the ones showing. ## Where it shows On a screen narrower than 40rem, toasts span the width of the screen along the bottom, or along the top if `position` starts with `top`. From 40rem up, they're a column 22rem wide in the corner that `position` names. The newest toast is always the one nearest the edge of the screen. The list sits where you render `Toaster`, without a portal, so it picks up a `data-theme` from whatever is around it. ## Accessibility ### Keyboard | Key | What it does | | --- | --- | | F8 | Moves focus to the list of toasts, from anywhere on the page. | | Tab | Moves through the toasts and the buttons inside them. | | Esc | Closes the toast that has focus. | | Enter or Space | Presses the focused button. | ### What the component handles Most of this is Radix. The library chooses how each intent is announced. - Every toast is read out by screen readers when it appears. A `warning` or `danger` toast interrupts whatever is being read, as an [alert](page:components/alert) with that intent does. The others wait until the screen reader is idle. - No more than three toasts show at once. The rest wait their turn, and each is announced when it shows. - The list is a landmark named "Notifications (F8)", so it can be found again after the announcement. - The clock stops on hover and on focus, which gives people time to read a toast and reach its buttons. - The close button is a real button with an accessible name, and is at least 44 pixels on touch screens. - A toast can be swiped away to the right, with a finger or a mouse. - The list takes no clicks itself. Whatever is under an empty part of it still works. - The animations only run when the visitor hasn't asked for reduced motion. ### What you need to handle - Don't put anything essential in a toast. Some people will miss it however long it stays. - Give a toast with an action, or with a lot of text, a longer `duration`. - Write an `altText` that says how else to do the action, such as a keyboard shortcut or where to find it on the page. - Translate `closeLabel`, `toastLabel` and `label` along with the rest of your interface. ## CSS variables Set any of these on `Toaster` with a class or `style`, or on anything around it. ```css :root { --nuv-toast-width: 26rem; } ``` | Variable | Default | What it sets | | --- | --- | --- | | `--nuv-toast-width` | `22rem` | Width of a toast once the screen is at least 40rem wide. | | `--nuv-toast-border` | `var(--color-border)` | Border color. | | `--nuv-toast-radius` | `var(--radius-lg)` | Corner radius. | | `--nuv-toast-bg` | `var(--color-surface)` | Background color. | | `--nuv-toast-shadow` | `var(--shadow-lg)` | Shadow under each toast. | | `--nuv-toast-fg` | `var(--color-surface-foreground)` | Text color. | | `--nuv-toast-accent-width` | `4px` | Thickness of that edge. The padding beside it shrinks to match, so titles stay lined up. | | `--nuv-toast-accent` | `var(--color-primary)`, `var(--color-success)`, `var(--color-warning)`, `var(--color-danger)` | Color of the thick edge on a toast with an intent. | ## Classes | Class | What it's on | | --- | --- | | `.nuv-toast` | One toast. | | `.nuv-toast--danger` | A toast with intent "danger". | | `.nuv-toast--info` | A toast with intent "info". | | `.nuv-toast--success` | A toast with intent "success". | | `.nuv-toast--warning` | A toast with intent "warning". | | `.nuv-toast__action` | The action button. | | `.nuv-toast__close` | The close button. | | `.nuv-toast__content` | The title and the description together. | | `.nuv-toast__description` | The description. | | `.nuv-toast__title` | The title. | | `.nuv-toaster` | Toaster, which is the list the toasts sit in. | | `.nuv-toaster--center` | A position that ends with center. | | `.nuv-toaster--end` | A position that ends with end. | | `.nuv-toaster--start` | A position that ends with start. | | `.nuv-toaster--top` | A position that starts with top. | The list also gets `nuv-toaster--bottom`, and a toast gets `nuv-toast--neutral`, when those apply. No styles are attached to either, since they're the base. Radix sets `data-state="open"` or `data-state="closed"` on each toast, and `data-swipe` while one is being dragged. The animations hang off those. ## Server components `Toaster` is a client component. It carries `"use client"`, and the build checks that the directive is still there in the published files. You can render it from a server component, such as a root layout. `toast()` belongs in the browser. Call it from event handlers and effects in client components. If a client component calls it while it's being rendered on the server, nothing happens: there's nowhere to show it, and a list kept on the server would be shared between requests. Toasts sent before `Toaster` has mounted aren't lost. They show once it's there. ## Do and don't **Do** - Say what happened in a few words: "Changes saved", "Invitation sent". - Offer "Undo" in the toast when the thing can be undone. - Reuse an id for a message that repeats, so it doesn't stack up. **Don't** - Don't use a toast for an error in a form. Put the message next to the field. - Don't send a toast for every item in a batch. Only three show at a time, so the last ones arrive long after the work is done. Send one that covers them all. - Don't put a toast's only action somewhere people can't get to after it's gone.
