# VisuallyHidden Text that's in the page for screen readers and drawn nowhere. Use `VisuallyHidden` for words that someone looking at the page gets from the layout, and someone listening to it doesn't get at all: the name of a button that shows only an icon, the unit of a number in a badge, a heading for a column of buttons. ```tsx import { Button, VisuallyHidden } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function Example() { return ( ); } ``` ## Install ```sh pnpm add @nuvui/react ``` ## Import ```tsx import { VisuallyHidden } from "@nuvui/react"; ``` The styles come from `@nuvui/react/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app. [Getting started](page:index) covers that, and how to load only this component's CSS. Without the stylesheet the text shows. The hiding is a class, not an inline style. ## Props | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `focusable` | `boolean` | `false` | Show the content while it, or something inside it, has keyboard focus. This is what a "Skip to content" link needs. | | `asChild` | `boolean` | `false` | Render the single child element instead of a `span`, and give it the class and props. | Everything else is passed to the ``, including `ref`, `className` and `id`. ## How it hides `display: none` and `visibility: hidden` hide from everyone, screen readers included. This hides from the eye only: the element is one pixel in size, clipped to nothing, and taken out of the layout so it leaves no gap. `aria-label` does a similar job on a control, and is fine there. Hidden text has two things over it. Translation tools in the browser translate it, where they often skip attributes. And it works on elements that `aria-label` doesn't, such as a `` or a table cell. ## A skip link `focusable` shows the content while it, or something in it, has keyboard focus. That's the pattern for a "Skip to content" link: the first stop on the page for the Tab key, seen only by the people who use that key. Press Tab in the example to bring the link up. ```tsx import { Button, VisuallyHidden } from "@nuvui/react"; export default function Example() { return (

The article starts here.

); } ``` When shown, the content sits where it is in the page's flow. To float it over the page's corner, as most skip links do, position it with a class of your own. The link's target needs `tabIndex={-1}` if it isn't something that takes focus by itself. Otherwise some browsers scroll to it and leave focus where it was. ## In a table A column of buttons still needs a header for a screen reader to say with each cell. And each "Open" button needs to say what it opens. ```tsx import { Button, VisuallyHidden } from "@nuvui/react"; const rows = [ ["Northwind Traders", "Paid"], ["Contoso", "Overdue"], ]; export default function Example() { return ( {rows.map(([customer, status]) => ( ))}
Customer Status Actions
{customer} {status}
); } ``` ## Accessibility ### What the component handles - The text stays in the accessibility tree, in its place in the reading order. - It keeps its words apart. Text squeezed into one pixel can be read out with the spaces missing, and a `white-space` rule prevents that. - It takes no room, so it can't cause a scrollbar or a gap. ### What you need to handle - **Don't hide something that can take focus,** without `focusable`. A sighted keyboard user would tab to a control they can't see. - **Hidden text is for what the layout already shows.** If people who see the page would also be helped by the words, show the words. - A hidden heading is a fair way to give a region of the page a place in the outline. Don't add more than the page needs. - Speech input users say what they see. A button whose visible text is "Open" and whose full name is "Open Northwind Traders" works, because the name starts with the visible text. Keep it that way round. ## Classes | Class | What it's on | | --- | --- | | `.nuv-visually-hidden` | The hiding. | | `.nuv-visually-hidden--focusable` | focusable. Undoes the hiding while focus is on the element or inside it. | It has no CSS variables. ## Server components VisuallyHidden has no `"use client"` directive and uses no state, so it renders in a server component as it is. It's a class in the stylesheet and not Radix's primitive, which hides with inline styles. A class can be undone on focus, which is what `focusable` needs, and it doesn't put a `style` attribute in the server's HTML, which a strict content security policy would block. ## Do and don't **Do** - Use it for the name of an icon-only control when the control's own element can't take `aria-label` cleanly. - Write hidden text as carefully as visible text. It's the whole interface for some people. **Don't** - Don't use it to stuff keywords into a page. - Don't give screen reader users a different message from everyone else. Say the same thing, in the words the layout left out.

pages.markdown:
# Dates

The @nuvui/date-picker package. A calendar, a date field and a date range field, installed next to @nuvui/react, with locales and time zones.

Dates are a package of their own, `@nuvui/date-picker`. It has three components:

| Component | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| [Calendar](page:date-picker/calendar) | A month of days to pick from: one day, several, or a range. |
| [DatePicker](page:date-picker/date-picker) | A field a date is typed into, with a button that opens a calendar. |
| [DateRangePicker](page:date-picker/date-range-picker) | Two fields, for the first and the last day, and one calendar for both. |

It's separate from `@nuvui/react` because of what it brings with it. The calendar is [react-day-picker](https://daypicker.dev), which depends on [date-fns](https://date-fns.org). An app that only wants buttons and dialogs shouldn't have to install, review and update a date library.

## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/date-picker @nuvui/react
```

`@nuvui/react` is a peer dependency: the date fields are built from its input group, popover and dialog, so your app has to have it. `react-day-picker`, `date-fns` and `@date-fns/tz` come along as ordinary dependencies. You don't install them yourself.

## Load the styles

Import the package's stylesheet once, after the core's:

```tsx title="app/layout.tsx"
import "@nuvui/react/styles.css";
import "@nuvui/date-picker/styles.css";
```

It holds the calendar and what the two fields add to an input group. It reads the same tokens as every other component, so a [theme](page:theming), a preset or a density you've set applies to it with nothing more to do.

Both files open with the same line naming the cascade layers, so the order you import them in doesn't decide which rule wins. To load one component's styles on their own, there's `@nuvui/date-picker/css/calendar.css` and `@nuvui/date-picker/css/date-picker.css`. The second needs the first, and the core's input, input group, popover and dialog styles.

The package doesn't use react-day-picker's own stylesheet. Don't import it.

## Use a component

```tsx
import { DatePicker } from "@nuvui/date-picker";

export default function Page() {
  return <DatePicker aria-label="Due date" name="due" />;
}
```

Each component also has an entry of its own, `@nuvui/date-picker/calendar` and `@nuvui/date-picker/date-picker`, for a bundler that doesn't remove unused code from the main one.

## Dates are `Date` objects

What you pass in and what you get back are JavaScript `Date`s, set to midnight at the start of the day. An empty date field is `null`.

A form doesn't get a `Date`. Give a field a `name` and it submits the day as `yyyy-MM-dd`, such as `2026-10-15`, which is what a `<input type="date">` sends and what a database's date column takes.

Don't turn one of these dates into text with `toISOString()`. That gives the day in UTC, which is the day before for anyone east of Greenwich looking at midnight. Use date-fns' `format(date, "yyyy-MM-dd")`, or the form value.

## Languages

Everything a calendar shows and says comes from a locale: the names of months and days, the day a week starts on, the order a date is typed in, and the labels a screen reader hears on the buttons. English as used in the United States is the default.

```tsx
import { DatePicker } from "@nuvui/date-picker";
import { de } from "@nuvui/date-picker/locale";

<DatePicker locale={de} />;
```

`@nuvui/date-picker/locale` has every locale that react-day-picker has. Import the ones you use by name and a bundler leaves the rest out.

A locale doesn't translate the few strings the fields add themselves. Those are props, with English defaults:

| Prop | Default | On |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `calendarLabel` | `"Choose date"`, or `"Choose dates"` for a range | The button that opens the calendar. |
| `title` | The same | The calendar's panel, and the heading of the sheet on a phone. |
| `closeLabel` | `"Close"` | The sheet's close button. |
| `invalidMessage` | `"Enter a valid date."` | What the browser shows for text that isn't a date. |
| `startLabel` and `endLabel` | `"Start date"` and `"End date"` | The two fields of a range. |
| `orderMessage` | `"The end date is before the start date."` | A range typed the wrong way round. |

## Time zones

Left alone, a day is a day in the browser's time zone. That's right for most forms: a due date, a birthday, a booking at a place the person is in.

It's wrong when the day belongs to somewhere else, such as a launch at midnight in Tokyo or a report for a company's financial day in New York. Pass `timeZone` with an [IANA name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones):

```tsx
<DatePicker timeZone="Asia/Tokyo" name="launch" />
```

Today is then today in Tokyo, the dates you're handed are midnight in Tokyo, and the form value is the day in Tokyo. The dates are `TZDate` objects, from [`@date-fns/tz`](https://github.com/date-fns/tz). A `TZDate` is a `Date` that knows its zone, so `date.getDate()` and date-fns' functions answer for Tokyo. Its `toISOString()` gives the time with Tokyo's offset on the end, not in UTC. `date.getTime()` is the same moment either way.

With `timeZone` set, give `value`, `min` and `max` as `TZDate`s in the same zone. The package exports the class:

```tsx
import { DatePicker, TZDate } from "@nuvui/date-picker";

<DatePicker
  timeZone="Asia/Tokyo"
  min={new TZDate(2026, 9, 1, "Asia/Tokyo")}
/>;
```

A plain `Date` is read as the moment it is. One moment is two different days in two places, so `new Date(2026, 9, 1)` made in London is still 30 September in Honolulu.

## Server components

All three are client components. They carry `"use client"`, and the build checks that the directive is still there in the published files. You can render any of them from a server component. A client component of your own is only needed where you pass a function, such as `onValueChange`.

A server can't know what day it is for the person who'll look at the page, which may have been rendered hours earlier or in another time zone. The components allow for that. The date fields render no calendar until one is opened, in the browser. A [calendar that's on the page from the start](page:date-picker/calendar#server-rendering) marks today once the browser has taken over.

A `Date` made on a server is midnight in the server's time zone. Sent to a browser in another zone as `defaultValue`, it's a different time of day there, and can be the day before. For a date that a server component passes down, say which zone it's in on both sides: make it with `Date.UTC` and set `timeZone="UTC"`, or make the `Date` in a client component from the `yyyy-MM-dd` text.

## What's not here

- **A time of day.** These pick days. A time picker is planned for after 1.0.
- **A month or year picker** on its own.
- **A field with a part for each of day, month and year**, where the arrow keys step through them. The fields here are one text field each, which is simpler to paste into and to correct.

| `title` | The same | The calendar's panel, and the heading of the sheet on a phone. |
| `closeLabel` | `"Close"` | The sheet's close button. |
| `invalidMessage` | `"Enter a valid date."` | What the browser shows for text that isn't a date. |
| `startLabel` and `endLabel` | `"Start date"` and `"End date"` | The two fields of a range. |
| `orderMessage` | `"The end date is before the start date."` | A range typed the wrong way round. |

sections.heading: Time zones
sections.markdown:
## Time zones

Left alone, a day is a day in the browser's time zone. That's right for most forms: a due date, a birthday, a booking at a place the person is in.

It's wrong when the day belongs to somewhere else, such as a launch at midnight in Tokyo or a report for a company's financial day in New York. Pass `timeZone` with an [IANA name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones):

```tsx
<DatePicker timeZone="Asia/Tokyo" name="launch" />
```

Today is then today in Tokyo, the dates you're handed are midnight in Tokyo, and the form value is the day in Tokyo. The dates are `TZDate` objects, from [`@date-fns/tz`](https://github.com/date-fns/tz). A `TZDate` is a `Date` that knows its zone, so `date.getDate()` and date-fns' functions answer for Tokyo. Its `toISOString()` gives the time with Tokyo's offset on the end, not in UTC. `date.getTime()` is the same moment either way.

With `timeZone` set, give `value`, `min` and `max` as `TZDate`s in the same zone. The package exports the class:

```tsx
import { DatePicker, TZDate } from "@nuvui/date-picker";

<DatePicker
  timeZone="Asia/Tokyo"
  min={new TZDate(2026, 9, 1, "Asia/Tokyo")}
/>;
```

A plain `Date` is read as the moment it is. One moment is two different days in two places, so `new Date(2026, 9, 1)` made in London is still 30 September in Honolulu.

sections.heading: Server components
sections.markdown:
## Server components

All three are client components. They carry `"use client"`, and the build checks that the directive is still there in the published files. You can render any of them from a server component. A client component of your own is only needed where you pass a function, such as `onValueChange`.

A server can't know what day it is for the person who'll look at the page, which may have been rendered hours earlier or in another time zone. The components allow for that. The date fields render no calendar until one is opened, in the browser. A [calendar that's on the page from the start](page:date-picker/calendar#server-rendering) marks today once the browser has taken over.

A `Date` made on a server is midnight in the server's time zone. Sent to a browser in another zone as `defaultValue`, it's a different time of day there, and can be the day before. For a date that a server component passes down, say which zone it's in on both sides: make it with `Date.UTC` and set `timeZone="UTC"`, or make the `Date` in a client component from the `yyyy-MM-dd` text.

sections.heading: What's not here
sections.markdown:
## What's not here

- **A time of day.** These pick days. A time picker is planned for after 1.0.
- **A month or year picker** on its own.
- **A field with a part for each of day, month and year**, where the arrow keys step through them. The fields here are one text field each, which is simpler to paste into and to correct.

pages.title: Calendar
pages.description: A month of days to pick from. It holds one day, several days or a range, moves by keyboard, and takes a locale, a week start and a time zone.

sections.markdown:
## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/date-picker @nuvui/react
```

sections.heading: Import
sections.markdown:
## Import

```tsx
import { Calendar } from "@nuvui/date-picker";
```

The styles come from `@nuvui/date-picker/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app, after `@nuvui/react/styles.css`. [Dates](page:date-picker/index) covers that.

sections.heading: Props
sections.markdown:
## Props

`Calendar` is [react-day-picker](https://daypicker.dev)'s `DayPicker` with this library's styles and markup. It takes what `DayPicker` takes, and these are the ones you're most likely to set:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mode` | `"multiple" \| "range" \| "single"` |  | What can be picked: `"single"` for one day, `"multiple"` for several, `"range"` for a first and a last day. Left out, the calendar only shows days. |
| `required` | `boolean` |  | With `true`, there's always something picked: pressing the picked day doesn't clear it. |
| `disabled` | `Matcher[] \| Matcher` |  | Days that can't be picked. A date, a list of them, `{ before }`, `{ after }`, `{ from, to }`, `{ dayOfWeek: [0, 6] }`, or a function that's given a date. |
| `defaultMonth` | `Date` |  | The month shown to begin with. Left out, it's this month. |
| `month` | `Date` |  | The month shown, when you control it. Use it with `onMonthChange`. |
| `onMonthChange` | `MonthChangeEventHandler` |  | Called when the month shown changes. |
| `startMonth` | `Date` |  | The earliest month that can be gone to. |
| `endMonth` | `Date` |  | The latest month that can be gone to. |
| `numberOfMonths` | `number` |  | How many months are shown side by side. One by default. |
| `captionLayout` | `"dropdown" \| "dropdown-months" \| "dropdown-years" \| "label"` |  | `"dropdown"` makes the month and the year lists to choose from. `"dropdown-months"` and `"dropdown-years"` do it for one of them. |
| `showOutsideDays` | `boolean` |  | Fills the first and last week with days from the months either side. |
| `showWeekNumber` | `boolean` |  | Adds a column with the number of each week. |
| `fixedWeeks` | `boolean` |  | Always draws six weeks, so the calendar doesn't change height from month to month. |
| `weekStartsOn` | `0 \| 1 \| 2 \| 3 \| 4 \| 5 \| 6` |  | The day a week starts on, from 0 for Sunday. Left out, it's the locale's. |
| `locale` | `Partial<DayPickerLocale>` |  | The language. Take one from `@nuvui/date-picker/locale`. |
| `timeZone` | `string` |  | The time zone the days are in, as an IANA name such as `"Asia/Tokyo"`. |
| `today` | `Date` |  | The day marked as today. Left out, it's today. |
| `labels` | `Partial<Labels>` |  | Functions that give the accessible names of the buttons and the grid, to replace the locale's. |
| `footer` | `ReactNode` |  | Text under the days. It's a live region, so a screen reader says it when it changes. |
| `navLayout` | `"after" \| "around"` |  | Where the two month buttons go. `"around"`, either side of the month's name, is the default here. |

What's picked is in `selected`, and `onSelect` is called with the new value. Their types follow `mode`:

| `mode` | `selected` | `onSelect` is called with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"single"` | `Date` | The day, or `undefined` when the picked day was pressed again. |
| `"multiple"` | `Date[]` | The list of days. |
| `"range"` | `{ from, to }` | The range. `to` is `undefined` until a second day is picked. |

Pass both, or neither. With neither, the calendar keeps what's picked itself. With `onSelect` and no `selected`, nothing shows as picked.

`animate` is the one `DayPicker` prop that's left out. Its slide between months is drawn by react-day-picker's own stylesheet, which this package doesn't use. The [react-day-picker reference](https://daypicker.dev/api/interfaces/PropsBase) lists every prop.

sections.heading: Several days
A range
Days that can't be picked
A date far from today
Languages
Right to left
sections.markdown:
## Right to left

Inside a [`DirectionProvider`](page:right-to-left) with `dir="rtl"`, the days run from right to left, the button for the month before is on the right, and the left arrow key moves to the next day. Without the provider, pass `dir="rtl"` to the calendar.

sections.heading: Server rendering
sections.markdown:
## Server rendering

A server can't know which day is today for the person looking at the page. It may have rendered the page an hour ago, or yesterday for a site that's built ahead of time, and its clock may be in another time zone. A calendar that marked the server's today would be wrong for some people, and React would report that the page it was sent doesn't match.

So a calendar rendered on a server marks no day as today. The browser adds the mark once React has taken over the page.

A calendar that has no `month` or `defaultMonth` has nothing but today to choose its month by. On a server it renders an empty month, hidden, that holds its place in the page, and the real one appears in the browser. To have the days in the HTML from the start, say which month to show:

```tsx
<Calendar mode="single" defaultMonth={new Date(2026, 9)} />
```

Passing `today` yourself turns all of this off, and the calendar renders the same on the server and in the browser. A calendar that's first rendered in the browser, as the one inside a date picker is, isn't affected.

sections.heading: On small screens
sections.markdown:
## On small screens

A day is 44 pixels each way on a touch screen, and so are the two month buttons. With a mouse a day is 40 pixels, and [density](page:theming#density) moves it to 36 or 44. Seven days across is 308 pixels on a touch screen, which fits a 360 pixel phone with the usual margins.

`--nuv-calendar-cell-size` sets the size of a day everywhere at once. Don't go under 44 pixels on a touch screen.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### Keyboard

<kbd>Tab</kbd> stops at the button for the month before, the button for the month after, and one day: the picked one, or today. From that day:

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>←</kbd> and <kbd>→</kbd> | Move to the day before or after. They swap in a right-to-left calendar. |
| <kbd>↑</kbd> and <kbd>↓</kbd> | Move to the same day the week before or after. |
| <kbd>Home</kbd> and <kbd>End</kbd> | Move to the first or last day of the week. |
| <kbd>Page Up</kbd> and <kbd>Page Down</kbd> | Move to the same day the month before or after. |
| <kbd>Shift</kbd> with <kbd>Page Up</kbd> or <kbd>Page Down</kbd> | Move a year. |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Space</kbd> | Picks the day. |

Moving past the end of the month shows the next one and keeps focus on the day.

### What the component handles

- Each month is a `table` with `role="grid"`, named for its month and year. With `mode="multiple"` or `"range"` it has `aria-multiselectable`.
- Each day is a button named with its whole date, such as "Thursday, October 15th, 2026". Today's name starts with "Today", and a picked day's ends with "selected". The cell around a picked day has `aria-selected`.
- The row of day names is hidden from screen readers, because every day already says which day of the week it is.
- The month's name is a live region. When the month changes, a screen reader says the new one.
- A picked day is filled with the primary color, which has at least 3:1 contrast with what's behind it, and the number on it keeps 4.5:1. Where the browser forces its own colors, as Windows high contrast does, the fill is the system's color for something selected.
- Today has a ring around it. Color alone wouldn't tell it from the days next to it.
- A disabled day is a disabled button, so it's skipped by a screen reader's list of buttons and can't be pressed.
- A month button that can't go further stays in place with `aria-disabled`. Removing it would throw keyboard focus out of the calendar when the last month is reached.

### What you need to handle

- Say what the calendar is for. Put a heading or a label before it. The grid's own name is the month.
- Don't rely on a disabled day to explain itself. If days are unavailable for a reason, say the reason in text near the calendar.
- With `footer`, keep it to a short sentence. It's read out whenever it changes.

### What hasn't been checked

The tests check the roles, names and states that a browser passes on to a screen reader. What each screen reader then says in a grid of dates hasn't been checked by a person.

sections.heading: What it's built on
sections.markdown:
## What it's built on

The calendar is [react-day-picker](https://daypicker.dev) 10, which does the date arithmetic with [date-fns](https://date-fns.org). Both are installed with the package.

Three things are done differently from react-day-picker on its own. The styles are this library's, read from its tokens, and react-day-picker's stylesheet isn't used. The month buttons sit either side of the month's name, so that the order <kbd>Tab</kbd> goes through them is the order they're drawn in. And the calendar can be rendered on a server without marking the wrong day as today.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Open on the month people are most likely to want. For a booking that's this month. For a date of birth it isn't.
- Limit the months with `startMonth` and `endMonth` when only some dates make sense.
- Show two months for a range.

**Don't**

- Don't use an inline calendar for a date in a long form. A [date picker](page:date-picker/date-picker) takes one line.
- Don't make people page month by month to a year far away. Use `captionLayout="dropdown"`.
- Don't mark days with color alone. Say what a marked day means in text.

pages.title: DatePicker
pages.description: A date field you can type into, with a button that opens a calendar. It works with a label, the keyboard and plain forms, and opens as a sheet on a phone.

sections.markdown:
## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/date-picker @nuvui/react
```

sections.heading: Import
sections.markdown:
## Import

```tsx
import { DatePicker } from "@nuvui/date-picker";
```

The styles come from `@nuvui/date-picker/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app, after `@nuvui/react/styles.css`. [Dates](page:date-picker/index) covers that.

sections.heading: Props
sections.markdown:
## Props

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value` | `Date \| null` |  | The picked date, or `null` for none. Use it with `onValueChange`. |
| `defaultValue` | `Date \| null` |  | The date picked to begin with. |
| `onValueChange` | `((date: Date \| null) => void)` |  | Called with the new date when one is picked or typed. |
| `name` | `string` |  | The name the date is submitted under, as `yyyy-MM-dd`. Without one, nothing is submitted. |
| `calendar` | `DatePickerCalendarProps` |  | More of the calendar's own options, such as `captionLayout` and `showWeekNumber`. |
| `open` | `boolean` |  | Whether the calendar is open. Use it with `onOpenChange`. |
| `defaultOpen` | `boolean` | `false` | Whether the calendar starts out open. |
| `onOpenChange` | `((open: boolean) => void)` |  | Called when the calendar opens or closes. |
| `min` | `Date` |  | The earliest day that can be picked or typed. |
| `max` | `Date` |  | The latest day that can be picked or typed. |
| `disabledDates` | `Matcher[] \| Matcher` |  | Days that can't be picked or typed: a date, a list of them, a range, `{ dayOfWeek: [0, 6] }` for weekends, or a function that's given a date. |
| `locale` | `CalendarLocale` | `enUS` | The language of the calendar, and the order a typed date is read in. Take one from `@nuvui/date-picker/locale`. |
| `weekStartsOn` | `0 \| 1 \| 2 \| 3 \| 4 \| 5 \| 6` |  | The day a week starts on, from 0 for Sunday. Left out, it's the locale's. |
| `timeZone` | `string` |  | The time zone the days are in, as an IANA name such as `"Asia/Tokyo"`. Left out, it's the browser's. Dates are then handed back as `TZDate`s. |
| `format` | `string` | `"P"` | The pattern a typed date is read and written in, in date-fns' tokens. `"P"` is the locale's own short date, `MM/dd/yyyy` in the United States. |
| `invalidMessage` | `string` | `"Enter a valid date."` | What the browser is told when the text isn't a date, or is one that can't be picked. It's shown when a form with the field is submitted. |
| `calendarLabel` | `string` | `"Choose date"` | Accessible name of the button that opens the calendar. The picked date is read after it. |
| `title` | `string` | `"Choose date"` | Accessible name of the calendar's panel, and the heading of the sheet it opens in on a phone. |
| `closeLabel` | `string` | `"Close"` | Accessible name of the sheet's close button. |
| `form` | `string` |  | The `id` of the form the value belongs to, when the field is outside it. |
| `container` | `DocumentFragment \| Element \| null` | `document.body` | The element the calendar is rendered into. Set this when it should pick up a `data-theme` from a section of the page. |

Everything else goes to the text field, which is an `input`: `id`, `required`, `disabled`, `readOnly`, `placeholder`, `aria-label` and so on. The ref is the text field too. `className` and `style` go on the box around the field and the button.

sections.heading: Typing a date
sections.markdown:
## Typing a date

The field takes a date in the order the locale writes it. In the United States that's month, day, year, and the placeholder says so: `mm/dd/yyyy`.

- A date typed in full, such as `10/15/2026`, becomes the value at the last keystroke.
- A looser form is taken when the person leaves the field or presses <kbd>Enter</kbd>, and rewritten in full. `1/5/26` becomes `01/05/2026`.
- Text that isn't a date by then stays as it was typed, so that it can be corrected. The value becomes `null` and the field is marked invalid.
- Clearing the field clears the value.

A year of two digits is read as the nearest one to today, so `26` is 2026. To mean the year 26, write `0026`.

`format` sets another pattern, in [date-fns' tokens](https://date-fns.org/docs/format). `"yyyy-MM-dd"` suits a tool for people who work with data. `"P"`, the default, is the locale's own short date.

sections.heading: Controlling it
Earliest, latest and days ruled out
In a form
Languages
Time zones
More of the calendar
sections.markdown:
## More of the calendar

`calendar` takes the [calendar's](page:date-picker/calendar) own options for the ones the picker doesn't set: `captionLayout`, `showWeekNumber`, `showOutsideDays`, `numberOfMonths`, `labels` and the rest.

```tsx
<DatePicker
  aria-label="Date of birth"
  max={new Date()}
  calendar={{ captionLayout: "dropdown", defaultMonth: new Date(1990, 0) }}
/>
```

sections.heading: Width
sections.markdown:
## Width

The box fills its container. Set `--nuv-date-picker-width`, or a width on the element around it, to make it narrower.

sections.heading: On small screens
sections.markdown:
## On small screens

Below 640 pixels wide, the calendar opens as a sheet across the bottom of the screen, with a heading and a close button. That's the [dialog](page:components/dialog) from `@nuvui/react`. Wider than that, it opens in a [popover](page:components/popover) under the field.

The box is 44 pixels tall on a touch screen and 40 with a mouse. The field's text is 16 pixels on a touch screen, because iOS zooms the page in when a field with smaller text takes focus. A day in the calendar is 44 pixels each way.

The field has no `inputMode`. A numeric keypad on a phone has no slash or dot to type between the numbers. People on a phone mostly use the button.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### Keyboard

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Moves from the field to the button, and on. |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Space</kbd> | On the button, opens the calendar with focus on the picked day, or on today. |
| <kbd>Alt</kbd> with <kbd>↓</kbd> | In the field, opens the calendar. |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> | In the field, takes what was typed. In a form it then submits. |
| Arrow keys and the rest | In the calendar, move between days. The [calendar's page](page:date-picker/calendar#keyboard) lists them. |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Space</kbd> | On a day, picks it, closes the calendar and puts focus back on the button. |
| <kbd>Esc</kbd> | Closes the calendar, keeps the date and puts focus back on the button. |

### What the component handles

- The field is a plain text `input`, so it's read, labelled and autofilled like any other.
- The button has `aria-haspopup="dialog"` and `aria-expanded`. Its name is `calendarLabel` followed by the picked date written out, such as "Choose date, Thursday, October 15th, 2026".
- The calendar opens in a dialog named by `title`. On a phone that's a modal sheet, and the page behind is hidden from screen readers while it's open.
- Focus moves into the calendar when it opens and back to the button when it closes, however it was closed.
- Text that isn't a date sets `aria-invalid` on the field and turns the box's edge to the danger color. That happens when the person leaves the field, not while they're still typing.
- The ring that shows keyboard focus goes around the whole box.
- The calendar only animates when the visitor hasn't asked for reduced motion.

### What you need to handle

- Give the field a name. Use a `<label>` whose `htmlFor` matches the picker's `id`, a [field](page:components/field), or `aria-label`.
- The placeholder shows the pattern, and a placeholder goes away at the first keystroke. If people get the order wrong, put the pattern in the field's description as well.
- When a date is refused, say why in text. `aria-invalid` only says that something is wrong.
- Translate `calendarLabel`, `title`, `closeLabel` and `invalidMessage` with the rest of your interface, and pass a `locale`.

### What hasn't been checked

The tests check the roles, names and states that a browser passes on to a screen reader. What each screen reader then says hasn't been checked by a person.

sections.heading: CSS variables
sections.markdown:
## CSS variables

The box is an [input group](page:components/input-group), and its variables apply here too: `--nuv-input-group-height`, `--nuv-input-group-border` and the rest. The panel is a popover, so `--nuv-popover-radius` and its other variables apply to it. These are the ones the date picker adds:

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-date-picker-width` | `100%` | Width of the box. Set a length to stop it filling its container. |
| `--nuv-date-picker-separator-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of the dash between the two fields of a range. |
| `--nuv-date-picker-icon-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of the calendar icon. |
| `--nuv-date-picker-padding` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 3)` | Space between the edge of the calendar's panel and the calendar. |

The panel renders at the end of `<body>`, so set `--nuv-date-picker-padding` and the [calendar's variables](page:date-picker/calendar#css-variables) on `:root` or `body` to reach it.

sections.markdown:
## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-date-picker` | The box around the field and the button. It also has nuv-input-group. |
| `.nuv-date-picker--range` | Added to the box of a DateRangePicker. |
| `.nuv-date-picker__button` | The button that opens the calendar. It also has nuv-input-group__button. |

sections.heading: Themed sections
sections.markdown:
## Themed sections

The calendar's panel is rendered at the end of the page, so one opened from inside a `data-theme="dark"` section doesn't inherit that theme. Pass the section's element as `container` and it will.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Put a visible label above the field.
- Let people type. Someone entering a date of birth knows it and doesn't want a calendar.
- Set `min` and `max` when only some dates make sense, and say which in the description.

**Don't**

- Don't make the field read-only to force people through the calendar. That's slower, and harder with a screen reader.
- Don't use one for a date and a time together. Add a separate field for the time.
- Don't use the placeholder as the label.

Use a date range picker for a span of days: a stay, a reporting period, the dates of a leave request. sections.heading: Install
sections.markdown:
## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/date-picker @nuvui/react
```

sections.heading: Import
sections.markdown:
## Import

```tsx
import { DateRangePicker } from "@nuvui/date-picker";
```

The styles come from `@nuvui/date-picker/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app, after `@nuvui/react/styles.css`. [Dates](page:date-picker/index) covers that.

sections.heading: Props
sections.markdown:
## Props

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value` | `DateRange \| null` |  | The picked range, or `null` for none. Use it with `onValueChange`. |
| `defaultValue` | `DateRange \| null` |  | The range picked to begin with. |
| `onValueChange` | `((range: DateRange \| null) => void)` |  | Called with the new range when a day is picked or typed. While only the first day has been chosen, `to` is `undefined`. |
| `startName` | `string` |  | The name the first day is submitted under, as `yyyy-MM-dd`. |
| `endName` | `string` |  | The name the last day is submitted under, as `yyyy-MM-dd`. |
| `startLabel` | `string` | `"Start date"` | Accessible name of the field for the first day. |
| `endLabel` | `string` | `"End date"` | Accessible name of the field for the last day. |
| `orderMessage` | `string` | `"The end date is before the start date."` | What the browser is told when the last day comes before the first. |

| `max` | `Date` |  | The latest day that can be picked or typed. |
| `disabledDates` | `Matcher[] \| Matcher` |  | Days that can't be picked or typed: a date, a list of them, a range, `{ dayOfWeek: [0, 6] }` for weekends, or a function that's given a date. |
| `locale` | `CalendarLocale` | `enUS` | The language of the calendar, and the order a typed date is read in. Take one from `@nuvui/date-picker/locale`. |
| `weekStartsOn` | `0 \| 1 \| 2 \| 3 \| 4 \| 5 \| 6` |  | The day a week starts on, from 0 for Sunday. Left out, it's the locale's. |
| `timeZone` | `string` |  | The time zone the days are in, as an IANA name such as `"Asia/Tokyo"`. Left out, it's the browser's. Dates are then handed back as `TZDate`s. |

| `invalidMessage` | `string` | `"Enter a valid date."` | What the browser is told when the text isn't a date, or is one that can't be picked. It's shown when a form with the field is submitted. |

Everything else goes to both text fields, apart from `id`, which goes to the first, and `aria-label` and `aria-labelledby`, which name the group around the two. The ref is the first field.

sections.heading: The value
sections.markdown:
## The value

The value is an object with the two days, or `null` for none:

```ts
{ from: Date | undefined, to: Date | undefined }
```

`onValueChange` is called each time either day changes. After the first press in the calendar, `to` is still `undefined`. Check for both before using the range.

sections.heading: Picking a range
sections.markdown:
## Picking a range

The first press in the calendar sets the first day, and the calendar stays open. The second sets the last day and closes it. If the second day is earlier than the first, the two swap.

With a whole range already picked, the next press starts a new one. It doesn't move the nearer end. That keeps it clear when someone has finished: the calendar closes on the press that completes a range, and only then.

The calendar shows two months side by side. `numberOfMonths` changes that, and on a phone it's always one.

sections.heading: Typing a range
sections.markdown:
## Typing a range

Each field takes a date the way a [date picker's](page:date-picker/date-picker#typing-a-date) does. A last day that's before the first is refused, and so is a first day after the last. The field that was typed in is marked invalid, with `orderMessage` as the browser's message.

sections.heading: In a form
The length of a range
On small screens
sections.markdown:
## On small screens

Both fields, the dash and the button fit a 360 pixel phone with the usual margins, with a date such as `10/15/2026` in each. A longer `format` needs more room. Give the picker a line to itself there.

The calendar opens as a sheet with one month in it. The box is 44 pixels tall on a touch screen and 40 with a mouse.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### Keyboard

The keys are the [date picker's](page:date-picker/date-picker#keyboard). <kbd>Tab</kbd> goes through the first field, the second field and the button. In the calendar, the first <kbd>Enter</kbd> on a day sets the first day and the second sets the last.

### What the component handles

- The box has `role="group"` and takes the label's name. The two fields inside are named by `startLabel` and `endLabel`, so a screen reader says "Stay, group", then "Start date" and "End date".
- The button's name is `calendarLabel` followed by the days that are picked, written out.
- The calendar's grid has `aria-multiselectable`, and every day in the range has `aria-selected`.
- The days between the two ends are joined by a fill. Where the browser forces its own colors, that fill is the system's color for something selected.
- The dash between the fields is hidden from screen readers.

### What you need to handle

- Give the group a name: a [field](page:components/field), or `aria-label`. With a plain `<label>`, point `htmlFor` at the picker's `id` and name the group with `aria-labelledby`, as the first example does.
- Translate `startLabel`, `endLabel`, `orderMessage` and the strings a date picker has.
- When a range is refused for its length, say what's allowed in text.

### What hasn't been checked

The tests check the roles, names and states that a browser passes on to a screen reader. What each screen reader then says hasn't been checked by a person.

sections.heading: CSS variables and classes
sections.markdown:
## CSS variables and classes

They're the [date picker's](page:date-picker/date-picker#css-variables). The box has `nuv-date-picker--range` as well, and `--nuv-date-picker-separator-fg` colors the dash.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Name the two fields for what they are: "Check-in" and "Check-out" say more than "Start date" and "End date".
- Set `max` to today for a report on the past, and `min` to today for a booking.
- Say how long a range may be before people pick one.

**Don't**

- Don't use one where the two dates aren't a span, such as a date of issue and a date of expiry years apart. Two date pickers are clearer.
- Don't treat a range with only its first day as finished. `to` is `undefined` until the second day is picked.

pages.title: Tables
pages.description: The @nuvui/table package. Styled table elements, and a data table on TanStack Table 9 with sorting, filtering, pagination, selection, pinned and resizable columns, expanding rows, a server mode and virtual rows.

sections.heading: Install
sections.markdown:
## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/table @nuvui/react @tanstack/react-table
```

Both `@nuvui/react` and `@tanstack/react-table` are peer dependencies. The controls are built from the core's button, checkbox, input and menu. And your columns are written with TanStack's own helpers and types, so your app has to own that version: a new major of TanStack Table is then a new major of this one package, and not something that arrives inside another dependency.

This package needs TanStack Table 9. Version 8 is a different API, and [coming from version 8](page:table/migrating) says what changes.

For [virtual rows](page:table/virtualization), add `@tanstack/react-virtual` as well. It's an optional peer: nothing else in the package needs it.

sections.heading: Load the styles
sections.markdown:
## Load the styles

Import the package's stylesheet once, after the core's:

```tsx title="app/layout.tsx"
import "@nuvui/react/styles.css";
import "@nuvui/table/styles.css";
```

It reads the same tokens as every other component, so a [theme](page:theming), a preset or a density you've set applies to tables with nothing more to do.

Both files open with the same line naming the cascade layers, so the order you import them in doesn't decide which rule wins. To load one part's styles on their own, there's `@nuvui/table/css/table.css` and `@nuvui/table/css/data-table.css`. The second needs the first, and the core's button, checkbox, input, native select, dropdown menu and skeleton styles.

sections.heading: A table in two steps
Features are opt-in
What the hook adds
sections.markdown:
## What the hook adds

A table from `useDataTable` has the controls on it, so they can be placed without importing each one:

| On | Parts |
| --- | --- |
| The table | `table.Toolbar`, `table.Filter`, `table.ColumnChooser`, `table.BulkActions`, `table.Pagination` |
| A column's `header` | `header.ColumnHeader`, `header.ColumnFilter`, `header.SelectAll` |
| A column's `cell` | `cell.SelectRow`, `cell.ExpandToggle` |

The column helper is TanStack's, with two columns added: `helper.select()` for a column of checkboxes, and `helper.expand()` for a column of buttons that open a row.

Every one of these is also an export of its own, such as `DataTablePagination`, for a table that didn't come from the hook.

sections.heading: The entries
sections.markdown:
## The entries

| Import from | For |
| --- | --- |
| `@nuvui/table` | Everything except the two below. |
| `@nuvui/table/full` | The hook with all nine features. Separate because importing it brings all nine in. |
| `@nuvui/table/virtual` | The virtual table. Separate because it needs `@tanstack/react-virtual`. |
| `@nuvui/table/table` | The styled elements alone, with no TanStack code. |
| `@nuvui/table/data-table` | The data table alone. |

The package is published as ES modules only. `@tanstack/react-table` is too, so a CommonJS build would run in exactly the places an ES module can already be loaded from, and nowhere else.

sections.heading: Server components
sections.markdown:
## Server components

The styled elements can be rendered from a server component. A data table can't be made in one: the hook holds state, so the component that calls `useDataTable` has `"use client"` at the top. Fetch the rows in a server component and pass them down as a prop.

For rows that are sorted, filtered and paged by a database, see [the server mode](page:table/server).

sections.heading: What's not here
sections.markdown:
## What's not here

These are things TanStack Table can do that this package has no controls or markup for yet. A table made with those features still works, and `DataTable` draws it, without anything for them.

- **Grouping rows** under a shared value, and totals for a group.
- **Faceted filters**: the list of values a column has, with a count for each.
- **Dragging columns** into a new order.
- **Pinned rows**, and selecting cells.
- **Virtual columns.** The virtual table draws a window of rows, and all of the columns.

pages.title: Table
pages.description: The elements of a table, styled. A real table with a caption, column and row headings, a sticky header, a pinned column, and a box that scrolls sideways and can be reached from the keyboard.
pages.markdown:
# Table The elements of a table, styled. A real table with a caption, column and row headings, a sticky header, a pinned column, and a box that scrolls sideways and can be reached from the keyboard. Use these for a table you write out yourself: a price list, a comparison, the lines of an invoice. Nothing in them sorts or pages. For rows that people sort, filter or select, use a [data table](page:table/data-table), which is drawn with these same elements. ```tsx import { Table, TableBody, TableCaption, TableCell, TableContainer, TableFooter, TableHead, TableHeader, TableRow, } from "@nuvui/table"; const invoices = [ { id: "INV-001", customer: "Acme", status: "Paid", total: "$250.00" }, { id: "INV-002", customer: "Globex", status: "Pending", total: "$1,150.00" }, { id: "INV-003", customer: "Initech", status: "Overdue", total: "$350.00" }, { id: "INV-004", customer: "Umbrella", status: "Paid", total: "$450.00" }, ]; export default function Example() { return ( Invoices sent in October Invoice Customer Status Total {invoices.map((invoice) => ( {invoice.id} {invoice.customer} {invoice.status} {invoice.total} ))} Total $2,200.00
); } ``` ## Install ```sh pnpm add @nuvui/table @nuvui/react @tanstack/react-table ``` ## Import ```tsx import { Table, TableBody, TableCaption, TableCell, TableContainer, TableFooter, TableHead, TableHeader, TableRow, } from "@nuvui/table"; ``` The styles come from `@nuvui/table/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app, after `@nuvui/react/styles.css`. [Tables](page:table/index) covers that. These elements have no TanStack code in them. An app that only uses them can import from `@nuvui/table/table`, and a bundler that doesn't remove unused code then leaves the data table out. ## The parts Each part is the HTML element it's named for, with a class. It takes that element's attributes and a `ref`. | Part | Element | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | | `TableContainer` | `div` | The box the table scrolls in. | | `Table` | `table` | The table. | | `TableCaption` | `caption` | The table's name. | | `TableHeader` | `thead` | The rows of headings. | | `TableBody` | `tbody` | The rows of data. | | `TableFooter` | `tfoot` | Totals. | | `TableRow` | `tr` | A row. | | `TableHead` | `th` | A column's heading. It has `scope="col"`. | | `TableCell` | `td` | A cell. With `rowHeader` it's a `th` with `scope="row"`. | ## Props ### Table | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `striped` | `boolean` | `false` | Shade every second row of the body. | | `stickyHeader` | `boolean` | `false` | Keep the header row in view while the body scrolls under it. It sticks to the top of the nearest thing that scrolls: a `TableContainer` with a height, or the page. | | `layout` | `"auto" \| "fixed"` | `"auto"` | `"auto"` sizes each column to what's in it. `"fixed"` takes each column's width from its first row or its `col`, and is what a table with set column widths needs. | ### TableCaption | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `visuallyHidden` | `boolean` | `false` | Keep the caption for screen readers and show nothing. For a table whose heading is already on the page above it. | ### TableRow | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `selected` | `boolean` | `false` | Mark the row as picked. It gets the selected background and `data-state="selected"`. | ### TableHead and TableCell Both take these: | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `align` | `"center" \| "end" \| "start"` | `"start"` | Which side the content sits on. `"end"` is for numbers, so their digits line up. | | `pinned` | `"end" \| "start"` | | Keep the cell in view while the table scrolls sideways. Do it for every cell of the column, the header's too. With one pinned column a side that's all there is to it. With more, each one after the first needs an `inset-inline-start` or `inset-inline-end` of its own. | | `pinnedEdge` | `boolean` | `false` | Draw the line that separates pinned columns from the ones that scroll. For the last column pinned to the start and the first pinned to the end. | `TableCell` also takes `rowHeader`, which makes it the heading of its row. ## Name the table A screen reader reads a table's name when it reaches it, and lists tables by name. Give every table one. `TableCaption` is the usual way. It's drawn under the table. Where a heading above the table already says what it is, pass `visuallyHidden` to keep the caption for screen readers only, or leave the caption out and point `aria-labelledby` on the `Table` at the heading. ## Headings for rows A column's heading tells a screen reader what a cell is. A row's heading tells it whose. Mark the cell that names the row, such as the invoice number above or a person's name, with `rowHeader`. A screen reader can then say which invoice a cell belongs to as it moves down a column. ## A table wider than its space Put the table in a `TableContainer`. A table too wide for it then scrolls sideways inside the box, and the page stays as wide as the screen. While there's something to scroll, the box takes keyboard focus, and the arrow keys scroll it. Without that, someone who doesn't use a mouse or a touch screen couldn't reach the columns that are out of view. Give the box an `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` and it's also a region with that name, so a screen reader says what's being scrolled. While everything fits, the box isn't a stop for Tab. ```tsx import { Table, TableBody, TableCell, TableContainer, TableHead, TableHeader, TableRow, } from "@nuvui/table"; const months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug"]; const regions = [ "Austria", "Belgium", "Croatia", "Denmark", "Estonia", "Finland", "Germany", "Hungary", "Ireland", "Latvia", ]; export default function Example() { return ( Country {months.map((month) => ( {month} ))} {regions.map((region, row) => ( {region} {months.map((month, column) => ( {(1200 + row * 310 + column * 127).toLocaleString("en-US")} ))} ))}
); } ``` That table also keeps its headings and its first column in view: - `stickyHeader` on the `Table` keeps the header row at the top of whatever scrolls. Give the `TableContainer` a height, or a `max-block-size`, and that's the box. With no height it's the page. - `pinned="start"` on every cell of a column, the heading's too, keeps the column at the start edge. `pinnedEdge` draws the line between it and the columns that scroll. One pinned column on each side needs nothing more. A second on the same side has to start where the first one ends, so it needs an `inset-inline-start` of the first one's width. A [data table](page:table/column-pinning) measures the columns and does that for you. ## Numbers `align="end"` puts a column's content at its end edge, which lines digits up so that amounts can be compared down the column. Put it on the heading as well. The table asks the font for digits of equal width, so `1,150.00` and `250.00` line up in a font that has them. ## Density A row is at least as tall as a control: 40 pixels with a mouse, and 36 or 44 with the [density](page:theming#density) set to compact or comfortable. A cell with more than one line of text makes its row taller. On a touch screen a row is at least 44 pixels whatever the density. A checkbox or a button in a row answers a tap anywhere in 44 pixels around it, and in shorter rows those areas would overlap. `--nuv-table-row-height` sets the least height yourself, and `--nuv-table-cell-padding-x` and `--nuv-table-cell-padding-y` the padding. ## Right to left The parts use logical properties, so inside `dir="rtl"` text starts at the right, `align="end"` is the left, and `pinned="start"` pins to the right. ## Accessibility ### What the component handles - The markup is a real `table`, with `thead`, `tbody` and `tfoot`. A screen reader's table commands, such as moving down a column, work in it. - `TableHead` is a `th` with `scope="col"`, and a `TableCell` with `rowHeader` is a `th` with `scope="row"`. That's what ties every cell to its headings. - A `TableContainer` with something to scroll takes keyboard focus and scrolls with the arrow keys. Its focus ring is drawn inside the box, where it can't be clipped. - A selected row has `data-state="selected"` and a background. Where the browser forces its own colors, as Windows high contrast does, backgrounds aren't drawn, and the row gets a bar at its start edge. - Pinned cells and a sticky header are painted, so what scrolls under them doesn't show through. ### What you need to handle - Name the table, with a caption or a label. - Mark the cell that names each row with `rowHeader`. - Name a `TableContainer` that may scroll, with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`. - `selected` on a row is a look. If rows can be selected, there has to be a control that does it and says so, such as a checkbox with a label. A [data table](page:table/row-selection) has one. - Don't use a table to lay out a page. A screen reader announces it as data. ## CSS variables ```css .pricing { --nuv-table-row-height: 3.5rem; --nuv-table-header-bg: transparent; } ``` | Variable | Default | What it sets | | --- | --- | --- | | `--nuv-table-container-max-height` | `none` | The most height the box takes before its rows scroll. | | `--nuv-table-container-border-width` | `var(--nuv-border-width)` | Width of the box's border. Set it to 0 for a table inside a card. | | `--nuv-table-border` | `var(--color-border)` | Color of the lines between rows, and of the box. | | `--nuv-table-container-radius` | `var(--radius-lg)` | Corner radius of the box. | | `--nuv-table-bg` | `var(--color-surface)` | Background of the box and of a row. | | `--nuv-table-fg` | `var(--color-surface-foreground)` | Text color. | | `--nuv-table-font-size` | `var(--text-sm)` | Size of the text. | | `--nuv-table-cell-padding-y` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 1.5)` | Space above and below a cell's content. | | `--nuv-table-cell-padding-x` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 3)` | Space at the start and end of a cell. | | `--nuv-table-caption-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of the caption. | | `--nuv-table-caption-side` | `bottom` | Where the caption goes: bottom or top. | | `--nuv-table-row-bg` | `var(--nuv-table-bg, var(--color-surface))` | Background of a row. Set it on a row to give that row a color of its own. | | `--nuv-table-row-height` | `var(--nuv-touch-size)`, `var(--nuv-control-height-md)` | The least height of a row. The default is a control's height at the current density, and 44 pixels on a touch screen. | | `--nuv-table-header-bg` | `var(--color-muted)` | Background of a heading. | | `--nuv-table-header-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of a heading's text. | | `--nuv-table-last-row-border-width` | `0` | Width of the line under the last row. Zero by default, because the box has a border there. | | `--nuv-table-footer-bg` | `var(--color-muted)` | Background of the footer's rows. | | `--nuv-table-stripe-bg` | `var(--color-muted)` | Background of every second row with striped. | | `--nuv-table-row-hover-bg` | `var(--color-muted)` | Background of a row under the pointer. | | `--nuv-table-row-selected-bg` | `color-mix(in oklab, var(--color-primary) 12%, var(--color-surface))` | Background of a selected row. | ## Classes | Class | What it's on | | --- | --- | | `.nuv-table` | The table. | | `.nuv-table--fixed` | With layout="fixed". | | `.nuv-table--sticky-header` | With stickyHeader. | | `.nuv-table-container` | The box the table scrolls in. | | `.nuv-table__body` | The tbody. | | `.nuv-table__body--striped` | The tbody of a table with striped. | | `.nuv-table__caption` | The caption. | | `.nuv-table__caption--hidden` | A caption kept for screen readers only. | | `.nuv-table__cell` | A cell. | | `.nuv-table__cell--align-center` | A cell with its content in the middle. | | `.nuv-table__cell--align-end` | A cell with its content at the end. | | `.nuv-table__cell--pinned-edge` | A pinned cell with the dividing line. | | `.nuv-table__cell--pinned-end` | A cell pinned to the end. | | `.nuv-table__cell--pinned-start` | A cell pinned to the start. | | `.nuv-table__cell--row-header` | The cell that's the heading of its row. | | `.nuv-table__footer` | The tfoot. | | `.nuv-table__head` | A column's heading. | | `.nuv-table__head--align-center` | A heading with its content in the middle. | | `.nuv-table__head--align-end` | A heading with its content at the end. | | `.nuv-table__head--pinned-edge` | A pinned heading with the dividing line. | | `.nuv-table__head--pinned-end` | A heading pinned to the end. | | `.nuv-table__head--pinned-start` | A heading pinned to the start. | | `.nuv-table__row` | A row. | `nuv-table__header` is on the `thead`. It has no styles of its own and is there to hook yours on. ## Do and don't **Do** - Put every table in a `TableContainer`, so a phone can scroll it. - Align numbers to the end, headings included. - Keep a heading to a word or two. Explain it in the caption or in text near the table. **Don't** - Don't leave a table without a name. - Don't use an empty cell to mean "none" or "not applicable". Write it, so a screen reader has something to read. - Don't put more in a hand-written table than fits on a screen or two. Past that, people need to sort and search: use a [data table](page:table/data-table).

sections.heading: Install
sections.markdown:
## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/table @nuvui/react @tanstack/react-table
```

sections.heading: Import
sections.markdown:
## Import

```tsx
import {
  Table,
  TableBody,
  TableCaption,
  TableCell,
  TableContainer,
  TableFooter,
  TableHead,
  TableHeader,
  TableRow,
} from "@nuvui/table";
```

The styles come from `@nuvui/table/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app, after `@nuvui/react/styles.css`. [Tables](page:table/index) covers that.

These elements have no TanStack code in them. An app that only uses them can import from `@nuvui/table/table`, and a bundler that doesn't remove unused code then leaves the data table out.

sections.heading: The parts
sections.markdown:
## The parts

Each part is the HTML element it's named for, with a class. It takes that element's attributes and a `ref`.

| Part | Element | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TableContainer` | `div` | The box the table scrolls in. |
| `Table` | `table` | The table. |
| `TableCaption` | `caption` | The table's name. |
| `TableHeader` | `thead` | The rows of headings. |
| `TableBody` | `tbody` | The rows of data. |
| `TableFooter` | `tfoot` | Totals. |
| `TableRow` | `tr` | A row. |
| `TableHead` | `th` | A column's heading. It has `scope="col"`. |
| `TableCell` | `td` | A cell. With `rowHeader` it's a `th` with `scope="row"`. |

sections.heading: Props
sections.markdown:
## Props

### Table

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `striped` | `boolean` | `false` | Shade every second row of the body. |
| `stickyHeader` | `boolean` | `false` | Keep the header row in view while the body scrolls under it. It sticks to the top of the nearest thing that scrolls: a `TableContainer` with a height, or the page. |
| `layout` | `"auto" \| "fixed"` | `"auto"` | `"auto"` sizes each column to what's in it. `"fixed"` takes each column's width from its first row or its `col`, and is what a table with set column widths needs. |

### TableCaption

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `visuallyHidden` | `boolean` | `false` | Keep the caption for screen readers and show nothing. For a table whose heading is already on the page above it. |

### TableRow

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `selected` | `boolean` | `false` | Mark the row as picked. It gets the selected background and `data-state="selected"`. |

### TableHead and TableCell

Both take these:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `align` | `"center" \| "end" \| "start"` | `"start"` | Which side the content sits on. `"end"` is for numbers, so their digits line up. |
| `pinned` | `"end" \| "start"` |  | Keep the cell in view while the table scrolls sideways. Do it for every cell of the column, the header's too. With one pinned column a side that's all there is to it. With more, each one after the first needs an `inset-inline-start` or `inset-inline-end` of its own. |
| `pinnedEdge` | `boolean` | `false` | Draw the line that separates pinned columns from the ones that scroll. For the last column pinned to the start and the first pinned to the end. |

`TableCell` also takes `rowHeader`, which makes it the heading of its row.

sections.heading: Name the table
sections.markdown:
## Name the table

A screen reader reads a table's name when it reaches it, and lists tables by name. Give every table one.

`TableCaption` is the usual way. It's drawn under the table. Where a heading above the table already says what it is, pass `visuallyHidden` to keep the caption for screen readers only, or leave the caption out and point `aria-labelledby` on the `Table` at the heading.

sections.heading: Headings for rows
sections.markdown:
## Headings for rows

A column's heading tells a screen reader what a cell is. A row's heading tells it whose. Mark the cell that names the row, such as the invoice number above or a person's name, with `rowHeader`. A screen reader can then say which invoice a cell belongs to as it moves down a column.

sections.heading: A table wider than its space
Numbers
sections.markdown:
## Numbers

`align="end"` puts a column's content at its end edge, which lines digits up so that amounts can be compared down the column. Put it on the heading as well. The table asks the font for digits of equal width, so `1,150.00` and `250.00` line up in a font that has them.

sections.heading: Density
sections.markdown:
## Density

A row is at least as tall as a control: 40 pixels with a mouse, and 36 or 44 with the [density](page:theming#density) set to compact or comfortable. A cell with more than one line of text makes its row taller.

On a touch screen a row is at least 44 pixels whatever the density. A checkbox or a button in a row answers a tap anywhere in 44 pixels around it, and in shorter rows those areas would overlap.

`--nuv-table-row-height` sets the least height yourself, and `--nuv-table-cell-padding-x` and `--nuv-table-cell-padding-y` the padding.

sections.heading: Right to left
sections.markdown:
## Right to left

The parts use logical properties, so inside `dir="rtl"` text starts at the right, `align="end"` is the left, and `pinned="start"` pins to the right.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### What the component handles

- The markup is a real `table`, with `thead`, `tbody` and `tfoot`. A screen reader's table commands, such as moving down a column, work in it.
- `TableHead` is a `th` with `scope="col"`, and a `TableCell` with `rowHeader` is a `th` with `scope="row"`. That's what ties every cell to its headings.
- A `TableContainer` with something to scroll takes keyboard focus and scrolls with the arrow keys. Its focus ring is drawn inside the box, where it can't be clipped.
- A selected row has `data-state="selected"` and a background. Where the browser forces its own colors, as Windows high contrast does, backgrounds aren't drawn, and the row gets a bar at its start edge.
- Pinned cells and a sticky header are painted, so what scrolls under them doesn't show through.

### What you need to handle

- Name the table, with a caption or a label.
- Mark the cell that names each row with `rowHeader`.
- Name a `TableContainer` that may scroll, with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.
- `selected` on a row is a look. If rows can be selected, there has to be a control that does it and says so, such as a checkbox with a label. A [data table](page:table/row-selection) has one.
- Don't use a table to lay out a page. A screen reader announces it as data.

sections.markdown:
## CSS variables

```css
.pricing {
  --nuv-table-row-height: 3.5rem;
  --nuv-table-header-bg: transparent;
}
```

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-table-container-max-height` | `none` | The most height the box takes before its rows scroll. |
| `--nuv-table-container-border-width` | `var(--nuv-border-width)` | Width of the box's border. Set it to 0 for a table inside a card. |
| `--nuv-table-border` | `var(--color-border)` | Color of the lines between rows, and of the box. |
| `--nuv-table-container-radius` | `var(--radius-lg)` | Corner radius of the box. |
| `--nuv-table-bg` | `var(--color-surface)` | Background of the box and of a row. |
| `--nuv-table-fg` | `var(--color-surface-foreground)` | Text color. |
| `--nuv-table-font-size` | `var(--text-sm)` | Size of the text. |
| `--nuv-table-cell-padding-y` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 1.5)` | Space above and below a cell's content. |
| `--nuv-table-cell-padding-x` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 3)` | Space at the start and end of a cell. |
| `--nuv-table-caption-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of the caption. |
| `--nuv-table-caption-side` | `bottom` | Where the caption goes: bottom or top. |
| `--nuv-table-row-bg` | `var(--nuv-table-bg, var(--color-surface))` | Background of a row. Set it on a row to give that row a color of its own. |
| `--nuv-table-row-height` | `var(--nuv-touch-size)`, `var(--nuv-control-height-md)` | The least height of a row. The default is a control's height at the current density, and 44 pixels on a touch screen. |
| `--nuv-table-header-bg` | `var(--color-muted)` | Background of a heading. |
| `--nuv-table-header-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of a heading's text. |
| `--nuv-table-last-row-border-width` | `0` | Width of the line under the last row. Zero by default, because the box has a border there. |
| `--nuv-table-footer-bg` | `var(--color-muted)` | Background of the footer's rows. |
| `--nuv-table-stripe-bg` | `var(--color-muted)` | Background of every second row with striped. |
| `--nuv-table-row-hover-bg` | `var(--color-muted)` | Background of a row under the pointer. |
| `--nuv-table-row-selected-bg` | `color-mix(in oklab, var(--color-primary) 12%, var(--color-surface))` | Background of a selected row. |

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Put every table in a `TableContainer`, so a phone can scroll it.
- Align numbers to the end, headings included.
- Keep a heading to a word or two. Explain it in the caption or in text near the table.

**Don't**

- Don't leave a table without a name.
- Don't use an empty cell to mean "none" or "not applicable". Write it, so a screen reader has something to read.
- Don't put more in a hand-written table than fits on a screen or two. Past that, people need to sort and search: use a [data table](page:table/data-table).

pages.title: DataTable
pages.description: A finished table from a TanStack Table instance. Headings that sort, a search field, a column chooser, checkboxes and a pagination bar, each one there when the table has the feature for it, with loading, empty and error states.
pages.markdown:
# DataTable A finished table from a TanStack Table instance. Headings that sort, a search field, a column chooser, checkboxes and a pagination bar, each one there when the table has the feature for it, with loading, empty and error states. Use a data table for rows that people work with: sort, search, page through, select and act on. For a short table that's only read, the [table elements](page:table/table) on their own are enough. ```tsx "use client"; import { DataTable } from "@nuvui/table"; import { createColumnHelper, useDataTable } from "@nuvui/table/full"; import { type Person, people } from "./people"; const helper = createColumnHelper(); const columns = helper.columns([ helper.accessor("name", { header: "Name" }), helper.accessor("email", { header: "Email" }), helper.accessor("role", { header: "Role" }), helper.accessor("seats", { header: "Seats", meta: { align: "end" } }), ]); export default function Example() { const table = useDataTable({ columns, data: people, getRowId: (person) => person.id, }); return ; } ``` ## Install ```sh pnpm add @nuvui/table @nuvui/react @tanstack/react-table ``` ## Import ```tsx import { DataTable } from "@nuvui/table"; import { createColumnHelper, useDataTable } from "@nuvui/table/full"; ``` `@nuvui/table/full` is the hook with every feature. [Tables](page:table/index#features-are-opt-in) shows how to make one with only the features you use, and how to load the styles. ## How it fits together There are three steps, and the first two are TanStack Table's. 1. **Columns.** `helper.accessor("name", { header: "Name" })` is a column that reads `name` from each row. A `header` that's a string is all a column needs: where the column can be sorted, the heading becomes a button that sorts it. 2. **The table.** `useDataTable({ columns, data })` returns a TanStack table. It holds the sorting, the filters, the page and the selection, and works out which rows to show. 3. **`DataTable`.** It takes the table and draws it. `DataTable` looks at what the table can do and adds the controls for it: | The table has | `DataTable` adds | | --- | --- | | [Sorting](page:table/sorting) | A button in each heading that can sort. | | [A global filter](page:table/filtering) | A search field above the table. | | [Column visibility](page:table/column-visibility) | A "Columns" button above the table. | | [Pagination](page:table/pagination) | A bar under the table. | | [Row selection](page:table/row-selection) | Nothing by itself. Add `helper.select()` to the columns. | | [Column pinning](page:table/column-pinning) | Pinned columns that stay in view. | | [Column resizing](page:table/column-resizing) | A grip on each heading, with `layout="fixed"`. | | [Expanding rows](page:table/expanding) | Nothing by itself. Add `helper.expand()`, or `cell.ExpandToggle` in a cell. | ## Props | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `table` (required) | `ReactTable` | | The table, from `useDataTable` or from TanStack's own `useTable`. | | `labels` | `Partial` | | Text the table writes itself, to change or translate. | | `rowHeader` | `string` | | The id of the column that names each row, such as a person's name. Its cells become the row's heading, and the row's checkbox and expand button are named after it: "Select Ada Lovelace". | | `getRowLabel` | `((row: Row) => string)` | | A name for a row, where no one column gives it. It's used the way `rowHeader` is, for the names of the row's controls. | | `loading` | `boolean` | `false` | Rows are on their way. With none yet, the table shows placeholders. With some, it keeps them and marks itself busy. | | `error` | `ReactNode` | | The rows couldn't be loaded. A message of your own, or `true` for the standard one. It's shown in place of the rows. | | `onRetry` | `(() => void)` | | With `error`, adds a button that calls this. | What goes around the table: | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `toolbar` | `ReactNode` | | What goes above the table. Left out, it's the search field and the column chooser, where the table has those features. `false` for nothing. | | `bulkActions` | `((rows: Row[]) => ReactNode) \| ReactNode` | | Actions for the selected rows. They show in a bar above the table while anything is selected. As a function it's given the selected rows that are loaded. | | `pagination` | `ReactNode` | | What goes under the table. Left out, it's the pagination bar, where the table has pages. `false` for nothing. | | `pageSizes` | `number[]` | `[10, 20, 50, 100]` | The choices for rows per page. | And the table itself: | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `captionHidden` | `boolean` | `false` | Keep the caption for screen readers and show nothing. | | `stickyHeader` | `boolean` | `false` | Keep the header row in view while the rows scroll. Give the table a height to scroll in with `--nuv-table-container-max-height`. | | `striped` | `boolean` | `false` | Shade every second row. | | `layout` | `"auto" \| "fixed"` | `"auto"` | `"auto"` sizes each column to what's in it. `"fixed"` gives each column the width TanStack holds for it, which needs `columnSizingFeature`, and puts a grip on every column that can be resized. | | `renderDetail` | `((row: Row) => ReactNode)` | | What a row shows under itself when it's open. It's drawn under the table, or kept for screen readers with `captionHidden`. | | `aria-labelledby` | A heading above the table already names it. Pass the heading's `id`. | | `aria-label` | The name shouldn't be on show at all. | ## Name the rows `rowHeader` takes the id of the column that names each row, such as a person's name or an order number. It does two things. That column's cells become the headings of their rows, so a screen reader can say whose row a cell is in. And the row's own controls are named after it: "Select Ada Lovelace", "Show details for Ada Lovelace". Without it, a row is named by its place: "Select row 3". Where no single column names a row, pass `getRowLabel`: ```tsx `order ${row.original.number}`} /> ``` ## Columns A column is TanStack's. These are the parts of one that the data table reads. `header` as a string is the heading, and the column's name in the column chooser and for screen readers. As a function it draws the heading itself, and is given the registered parts: ```tsx helper.accessor("email", { meta: { label: "Email" }, header: ({ header }) => ( <> ), }); ``` `header.ColumnHeader` is the heading with its sort button. A column whose `header` is a function has no text for the chooser to list, so give it a `meta.label`. Without one, the column's id is used. `cell` is what a cell shows. Left out, it's the row's value as text, which suits a name. A number, a date or a status wants more, and `cell` is given the value to draw it from: ```tsx import { Badge, FormattedNumber } from "@nuvui/react"; // A date with no time is written as UTC, or a reader west of Greenwich // sees the day before. const day = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "medium", timeZone: "UTC", }); helper.columns([ helper.accessor("total", { header: "Total", meta: { align: "end" }, cell: (cell) => , }), helper.accessor("placed", { header: "Placed", cell: (cell) => ( {day.format(cell.getValue())} ), }), helper.accessor("status", { header: "Status", cell: (cell) => {cell.getValue()}, }), ]); ``` Sorting and filtering go by the value and not by what `cell` draws, so a total sorts as a number however it's written. `cell.row.original` is the whole row, for a cell that needs more than its own value. `meta` takes three things: | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `label` | `string` | | The column's name in the column chooser and for screen readers. A column whose `header` is a string doesn't need one. | | `align` | `"center" \| "end" \| "start"` | | Which side the column's cells and heading sit on. | | `control` | `boolean` | | The column only holds a control, such as a checkbox. It's kept as narrow as the control. | With `@nuvui/table/full`, `meta` is typed. In a hook of your own, register the type to get the same: ```tsx import type { DataTableColumnMeta } from "@nuvui/table"; import { metaHelper, tableFeatures } from "@tanstack/react-table"; tableFeatures({ columnMeta: metaHelper(), }); ``` A `footer` on any column adds a footer row. ## Loading, empty and failed ```tsx "use client"; import { ToggleGroup, ToggleGroupItem } from "@nuvui/react"; import { DataTable } from "@nuvui/table"; import { createColumnHelper, useDataTable } from "@nuvui/table/full"; import { useState } from "react"; import { type Person, people } from "./people"; const helper = createColumnHelper(); const columns = helper.columns([ helper.accessor("name", { header: "Name" }), helper.accessor("team", { header: "Team" }), helper.accessor("role", { header: "Role" }), ]); const rows = people.slice(0, 4); const none: Person[] = []; type State = "rows" | "first load" | "reload" | "empty" | "error"; export default function Example() { const [state, setState] = useState("first load"); const table = useDataTable({ columns, data: state === "rows" || state === "reload" ? rows : none, }); return (
