With rows already there, it keeps them, so a reload doesn't flash the table empty. Either way the table has `aria-busy`. - **No rows** shows "No rows.", or what you pass as `empty`. When a filter is why there are none, it says "No rows match." with a button that clears the filters. - **`error`** shows a message in place of the rows, and reads it out at once. Pass a message of your own or `true` for the standard one. With `onRetry` there's a "Try again" button. ## Arrange the parts yourself `DataTable` is a `DataTableRoot` with four parts in it: the toolbar, the bar for selected rows, the table and the pagination bar. To put them somewhere else, or something else between them, use the root and place the parts: ```tsx "use client"; import { DataTableContent, DataTablePagination, DataTableRoot, } from "@nuvui/table"; import { createColumnHelper, useDataTable } from "@nuvui/table/full"; import { type Person, people } from "./people"; const helper = createColumnHelper(); const columns = helper.columns([ helper.accessor("name", { header: "Name" }), helper.accessor("team", { header: "Team" }), helper.accessor("role", { header: "Role" }), ]); export default function Example() { const table = useDataTable({ columns, data: people, initialState: { pagination: { pageIndex: 0, pageSize: 5 } }, }); return (

Every part has to be inside one. | | `DataTableContent` | The table. Takes the name, `stickyHeader`, `striped`, `layout`, `renderDetail`, `empty` and `loadingRows`. | | `DataTableToolbar` | A row for controls. Empty, it holds the search field and the column chooser. | | `DataTableFilter` | The search field. | | `DataTableColumnFilter` | A text filter for one column. | | `DataTableColumnChooser` | The "Columns" button. | | `DataTableBulkActions` | The bar that shows while rows are selected. | | `DataTablePagination` | The pagination bar. | | `DataTableColumnHeader` | A heading with its sort button. | | `DataTableSelectAll` and `DataTableSelectRow` | The checkboxes. | | `DataTableExpandToggle` | The button that opens a row. | On a table from the hook the same parts are there as `table.Filter`, `table.Pagination` and so on. The `toolbar` and `pagination` props of `DataTable` cover the common changes without going this far. Pass your own, or `false` for none. ## Text and translation Everything the data table writes itself is in `labels`: the button names, "No rows.", "Page 2 of 5", and what's read out after a sort. Pass the ones to change: ```tsx `Seite ${page} von ${pages}`, selected: (count) => `${count} ausgewählt`, }} /> ``` | Prop | Type | Default | What it's for | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `search` when there are none. | | `noMatches` (required) | `string` | | Shown in place of rows when a filter leaves none. | | `clearFilters` (required) | `string` | | | | `error` (required) | `string` | | checkbox of a table with pages. | | `selectRow` (required) | `(row: string) => string` | | | | `rowName` (required) | `(position: number) => string` | | A row's name when it has no `rowHeader` column: after a filter changes how many rows there are. | Numbers in the labels are plain. Format them in your own functions if your language groups digits. ## On small screens The toolbar wraps, and the search field takes a row of its own. The pagination bar puts the page buttons on their own row, spread across the width. The table scrolls sideways inside its box, and the box can be scrolled from the keyboard. A table with many columns is hard to use on a phone however it scrolls. [Pin](page:table/column-pinning) the column that names the row, so it stays in view, and [hide](page:table/column-visibility) the columns that matter least. On a touch screen every control is 44 pixels: the sort buttons, the page buttons and the area around each checkbox. ## Accessibility ### Keyboard Every control is a button, a checkbox, a text field or a select, and works the way those do: Tab to reach it, Enter or Space to use it. Each feature's page has the keys that are particular to it. | Key | Where | What it does | | --- | --- | --- | | Enter or Space | A heading | Sorts by the column. | | Shift with Enter | A heading | Adds the column to the sort. | | Space | A checkbox | Selects the row. | | ← → ↑ ↓ | The table's box, when it scrolls | Scrolls it. | | ← and → | A column's grip | Makes the column narrower or wider. | ### What the component handles - The table is a real `table` with a name, column headings with `scope`, and a heading for each row when `rowHeader` is set. - A sorted column's heading has `aria-sort`. With a sort by several columns, the first has it. - Every checkbox, expand button and grip has a name that says which row or column it's for. - A sort, a filter, a change of page and a change in the selection are each read out by a polite live region: "Sorted by Name, ascending", "4 rows", "Page 2 of 5", "3 selected". With a [server](page:table/server) doing the work, the message waits for the rows to arrive. - A page button with no page to go to keeps keyboard focus and is marked `aria-disabled`. A disabled button would drop focus onto the page the moment "Next" reached the last page. - When the bar for selected rows goes, because the selection was cleared from inside it, focus moves to the table's first checkbox. - An error is in an alert, so it's read out when it appears. - The heading of a column of checkboxes isn't a column heading, so a screen reader doesn't read "Select all rows" before every cell under it. ### What you need to handle - Name the table, and set `rowHeader` or `getRowLabel`. - Give a column whose `header` is a function a `meta.label`. - What you put in a cell is yours. A button made of an icon needs a name that says which row it acts on. - Translate `labels` with the rest of your interface. ### What hasn't been checked The tests check the roles, names and states that a browser passes on to a screen reader, and that the live region's text changes. What each screen reader then says, and when, hasn't been checked by a person. ## CSS variables The table inside is made of the [table elements](page:table/table#css-variables), and their variables apply here: `--nuv-table-row-height`, `--nuv-table-header-bg` and the rest. Read it, don't set it. | | `--nuv-data-table-expand-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of that button's arrow. | | `--nuv-data-table-detail-bg` | `var(--color-background)` | Background of a row's open panel. | | `--nuv-data-table-detail-padding` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 4)` | Padding of that panel. | | `--nuv-data-table-message-padding` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 10)` | Space above and below what's shown in place of rows. | | `--nuv-data-table-message-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of that text. | | `--nuv-data-table-pagination-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Text color of the pagination bar. | ## Classes | Class | What it's on | | --- | --- | | `.nuv-data-table` | The root element. | | `.nuv-data-table__bulk` | The bar for selected rows. | | `.nuv-data-table__bulk-actions` | The element around your actions. | | `.nuv-data-table__bulk-count` | How many are selected. | | `.nuv-data-table__cell--control` | A cell of a column that only holds a control. | | `.nuv-data-table__column-filter` | A column's filter field. | | `.nuv-data-table__detail` | The panel's cell. | | `.nuv-data-table__detail-row` | The row that holds an open panel. | | `.nuv-data-table__expand` | The button that opens a row. | | `.nuv-data-table__expand-gap` | The space a row with nothing to open has in its place. | | `.nuv-data-table__expand-icon` | The arrow in the button. | | `.nuv-data-table__filter` | The search field. | | `.nuv-data-table__head--resizable` | A heading with a grip. | | `.nuv-data-table__heading` | The text of a heading. | | `.nuv-data-table__loading-row` | A placeholder row. | | `.nuv-data-table__message` | Its cell. | | `.nuv-data-table__message-row` | The row shown in place of rows. | | `.nuv-data-table__page` | The page it is. | | `.nuv-data-table__page-button` | A page button. | | `.nuv-data-table__page-icon` | The arrow in it. | | `.nuv-data-table__page-range` | Which rows are showing, out of how many. | | `.nuv-data-table__page-size` | The rows per page label and select. | | `.nuv-data-table__pages` | The page buttons and the page between them. | | `.nuv-data-table__pagination` | The pagination bar. | | `.nuv-data-table__resize` | The grip. | | `.nuv-data-table__sort` | A heading's sort button. | | `.nuv-data-table__sort-icon` | The arrows in it. | | `.nuv-data-table__sort-index` | The number that shows a column's place in a sort by several. | | `.nuv-data-table__status` | The live region. It's in the page and not on show. | | `.nuv-data-table__toolbar` | The row of controls above the table. | | `.nuv-data-table__toolbar-gap` | The space that pushes the column chooser to the end. | `nuv-data-table__container` is on the table's box, `nuv-data-table__chooser` on the "Columns" button and `nuv-data-table__page-size-label` on the rows per page label. They have no styles of their own and are there to hook yours on. ## What it's built on [TanStack Table](https://tanstack.com/table) 9 holds the state and works out the rows. The markup, the styles, the controls and the accessibility on this page are this package's. The controls are `@nuvui/react`'s button, checkbox, input, native select and dropdown menu. ## Do and don't **Do** - Set `getRowId` when rows have an id. Selection and open rows are then kept by id, and survive a sort or a reload. - Keep `columns` and `data` the same arrays between renders, unless they've changed. - Use the [server mode](page:table/server) once there are more rows than you'd send to a browser in one go. **Don't** - Don't put a table inside a row's cell. Use a [panel under the row](page:table/expanding). - Don't hide the pagination bar while the rows run past one page. The rows after the first page couldn't be reached. A table whose rows all fit on one page, ten unless you set another size, can leave the bar out, as the short examples on these pages do. - Don't rely on color in a cell to carry meaning. Write the status.

sections.heading: Install
sections.markdown:
## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/table @nuvui/react @tanstack/react-table
```

sections.heading: Import
How it fits together
sections.markdown:
## How it fits together

There are three steps, and the first two are TanStack Table's.

1. **Columns.** `helper.accessor("name", { header: "Name" })` is a column that reads `name` from each row. A `header` that's a string is all a column needs: where the column can be sorted, the heading becomes a button that sorts it.
2. **The table.** `useDataTable({ columns, data })` returns a TanStack table. It holds the sorting, the filters, the page and the selection, and works out which rows to show.
3. **`DataTable`.** It takes the table and draws it.

`DataTable` looks at what the table can do and adds the controls for it:

| The table has | `DataTable` adds |
| --- | --- |
| [Sorting](page:table/sorting) | A button in each heading that can sort. |
| [A global filter](page:table/filtering) | A search field above the table. |
| [Column visibility](page:table/column-visibility) | A "Columns" button above the table. |
| [Pagination](page:table/pagination) | A bar under the table. |
| [Row selection](page:table/row-selection) | Nothing by itself. Add `helper.select()` to the columns. |
| [Column pinning](page:table/column-pinning) | Pinned columns that stay in view. |
| [Column resizing](page:table/column-resizing) | A grip on each heading, with `layout="fixed"`. |
| [Expanding rows](page:table/expanding) | Nothing by itself. Add `helper.expand()`, or `cell.ExpandToggle` in a cell. |

sections.heading: Props
sections.markdown:
## Props

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `table` (required) | `ReactTable<TFeatures, TData, any>` |  | The table, from `useDataTable` or from TanStack's own `useTable`. |
| `labels` | `Partial<DataTableLabels>` |  | Text the table writes itself, to change or translate. |
| `rowHeader` | `string` |  | The id of the column that names each row, such as a person's name. Its cells become the row's heading, and the row's checkbox and expand button are named after it: "Select Ada Lovelace". |
| `getRowLabel` | `((row: Row<TFeatures, TData>) => string)` |  | A name for a row, where no one column gives it. It's used the way `rowHeader` is, for the names of the row's controls. |
| `loading` | `boolean` | `false` | Rows are on their way. With none yet, the table shows placeholders. With some, it keeps them and marks itself busy. |
| `error` | `ReactNode` |  | The rows couldn't be loaded. A message of your own, or `true` for the standard one. It's shown in place of the rows. |
| `onRetry` | `(() => void)` |  | With `error`, adds a button that calls this. |

What goes around the table:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `toolbar` | `ReactNode` |  | What goes above the table. Left out, it's the search field and the column chooser, where the table has those features. `false` for nothing. |
| `bulkActions` | `((rows: Row<TFeatures, TData>[]) => ReactNode) \| ReactNode` |  | Actions for the selected rows. They show in a bar above the table while anything is selected. As a function it's given the selected rows that are loaded. |
| `pagination` | `ReactNode` |  | What goes under the table. Left out, it's the pagination bar, where the table has pages. `false` for nothing. |
| `pageSizes` | `number[]` | `[10, 20, 50, 100]` | The choices for rows per page. |

And the table itself:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `captionHidden` | `boolean` | `false` | Keep the caption for screen readers and show nothing. |
| `stickyHeader` | `boolean` | `false` | Keep the header row in view while the rows scroll. Give the table a height to scroll in with `--nuv-table-container-max-height`. |
| `striped` | `boolean` | `false` | Shade every second row. |
| `layout` | `"auto" \| "fixed"` | `"auto"` | `"auto"` sizes each column to what's in it. `"fixed"` gives each column the width TanStack holds for it, which needs `columnSizingFeature`, and puts a grip on every column that can be resized. |
| `renderDetail` | `((row: Row<TFeatures, TData>) => ReactNode)` |  | What a row shows under itself when it's open. With this set, a row can be opened if `getRowCanExpand` says so. |
| `empty` | `ReactNode` |  | Shown in place of rows when there are none. |
| `loadingRows` | `number` | `the page size, up to 10` | How many placeholder rows to show while the first rows load. |
| `className` | `string` |  |  |

A data table also needs a name. Pass one of `caption`, `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`. TypeScript reports a table with none of them.

| Prop | When |
| --- | --- |
| `caption` | Nothing else on the page names the table. It's drawn under the table, or kept for screen readers with `captionHidden`. |
| `aria-labelledby` | A heading above the table already names it. Pass the heading's `id`. |
| `aria-label` | The name shouldn't be on show at all. |

sections.heading: Name the rows
sections.markdown:
## Name the rows

`rowHeader` takes the id of the column that names each row, such as a person's name or an order number. It does two things. That column's cells become the headings of their rows, so a screen reader can say whose row a cell is in. And the row's own controls are named after it: "Select Ada Lovelace", "Show details for Ada Lovelace".

Without it, a row is named by its place: "Select row 3". Where no single column names a row, pass `getRowLabel`:

```tsx
<DataTable
  table={table}
  caption="Orders"
  getRowLabel={(row) => `order ${row.original.number}`}
/>
```

## Text and translation

Everything the data table writes itself is in `labels`: the button names, "No rows.", "Page 2 of 5", and what's read out after a sort. Pass the ones to change:

  table={table}
  caption="Personen"
  labels={{
    search: "Suchen",
    columns: "Spalten",
    rowsPerPage: "Zeilen pro Seite",
    page: (page, pages) => `Seite ${page} von ${pages}`,
    selected: (count) => `${count} ausgewählt`,

| `rowsPerPage` (required) | `string` |  |  |
| `pageRange` (required) | `(from: number, to: number, total: number) => string` |  | "21-40 of 143". |
| `page` (required) | `(page: number, pages: number) => string` |  |  |
| `firstPage` (required) | `string` |  |  |
| `previousPage` (required) | `string` |  |  |
| `nextPage` (required) | `string` |  |  |
| `lastPage` (required) | `string` |  |  |
| `resizeColumn` (required) | `(column: string) => string` |  |  |
| `filterColumn` (required) | `(column: string) => string` |  |  |
| `sortedAscending` (required) | `(column: string) => string` |  | Read out after a sort. |
| `sortedDescending` (required) | `(column: string) => string` |  |  |
| `sortCleared` (required) | `string` |  |  |
| `results` (required) | `(count: number) => string` |  | Read out after a filter changes how many rows there are. |

Numbers in the labels are plain. Format them in your own functions if your language groups digits.

sections.heading: On small screens
sections.markdown:
## On small screens

The toolbar wraps, and the search field takes a row of its own. The pagination bar puts the page buttons on their own row, spread across the width. The table scrolls sideways inside its box, and the box can be scrolled from the keyboard.

A table with many columns is hard to use on a phone however it scrolls. [Pin](page:table/column-pinning) the column that names the row, so it stays in view, and [hide](page:table/column-visibility) the columns that matter least.

On a touch screen every control is 44 pixels: the sort buttons, the page buttons and the area around each checkbox.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### Keyboard

Every control is a button, a checkbox, a text field or a select, and works the way those do: <kbd>Tab</kbd> to reach it, <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Space</kbd> to use it. Each feature's page has the keys that are particular to it.

| Key | Where | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Space</kbd> | A heading | Sorts by the column. |
| <kbd>Shift</kbd> with <kbd>Enter</kbd> | A heading | Adds the column to the sort. |
| <kbd>Space</kbd> | A checkbox | Selects the row. |
| <kbd>←</kbd> <kbd>→</kbd> <kbd>↑</kbd> <kbd>↓</kbd> | The table's box, when it scrolls | Scrolls it. |
| <kbd>←</kbd> and <kbd>→</kbd> | A column's grip | Makes the column narrower or wider. |

### What the component handles

- The table is a real `table` with a name, column headings with `scope`, and a heading for each row when `rowHeader` is set.
- A sorted column's heading has `aria-sort`. With a sort by several columns, the first has it.
- Every checkbox, expand button and grip has a name that says which row or column it's for.
- A sort, a filter, a change of page and a change in the selection are each read out by a polite live region: "Sorted by Name, ascending", "4 rows", "Page 2 of 5", "3 selected". With a [server](page:table/server) doing the work, the message waits for the rows to arrive.
- A page button with no page to go to keeps keyboard focus and is marked `aria-disabled`. A disabled button would drop focus onto the page the moment "Next" reached the last page.
- When the bar for selected rows goes, because the selection was cleared from inside it, focus moves to the table's first checkbox.
- An error is in an alert, so it's read out when it appears.
- The heading of a column of checkboxes isn't a column heading, so a screen reader doesn't read "Select all rows" before every cell under it.

### What you need to handle

- Name the table, and set `rowHeader` or `getRowLabel`.
- Give a column whose `header` is a function a `meta.label`.
- What you put in a cell is yours. A button made of an icon needs a name that says which row it acts on.
- Translate `labels` with the rest of your interface.

### What hasn't been checked

The tests check the roles, names and states that a browser passes on to a screen reader, and that the live region's text changes. What each screen reader then says, and when, hasn't been checked by a person.

sections.heading: CSS variables
sections.markdown:
## CSS variables

The table inside is made of the [table elements](page:table/table#css-variables), and their variables apply here: `--nuv-table-row-height`, `--nuv-table-header-bg` and the rest. These are the data table's own:

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-data-table-gap` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 3)` | Space between the toolbar, the table and the pagination bar. |
| `--nuv-data-table-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Text color of the toolbar and the bars. |
| `--nuv-data-table-filter-width` | `16rem` | Width of the search field from the sm breakpoint up. |
| `--nuv-data-table-column-filter-min-width` | `6rem` | The least width of a column's filter field. |
| `--nuv-data-table-bulk-border` | `var(--color-border)` | Border color of the bar for selected rows. |
| `--nuv-data-table-bulk-radius` | `var(--radius-lg)` | Corner radius of that bar. |
| `--nuv-data-table-bulk-bg` | `var(--color-muted)` | Background of that bar. |
| `--nuv-data-table-sort-hover-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Color of a heading's sort button under the pointer. |
| `--nuv-data-table-sorted-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Color of the heading of a sorted column. |
| `--nuv-data-table-resize-color` | `var(--color-border-strong)` | Color of the line on a column's grip. |
| `--nuv-data-table-resize-active-color` | `var(--color-primary)` | Color of that line under the pointer and while the column is being resized. |
| `--nuv-data-table-expand-size` | `1.5rem` | Width and height of the button that opens a row. |
| `--nuv-data-table-indent` | `1.25rem` | How far each level of a tree is indented. |
| `--nuv-data-table-depth` | `0` | Set by the component on each expand button: how deep its row is in a tree. Read it, don't set it. |
| `--nuv-data-table-expand-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of that button's arrow. |
| `--nuv-data-table-detail-bg` | `var(--color-background)` | Background of a row's open panel. |
| `--nuv-data-table-detail-padding` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 4)` | Padding of that panel. |
| `--nuv-data-table-message-padding` | `calc(var(--spacing) * 10)` | Space above and below what's shown in place of rows. |
| `--nuv-data-table-message-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of that text. |
| `--nuv-data-table-pagination-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Text color of the pagination bar. |

sections.markdown:
## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-data-table` | The root element. |

| `.nuv-data-table__expand` | The button that opens a row. |
| `.nuv-data-table__expand-gap` | The space a row with nothing to open has in its place. |
| `.nuv-data-table__expand-icon` | The arrow in the button. |
| `.nuv-data-table__filter` | The search field. |
| `.nuv-data-table__head--resizable` | A heading with a grip. |
| `.nuv-data-table__heading` | The text of a heading. |
| `.nuv-data-table__loading-row` | A placeholder row. |
| `.nuv-data-table__message` | Its cell. |

| `.nuv-data-table__pages` | The page buttons and the page between them. |

`nuv-data-table__container` is on the table's box, `nuv-data-table__chooser` on the "Columns" button and `nuv-data-table__page-size-label` on the rows per page label. They have no styles of their own and are there to hook yours on.

sections.heading: What it's built on
sections.markdown:
## What it's built on

[TanStack Table](https://tanstack.com/table) 9 holds the state and works out the rows. The markup, the styles, the controls and the accessibility on this page are this package's. The controls are `@nuvui/react`'s button, checkbox, input, native select and dropdown menu.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Set `getRowId` when rows have an id. Selection and open rows are then kept by id, and survive a sort or a reload.
- Keep `columns` and `data` the same arrays between renders, unless they've changed.
- Use the [server mode](page:table/server) once there are more rows than you'd send to a browser in one go.

**Don't**

- Don't put a table inside a row's cell. Use a [panel under the row](page:table/expanding).
- Don't hide the pagination bar while the rows run past one page. The rows after the first page couldn't be reached. A table whose rows all fit on one page, ten unless you set another size, can leave the bar out, as the short examples on these pages do.
- Don't rely on color in a cell to carry meaning. Write the status.

pages.title: Sorting
pages.description: Sort a data table by clicking a heading. Ascending, descending and off, a sort by several columns with Shift, aria-sort on the heading, and a message read out after each sort.

sections.heading: What to register
Which columns sort
The order of the presses
sections.markdown:
## The order of the presses

Text sorts from A to Z first. Numbers sort from the largest first. Both are TanStack's defaults. Set `sortDescFirst` on a column, or on the table, to choose.

The third press takes the sort off. For a table that should always be sorted by something, pass `enableSortingRemoval: false` to the hook, and the presses go back and forth between the two directions.

sections.heading: Sorted to begin with
By several columns
sections.markdown:
## By several columns

Hold <kbd>Shift</kbd> and press a second heading to sort by it within the first. Each sorted heading then shows a number for its place in the order. A press without <kbd>Shift</kbd> goes back to one column.

`enableMultiSort: false` on the table turns this off.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### Keyboard

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Moves to the next heading that sorts. |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Space</kbd> | Sorts by the column, reverses the sort, then takes it off. |
| <kbd>Shift</kbd> with <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Space</kbd> | Adds the column to the sort. |

### What the component handles

- The heading is a `button` inside the `th`, so it's in the tab order and a screen reader says it can be pressed.
- The `th` of the sorted column has `aria-sort="ascending"` or `"descending"`. With several sorted columns only the first has it, since a table may only name one.
- After a sort, a polite live region says "Sorted by Name, ascending", or "Sorting cleared".
- The arrows are decoration, hidden from screen readers. Both show on a heading that isn't sorted, and one on a heading that is, so the state isn't carried by color.
- On a touch screen the button is 44 pixels tall.
- <kbd>Shift</kbd> counts for a press from the keyboard as it does for a click. Firefox doesn't pass it on by itself, so the component does.

### What you need to handle

- Don't sort the rows yourself as well. With `manualSorting`, the table shows the rows in the order you give them.
- If the order matters to what a row means, such as a ranking, say so in a column. A screen reader user moving through cells doesn't see the row's position.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Turn sorting off for columns where an order means nothing: a column of buttons, a description.
- Start a table sorted the way most people want it.

**Don't**

- Don't sort a table with a few rows that are already in a meaningful order.
- Don't expect a sort by several columns to be found. Say it's there if it matters.

pages.title: Filtering
pages.description: Filter a data table with a search field over every column, a filter on one column, or both. With a debounce, a count read out for screen readers, and a way back when nothing matches.

sections.heading: What to register
The search field
sections.markdown:
## The search field

A table with the global filter gets a search field above it. It matches text anywhere in a column, ignoring case, in every column whose values are text or numbers.

To leave a column out of the search, set `enableGlobalFilter: false` on it.

`DataTableFilter`, or `table.Filter`, is the field on its own, for a toolbar you lay out yourself. It takes an input's props, so `placeholder` and `aria-label` can be changed, and:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `debounce` | `number` | `0` | How long to wait after the last keystroke before filtering, in milliseconds. Set it when each change asks a server. |

sections.heading: Filtering one column
When nothing matches
sections.markdown:
## When nothing matches

The table says "No rows match." and shows a "Clear filters" button, which empties the search field and takes off every column filter. Without it, someone who's filtered everything away has to work out which filter did it.

sections.heading: Back to the first page
sections.markdown:
## Back to the first page

When a filter changes, the table goes back to its first page. The fourth page of the old results may not exist in the new ones. TanStack does this when it does the paging. With a server doing it, [`useDataTableRequest`](page:table/server) does the same.

sections.heading: Filtered to begin with
Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### What the component handles

- The search field is an `input` of type `search` named "Search". A column's filter is named for its column.
- After a filter changes, a polite live region says how many rows are left: "4 rows". With pages, that's the count across all of them.
- "No rows match." is in the table, in a cell that spans it, so it's found where the rows would be.

### What you need to handle

- A filter control of your own needs a label: an `aria-label`, or a visible one.
- Set `debounce` on the search field when each change is a request. Around 300 milliseconds is usual. Without it, the count is read out after every key.
- Show which filters are on. A select that says "Admin" does. A filter set from somewhere else on the page, with nothing showing it near the table, leaves people wondering where the rows went.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Use the search field for "find this one", and column filters for "show me this kind".
- Use a control that fits the column: a select for a few fixed values, a text field for names.

**Don't**

- Don't put a filter in every heading by default. It makes the header tall and is rarely used on most columns.
- Don't filter on a formatted value. Filter the value the column reads, and format it in `cell`.

pages.title: Table pagination
pages.description: Split a data table into pages. A bar with rows per page, which rows are showing out of how many, and buttons for the first, previous, next and last page that keep keyboard focus.

sections.heading: What to register
The page size
The bar
sections.markdown:
## The bar

`DataTablePagination`, or `table.Pagination`, is the bar on its own:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pageSizes` | `number[]` | `[10, 20, 50, 100]` | The choices for rows per page. The size the table has now is added if it isn't one of them. Pass an empty list to leave the select out. |

It reads everything else from the table. `pagination={false}` on `DataTable` leaves it out, and `pagination={<Something />}` puts your own in its place. A bar of your own can call `table.nextPage()`, `table.setPageIndex(3)` and the rest of [TanStack's pagination methods](https://tanstack.com/table).

sections.heading: What resets the page
sections.markdown:
## What resets the page

A new sort or a new filter goes back to the first page. So does new `data`. To stay on the page when the data is replaced, as after saving an edit to a row, pass `autoResetPageIndex: false` to the hook. You then have to deal with a page that no longer exists, for instance after the last row on the last page is deleted.

sections.heading: Pages or a long scroll
sections.markdown:
## Pages or a long scroll

Pages suit a table people look things up in: they give a place to come back to, and the page stays light. For a table people scan from top to bottom, such as a log, [virtual rows](page:table/virtualization) keep everything in one scroll.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### Keyboard

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Moves through the select and the four buttons. |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Space</kbd> | On a button, goes to that page. |
| <kbd>↑</kbd> and <kbd>↓</kbd> | On the select, changes the rows per page. |

### What the component handles

- The bar is a group named "Pagination". It isn't a `nav`: these are a table's controls, not links to other places, and a page with two tables would have two landmarks with the same name.
- Each button is named: "First page", "Previous page", "Next page", "Last page".
- A button with no page to go to has `aria-disabled` and stays where it is, with keyboard focus if it had it. A disabled button would drop focus onto the page the moment "Next" reached the last page, and the next <kbd>Tab</kbd> would start from the top.
- After a change of page, a polite live region says "Page 2 of 5".
- "Rows per page" is a label for its select, and the select is the browser's own, which opens the system picker on a phone.
- The arrows turn around in a right-to-left layout.

### What you need to handle

- Translate the six labels: `pagination`, `rowsPerPage`, `firstPage`, `previousPage`, `nextPage`, `lastPage`, and the two functions `page` and `pageRange`.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Offer page sizes that suit the rows. Ten tall rows fill a screen. Fifty short ones do too.
- Keep the bar directly under the table.

**Don't**

- Don't page a table that fits on one page. A table from `@nuvui/table/full` can pass `pagination={false}`, with a page size that holds every row. The size is ten unless you set another, so a table that can grow past ten sets `initialState.pagination.pageSize` as well.
- Don't use pages for a table that has to be compared from top to bottom.

pages.title: Row selection
pages.description: Select rows in a data table with a checkbox on each row and one for all of them, select a range with Shift, and act on the selection from a bar that shows while anything is selected.

sections.heading: What to register
The checkbox column
sections.markdown:
## The checkbox column

```tsx
const columns = helper.columns([
  helper.select(),
  helper.accessor("name", { header: "Name" }),
]);
```

`helper.select()` is a column with `DataTableSelectAll` in its heading and `DataTableSelectRow` in each cell. It can't be sorted, hidden or resized. Pass it options to change that or its `id`, which is `"select"`.

To put the checkbox in a column of your own, use the parts: `cell.SelectRow` in a `cell`, and `header.SelectAll` in a `header`.

sections.heading: Give rows an id
Acting on the selection
sections.markdown:
## Acting on the selection

`bulkActions` on `DataTable` is what the bar holds: usually a button or two. The bar is there while anything is selected, says how many rows that is, and has a button that clears the selection.

As a function, `bulkActions` is given the selected rows:

```tsx
<DataTable
  table={table}
  caption="People"
  bulkActions={(rows) => (
    <Button size="sm" onClick={() => exportPeople(rows.map((row) => row.original))}>
      Export
    </Button>
  )}
/>
```

Those are the selected rows the table has loaded. With a [server](page:table/server) doing the paging, rows selected on other pages aren't in the browser, so they aren't in that list. `table.getSelectedRowIds()` has every selected id, whichever page it's on. Send the ids to the server and let it find the rows.

The table doesn't forget a row because it's gone from `data`. After deleting the selected rows, clear the selection with `table.resetRowSelection(true)`, as the example does.

sections.heading: A range
sections.markdown:
## A range

Click one checkbox, hold <kbd>Shift</kbd> and click another: every row between them takes the state of the second. It works across pages when the table does its own paging.

sections.heading: All of them
sections.markdown:
## All of them

The heading's checkbox selects the rows on the page, and is named "Select all rows on this page". In a table without pagination it selects every row and is named "Select all rows". It shows a dash while some of them are selected and not all.

For "select all 4,312 results", across pages the browser hasn't loaded, there's nothing in the table to tick. Keep that as a flag of your own and send it to the server with the filters.

sections.heading: Which rows can be selected
Selected to begin with
sections.markdown:
## Selected to begin with

```tsx
initialState: { rowSelection: { "person-2": true } }
```

To hold the selection yourself, pass `state: { rowSelection }` and `onRowSelectionChange` together.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### Keyboard

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Moves to the next checkbox. |
| <kbd>Space</kbd> | Selects the row, or all rows from the heading. |
| <kbd>Shift</kbd> with <kbd>Space</kbd> | Selects the range from the last row selected to this one. |

### What the component handles

- Each checkbox is named for its row: "Select Ada Lovelace" with `rowHeader` set, "Select row 3" without.
- A selected row has `data-state="selected"` and a background. The checkbox carries the state for screen readers, and for anyone whose browser forces its own colors, the row also gets a bar at its start edge.
- A change in the selection is read out: "3 selected".
- The bar is a group named "Selected rows". When clearing the selection from inside it makes it go, focus moves to the heading's checkbox, so it isn't left on nothing.
- The cell in the heading that holds the checkbox isn't a column heading, so a screen reader doesn't say "Select all rows on this page" before every cell under it.
- On a touch screen a checkbox answers a tap anywhere in 44 pixels around it, and rows are tall enough that those areas don't overlap.

### What you need to handle

- Set `rowHeader` or `getRowLabel`, so the checkboxes are named for their rows.
- Name your actions for what they do to the selection: "Remove", "Export". The count is next to them.
- Confirm an action that can't be undone. An [alert dialog](page:components/alert-dialog) is the place.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Put the checkbox column first, and [pin it](page:table/column-pinning) in a wide table.
- Say how many rows an action will touch before it does.

**Don't**

- Don't use selection for an action on one row. Put a button or a menu in the row.
- Don't select a row when its text is clicked. People click text to select it for copying.

pages.title: Column visibility
pages.description: Let people choose which columns a data table shows, from a menu with a tick for each column. Columns can start hidden, and some can be kept from being hidden.

sections.heading: What to register
Hidden to begin with
sections.markdown:
## Hidden to begin with

Visibility is a map from a column's id to `false` for the hidden ones. A column that isn't in it is showing.

```tsx
const table = useDataTable({
  columns,
  data,
  initialState: { columnVisibility: { joined: false } },
});
```

A column's id is its accessor key, such as `"joined"`, unless it has an `id` of its own.

To remember what someone chose, hold the state yourself with `state: { columnVisibility }` and `onColumnVisibilityChange`, and save it.

sections.heading: Columns that stay
sections.markdown:
## Columns that stay

`enableHiding: false` on a column keeps it in the table and out of the menu. Do that for the column that names the row: a table of people with the names hidden is a table of nothing.

`helper.select()` and `helper.expand()` can't be hidden.

sections.heading: What the menu calls a column
The button
sections.markdown:
## The button

`DataTableColumnChooser`, or `table.ColumnChooser`, is the button on its own, for a toolbar you lay out yourself. With no column that can be hidden, it isn't shown.

sections.heading: Hiding and searching
sections.markdown:
## Hiding and searching

A hidden column is still searched by the [search field](page:table/filtering), and still sorts the table if it was sorted by. That's TanStack's behavior. If a match in a column nobody can see would confuse, set `enableGlobalFilter: false` on columns that start hidden.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### Keyboard

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd>, <kbd>Space</kbd> or <kbd>↓</kbd> | On the button, opens the menu. |
| <kbd>↑</kbd> and <kbd>↓</kbd> | Move through the columns. |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Space</kbd> | Shows or hides the column. The menu stays open. |
| <kbd>Esc</kbd> | Closes the menu and returns focus to the button. |

### What the component handles

- The menu is the core's [dropdown menu](page:components/dropdown-menu), and each column is a `menuitemcheckbox` that says whether it's ticked.
- The menu stays open after a choice, so several columns can be set without opening it again each time.
- A hidden column is taken out of the table, headings and cells both, so a screen reader's count of columns is right.

### What you need to handle

- Give every column a name the menu can show: a string `header` or a `meta.label`.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Start with the columns most people need, and let the rest be turned on.
- Remember the choice between visits for a table people come back to.

**Don't**

- Don't let the column that names the row be hidden.
- Don't use hidden columns to keep data out of sight. It's still in the page's data.

pages.title: Column pinning
pages.description: Keep columns in view while a data table scrolls sideways. Pin to the start or the end, several to a side, with offsets that are measured for you and follow the direction of the text.

sections.heading: What to register
Pin columns
How wide a pinned column is
sections.markdown:
## How wide a pinned column is

A second pinned column has to sit where the first one ends, so the table needs to know how wide the first one is. `DataTable` measures the pinned headings in the browser and places each column from that. It measures again when one changes width, so it works with columns sized by their content, with [resized columns](page:table/column-resizing), and when a web font arrives late.

TanStack's own examples take the offsets from the widths it holds in state, which needs `columnSizingFeature` and a fixed layout. Here neither is needed.

On a page rendered by a server, the offsets aren't known until the browser has the page. Until then every pinned column sits at its own edge, which only shows if the table is scrolled sideways in that moment.

sections.heading: Don't pin too much
sections.markdown:
## Don't pin too much

Pinned columns take their width from what's left for the others. On a phone, two pinned columns can leave no room to scroll anything through. Pin one narrow column on small screens, or none.

Nothing here changes the pinning by screen size for you. Hold the state yourself and set it from a media query if you need that.

sections.heading: With a sticky header
sections.markdown:
## With a sticky header

`stickyHeader` and pinned columns work together. The heading of a pinned column stays in the corner, over both the rows that scroll up under the header and the columns that scroll sideways under it.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### What the component handles

- Pinning changes where a column is drawn, and where it is in the markup with it, so the order a screen reader reads the cells in is the order they're seen in.
- A pinned cell is painted, so the cells that scroll under it don't show through its text.
- The last column pinned to the start, and the first pinned to the end, have a line at their edge. A shadow would be lost where the browser forces its own colors, and a line isn't.
- The table's box takes keyboard focus while it scrolls, and the arrow keys scroll it.

### What you need to handle

- Leave room. Check the table at 320 pixels wide with the columns you've pinned.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Pin the column that names the row, and the checkbox column next to it.
- Pin a column of row actions to the end, so it can be reached without scrolling.

**Don't**

- Don't pin more than two columns to a side.
- Don't pin a column whose content can be very wide.

pages.title: Column resizing
pages.description: Let people drag the edge of a data table's column to resize it, or do it from the keyboard. Columns have set widths in a fixed layout, with a least and a most.
pages.markdown:
# Column resizing

Let people drag the edge of a data table's column to resize it, or do it from the keyboard. Columns have set widths in a fixed layout, with a least and a most.

With `layout="fixed"`, every column has a set width and a grip at the end of its heading. Drag the grip to resize the column.

```tsx
"use client";

import { DataTable } from "@nuvui/table";
import { createColumnHelper, useDataTable } from "@nuvui/table/full";
import { type Person, people } from "./people";

const helper = createColumnHelper<Person>();
const columns = helper.columns([
  helper.accessor("name", { header: "Name", size: 200, minSize: 120 }),
  helper.accessor("email", { header: "Email", size: 240, minSize: 120 }),
  helper.accessor("team", { header: "Team", size: 140, maxSize: 240 }),
  // This one keeps its width.
  helper.accessor("role", { header: "Role", size: 120, enableResizing: false }),
]);
const firstSix = people.slice(0, 6);

export default function Example() {
  const table = useDataTable({ columns, data: firstSix });

  return (
    <DataTable
      table={table}
      aria-label="People"
      rowHeader="name"
      layout="fixed"
      toolbar={false}
      pagination={false}
    />
  );
}
```

## What to register

`@nuvui/table/full` has both features. In a hook of your own:

```tsx
import {
  columnResizingFeature,
  columnSizingFeature,
  tableFeatures,
} from "@tanstack/react-table";

tableFeatures({ columnSizingFeature, columnResizingFeature });
```

`columnSizingFeature` is the widths. `columnResizingFeature` is the dragging, and needs the first. With only the first, columns have their set widths and no grips.

## The fixed layout

By default a table is laid out by the browser: each column is as wide as its content needs, and the table fills its box. That's `layout="auto"`, and nothing in it has a set width, so there's nothing to resize.

`layout="fixed"` gives each column the width TanStack holds for it:

```tsx
<DataTable table={table} caption="People" layout="fixed" />
```

The table is then exactly as wide as its columns add up to. Narrower than its box, it leaves space at the end. Wider, it scrolls. It isn't stretched to fill the box, because then every column would be wider than the width a resize had just given it.

## Widths

A column is 150 pixels unless it says otherwise, which is TanStack's default.

```tsx
helper.accessor("name", {
  header: "Name",
  size: 200,
  minSize: 120,
  maxSize: 400,
});
```

`size` is where it starts, and `minSize` and `maxSize` are how far it can be dragged. Without them a column can go down to 20 pixels and has no upper limit. Text that doesn't fit a narrow column wraps onto more lines.

`enableResizing: false` on a column takes its grip away. `enableColumnResizing: false` on the hook takes them all.

Sizes are numbers of pixels. TanStack doesn't take percentages.

## Remembering widths

The widths people set are in the table's `columnSizing` state, as a map from column id to pixels. To keep them between visits, hold that state yourself with `state: { columnSizing }` and `onColumnSizingChange`, and save it.

`column.resetSize()` puts one column back, and `table.resetColumnSizing()` all of them.

## Right to left

In a right-to-left layout the grip is at the left end of its heading, and dragging left makes the column wider. `useDataTable` reads the direction from the [`DirectionProvider`](page:right-to-left) and tells TanStack. With TanStack's plain `useTable`, pass `columnResizeDirection: "rtl"` yourself.

## Accessibility

### Keyboard

TanStack's own resizing follows a mouse or a finger. The keyboard is added here. <kbd>Tab</kbd> stops at each grip, after its heading's sort button.

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>→</kbd> | Makes the column 16 pixels wider. |
| <kbd>←</kbd> | Makes it 16 pixels narrower. The two swap in a right-to-left layout. |
| <kbd>Shift</kbd> with an arrow | Moves 64 pixels. |
| <kbd>Home</kbd> | Goes to the least width. |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> | Puts the column back to the width it started with. |

A double click on a grip also puts the column back.

### What the component handles

- The grip is a `separator` that takes focus, named "Resize Name" for its column, with the width as its value and the least and most as its limits. That's the role for a divider that can be moved.
- The heading keeps its own name. A heading is named by what's in it, and with the grip inside it every cell in the column would be read out as "Name Resize Name", so the heading is given the column's label.
- The grip is 8 pixels wide with a mouse and 16 on a touch screen, and shows a line that's 2 pixels wide. The line is full height and in the primary color while the column is being resized.

### What you need to handle

- Set a `minSize` that still shows something useful. A column dragged to 20 pixels can't be read.
- Give a column whose `header` is a function a `meta.label`. The grip and the heading are both named from it.

## Do and don't

**Do**

- Set `size` on every column, so the table starts out looking deliberate.
- Save the widths for a table people use every day.

**Don't**

- Don't use the fixed layout only to line columns up. The automatic layout does that with less to maintain.
- Don't expect resizing to be found on a touch screen. Keep the default widths good enough.

pages.title: Expanding rows
pages.description: Open a data table's row to show a panel of details under it, or the rows nested under it in a tree. With a named button that says whether the row is open.

sections.heading: A panel under the row
Rows under a row
What to register
Open to begin with
sections.markdown:
## Open to begin with

Which rows are open is a map from row id to `true`, or just `true` for all of them:

```tsx
initialState: { expanded: { "person-2": true } }
```

Set `getRowId` so the ids are your own. Without it a row's id is its position, and a nested row's is its parent's and its own joined with a dot, such as `"0.1"`.

`table.toggleAllRowsExpanded()` opens or closes every row, for a button of your own.

sections.heading: With other features
sections.markdown:
## With other features

- **Sorting and filtering** apply to every level of a tree. A filter keeps a parent whose own values match. To keep a parent because something under it matches, pass `filterFromLeafRows: true` to the hook.
- **Pagination** counts the rows of an open tree. A page of ten holds ten rows, nested ones included, so opening a row pushes others to the next page. `paginateExpandedRows: false` keeps a parent's rows with it, and lets a page grow.
- **Selection**: selecting a parent selects the rows under it. Its checkbox shows a dash while some of them are selected.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### Keyboard

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Moves to the next button. |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Space</kbd> | Opens or closes the row. |

### What the component handles

- The button has `aria-expanded`, and is named for its row: "Show details for Ada Lovelace", then "Hide details for Ada Lovelace".
- A panel is a row of the same table, directly after the row it belongs to, so it's read in order.
- On a touch screen the button answers a tap anywhere in 44 pixels around it.
- The arrow points the other way in a right-to-left layout.

### What you need to handle

- The names say "details". For a tree, rename them with `labels`, as below.
- A tree here is a table with indented rows, not a `treegrid`. A screen reader isn't told a row's level or how many rows are under it. Where that matters, say it in the row: "Design, 2 folders".
- Keep a panel short. It sits inside a table, and a long form or another table in it is hard to move through.

```tsx
<DataTable
  table={table}
  caption="Folders"
  labels={{
    expandRow: (row) => `Open ${row}`,
    collapseRow: (row) => `Close ${row}`,
  }}
/>
```

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Put in a panel what's too long for a cell and not needed to compare rows.
- Keep a tree to two or three levels.

**Don't**

- Don't hide in a panel something people need in order to choose a row.
- Don't put the open button at the end of the row. It's expected at the start.

pages.title: Server mode
pages.description: A data table whose sorting, filtering and paging are done by your API. The table reports what's being asked for, you fetch it, and it shows what comes back, with loading and error states.

sections.heading: The request
sections.markdown:
## The request

`useDataTableRequest` holds what the table is asking for, and returns it with the options that put the table in server mode:

```tsx
import { useDataTableRequest } from "@nuvui/table";

const [request, options] = useDataTableRequest({
  pagination: { pageIndex: 0, pageSize: 20 },
});
```

`request` is what to send:

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `pagination` | `{ pageIndex, pageSize }`. The first page is 0. |
| `sorting` | A list of `{ id, desc }`, in order. Empty for no sort. |
| `columnFilters` | A list of `{ id, value }`. |
| `globalFilter` | The text in the search field. |

`options` goes into the hook. It holds that state, the functions that change it, and `manualPagination`, `manualSorting` and `manualFiltering`, which are what tell TanStack to leave the rows as they come:

```tsx
const table = useDataTable({
  columns,
  data: page?.rows ?? none,
  rowCount: page?.total,
  getRowId: (person) => person.id,
  ...options,
});
```

Three things in that matter:

- **`rowCount`** is how many rows match in all, from your API. The pagination bar needs it for "21-40 of 143" and to know when there's no next page.
- **`none`** is an empty array made once, outside the component. A new `[]` on every render would be new `data` every time, and TanStack would work the table out again every time.
- **`getRowId`** keeps the selection on the right rows. A row's position means nothing when each page is a different set of rows.

`request` is a new object whenever anything in it changes, and the same object otherwise, so it can go straight into an effect's dependencies or a query key.

sections.heading: Fetching
What your API does with it
Loading and errors
sections.markdown:
## Loading and errors

- `loading` while a request is out. The first time, with no rows, the table shows placeholders. After that it keeps the rows it has and marks itself busy, so the table doesn't jump.
- `error` when a request fails, with `onRetry` to try again.

The message a screen reader hears after a sort or a filter, such as "4 rows", waits for the answer, so it describes the rows that arrived and not the ones that were there before. It's said once `loading` has been set and cleared, or once `data` is a new array, whichever the table sees. Pass `loading`: without it, an answer that's the very same array as before is never noticed.

sections.heading: The search field
sections.markdown:
## The search field

Each key in the search field is a new request. Set `debounce` on it so the request waits for a pause in the typing:

```tsx
<DataTable
  table={table}
  caption="People"
  toolbar={
    <DataTableToolbar>
      <table.Filter debounce={300} />
    </DataTableToolbar>
  }
/>
```

sections.heading: Back to the first page
sections.markdown:
## Back to the first page

A new sort or filter sets `pageIndex` to 0. The seventh page of the old results is usually past the end of the new ones. TanStack does this itself when it does the paging and not when a server does, so `useDataTableRequest` does it.

sections.heading: Selection across pages
sections.markdown:
## Selection across pages

Selection is kept by row id, so ticks stay when the page changes and come back with the row. `table.getSelectedRowIds()` has all of them. The rows for ids on other pages aren't in the browser: an action on the selection sends the ids, and the server finds the rows.

<kbd>Shift</kbd> and a click selects a range within the page that's showing. It can't reach rows that haven't been loaded.

sections.heading: Some of it on the server
sections.markdown:
## Some of it on the server

The three `manual` options are separate. A table that fetches every matching row but lets the browser page them can override one:

```tsx
useDataTable({ columns, data, ...options, manualPagination: false });
```

It then needs `paginatedRowModel` in its features. The usual mistake goes the other way: paging on the server and sorting in the browser, which sorts only the rows on the page.

sections.heading: Without the helper
sections.markdown:
## Without the helper

`useDataTableRequest` is a `useState` and four setters. To keep the state somewhere else, such as the URL, pass `state`, the `on...Change` functions and the three `manual` options yourself. Remember to reset the page when the sort or a filter changes.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

Everything on the [DataTable page](page:table/data-table#accessibility) applies. Two things are particular to this mode:

- The table has `aria-busy` while `loading` is set.
- What's read out after a change waits for the rows.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Send the total with every page.
- Keep the old rows on screen while the next page loads.
- Cancel or ignore a request that's been replaced.

**Don't**

- Don't sort or filter the returned page in the browser as well.
- Don't make `data` a new array on every render.
- Don't put a column id from the request into a query without checking it against a list.

pages.title: Virtual rows
pages.description: A data table that draws only the rows in view, for thousands of rows in one scroll. Real table rows, a sticky header, keyboard focus that survives scrolling, and row counts for screen readers.
pages.markdown:
# Virtual rows

A data table that draws only the rows in view, for thousands of rows in one scroll. Real table rows, a sticky header, keyboard focus that survives scrolling, and row counts for screen readers.

A browser slows down long before it runs out of rows it could hold. Ten thousand table rows with five cells each is sixty thousand elements before anything is put in a cell. A virtual table keeps all the rows in memory and puts only the ones in view, and a few either side, in the page.

```tsx
"use client";

import { createColumnHelper, useDataTable } from "@nuvui/table/full";
import { DataTableVirtual } from "@nuvui/table/virtual";
import { manyPeople, type Person } from "./people";

const helper = createColumnHelper<Person>();
const columns = helper.columns([
  helper.select(),
  helper.accessor("name", { header: "Name" }),
  helper.accessor("email", { header: "Email" }),
  helper.accessor("team", { header: "Team" }),
  helper.accessor("seats", { header: "Seats", meta: { align: "end" } }),
]);
const tenThousand = manyPeople(10_000);

export default function Example() {
  const table = useDataTable({
    columns,
    data: tenThousand,
    getRowId: (person) => person.id,
    // The ready-made hook has pages. One page holds every row here.
    initialState: {
      pagination: { pageIndex: 0, pageSize: tenThousand.length },
    },
  });

  return (
    <DataTableVirtual
      table={table}
      caption="Ten thousand people"
      rowHeader="name"
      height={360}
      pagination={false}
    />
  );
}
```

## Install

```sh
pnpm add @tanstack/react-virtual
```

It's an optional peer dependency of `@nuvui/table`, so it's only needed by an app that uses this entry.

## Import

```tsx
import { DataTableVirtual } from "@nuvui/table/virtual";
```

It's an entry of its own, so that the main one can be imported without `@tanstack/react-virtual` installed.

## Use it

`DataTableVirtual` takes what [`DataTable`](page:table/data-table#props) takes, and these:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `height` | `string \| number` | `480` | How tall the table may get before its rows scroll. A number is pixels. The window of rows is cut to this, so it has to be set. |
| `estimateRowHeight` | `number` | `40` | A guess at a row's height in pixels, used for rows that haven't been drawn yet. Each row is measured when it is. |
| `overscan` | `number` | `10` | How many rows to draw beyond each edge of what's in view. |

```tsx
<DataTableVirtual
  table={table}
  caption="Events"
  rowHeader="name"
  height={480}
  pagination={false}
/>
```

`height` is the most the table takes before it scrolls. It has to be set to something: with no limit every row would be in view, and all of them would be drawn.

The header stays at the top while the rows scroll. Pass `stickyHeader={false}` to let it scroll away.

## Without pages

Virtual rows are an answer to the same problem as pages, so a table usually has one or the other. With a hook of your own, leave `rowPaginationFeature` out. `@nuvui/table/full` has it, so there, give the table one page that holds everything, and hide the bar:

```tsx
const table = useDataTable({
  columns,
  data,
  initialState: { pagination: { pageIndex: 0, pageSize: data.length } },
});

<DataTableVirtual table={table} caption="Events" pagination={false} />;
```

Sorting, filtering and selection work on every row, in view or not. They're TanStack's, and it has all the rows.

## Row heights

Rows don't have to be the same height. `estimateRowHeight` is used for rows that haven't been drawn, and each row is measured when it is, so the scroll bar gets more exact as the table is scrolled. A guess that's close keeps it from jumping. The default, 40, is a one-line row with a mouse at the default density. On a touch screen a row is 44, and rows with two lines of text are taller: set it to what your rows are.

A row's [open panel](page:table/expanding) is counted in its height.

## How it's drawn

The rows in view are ordinary `tr` elements in the `tbody`, in their usual flow. An empty row above them and one below stand in for the rows that aren't drawn, and are as tall as those rows would be. Nothing is positioned by hand, so the browser lays the columns out as it does for any table, and the columns line up with their headings whatever is in them.

The column widths come from the rows that are drawn. With `layout="auto"` a column can change width as rows with longer content scroll in. Use [`layout="fixed"`](page:table/column-resizing) with a `size` on each column to keep them still.

## Loading more as it scrolls

This draws a window over rows that are already loaded. For rows that arrive as the table is scrolled, load them in your own code and add them to `data`. With TanStack Query that's `useInfiniteQuery`, with `fetchNextPage` called from an effect that watches the table's box scroll near its end.

For a table too big to load at all, use [the server mode](page:table/server) with pages.

## Accessibility

### Keyboard

| Key | Where | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <kbd>↑</kbd> <kbd>↓</kbd> <kbd>Page Up</kbd> <kbd>Page Down</kbd> | The table's box | Scroll the rows. |
| <kbd>Home</kbd> and <kbd>End</kbd> | The table's box | Go to the first and the last row. |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Anywhere | Moves through the controls of the rows that are drawn. |

### What the component handles

- The table has `aria-rowcount` with the number of rows there really are, and each row has `aria-rowindex` with its place. A screen reader can then say "row 5,012 of 10,001" where it would otherwise count only the rows in the page.
- The row that holds keyboard focus stays in the page when it's scrolled out of view. If it were taken out, focus would fall to the page, and the next <kbd>Tab</kbd> would start from the top of the document. It's let go once focus has moved on.
- The table's box takes keyboard focus, so the rows can be scrolled without a mouse.
- The rows that stand in for the ones not drawn are hidden from screen readers.

### What you need to handle

- <kbd>Tab</kbd> only reaches rows that are drawn. To get to a row far away by keyboard, scroll the box first, or give people a search field. A table of thousands of rows needs one anyway.
- A browser's own find, <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> <kbd>F</kbd>, only finds text in rows that are drawn. Say so, or provide the search.
- Printing prints the rows in view. Offer an export if people need all of them on paper.

### What hasn't been checked

The tests check the row counts and that focus is kept. How each screen reader moves through a table whose rows come and go hasn't been checked by a person.

## Do and don't

**Do**

- Use it for a table people scan or scroll: a log, a feed, a long list they recognize things in.
- Set `getRowId`, so a row keeps its state when it leaves the page and comes back.

**Don't**

- Don't use it for a few hundred rows. A plain table draws those without trouble and has none of the limits above.
- Don't hold state inside a row's cells. A row that scrolls out of view is taken out of the page, and its state goes with it. Keep it in your data.

sections.heading: Install
sections.markdown:
## Install

```sh
pnpm add @tanstack/react-virtual
```

It's an optional peer dependency of `@nuvui/table`, so it's only needed by an app that uses this entry.

sections.heading: Import
sections.markdown:
## Import

```tsx
import { DataTableVirtual } from "@nuvui/table/virtual";
```

It's an entry of its own, so that the main one can be imported without `@tanstack/react-virtual` installed.

sections.heading: Use it
sections.markdown:
## Use it

`DataTableVirtual` takes what [`DataTable`](page:table/data-table#props) takes, and these:

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `height` | `string \| number` | `480` | How tall the table may get before its rows scroll. A number is pixels. The window of rows is cut to this, so it has to be set. |
| `estimateRowHeight` | `number` | `40` | A guess at a row's height in pixels, used for rows that haven't been drawn yet. Each row is measured when it is. |
| `overscan` | `number` | `10` | How many rows to draw beyond each edge of what's in view. |

```tsx
<DataTableVirtual
  table={table}
  caption="Events"
  rowHeader="name"
  height={480}
  pagination={false}
/>
```

`height` is the most the table takes before it scrolls. It has to be set to something: with no limit every row would be in view, and all of them would be drawn.

The header stays at the top while the rows scroll. Pass `stickyHeader={false}` to let it scroll away.

sections.heading: Without pages
Row heights
sections.markdown:
## Row heights

Rows don't have to be the same height. `estimateRowHeight` is used for rows that haven't been drawn, and each row is measured when it is, so the scroll bar gets more exact as the table is scrolled. A guess that's close keeps it from jumping. The default, 40, is a one-line row with a mouse at the default density. On a touch screen a row is 44, and rows with two lines of text are taller: set it to what your rows are.

A row's [open panel](page:table/expanding) is counted in its height.

sections.heading: How it's drawn
sections.markdown:
## How it's drawn

The rows in view are ordinary `tr` elements in the `tbody`, in their usual flow. An empty row above them and one below stand in for the rows that aren't drawn, and are as tall as those rows would be. Nothing is positioned by hand, so the browser lays the columns out as it does for any table, and the columns line up with their headings whatever is in them.

The column widths come from the rows that are drawn. With `layout="auto"` a column can change width as rows with longer content scroll in. Use [`layout="fixed"`](page:table/column-resizing) with a `size` on each column to keep them still.

sections.heading: Loading more as it scrolls
sections.markdown:
## Loading more as it scrolls

This draws a window over rows that are already loaded. For rows that arrive as the table is scrolled, load them in your own code and add them to `data`. With TanStack Query that's `useInfiniteQuery`, with `fetchNextPage` called from an effect that watches the table's box scroll near its end.

For a table too big to load at all, use [the server mode](page:table/server) with pages.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

### Keyboard

| Key | Where | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <kbd>↑</kbd> <kbd>↓</kbd> <kbd>Page Up</kbd> <kbd>Page Down</kbd> | The table's box | Scroll the rows. |
| <kbd>Home</kbd> and <kbd>End</kbd> | The table's box | Go to the first and the last row. |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Anywhere | Moves through the controls of the rows that are drawn. |

### What the component handles

- The table has `aria-rowcount` with the number of rows there really are, and each row has `aria-rowindex` with its place. A screen reader can then say "row 5,012 of 10,001" where it would otherwise count only the rows in the page.
- The row that holds keyboard focus stays in the page when it's scrolled out of view. If it were taken out, focus would fall to the page, and the next <kbd>Tab</kbd> would start from the top of the document. It's let go once focus has moved on.
- The table's box takes keyboard focus, so the rows can be scrolled without a mouse.
- The rows that stand in for the ones not drawn are hidden from screen readers.

### What you need to handle

- <kbd>Tab</kbd> only reaches rows that are drawn. To get to a row far away by keyboard, scroll the box first, or give people a search field. A table of thousands of rows needs one anyway.
- A browser's own find, <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> <kbd>F</kbd>, only finds text in rows that are drawn. Say so, or provide the search.
- Printing prints the rows in view. Offer an export if people need all of them on paper.

### What hasn't been checked

The tests check the row counts and that focus is kept. How each screen reader moves through a table whose rows come and go hasn't been checked by a person.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Use it for a table people scan or scroll: a log, a feed, a long list they recognize things in.
- Set `getRowId`, so a row keeps its state when it leaves the page and comes back.

**Don't**

- Don't use it for a few hundred rows. A plain table draws those without trouble and has none of the limits above.
- Don't hold state inside a row's cells. A row that scrolls out of view is taken out of the page, and its state goes with it. Keep it in your data.

pages.title: Coming from TanStack Table 8
pages.description: What changes in your table code between TanStack Table 8 and 9, for people bringing version 8 tables to @nuvui/table. The hook, features, row models, state, pinning, sizing and sorting names.
pages.markdown:
# Coming from TanStack Table 8

What changes in your table code between TanStack Table 8 and 9, for people bringing version 8 tables to @nuvui/table. The hook, features, row models, state, pinning, sizing and sorting names.

`@nuvui/table` is built on TanStack Table 9. Version 9 is a different API from version 8, and version 8 code doesn't run on it unchanged. If you have tables written for version 8, with `useReactTable`, this page is what changes in them.

It covers what you'll meet using this package. TanStack's own [migration guide](https://tanstack.com/table) is the full list.

## The short version

A version 8 table:

```tsx
import {
  getCoreRowModel,
  getSortedRowModel,
  useReactTable,
} from "@tanstack/react-table";

const table = useReactTable({
  columns,
  data,
  getCoreRowModel: getCoreRowModel(),
  getSortedRowModel: getSortedRowModel(),
});
```

The same table here:

```tsx
import { createColumnHelper, useDataTable } from "@nuvui/table/full";

const table = useDataTable({ columns, data });
```

The row models are gone from the options because they're part of the features the hook was made with. With `@nuvui/table/full` that's all of them. With a hook of your own, it's the ones you listed.

## Features are listed, not assumed

Version 8 shipped every feature in every table. Version 9 has a table say which it uses:

```tsx
import {
  createSortedRowModel,
  rowSortingFeature,
  sortFn_text,
  tableFeatures,
} from "@tanstack/react-table";

const features = tableFeatures({
  rowSortingFeature,
  sortedRowModel: createSortedRowModel(),
  sortFns: { text: sortFn_text },
});
```

A method that isn't there, such as `column.getCanSort`, usually means the feature wasn't registered, not that version 9 removed it. TypeScript says so too: the methods of a feature are only on the types of a table made with it.

| Version 8 | Version 9 |
| --- | --- |
| `useReactTable(options)` | `useTable({ features, ...options })`, or `useDataTable(options)` here |
| `getCoreRowModel: getCoreRowModel()` | Nothing. The core row model is automatic. |
| `getSortedRowModel: getSortedRowModel()` | `sortedRowModel: createSortedRowModel()` in `tableFeatures` |
| `getFilteredRowModel: getFilteredRowModel()` | `filteredRowModel: createFilteredRowModel()` in `tableFeatures` |
| `getPaginationRowModel: getPaginationRowModel()` | `paginatedRowModel: createPaginatedRowModel()` in `tableFeatures` |
| `getExpandedRowModel: getExpandedRowModel()` | `expandedRowModel: createExpandedRowModel()` in `tableFeatures` |
| `filterFns` and `sortingFns` as table options | `filterFns` and `sortFns` in `tableFeatures` |

Two features need another registered before them: `globalFilteringFeature` needs `columnFilteringFeature`, and `columnResizingFeature` needs `columnSizingFeature`.

## Column helpers know the features

The column helper takes the features as well as the row type, so that a column's options are the ones its table has:

```tsx
// Version 8
const helper = createColumnHelper<Person>();

// Version 9, plain
const helper = createColumnHelper<typeof features, Person>();

// Version 9, from this package's hook: the features are already bound
const helper = createColumnHelper<Person>();
```

Wrap the list in `helper.columns([...])`. It keeps each column's value type, where a plain array would widen them all.

## State

| Version 8 | Version 9 |
| --- | --- |
| `table.getState()` | `table.state` |
| `onStateChange` for everything | One function per slice: `onSortingChange`, `onPaginationChange` and so on |
| `state: { sorting }` with `onSortingChange` | The same. This still works as it did. |

`useTable` takes a second argument, a function that picks which state the component follows, for a component that should only draw again for some changes. `DataTable` follows all of the table's state itself, whatever the table handed to it was told to follow, so its controls are never stale.

## Sorting names

`sorting` in function and type names became `sort`:

| Version 8 | Version 9 |
| --- | --- |
| `sortingFn` on a column | `sortFn` |
| `SortingFn` | `SortFn` |
| `sortingFns` | `sortFns` |
| `column.getSortingFn()` | `column.getSortFn()` |

The state is still `sorting`, and `SortingState` is still its type.

## Pinning is by start and end

Version 9 has no `left` and `right`. Pinned columns are at the `start` or the `end`, which follow the direction of the text:

| Version 8 | Version 9 |
| --- | --- |
| `columnPinning: { left, right }` | `columnPinning: { start, end }` |
| `column.pin("left")` | `column.pin("start")` |
| `column.getIsPinned() === "left"` | `=== "start"` |
| `table.getLeftHeaderGroups()` | `table.getStartHeaderGroups()` |
| `row.getLeftVisibleCells()` | `row.getStartVisibleCells()` |
| `enablePinning` on the table | `enableColumnPinning` |

With `DataTable` you don't write the sticky positioning these were used for. It [measures and places](page:table/column-pinning) pinned columns itself.

## Sizing and resizing are two features

| Version 8 | Version 9 |
| --- | --- |
| One feature for widths and dragging | `columnSizingFeature` for widths, `columnResizingFeature` for dragging |
| `columnSizingInfo` state | `columnResizing` |
| `onColumnSizingInfoChange` | `onColumnResizingChange` |

## Selection

`table.getIsSomeRowsSelected()` and `table.getIsSomePageRowsSelected()` now mean "at least one", and are true when all are selected too. In version 8 they meant "some and not all". A checkbox of your own that shows a dash needs both tests:

```tsx
const some = table.getIsSomeRowsSelected() && !table.getIsAllRowsSelected();
```

`DataTableSelectAll` does this.

## Methods stay on their object

In version 9 the methods of a row, a column, a cell and a header are shared through a prototype. Call them on the object:

```tsx
// Works
row.getValue("name");

// Doesn't: the method has lost the row it belongs to
const { getValue } = row;
getValue("name");
```

For the same reason, spreading a row into a new object leaves its methods behind.

## Rendering

`flexRender(cell.column.columnDef.cell, cell.getContext())` still works. There's also a component, `<table.FlexRender cell={cell} />`. With `DataTable` you write neither: it draws the headings and the cells.

## What you can delete

A version 8 table usually came with markup of your own: the `table`, the `thead`, the loop over header groups, the sort button, the pagination buttons, the `aria-sort`. `DataTable` is that markup. What's left of a migrated table is the columns, the hook and one element.

## A way to move a table at a time

TanStack ships `useLegacyTable` in `@tanstack/react-table/legacy`, which takes version 8 options and returns a version 9 table. It includes every feature, and TanStack marks it as deprecated: it's there to keep an app running while its tables are moved one by one, not to stay on. A table from it can be given to `DataTable`.
