pages.markdown:
# Charts

The @nuvui/charts package. Recharts 3 charts that take their colors from the theme, with a tooltip and a legend that match the library, pattern fills, and a table of the same numbers for screen readers.

Charts are a package of their own, `@nuvui/charts`. You build a chart from [Recharts](https://recharts.github.io)' own parts, `BarChart`, `Line`, `XAxis` and the rest, and this package is what goes around them:

| | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `ChartContainer` | Sizes the chart, gives each series a color from the theme, and styles Recharts' axes, grid and labels from the tokens. |
| `ChartTooltip` | Recharts' tooltip, drawn like the library's other floating panels. |
| `ChartLegend` | Recharts' legend, with the series' labels. |
| `ChartTable` | The same numbers as a table, for screen readers or for everyone. |

```tsx
"use client";

import {
  ChartContainer,
  ChartLegend,
  ChartTable,
  ChartTooltip,
  chartFill,
} from "@nuvui/charts";
import { Bar, BarChart, CartesianGrid, XAxis } from "recharts";
import { short, visitors, visitorsConfig } from "./data";

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <ChartContainer
      config={visitorsConfig}
      aria-label="Visitors by month, on desktop and mobile"
      table={
        <ChartTable data={visitors} category="month" categoryLabel="Month" />
      }
    >
      <BarChart data={visitors}>
        <CartesianGrid vertical={false} />
        <XAxis
          dataKey="month"
          tickFormatter={short}
          tickLine={false}
          axisLine={false}
        />
        <ChartTooltip />
        <ChartLegend />
        <Bar dataKey="desktop" fill={chartFill("desktop")} radius={4} />
        <Bar dataKey="mobile" fill={chartFill("mobile")} radius={4} />
      </BarChart>
    </ChartContainer>
  );
}
```

Recharts does the drawing: the scales, the shapes, the axes, the animation and the keyboard. Nothing of it is wrapped or renamed, so its [documentation](https://recharts.github.io/en-US/api) applies as written.

## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/charts @nuvui/react recharts
```

`@nuvui/react` and `recharts` are peer dependencies. You import the chart's parts from `recharts` yourself, so your app has to own that version. This package needs Recharts 3.

Recharts asks for `react-is` as a peer of its own. Most package managers install it for you. If yours reports it missing, add it at the same version as `react`.

## Load the styles

Import the package's stylesheet once, after the core's:

```tsx title="app/layout.tsx"
import "@nuvui/react/styles.css";
import "@nuvui/charts/styles.css";
```

Both files open with the same line naming the cascade layers, so the order you import them in doesn't decide which rule wins.

## A chart in three steps

**Describe the series.** The config has an entry for each series, under the key it has in the data:

```tsx
import type { ChartConfig } from "@nuvui/charts";

const config = {
  desktop: { label: "Desktop" },
  mobile: { label: "Mobile" },
} satisfies ChartConfig;
```

**Put a Recharts chart in a container.** The container needs the config and a name:

```tsx
"use client";

import { ChartContainer, ChartLegend, ChartTooltip, chartFill } from "@nuvui/charts";
import { Bar, BarChart, CartesianGrid, XAxis } from "recharts";

export function Visitors({ data }: { data: Row[] }) {
  return (
    <ChartContainer config={config} aria-label="Visitors by month">
      <BarChart data={data}>
        <CartesianGrid vertical={false} />
        <XAxis dataKey="month" />
        <ChartTooltip />
        <ChartLegend />
        <Bar dataKey="desktop" fill={chartFill("desktop")} />
        <Bar dataKey="mobile" fill={chartFill("mobile")} />
      </BarChart>
    </ChartContainer>
  );
}
```

**Color each series with its variable.** `chartFill("desktop")` is the text `var(--chart-desktop-fill)`. The container sets that variable from the config, so the color is CSS: it changes with the theme without the chart being drawn again.

[ChartContainer](page:charts/chart) has all of it: colors, patterns, sizes, the table and the reference.

## Client components

A chart is a client component. Recharts measures the page and keeps state, and neither can happen on a server. Put `"use client"` at the top of the file a chart is written in, as the example above does. The page around it can stay a server component.

On the server a chart renders its container, at its final size, and its table. The drawing arrives in the browser, so nothing moves when it does.

## Kinds of chart

| Page | Recharts parts |
| --- | --- |
| [Area](page:charts/area) | `AreaChart`, `Area` |
| [Bar](page:charts/bar) | `BarChart`, `Bar` |
| [Line](page:charts/line) | `LineChart`, `Line` |
| [Pie](page:charts/pie) | `PieChart`, `Pie` |
| [Radar](page:charts/radar) | `RadarChart`, `Radar` |
| [Radial](page:charts/radial) | `RadialBarChart`, `RadialBar` |
| [Tooltip](page:charts/tooltip) | `ChartTooltip` in each of them |
| [Composed](page:charts/composed) | `ComposedChart`, with bars, lines and a target |
| [Scatter](page:charts/scatter) | `ScatterChart`, `Scatter` |

Any other Recharts chart works in a container the same way.

## Accessibility

A chart is a picture of numbers, and a picture needs a text that says the same. Three things in this package are for that:

- **A name.** `ChartContainer` won't compile without `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`. Say what the chart shows, not what kind of chart it is.
- **A table.** [`ChartTable`](page:charts/chart#the-same-numbers-as-a-table) puts the numbers in the page as a real table. A screen reader reads it with its table commands, which is a better way through forty numbers than hearing them one at a time.
- **More than color.** [Patterns](page:charts/chart#patterns) fill each series differently and dash each line differently, for people who can't tell the colors apart and for a page printed in gray.

Recharts adds the keyboard: a chart is one stop for <kbd>Tab</kbd>, and the arrow keys move from point to point. Each kind of chart's page says what that's like. All of it is tested with axe and by keyboard, and none of it has been checked with a screen reader yet.

# ChartContainer

The box a Recharts chart goes in. It sizes the chart, sets a CSS variable for each series from a config, styles the axes and grid from the tokens, and holds the legend, the patterns and a table of the same numbers.

Every chart goes in a `ChartContainer`. It takes one Recharts chart as its child and does what Recharts leaves to you: the size, the colors, and the text that stands in for the picture.

```tsx
"use client";

import {
  ChartContainer,
  ChartLegend,
  ChartTable,
  ChartTooltip,
  chartFill,
} from "@nuvui/charts";
import { Bar, BarChart, CartesianGrid, XAxis } from "recharts";
import { short, visitors, visitorsConfig } from "./data";

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <ChartContainer
      config={visitorsConfig}
      aria-label="Visitors by month, on desktop and mobile"
      table={
        <ChartTable data={visitors} category="month" categoryLabel="Month" />
      }
    >
      <BarChart data={visitors}>
        <CartesianGrid vertical={false} />
        <XAxis
          dataKey="month"
          tickFormatter={short}
          tickLine={false}
          axisLine={false}
        />
        <ChartTooltip />
        <ChartLegend />
        <Bar dataKey="desktop" fill={chartFill("desktop")} radius={4} />
        <Bar dataKey="mobile" fill={chartFill("mobile")} radius={4} />
      </BarChart>
    </ChartContainer>
  );
}
```

## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/charts @nuvui/react recharts
```

## Import

```tsx
import {
  ChartContainer,
  ChartLegend,
  ChartTable,
  ChartTooltip,
  chartColor,
  chartDash,
  chartFill,
  type ChartConfig,
} from "@nuvui/charts";
```

The styles come from `@nuvui/charts/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app, after `@nuvui/react/styles.css`. [Charts](page:charts/index) covers that.

## The config

The config lists the chart's series. The key is the name the series has in your data, and what its CSS variables are named after:

```tsx
const config = {
  desktop: { label: "Desktop" },
  mobile: { label: "Mobile" },
} satisfies ChartConfig;
```

`satisfies` checks the object and keeps its keys, so `config.desktop` is still known to exist.

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `label` | `ReactNode` |  | The name shown in the tooltip, the legend and the table. |
| `color` | `string` |  | Any CSS color. Left out, the series takes the next of the theme's eight chart colors, `--color-chart-1` to `--color-chart-8`, by its place in the config. |
| `pattern` | `"cross" \| "diagonal" \| "dots" \| "grid" \| "horizontal" \| "reverse-diagonal" \| "solid" \| "vertical"` |  | The fill of this series, always. Left out, the series is filled with its color, and with a pattern of its own when the container has `patterns` or the browser is forcing colors. |
| `dash` | `"dash-dot" \| "dash-dot-dot" \| "dashed" \| "dotted" \| "long-dash" \| "long-short" \| "short-dash" \| "solid"` |  | The same for its line. |

Make the config once, outside the component, or with `useMemo`. A new object on every render makes the container work its variables out again every time.

## Colors

For each series the container sets three variables on itself. For a series called `desktop`:

| Variable | Helper | What it holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--chart-desktop` | `chartColor("desktop")` | The series' color. |
| `--chart-desktop-fill` | `chartFill("desktop")` | Its fill: the color, or a pattern. |
| `--chart-desktop-dash` | `chartDash("desktop")` | The dashes of its line, for `strokeDasharray`. |

A helper returns the text `var(--chart-desktop)`, which goes straight into a Recharts prop:

```tsx
<Bar dataKey="desktop" fill={chartFill("desktop")} />
<Line dataKey="desktop" stroke={chartColor("desktop")} strokeDasharray={chartDash("desktop")} />
```

Use `chartFill` for anything filled and `chartColor` for a line. The variables work in your own CSS too, anywhere inside the container.

A series with no `color` takes the next of the theme's eight chart colors, `--color-chart-1` to `--color-chart-8`, by its place in the config. Those are chosen to stand 3:1 against the page in every theme the library ships, and ordered so that neighbours stay apart for people with the common kinds of color blindness. A ninth series starts again at the first.

To choose a color, give any CSS color. A token changes with the theme, and a fixed color doesn't:

```tsx
"use client";

import {
  type ChartConfig,
  ChartContainer,
  ChartLegend,
  ChartTooltip,
  chartFill,
} from "@nuvui/charts";
import { Bar, BarChart, CartesianGrid, XAxis } from "recharts";
import { short, visitors } from "./data";

const config = {
  // A token, so it changes with the theme.
  desktop: { label: "Desktop", color: "var(--color-primary)" },
  // The sixth chart color, out of order.
  mobile: { label: "Mobile", color: "var(--color-chart-6)" },
} satisfies ChartConfig;

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <ChartContainer config={config} aria-label="Visitors by month">
      <BarChart data={visitors}>
        <CartesianGrid vertical={false} />
        <XAxis
          dataKey="month"
          tickFormatter={short}
          tickLine={false}
          axisLine={false}
        />
        <ChartTooltip />
        <ChartLegend />
        <Bar dataKey="desktop" fill={chartFill("desktop")} radius={4} />
        <Bar dataKey="mobile" fill={chartFill("mobile")} radius={4} />
      </BarChart>
    </ChartContainer>
  );
}
```

Because a color is a variable, switching the theme recolors a chart in CSS. Nothing is rendered again.

A key that can't be part of a variable's name, one with a space in it say, has each such character replaced by a hyphen. The helpers do the same, so `chartFill("north america")` finds `--chart-north-america-fill`.

## Patterns

About one man in twelve can't tell some colors apart, and a chart that's printed or photocopied has no colors at all. `patterns` gives each series a second way to be told from the others: a fill of its own, and a line dashed its own way.

```tsx
"use client";

import {
  ChartContainer,
  ChartLegend,
  ChartTooltip,
  chartFill,
} from "@nuvui/charts";
import { Bar, BarChart, CartesianGrid, XAxis } from "recharts";
import { short, visitors, visitorsConfig } from "./data";

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <ChartContainer
      config={visitorsConfig}
      aria-label="Visitors by month, on desktop and mobile"
      patterns
    >
      <BarChart data={visitors}>
        <CartesianGrid vertical={false} />
        <XAxis
          dataKey="month"
          tickFormatter={short}
          tickLine={false}
          axisLine={false}
        />
        <ChartTooltip />
        <ChartLegend />
        <Bar dataKey="desktop" fill={chartFill("desktop")} radius={4} />
        <Bar dataKey="mobile" fill={chartFill("mobile")} radius={4} />
      </BarChart>
    </ChartContainer>
  );
}
```

The first series stays plain, and the next seven each get a different pattern and a different dash. The legend and the tooltip show the same pattern as the series.

Three things decide whether a series is patterned:

- `patterns` on the container turns them on for every series.
- `pattern` or `dash` on a series in the config sets that one for good, whatever the container says. `"solid"` keeps it plain.
- Where the browser is forcing colors, as Windows high contrast does, patterns are on whatever you set. A forced palette doesn't reach inside a drawing, so there every series is drawn in the system's text color and the patterns are what tell them apart.

This only works for series colored with `chartFill` and `chartDash`. A series given a color directly has no pattern to switch to.

Patterns are one way to meet [WCAG 1.4.1](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/use-of-color.html), which asks that color isn't the only way to tell things apart. A label written on each series, or a visible table, are others.

## The same numbers as a table

`ChartTable` writes the chart's data as a table, and goes in the container's `table`:

```tsx
<ChartContainer
  config={config}
  aria-label="Visitors by month"
  table={<ChartTable data={data} category="month" categoryLabel="Month" />}
>
```

It has a column for each series in the config, headed by the series' label, and a row for each row of the data, headed by its `category`.

Without `visible` the table is in the page for screen readers and takes no room. With it, the table is drawn under the chart:

```tsx
"use client";

import { ChartContainer, ChartTable, chartColor } from "@nuvui/charts";
import { CartesianGrid, Line, LineChart, XAxis } from "recharts";
import { short, visitors, visitorsConfig } from "./data";

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <ChartContainer
      config={visitorsConfig}
      aria-label="Visitors by month"
      table={
        <ChartTable
          data={visitors}
          category="month"
          categoryLabel="Month"
          caption="Visitors by month, January to June"
          visible
        />
      }
    >
      <LineChart data={visitors}>
        <CartesianGrid vertical={false} />
        <XAxis
          dataKey="month"
          tickFormatter={short}
          tickLine={false}
          axisLine={false}
        />
        <Line
          dataKey="desktop"
          stroke={chartColor("desktop")}
          strokeWidth={2}
          dot={false}
        />
        <Line
          dataKey="mobile"
          stroke={chartColor("mobile")}
          strokeWidth={2}
          dot={false}
        />
      </LineChart>
    </ChartContainer>
  );
}
```

Give every chart a table unless the same numbers are already in the page as text. It's the only part of a chart a screen reader can read as data, and with `visible` it's also how anyone reads an exact number off a chart.

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `data` (required) | `readonly object[]` |  | The rows the chart was drawn from. |
| `category` (required) | `string` |  | The field that names each row, such as the month. It's the heading of the row. |
| `categoryLabel` (required) | `ReactNode` |  | The heading of that column. |
| `series` | `string[]` |  | The fields to show, in order. Left out, it's every key of the chart's config. |
| `visible` | `boolean` | `false` | Shows the table under the chart. Without it the table is there for screen readers only. |
| `caption` | `ReactNode` |  | A caption for the table. Without one the table has the chart's name. |
| `formatCategory` | `((value: number \| string) => ReactNode)` |  | How a category is written. |
| `formatValue` | `ChartValueFormatter` |  | How a value is written. The container's `formatValue` by default. |

`ChartTable` also takes a `table` element's attributes and a `ref`.

## Formatting numbers

`formatValue` on the container says how a value is written in the tooltip and in the table. It's given the value and the series' key:

```tsx
const number = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US");

<ChartContainer formatValue={(value) => number.format(Number(value))} ... >
```

Name the locale. The table is rendered on the server as well as in the browser, and a formatter that takes each one's default locale can write two different texts for one number, which React reports as an error. Without `formatValue` a value is shown as it is in the data.

The numbers on an axis are Recharts' own, set with `tickFormatter` on the axis.

## Size

The container is as wide as the space it's in, and the chart is drawn in a box shaped 16 to 9. Two variables change that:

```css
.revenue {
  --nuv-chart-aspect-ratio: 2 / 1;
}

.sparkline {
  --nuv-chart-height: 4rem;
  --nuv-chart-aspect-ratio: auto;
}
```

The chart follows the box when it changes size. Don't wrap it in Recharts' `ResponsiveContainer`, and don't give the chart a `width` or a `height`: the container sets `responsive` on it.

The container's child has to be the Recharts chart itself, `<BarChart>` or one of the others. The container hands it its size and its name as props, and a component of your own in between wouldn't pass them on. Put the container inside that component instead.

## Legend

`ChartLegend` is Recharts' `Legend` with the library's look. It lists the series in the config's order, with their labels and the same fill, pattern or dashes as the series:

```tsx
<ChartLegend />
<ChartLegend indicator="line" verticalAlign="top" />
```

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `indicator` | `"line" \| "square"` | `"square"` | The sample drawn next to each series. |
| `nameKey` | `string` |  | The field of a data row that holds the series' key. Only needed when neither the series' name nor its data key is a key of the config. |
| `className` | `string` |  |  |

It takes everything Recharts' `Legend` takes. The tooltip has [a page of its own](page:charts/tooltip).

## Props

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `config` (required) | `ChartConfig` |  | The series of the chart: a label, and optionally a color, for each. |
| `children` (required) | `ReactElement<unknown, string \| React.JSXElementConstructor<any>>` |  | One Recharts chart, such as `<BarChart>`. It's sized to the container and given the container's name. |
| `table` | `ReactNode` |  | The same numbers as a table, usually a `ChartTable`. It's drawn after the chart. |
| `patterns` | `boolean` | `false` | Fills each series with a pattern of its own and dashes its line, so that series can be told apart without color. Where the browser is forcing colors this happens whatever is set here. |
| `formatValue` | `ChartValueFormatter` |  | How a value is written in the tooltip and the table. Left out, a value is shown as it is in the data. |

`ChartContainer` also takes a `div`'s attributes and a `ref`, and one of `aria-label` and `aria-labelledby`.

## Accessibility

### Keyboard

A chart is one stop for <kbd>Tab</kbd>. With focus on it:

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>←</kbd> and <kbd>→</kbd> | Move to the point before or after, and show its tooltip. |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> | Hides the tooltip, or shows it again. |

This is Recharts' own keyboard layer, which is on unless a chart sets `accessibilityLayer={false}`.

### What the components handle

- The chart has the name you gave the container, and a focus ring when it has keyboard focus. Recharts gives it `role="application"`, which tells a screen reader to pass the arrow keys through.
- The tooltip is a live region, so a screen reader hears the point the arrow keys moved to.
- The axes, the grid and the labels take their colors from the tokens. Axis text is held to 4.5:1 against the page, and the eight chart colors to 3:1, in every theme the library ships.
- Animation is off for people who've asked their system to reduce motion. Recharts does this itself.
- Where the browser forces colors, every series is drawn in the system's text color with a pattern of its own.

### What you need to handle

- Name the chart for what it shows: "Visitors by month, on desktop and mobile".
- Give it a `ChartTable`.
- Turn `patterns` on, or label the series directly, when a chart has more than one.
- Don't put anything in a chart that's only in the tooltip. A tooltip can't be reached on a touch screen without a tap on the right spot.

### With a screen reader

Recharts' guidance is that VoiceOver users have to turn QuickNav off to move through a chart's points with the arrow keys, because QuickNav takes those keys for itself.

None of this has been checked with a screen reader yet: what's said when focus lands on a chart, and how the tooltip's text is read as it changes. The table doesn't depend on any of it.

## CSS variables

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-chart-fg` | `var(--color-muted-foreground)` | Color of the text on the axes. |
| `--nuv-chart-font-size` | `var(--text-xs)` | Size of the text on the axes. |
| `--nuv-chart-height` | `auto` | Height of the box the chart is drawn in. Set the aspect ratio to auto with it. |
| `--nuv-chart-aspect-ratio` | `16/9` | Shape of the box, while it has no height. |
| `--nuv-chart-tooltip-border` | `var(--color-border)` | Border color of the tooltip. |
| `--nuv-chart-tooltip-radius` | `var(--radius-lg)` | Corner radius of the tooltip. |
| `--nuv-chart-tooltip-bg` | `var(--color-surface)` | Background of the tooltip. |
| `--nuv-chart-tooltip-shadow` | `var(--shadow-lg)` | Shadow under the tooltip. |
| `--nuv-chart-tooltip-fg` | `var(--color-surface-foreground)` | Text color of the tooltip. |
| `--nuv-chart-legend-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Text color of the legend. |
| `--nuv-chart-table-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Text color of a visible table. |
| `--nuv-chart-table-border` | `var(--color-border)` | Color of the lines between its rows. |
| `--nuv-chart-label-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Color of a label written onto the chart. |
| `--nuv-chart-grid` | `var(--color-border)` | Color of the grid lines. |
| `--nuv-chart-axis` | `var(--color-border-strong)` | Color of the axis lines, their ticks and a reference line. |
| `--nuv-chart-cursor` | `var(--color-border-strong)`, `var(--color-muted)` | Color of what follows the pointer: the line on a line chart, the band behind a group of bars. Also the track behind a radial bar. |
| `--nuv-chart-backdrop` | `var(--color-background)` | The color behind the chart. It's drawn between the slices of a pie and around a dot. Set it when the chart is on a card. |

The stylesheet also sets three variables of its own on the container, `--nuv-chart-patterns`, `--nuv-chart-solid` and `--nuv-chart-forced-color`. They're the switches behind `patterns` and forced colors. Leave them alone.

## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-chart` | The container. |
| `.nuv-chart__data` | The box around the table. |
| `.nuv-chart__data--hidden` | That box, when the table is for screen readers only. |
| `.nuv-chart__legend` | The legend's list. |
| `.nuv-chart__legend-item` | One series in the legend. |
| `.nuv-chart__legend-item--inactive` | A series Recharts reports as hidden. |
| `.nuv-chart__patterns` | A hidden svg that holds the patterns. It takes no room. |
| `.nuv-chart__plot` | The box the chart is drawn in. |
| `.nuv-chart__swatch` | The sample of a series, in the tooltip and the legend. |
| `.nuv-chart__swatch--line` | A sample drawn as a line. |
| `.nuv-chart__table` | The table. |
| `.nuv-chart__tooltip` | The tooltip's panel. |
| `.nuv-chart__tooltip-item` | One series in the tooltip. |
| `.nuv-chart__tooltip-items` | The list of series. |
| `.nuv-chart__tooltip-label` | The line that says which point it is. |
| `.nuv-chart__tooltip-name` | Its label. |
| `.nuv-chart__tooltip-value` | Its value. |

Recharts' own elements keep Recharts' class names, such as `recharts-cartesian-grid`. The stylesheet colors them from the variables above, and they aren't part of this library's naming.

## Do and don't

**Do**

- Make the config once, outside the component.
- Color a series with `chartFill` or `chartColor`, so the theme and the patterns reach it.
- Give the chart a table.

**Don't**

- Don't wrap the chart in `ResponsiveContainer` or give it a size.
- Don't write a color straight into a series when its config has one.
- Don't use more than eight series in one chart. Past that the colors repeat, and no one can follow that many.

| `--nuv-chart-tooltip-shadow` | `var(--shadow-lg)` | Shadow under the tooltip. |
| `--nuv-chart-tooltip-fg` | `var(--color-surface-foreground)` | Text color of the tooltip. |
| `--nuv-chart-legend-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Text color of the legend. |
| `--nuv-chart-table-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Text color of a visible table. |
| `--nuv-chart-table-border` | `var(--color-border)` | Color of the lines between its rows. |
| `--nuv-chart-label-fg` | `var(--color-foreground)` | Color of a label written onto the chart. |
| `--nuv-chart-grid` | `var(--color-border)` | Color of the grid lines. |
| `--nuv-chart-axis` | `var(--color-border-strong)` | Color of the axis lines, their ticks and a reference line. |
| `--nuv-chart-cursor` | `var(--color-border-strong)`, `var(--color-muted)` | Color of what follows the pointer: the line on a line chart, the band behind a group of bars. Also the track behind a radial bar. |
| `--nuv-chart-backdrop` | `var(--color-background)` | The color behind the chart. It's drawn between the slices of a pie and around a dot. Set it when the chart is on a card. |

The stylesheet also sets three variables of its own on the container, `--nuv-chart-patterns`, `--nuv-chart-solid` and `--nuv-chart-forced-color`. They're the switches behind `patterns` and forced colors. Leave them alone.

sections.heading: Classes
sections.markdown:
## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-chart` | The container. |
| `.nuv-chart__data` | The box around the table. |
| `.nuv-chart__data--hidden` | That box, when the table is for screen readers only. |
| `.nuv-chart__legend` | The legend's list. |
| `.nuv-chart__legend-item` | One series in the legend. |
| `.nuv-chart__legend-item--inactive` | A series Recharts reports as hidden. |
| `.nuv-chart__patterns` | A hidden svg that holds the patterns. It takes no room. |
| `.nuv-chart__plot` | The box the chart is drawn in. |
| `.nuv-chart__swatch` | The sample of a series, in the tooltip and the legend. |
| `.nuv-chart__swatch--line` | A sample drawn as a line. |
| `.nuv-chart__table` | The table. |
| `.nuv-chart__tooltip` | The tooltip's panel. |
| `.nuv-chart__tooltip-item` | One series in the tooltip. |
| `.nuv-chart__tooltip-items` | The list of series. |
| `.nuv-chart__tooltip-label` | The line that says which point it is. |
| `.nuv-chart__tooltip-name` | Its label. |
| `.nuv-chart__tooltip-value` | Its value. |

Recharts' own elements keep Recharts' class names, such as `recharts-cartesian-grid`. The stylesheet colors them from the variables above, and they aren't part of this library's naming.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Make the config once, outside the component.
- Color a series with `chartFill` or `chartColor`, so the theme and the patterns reach it.
- Give the chart a table.

**Don't**

- Don't wrap the chart in `ResponsiveContainer` or give it a size.
- Don't write a color straight into a series when its config has one.
- Don't use more than eight series in one chart. Past that the colors repeat, and no one can follow that many.

pages.title: Area chart
pages.description: Area charts with Recharts' AreaChart in a ChartContainer. One series, stacked series and a gradient fill, colored from the theme.

sections.heading: How it's made
sections.markdown:
## How it's made

`AreaChart` and `Area` come from Recharts. An area has two colors: `fill` for the space and `stroke` for the line along its top.

```tsx
<Area
  dataKey="desktop"
  fill={chartFill("desktop")}
  fillOpacity={0.4}
  stroke={chartColor("desktop")}
/>
```

A see-through fill lets the grid show, and lets two areas that overlap both be seen.

sections.heading: Stacked
A gradient
Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

- <kbd>←</kbd> and <kbd>→</kbd> move along the points, and the tooltip reads out each one.
- Stacked areas are hard to read exactly: only the bottom series sits on a flat line. Give the chart a [table](page:charts/chart#the-same-numbers-as-a-table), which has every number.
- Two overlapping areas of different colors mix where they cross. With `patterns` each keeps a fill that can be told from the other.
- Name the chart for what it shows, and say that it's stacked if it is.

Everything on the [ChartContainer page](page:charts/chart#accessibility) applies.

pages.title: Bar chart
pages.description: Bar charts with Recharts' BarChart in a ChartContainer. Grouped, stacked with totals, and horizontal bars, colored from the theme, with pattern fills.

sections.heading: How it's made
sections.markdown:
## How it's made

`BarChart` and `Bar` come from Recharts. Each `Bar` is a series, and bars of different series sit side by side in each category.

```tsx
<Bar dataKey="desktop" fill={chartFill("desktop")} radius={4} />
```

Start the value axis at zero, which Recharts does by default. A bar's length is its value, and a bar cut off at the bottom shows a difference that isn't there.

sections.heading: Stacked, with totals
Horizontal
Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

- <kbd>←</kbd> and <kbd>→</kbd> move from category to category. The tooltip reads out every series in that category.
- In a horizontal chart the keys are still <kbd>←</kbd> and <kbd>→</kbd>, and it's <kbd>←</kbd> that moves down the list. <kbd>↑</kbd> and <kbd>↓</kbd> do nothing. That's Recharts' keyboard layer at this version, measured on the example above.
- Bars that touch, as in a stack, are told apart only by their fill. Turn on [`patterns`](page:charts/chart#patterns).
- A label written on a bar is in the theme's text color, on the page and not on the bar, so it keeps its contrast whatever the bar's color is. Put it above or beside the bar, not inside.
- Give the chart a [table](page:charts/chart#the-same-numbers-as-a-table). For a stacked chart, include the total as a column.

Everything on the [ChartContainer page](page:charts/chart#accessibility) applies.

pages.title: Line chart
pages.description: Line charts with Recharts' LineChart in a ChartContainer. Several series colored from the theme, with dashes that tell them apart without color.

sections.heading: How it's made
sections.markdown:
## How it's made

`LineChart` and `Line` come from Recharts. A line has a `stroke` and no fill:

```tsx
<Line
  dataKey="desktop"
  stroke={chartColor("desktop")}
  strokeDasharray={chartDash("desktop")}
  strokeWidth={2}
/>
```

Draw a line 2 pixels wide. At 1 pixel a color is hard to make out, and the 3:1 the chart colors are held to is measured on something at least that thick.

`indicator="line"` on the tooltip and the legend makes their samples short lines, which show a line's dashes where a square can't.

sections.heading: Dashes
Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

- <kbd>←</kbd> and <kbd>→</kbd> move along the points. The tooltip reads out every line's value at that point.
- Lines cross, and where they do, color is all that says which is which. Use dashes when there's more than one line.
- Dots on a line make its points easier to hit with a pointer, and show where the data really is. On a line with many points, `dot={false}` keeps it readable.
- More than four or five lines is hard for anyone to follow. Show fewer, or let people choose which.
- Give the chart a [table](page:charts/chart#the-same-numbers-as-a-table).

Everything on the [ChartContainer page](page:charts/chart#accessibility) applies.

pages.title: Pie chart
pages.description: Pie and donut charts with Recharts' PieChart in a ChartContainer. Each slice colored and named from the config, with pattern fills and a total in the middle.

sections.heading: How it's made
sections.markdown:
## How it's made

`PieChart` and `Pie` come from Recharts. A pie has one `Pie`, whose slices are the rows of its data:

```tsx
const slices = browsers.map((row) => ({
  ...row,
  fill: chartFill(row.browser),
}));

<Pie data={slices} dataKey="visitors" nameKey="browser" />
```

The config has an entry for each slice, under the value its row has in the `nameKey` field. A slice takes its color from a `fill` field in its row, which is where `chartFill` goes. The tooltip and the legend then find each slice's label in the config by its name.

A pie is as wide as it is tall. In the container's usual box, which is wider than it's tall, it would be small with empty space either side. The stylesheet above makes the box square with `--nuv-chart-aspect-ratio`, and stops it growing with a `max-inline-size`.

sections.heading: A donut
Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

- Slices touch, so their fill is all that separates them. Use [`patterns`](page:charts/chart#patterns), as the first example does.
- A legend makes people look back and forth between it and the pie. With few slices, a label on each slice is easier to read.
- The number in the middle of a donut is text in the chart, which a screen reader doesn't reach. Say it in the chart's name, as the example does, or in the page.
- Give the chart a [table](page:charts/chart#the-same-numbers-as-a-table). With `series` set to the one field that holds the values, it has a row for each slice.
- The arrow keys move from slice to slice.

Everything on the [ChartContainer page](page:charts/chart#accessibility) applies.

pages.title: Radar chart
pages.description: Radar charts with Recharts' RadarChart in a ChartContainer. Series compared across several axes, colored from the theme, with a polar grid styled from the tokens.

sections.heading: How it's made
sections.markdown:
## How it's made

`RadarChart`, `PolarGrid`, `PolarAngleAxis` and `Radar` come from Recharts. Each `Radar` is a series, with a fill and a line around it:

```tsx
<Radar
  dataKey="desktop"
  fill={chartFill("desktop")}
  fillOpacity={0.4}
  stroke={chartColor("desktop")}
/>
```

Keep the fill see-through. Two shapes overlap over most of their area, and a solid one hides the other.

The grid and the names around it take their colors from `--nuv-chart-grid` and `--nuv-chart-fg`.

Like a pie, a radar chart is as wide as it is tall, so the example gives it a square box and a width to stop at.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

- The arrow keys move from spoke to spoke, and the tooltip reads out every series there.
- Where two shapes overlap their colors mix. Dash the lines with `chartDash`, as the example does, and turn on [`patterns`](page:charts/chart#patterns).
- A radar chart's values are hard to read off even for someone who can see it. Give it a [table](page:charts/chart#the-same-numbers-as-a-table), and consider making that table `visible`.
- More than three series is too many for this chart.

Everything on the [ChartContainer page](page:charts/chart#accessibility) applies.

pages.title: Radial chart
pages.description: Radial bar charts with Recharts' RadialBarChart in a ChartContainer. Bars bent into rings, each colored and named from the config.

sections.heading: How it's made
sections.markdown:
## How it's made

`RadialBarChart` and `RadialBar` come from Recharts. As in a [pie](page:charts/pie), each row of the data is a ring, and takes its color from a `fill` field in the row:

```tsx
const bars = browsers.map((row) => ({
  ...row,
  fill: chartFill(row.browser),
}));

<RadialBarChart data={bars} innerRadius="25%" outerRadius="100%">
  <RadialBar dataKey="visitors" background />
</RadialBarChart>
```

`background` draws the track each ring runs along, in `--nuv-chart-cursor`.

Every ring is read from the same field, so the tooltip and the legend can't tell from the series which label to use. `nameKey="browser"` on each says which field of the row holds the config's key.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

- The rings don't say what they are. Keep the legend, or the names are only in the tooltip.
- Give the chart a [table](page:charts/chart#the-same-numbers-as-a-table). Nobody reads an exact value off a ring.
- Turn on [`patterns`](page:charts/chart#patterns) when the rings need to be told apart without color.
- The arrow keys move from ring to ring.

Everything on the [ChartContainer page](page:charts/chart#accessibility) applies.

pages.title: Chart tooltip
pages.description: ChartTooltip, Recharts' tooltip drawn like the library's other floating panels. It names each series from the config, shows its color or pattern, formats values, and is a live region for screen readers.

sections.heading: Import
sections.markdown:
## Import

```tsx
import { ChartTooltip, ChartTooltipContent } from "@nuvui/charts";
```

Put `<ChartTooltip />` inside the chart, where Recharts' `Tooltip` would go. It takes everything `Tooltip` takes, such as `cursor`, `trigger` and `defaultIndex`.

sections.heading: What it shows
sections.markdown:
## What it shows

- **The point**, on the first line: the category from the axis, such as the month. `hideLabel` leaves it out, for a pie, where each slice already says what it is.
- **A row for each series**, with a sample, the series' label from the config, and its value.

The sample is drawn from the series' own variables, so it has the same color, the same pattern and the same dashes. `indicator="line"` makes it a short line, for a line chart. The default is a square.

A series is matched to the config by its name, then by its `dataKey`. A series the config doesn't have is shown with Recharts' name and color for it. Where neither is a key of the config, as with the rings of a [radial chart](page:charts/radial), `nameKey` names the field of the data row that is.

sections.heading: Formatting
Props
sections.markdown:
## Props

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `indicator` | `"line" \| "square"` | `"square"` | The sample drawn next to each series. |
| `hideLabel` | `boolean` | `false` | Leaves out the line that says which point this is, for a chart where each row already says it. |
| `nameKey` | `string` |  | The field of a data row that holds the series' key. Only needed when neither the series' name nor its data key is a key of the config. |
| `formatValue` | `ChartValueFormatter` |  | How a value is written. The container's `formatValue` by default. |
| `className` | `string` |  |  |

sections.heading: Your own tooltip
Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

- The tooltip is a live region. When the arrow keys move to a point, a screen reader reads the tooltip's text: the point, then each series and its value.
- It's in the page from the start, empty and hidden, because a live region that arrives with its text already in it isn't read.
- <kbd>Enter</kbd> on a focused chart hides the tooltip and shows it again.
- The tooltip never takes focus and has nothing in it to press. Don't put links or buttons in one.
- On a touch screen a tooltip opens on a tap and covers part of the chart. Nothing should be in the tooltip only: the [table](page:charts/chart#the-same-numbers-as-a-table) has the same numbers.
- The tooltip's slide between points is Recharts' animation, and is off when the system asks for reduced motion.

How the text is read as it changes hasn't been checked with a screen reader yet. Recharts' guidance is that VoiceOver users have to turn QuickNav off for the arrow keys to reach the chart.

pages.title: Composed chart
pages.description: Bars, lines and a target line in one chart, with Recharts' ComposedChart in a ChartContainer.

sections.heading: How it's made
sections.markdown:
## How it's made

`ComposedChart` comes from Recharts, and takes `Bar`, `Line`, `Area` and `Scatter` together. They're drawn in the order they're written, so put bars first and lines after, or the bars cover the lines.

```tsx
<ComposedChart data={quarters}>
  <Bar dataKey="revenue" fill={chartFill("revenue")} />
  <Line dataKey="margin" stroke={chartColor("margin")} strokeWidth={2} />
  <ReferenceLine y={60} label="Target" />
</ComposedChart>
```

sections.heading: A target line
sections.markdown:
## A target line

`ReferenceLine` draws a line at a value on an axis. It isn't a series: it has no entry in the config, the tooltip and the legend leave it out, and it takes its color from `--nuv-chart-axis`. Its `label` says what it is.

Because it's in none of those, it isn't in the table either. Say the target in the chart's name, as the example does, or add it to the data as a column.

sections.heading: Two scales
sections.markdown:
## Two scales

Recharts can put a second `YAxis` on the right, with `yAxisId` tying each series to one of them. Think twice. Where two lines on two scales cross means nothing, since moving either scale moves the crossing, and people read meaning into it anyway. Two charts one above the other, sharing an `XAxis`, say the same thing without that.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

- <kbd>←</kbd> and <kbd>→</kbd> move along the categories. The tooltip reads out every series there, bars and lines alike.
- A bar and a line already differ in shape, which is a way to tell two series apart without color. Two lines, or two sets of bars, still need [dashes or patterns](page:charts/chart#patterns).
- A reference line's label is text in the chart. Repeat what it says in the chart's name.
- Give the chart a [table](page:charts/chart#the-same-numbers-as-a-table).

Everything on the [ChartContainer page](page:charts/chart#accessibility) applies.

pages.title: Scatter chart
pages.description: Scatter charts with Recharts' ScatterChart in a ChartContainer. Groups of points on two number axes, colored from the theme and told apart by shape.
pages.markdown:
# Scatter chart

Scatter charts with Recharts' ScatterChart in a ChartContainer. Groups of points on two number axes, colored from the theme and told apart by shape.

A scatter chart puts each thing at a point on two number axes, to show whether the two measures move together and which points stand apart.

```tsx
"use client";

import {
  type ChartConfig,
  ChartContainer,
  ChartLegend,
  ChartTooltip,
  chartFill,
} from "@nuvui/charts";
import { CartesianGrid, Scatter, ScatterChart, XAxis, YAxis } from "recharts";

const startups = [
  { seats: 12, days: 18 },
  { seats: 25, days: 24 },
  { seats: 8, days: 9 },
  { seats: 40, days: 31 },
  { seats: 18, days: 15 },
];
const enterprises = [
  { seats: 220, days: 84 },
  { seats: 340, days: 121 },
  { seats: 150, days: 66 },
  { seats: 480, days: 140 },
];

const config = {
  startup: { label: "Startup" },
  enterprise: { label: "Enterprise" },
} satisfies ChartConfig;

export default function Example() {
  return (
    <ChartContainer
      config={config}
      aria-label="Days to close a deal against seats sold, for startups and enterprises"
    >
      <ScatterChart margin={{ top: 8, right: 12, bottom: 20 }}>
        <CartesianGrid />
        <XAxis
          type="number"
          dataKey="seats"
          name="Seats"
          tickLine={false}
          label={{ value: "Seats", position: "insideBottom", offset: -12 }}
        />
        <YAxis
          type="number"
          dataKey="days"
          name="Days to close"
          tickLine={false}
          width={40}
        />
        <ChartTooltip hideLabel />
        <ChartLegend verticalAlign="top" />
        <Scatter
          name="startup"
          data={startups}
          fill={chartFill("startup")}
          shape="circle"
        />
        <Scatter
          name="enterprise"
          data={enterprises}
          fill={chartFill("enterprise")}
          shape="diamond"
        />
      </ScatterChart>
    </ChartContainer>
  );
}
```

## How it's made

`ScatterChart` and `Scatter` come from Recharts. Both axes are numbers, so each needs `type="number"` and the field it reads. Each `Scatter` is a group of points with data of its own:

```tsx
<XAxis type="number" dataKey="seats" name="Seats" />
<YAxis type="number" dataKey="days" name="Days to close" />
<Scatter name="startup" data={startups} fill={chartFill("startup")} shape="circle" />
<Scatter name="enterprise" data={enterprises} fill={chartFill("enterprise")} shape="diamond" />
```

The config has an entry for each group, under the `name` its `Scatter` has. That's what the legend lists.

The tooltip for a point has a row for each axis, named by the axis's `name`. Give both axes one.

Label the axes. A scatter chart's axes are two measures, and nothing else in the chart says which is which.

## Shapes

`shape` on a `Scatter` is what tells groups apart without color: `"circle"`, `"cross"`, `"diamond"`, `"square"`, `"star"`, `"triangle"` and `"wye"`. Give each group its own. Points are too small for a pattern to show, so [`patterns`](page:charts/chart#patterns) isn't the tool here.

## Accessibility

- The arrow keys step through the points of the first group, in the order of its data, and don't reach the other groups. That's how Recharts' keyboard layer treats a scatter chart at this version, measured on the example above. With one group, every point can be reached.
- That makes a text version matter more. `ChartTable` draws one table from one list of rows, which fits a chart with a single group. For several groups, write the table yourself, with a column that says which group each row is in.
- Say what the chart shows in its name: the two measures and what was found, such as "Days to close rise with seats sold".
- Give each group a shape of its own.

Everything on the [ChartContainer page](page:charts/chart#accessibility) applies.

sections.markdown:
## How it's made

`ScatterChart` and `Scatter` come from Recharts. Both axes are numbers, so each needs `type="number"` and the field it reads. Each `Scatter` is a group of points with data of its own:

```tsx

<YAxis type="number" dataKey="days" name="Days to close" />
<Scatter name="startup" data={startups} fill={chartFill("startup")} shape="circle" />
```

pages.title: Barcodes
pages.description: The @nuvui/barcodes package. Barcodes in seventeen kinds and QR codes, drawn as SVG, installed next to @nuvui/react.
pages.markdown:
# Barcodes

The @nuvui/barcodes package. Barcodes in seventeen kinds and QR codes, drawn as SVG, installed next to @nuvui/react.

Barcodes and QR codes are a package of their own, `@nuvui/barcodes`. It has two components:

| Component | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| [Barcode](page:barcodes/barcode) | Bars for a scanner at a till, a warehouse door or a pharmacy: Code 128, Code 39, EAN, UPC, ITF, MSI, Codabar and Pharmacode. |
| [QRCode](page:barcodes/qrcode) | A square code for a phone's camera, with four levels of error correction and room for a logo in the middle. |

It's separate from `@nuvui/react` because of what it brings with it. Working out the bars is [JsBarcode](https://github.com/lindell/JsBarcode)'s job and working out a QR code's squares is [uqr](https://github.com/unjs/uqr)'s. An app that only wants buttons and dialogs shouldn't have to install, review and update either.

## Install

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/barcodes @nuvui/react
```

`@nuvui/react` is a peer dependency: the codes take their colors and their font from its tokens. `jsbarcode` and `uqr` come along as ordinary dependencies, and neither has dependencies of its own. You don't install them yourself.

Only the encoders are used. The drawing is done here, so that a code is markup like any other component and not a canvas.

## Load the styles

Import the package's stylesheet once, after the core's:

```tsx title="app/layout.tsx"
import "@nuvui/react/styles.css";
import "@nuvui/barcodes/styles.css";
```

It's a few rules: the colors, the font of the text under a barcode, and the size a code shrinks to in a narrow space. Both files open with the same line naming the cascade layers, so the order you import them in doesn't decide which rule wins. To load one component's styles on their own, there's `@nuvui/barcodes/css/barcode.css` and `@nuvui/barcodes/css/qrcode.css`.

## Use a component

```tsx
import { Barcode, QRCode } from "@nuvui/barcodes";

export default function Page() {
  return (
    <>
      <Barcode value="ORD-2026-001042" aria-label="Order ORD-2026-001042" />
      <QRCode value="https://example.com/orders/1042" aria-label="Open the order" />
    </>
  );
}
```

Each component also has an entry of its own, `@nuvui/barcodes/barcode` and `@nuvui/barcodes/qrcode`. A page that shows only QR codes can import from the second and leave every barcode's tables out of its bundle, whatever the bundler does with unused code.

## Black on white, in every theme

A code keeps dark bars on a light ground when the rest of the page goes dark. A scanner reads the difference between the two, and many scanners don't read a light code on a dark ground at all. So the two colors are the palette's black and white and not the theme's foreground and background, and they stay as they are where the browser forces its own colors.

Both have a variable to change them. If you do, keep the bars much darker than the ground, keep the ground light, and try the result with the scanners your codes meet.

## Check a value before it's drawn

Not every value can be every kind of code: an EAN-13 is digits only, with a check digit that has to be right. Each component draws [an empty box with a line through it](page:barcodes/barcode#a-value-that-cant-be-a-barcode) for a value it can't encode, and never a code that reads as something else.

To find out without drawing, the encoders are exported. They need no browser, so they run in a form's validation, in a server action or in a script:

```tsx
import { encodeBarcode, encodeQRCode } from "@nuvui/barcodes";

encodeBarcode("590123412345", "ean13")?.text; // "5901234123457", with its check digit
encodeBarcode("5901-2341", "ean13"); // null
encodeQRCode("https://example.com")?.version; // 2
```

## Save a code as a file

`saveCode` downloads a code that's on the page as an SVG or a PNG. It takes the code's element, which each component gives through `ref`:

```tsx
"use client";

import { QRCode, saveCode } from "@nuvui/barcodes";
import { useRef } from "react";

export function Ticket() {
  const code = useRef<SVGSVGElement>(null);
  return (
    <>
      <QRCode ref={code} value="https://example.com/t/8841" aria-label="Ticket 8841" />
      <button
        type="button"
        onClick={() => code.current && saveCode(code.current, { name: "ticket-8841", format: "png" })}
      >
        Save
      </button>
    </>
  );
}
```

| Function | What it gives |
| --- | --- |
| `saveCode(code, { name, format, scale })` | Nothing: it starts a download named `name` with the format's ending. |
| `codeToBlob(code, { format, scale })` | The file's contents, to upload or to put in an email. |
| `codeToSvg(code)` | The SVG as text. |

`format` is `"svg"`, the default, or `"png"`. An SVG stays sharp at any size and is the one to print from. A PNG is `scale` times the size the code was made at, four times unless you say.

The file stands by itself: the colors and the font the stylesheet gives the code are written into it, and its name on the page becomes its title. A picture laid over a QR code is fetched and put into the file. If it's on another site that doesn't allow that, it's left out of a PNG.

There's no PDF. That would need a PDF library in every app that uses this package. An SVG goes into a PDF from any tool that makes one, and a page with a code on it prints.

These three are also at `@nuvui/barcodes/save`.

## Server components

Neither component has state, and neither needs a browser to work out or to draw a code. They carry no `"use client"`, so a code rendered in a server component is plain SVG in the HTML and sends no script.

`saveCode` and the other two functions for files do need a browser. Call them from a client component, in answer to a press.

## What's not here

- **Other two-dimensional codes:** Data Matrix, PDF417 and Aztec.
- **Code 93, and the EAN add-ons** of two and five digits printed beside a book's or a magazine's barcode.
- **Reading a code** with a camera. These draw codes.
- **Drawing on a canvas.** An SVG scales and prints sharply and can be styled, and `codeToBlob` gives a PNG where a picture is wanted.

```sh
pnpm add @nuvui/barcodes @nuvui/react
```

sections.heading: Load the styles

Import the package's stylesheet once, after the core's:

```tsx title="app/layout.tsx"
import "@nuvui/react/styles.css";
import "@nuvui/barcodes/styles.css";
```

sections.heading: Use a component
Black on white, in every theme
sections.markdown:
## Black on white, in every theme

A code keeps dark bars on a light ground when the rest of the page goes dark. A scanner reads the difference between the two, and many scanners don't read a light code on a dark ground at all. So the two colors are the palette's black and white and not the theme's foreground and background, and they stay as they are where the browser forces its own colors.

Both have a variable to change them. If you do, keep the bars much darker than the ground, keep the ground light, and try the result with the scanners your codes meet.

# Barcode Bars for a scanner, drawn as SVG. Code 128, Code 39, EAN, UPC, ITF, MSI, Codabar and Pharmacode, with the value written underneath. Use a barcode where a handheld or a fixed scanner reads it: a product at a till, a parcel's label, a shelf in a stock room, a patient's wristband. For a phone's camera, and for an address or any longer text, use a [QR code](page:barcodes/qrcode). ```tsx import { Barcode } from "@nuvui/barcodes"; export default function Example() { return ; } ``` ## Install ```sh pnpm add @nuvui/barcodes @nuvui/react ``` ## Import ```tsx import { Barcode } from "@nuvui/barcodes"; ``` The styles come from `@nuvui/barcodes/styles.css`, which you load once for the whole app, after `@nuvui/react/styles.css`. [Barcodes](page:barcodes/index) covers that. ```tsx ``` ## Kinds `type` says which kind of barcode to draw. Which one you need is decided by whatever reads it: a retail till wants an EAN or a UPC, a carrier's label a Code 128. The value is the application identifiers and their data, without the brackets. | Cartons and pallets in a supply chain. | | `"code39"` | Capitals, digits, the space and `-` `.` `$` `/` `+` `%`. Small letters are made capitals. | Older systems, in industry and defense. | | `"code39-mod43"` | The same, with a check character added. | Where a Code 39 has to be checked. | | `"ean13"` | Twelve digits, and the thirteenth is worked out. ## Props

Barcode also takes the attributes of an `<svg>`, and `ref` goes to it.

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value` (required) | `string` |  | What the barcode holds. |
| `type` | `"codabar" \| "code128" \| "code39" \| "code39-mod43" \| "ean13" \| "ean8" \| "gs1-128" \| "itf" \| "itf14" \| "msi" \| "msi-mod10" \| "msi-mod1010" \| "msi-mod11" \| "msi-mod1110" \| "pharmacode" \| "upca" \| "upce"` | `"code128"` | The kind of barcode. Each takes its own values: an EAN-13 is twelve or thirteen digits, a Code 39 is capitals, digits and a few signs, and a Code 128 is any ASCII text. |
| `barWidth` | `number` | `2` | The width of the narrowest bar, in pixels. A scanner needs it to be a whole number of the screen's or the printer's dots. |
| `height` | `number` | `64` | The height of the bars, in pixels. The text is under that. |
| `quietZone` | `number` | `10` | The empty space at each end, counted in narrowest bars. A scanner finds the barcode by it, and most kinds ask for ten. |
| `showText` | `boolean` | `true` | Writes the value under the bars, for someone to type when it won't scan. |
| `text` | `string` |  | Written under the bars in place of the value: the same number with spaces in it, say. An EAN or a UPC writes its own digits whatever this is. |
| `textSize` | `number` | `14` | The size of the text, in pixels. |

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.markdown:
## Accessibility

A barcode has nothing to press and nothing to focus.

### What the component handles

- It's an `<svg>` with `role="img"`, so a screen reader meets one picture and not a hundred shapes.
- It has a name. Without `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`, the name is the value with any check digit, which is what a person would type.
- The text under the bars is drawn at the size you set, 14 pixels by default, in black on white.
- The bars stay black on white in a dark theme and where the browser forces colors, because that's what scans. The contrast between them is as high as it goes.

### What you need to handle

- Name it for what it's for: "Order 1042", not only the digits. A screen reader's user wants to know which barcode this is.
- Never make a barcode the only way to get what it holds. Someone who can't scan it, because of the screen, the scanner or their sight, needs the value as text they can read and copy. The text underneath does that for a short value. For a long one, put it on the page.
- If you change the colors, keep the bars dark and the ground light, and try it with a real scanner.

sections.heading: On small screens
sections.markdown:
## On small screens

A barcode is as wide as its value makes it, and a long Code 128 at two pixels a bar is wider than a phone. It shrinks to its container's width, which keeps the page from scrolling sideways. A shrunk barcode has bars that aren't whole pixels, and may not scan off the screen. For a phone, use `barWidth={1}`, a shorter value, or a [QR code](page:barcodes/qrcode), which holds more in less room.

sections.heading: CSS variables
sections.markdown:
## CSS variables

Set any of these on the barcode, or on anything around it.

```css
.label {
  --nuv-barcode-font: var(--font-sans);
}
```

| Variable | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--nuv-barcode-bg` | `var(--color-white)` | Color of the ground. White in every theme by default. Keep it light. |
| `--nuv-barcode-fg` | `var(--color-black)` | Color of the bars and the text. Black in every theme by default. Keep it much darker than the ground. |
| `--nuv-barcode-font` | `var(--font-mono)` | Font of the text under the bars. |
| `--nuv-barcode-invalid` | `var(--color-danger)` | Color of the edge and the line of a barcode that can't be drawn. |

sections.heading: Classes
sections.markdown:
## Classes

| Class | What it's on |
| --- | --- |
| `.nuv-barcode` | Barcode: the svg. |
| `.nuv-barcode__bars` | The bars, as one path. |
| `.nuv-barcode__ground` | The rectangle behind the bars. |
| `.nuv-barcode__mark` | The edge and the line through a barcode that can't be drawn. |
| `.nuv-barcode__text` | A line of text under the bars. An EAN or a UPC has several. |

A barcode has `data-type`, its kind. One that can't be drawn has `data-invalid` instead.

sections.heading: Server components
sections.markdown:
## Server components

Barcode has no `"use client"`. Rendered in a server component, it's SVG in the HTML and sends no script. `saveCode` needs a browser, so the button that calls it is in a client component.

sections.heading: Do and don't
sections.markdown:
## Do and don't

**Do**

- Print one and scan it with the scanner it's meant for before you ship. A screen and a printer each change what a scanner sees.
- Keep the text underneath for anything a person might have to type.
- Check values where they're entered, with `encodeBarcode`.

**Don't**

- Don't put a barcode on a colored or patterned ground. Leave it its white, and space around it.
- Don't stretch or squeeze one with CSS. Change `barWidth` and `height`.
- Don't use it for an address or a sentence. That's a [QR code](page:barcodes/qrcode).


```tsx
<QRCode value="https://example.com/orders/1042" aria-label="Open order 1042" />
```

sections.heading: What it holds
sections.markdown:
## What it holds

`value` is text, and a QR code doesn't care what the text means. What happens when it's scanned is decided by how the text starts, and by the phone:

| The value | What a phone offers to do |
| --- | --- |
| `https://example.com/orders/1042` | Open the page. |
| `mailto:help@example.com` | Write an email. |
| `tel:+15555550100` | Call the number. |
| `sms:+15555550100` | Write a message. |
| `geo:47.3769,8.5417` | Show the place on a map. |
| `WIFI:T:WPA;S:Office;P:the password;;` | Join the network. |
| A vCard, starting `BEGIN:VCARD` | Add the contact. |

These forms are the phones' and not this component's: it encodes whatever you give it. Any text works, in any script.

The longer the value, the more squares the code has and the smaller each is at the same size. A short address reads from across a room. A paragraph has to be held close. Where you can, put an address in the code and the long text at the address.

sections.heading: Size
sections.markdown:
## Size

`size` is the width and the height in pixels, with the empty edge. A phone needs each square to be a few pixels across, so a long value wants a larger code.

`quietZone` is the empty space around the code, in its squares. The standard asks for four, and cameras find the code by it. Only lower it if the code sits on a light ground with nothing near it.

In a space narrower than `size` the code shrinks to fit and stays square.

sections.heading: Error correction
Something over the middle
A value that can't be a QR code
Saving it as a file
QRCode props
sections.markdown:
## QRCode props

QRCode also takes the attributes of an `<svg>`, and `ref` goes to it.

| Prop | Type | Default | What it's for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value` (required) | `string` |  | What the code holds: an address, most often, or any text. |
| `size` | `number` | `160` | The width and the height, in pixels, with the empty edge. |
| `errorCorrection` | `"H" \| "L" \| "M" \| "Q"` |  | How much of the code can be lost and still be read, from `"L"`, about 7%, to `"H"`, about 30%. Left out, it's `"M"`, or `"H"` when there's an `overlay`, which covers part of the code. |
| `quietZone` | `number` | `4` | The empty space around the code, counted in its squares. A scanner finds the code by it, and the standard asks for four. |
| `overlay` | `ReactNode` |  | Something drawn over the middle, such as a logo. It's SVG, drawn in a box 100 by 100: an `<image>`, shapes of your own, or `<QRCodeSwissCross />`. The squares under it are lost, which the error correction makes up for. |
| `overlaySize` | `number` | `0.2` | How much of the code's side the overlay takes, from 0.1 to 0.3. More than a fifth and some phones stop reading it: try the code you ship. |
| `fallback` | `ReactNode` |  | What's drawn when the value can't be a QR code: nothing to encode, or more than one holds. Without it there's an empty box with a line through it, which no scanner reads as anything. |

`QRCodeSwissCross` takes the attributes of an SVG `<g>`.
